So, this is a very interesting game with a lot of emergent gameplay.  It has some rough edges, like any indie dev game can but also it has brilliance.  The very sort of brilliance you can't find in AAA titles because no committee will ever agree upon things that are controversial.
While I wil admit there are some design choices I strongly dislike and that I think will inhibit the game's ultimate success, these are details and not reflective of the systems in the gameplay.
Now add to this, the numerous legitimate ways to die including taking on something tougher than you are
and you have a lot of sudden deaths.
Combine that with the lack of any remote places to respawn, and it ends up being a 'fly back to the spot' simulator at times, which is super not fun.
Secondly, the way loot is generated is awkward.  You can loot 'blueprints' for ship parts, however these blueprints aren't final until you 'reveal' them, and at that point they can randomly be useful, or junk.  If they are junk, you can alt-f4 and reload the game and try again until you get a result that is non-junk.  I don't know about you, but knowing this I am forced to save scum, and I find this method extremely unsatisfying.    I'd prefer less loot and have it all be real, personally.
That aside the engineering parts of the game are great.  Designing ships is a lot of fun, and using your own designs in combat is a nice experience.  There are a lot of emergent systems that reward careful and intelligent design.
The price is a touch high for the amount of content available, but the game was worth it to me because I've wanted to play a game like this for a while.
I have to admit, though the devs repeatedly deny it - I still hold out hope for multiplayer, and most certainly more crew options for the player.
All that said, if you are an engineer like myself, this game is a strong recommendation.

After three hours of Pillars of Eternity, I am gravely, gravely disappointed.
PoE is a love paean to the old Infinity Engine RPG's, which is good in a way, because some of them had excellent writing, great impact in terms of your stats and skills having an effect on what you could do, and lots of choices. And this, too, is in Pillars of Eternity. Though "great writing" may take a knock if you've played previous Black Isle/Obsidian RPG's because in short order you're going to realize that Avellone can really only write one story and he's whipped it out for us again.
In terms of mechanics, however... it's a mess. It's an absolute goddamn mess. The AI is terrible, the mechanics obtuse, the UI functional but only barely, status effect effects are hard to suss out, why skills sometimes work, why characters sometimes don't use their skills, whether a given skill affects friends, enemies or both... it's just frustrating and entirely un-engaging, thrown even more into perspective by Larian's recent amazing RPG, Divinity: Original Sin, which had much the same kind of combat(albeit fully turn-based) and did it
by making everything obvious and easily parsed, by giving you all the info you could ever want in, usually, an easily parsed fashion.
So it's a shame, a damn shame, that Obsidian didn't look around for a few clues here and there. The mechanics don't even work on the purely... mechanical level. Some people might complain that D&D can be a kludgy, convoluted mess, and I'll agree to that, especially when it comes to the old 2nd edition AD&D that the Infinity Engine games(Icewind Dale 2 excepted) were largely based on. But whatever monstrosity Obsidian's stitched together in their basement is even more confusing.
While I intend to play through the remainder of Pillars of Eternity, and may even come to be more positive about it. At the moment? I'm going to recommend that no one buy this game unless they already made the mistake of kickstarting or pre-ordering it, in which case they may as well wring what fun they can out of it.

Full disclosure: I bought this game on sale for under $7. For that price, the cons I listed don't bother me that much. I'm really just a little bummed Black Panther is missing. Had I paid $30, I would have been more upset about all of them. For under < $10, this game is a steal, particularly if you have kids in your home that like to play games with you.
Pros:
- Solid 3D Platformer with good level design
- Good graphics for a console port
- Impressive roster of characters who each bring a totally different style of gameplay
- Can change current character and sidekick any time without having to deal with the base/toys
- Takes up a lot less room in your living space than the console version, w/o all of the toys
- TONS of content; there is potentially 100+ hours of stuff to do
Cons:
- Several of the newer playable characters are missing (Black Panter, Vision, Ant-Man, etc.)
- No local multiplayer (which is ridiculous, why would that be removed??)
- No online multiplayer (makes more sense, still a bit of a bummer)
- Very few options to adjust graphics quality
Recommendation:
- If you find it on sale for $10 or less, buy it.
- If you fins it at $15 or less and think you'd really get a lot of play out of it, buy it.
- If Disney updates the game to include all of the missing characters and/or patches in local co-op, buy it even at $30.

Frankly this is probably old news to many of you reading this.  I'm ashamed that I didn't know about these Spiderweb titles previously.
Gather round me children, for there's a tale I'd like to share.  Once there was a time when video games entertained the player an immersive story and provocative challenges that kept you playing for hours.
I've never liked the term "dungeon
".  To me the crawler part implies slow which let's be honest, is generally associated with boring in the world of books, movies and video games.  When was the last time you couldn't wait to dig in to a slow book someone recommended?
So when I saw that genre ascribed to this and other Spiderweb titles I dismissed them pretty quickly.  I didn't feel like click-spamming my way through another shallow DC chasing the next-best weapon for hours on end - mindlessly racing to the next waypoint, only taking breaks to managing a mountain of gear (/cough...torchlight)...
So as I was browsing my games library through titles I'll never get to and I barely recognize, the term "turn-based" caught my eye.
"Turn-based"...dungeon-crawler?
Now that's a name I"ve not heard in a long time.  A long time.
I must have played through "Planescape: Torment" three times since it's release.  The same can be said for "Fallout 1/2".
I can't chalk up their awesome replayablility to nostalgia any more.  These are simply incredibly entertaining titles and the reason I've played them all so often is that nothing after (to my knowledge) ever properly took up where they left off.  Well that was until I discovered this game.
This game, like Planescape and Fallout 1&2 focus on story depth, simple, intuitive UI/game mechanics, and challenging "strategic" (yet simple) combat.  I don't mean simple as in "easy", I just mean you will very quickly become well-versed your battle playbook and the challenge lies in making good decisions as it is turn-based.
If you're familiar Fallout 1 & 2 or Planescape Torment then to put it simply this game is very similar to those but in a classic fantasy setting.    It's also a nice reminder of the days when RPG titles didn't hold your hand every step of the way.  The quest descriptions are clear, but the objectives are kept broad enough keep the players guessing as to how exactly to complete them.
Combine all of the above with perfectly classic "if-it-ain't-broke" fantasy RPG elements and you have this surprisingly impressive game.  I can't recommend this title enough for old-school PC nerds like myself as well as newcomers.

Credentials: I've played one character class to the current max level and toyed around with a few others.
This game has a solid combat and loot system, which are the most important parts of an ARPG.  Getting new loot drops can drastically increase your power, allowing you to venture into new areas and make faster progress.  Dungeons and gear both have level requirements, and leveling also nets you some stat and skill points.  Skill trees are straightforward and there's plenty of opportunities to move points around as you level.  Fighting above your level is appropriately difficult, and it is usually not productive without a party.

The various open world areas and instanced dungeons are well designed and interesting to work through whether solo or with a party.  Even in alpha they have a nice variety of enemies as well as levers, puzzles, and secret areas.  Checkpoints typically unlock progress and also keep death from being too much of an annoyance as they provide a place to respawn with no penalty upon death.  Dungeons are designed to be run multiple times, and each successful run counts toward unlocking harder and more rewarding versions of the dungeon - this is currently just higher level enemies, but there's other interesting things they could do with this.
The downside is typical alpha stuff - there's not a lot of content yet aside from going into dungeons, killing monsters, and taking their stuff.  The loot system is good, but it needs to be fleshed out with more uniques, sets, and interesting modifiers.  There's only one quest and it's standard collection fare, but it works pretty well and shows that the quest system is viable.  Harvesting and crafting are in, but they currently involve socketing one harvestable gem or one quest reward gem into items.  Not particularly interesting, but, again, it shows that these systems are working.
Controls are occasionally awkward with multi-key input inssues, but you eventually learn the quirks and learn to work around them.  Lag is sometimes a problem, but it has never been bad enough to cause me to quit a playing session.  It does occasionally result in death, but as I mentioned above, death is not a huge setback by any means.
The biggest positive for the game is that the dev staff are updating regularly, post regular articles about progress and future goals, and actively respond to community input and bug reports.
If you're looking for a finished game with tons of content, this is not for you, but if you're interested in a Secret of Mana MMO with Diablo-esque loot with a lot of potential, there's a lot of fun to be had.  The active community is small, which means it's easy to be listened to if you are willing to give thoughtful feedback.

this is a good game. i played a lot in early access but don't really remember it too well, so this will be taking the game as it is on launch.
the gameplay loop is: exploring, gathering materials and decorative items, then crafting and building.
the resource progression has you working your way up difficulty tiers of planets, as you need to visit harder planets to get materials to build radiation protection to visit radioactive planets, and so on. the power of enemies increases, as does the value of loot you can find (weapons, items needed to upgrade your gear, etc). this progression coupled with the gameplay loop has compelled me for dozens of hours now.
the main story works well for giving the player that little objective marker to push them towards exploring if they don't just jump into the sandbox. you explore for a bit, and it rewards you with a designed dungeon & boss fights. then it pushes you towards harder planets to explore, and gives you another dungeon.
the platforming controls are floaty, which can make some manuevering awkward. the combat is very basic, although there is weapon variety (swords, hammers, pistols, grenade launchers; and some come with alt-fire abilities). this can make some segments frustrating, although the first main story boss (
) is mostly a puzzle fight and plays to the game's strengths rather than its weaknesses.
the variety of stuff in this game - worlds, furniture, materials, NPCs, items - gives it an immense longevity. the multiplayer adds another layer, with friends able to ease some of the worst bits (the combat) and enhance the best (building a shanty town colony with friends can't be beat). this is a very good game.

They say 3rd time's the charm, but not in the case of Infinity sadly. First of all, if you're not a massive Star Wars fan there's almost no reason to get this one anyway...maybe for the toybox, but yeah, this only includes characters from SW and Inside Out I think. Anyway, onward to the "campaigns".
There are 4-ish, this time around.
Inside Out:
You play as any one of the emotions of the movie, going through about 20 or so 3D or 2D levels to collect stuff and solve some very easy puzzles. This is honestly the best of the bunch, even if it has barely any story. You just do, but at least the levels keep changing it up and get more challenging. There's a mechanic in this mode in which you have to switch to certain characters for a short time in order to solve some puzzles. Since you can freely change your character anyway, however, (without the time limit) I wonder why this mechanic is even still in there. Maybe the original game required the miniatures to be able to do so...but then again I wonder how you can beat the levels if you only have one of them...
Twilight of the Republic:
Hands down the best Infinity campaign to date. It follows a story loosely tied around the droid war and Grieveous. You will remember scenes from episodes 1 and 2 I think, but the story is really a bit separate and different. You can follow this story without interruptions and finish it in 2 hours or so. You'll visit Geonosis, Coruscant, Tattooine and finally Naboo. Lightsabers!
Rise against the Empire:
Oh boy, after Twilight I actually got my hopes up, but they were dashed just as quickly like a ship onto rocks. In Rise you "relive" the events of the original trilogy...in very very condensed fashion and with some minor adjustments. This one has so many issues: like how you start the game on Tattooine and have to collect 2,000 credits...by doing SIDE QUESTS! All of them basically. Go here, collect this, bring here...blabla. There's no fighting for the first hour of the game, unless you repeatedly kill the poor patrol. What were they thinking?! Then they introduce "base building" from Infinity 1.0 and 2.0 again...and guess what, once you're on Hoth, you have to earn credits again to purchase and place three buildings! And if that weren't enough, better do all the side quests, until new story progression missions pop up (the side quests actually progress the story, but they don't give you an indicator of that, other than you knowing that Imperial sentry droids on the surface of Hoth are a bad thing). Then you can tow AT-ATs down. Yay. When it's more fun to fight an AT-AT on foot and destroy it than to use Snow Speeders you're doing it wrong. Finally we'll get to Endor/Yavin (I forgot) and have to fight off some stoff for the Ewoks to disable the shields of the second death star...oh I forgot, you also destroy the first one...in a terrible approximation of a space sim. It's basically an on rails shooter and you can go up, down, left and right a bit...even the segments where you can freely fly around are heavily gated...there is no real 3D space...just a small canvas in which you can hover up or down...not even really fly up or down...just gradually glide. Ugh.
And then...The Force Awakens:
It's not as bad as Rise, but it's not very good either. You basically only relive the events of said movie, starting on Jakku...and yes, having to collect 2,000 scrap this time around...luckily you can now salvage scrap heaps to make this initial hurdle faster. After getting enough scrap, we flee from the First Order in another boring flight segment, but luckily the only such one in this campaign. Then we go to the planet, whose name nobody seems to ever recall, fight off more imperials, who are actually more of a challenge in this game than they were in any movie, and go to Starkiller base...before that we destroy a few Star Destroyers in a moderately fun space segment. Aaaaaand then we get to "fight" Kylo Ren...well, we don't really fight him, because we're weak and bla, so we contend ourselves with shooting at explosive barrels he tries to hit us with...in three separate fights by the way. Ugh. Han's death is neither shown nor even mentioned in the game by the way. He simply disappears after Starkiller base. Likewise some key characters weren't even included. You can see that this was simply tacked on quickly to make more money, but no actual effort was put into it.
And then there's the Toybox Takeover again and the Speedway, which is just a racing mode, but with different tracks at least.
Overall for the hefty price of this game I can't even begin to recommend it. You will spend about 8 or so hours completing it, yes, but most of that play time is boring or frustrating imho. Combat has been slightly improved, but that's it. I'm not even sure kids would enjoy this...maybe in creator mode.

Gattling defense has you using a Gattling gun that overheats to hold of waves of zombies, but by the time I figured out how to use it, everything was already killed off by my brother and cousin who were wielding machineguns in their hands.
With more guns, a more in depth upgrade system, and more content, I'd be inclined to change my mind, but as the game stands and with the devs calling the game "Almost finished" I just can't, in good conscious recommend this to anyone. The idea of it is more satisfying than the experience.

This mod has unique and interesting concepts that I still haven't seen copied in any other games, even 10 years after it's release.
On most maps, you quickly find a weapon and barricade yourself in a room, and either wait out the zombies as they tear your barricade down, or take pot shots at the zombies before they're able to tear down your fortifications. On some maps there's objectives for the human players to accomplish and an end goal of escaping from the zombie threat.
When players die, they become zombies, which is a cool enough concept in itself... but playing as a zombie is actually pretty fun in it's own right. You essentially have two forms of attack, a push and a sctrach. You can push objects out of the way in a barricade, or you can scratch them until they break. When you've broken your way into the human's base, you can also scratch them until they die. The goal of the zombie team is to eliminate all of the human players.
There's also "alpha zombies" which have a sort-of mating call that they can use, which lets the other zombie players know where they are. They can use this when they're nearby a human to signal the other zombie players to rush to them and attack.
Overall, it's a really interesting concept and makes for some great multiplayer fun. Well worth checking out!

As per usual, Artifex Mundi put out another high quality hidden object game. Game takes about 2 hours or so.
Graphically its not bad. Animations arent that great, but the backgrounds and still shots are beautiful (as you can see from the store page screenshots). Audio was pretty good. Music got a little old after awhile, but the sound effects were nice. Voice acting was better than Im used to from a hidden object game, which was a nice surprise.
Puzzles were your standard issue hidden object game puzzles. None of them were overly difficult, and if youve played other hidden object games, then youll recognize some repeated puzzle styles.
Where this game really shined for me, was the story. Slavic folklore is a pretty interesting topic for a story (in my opinion anyway), and I felt they did a pretty good job incorporating it into a lighter-hearted video game.  Without spoiling too much, the game had a cool side achievement for collecting these lore cards that were pretty cool reads if you wanted even more insight into the creatures in the lore, as well as some of the characters you meet. That said, the story still follows the "person gets kidnapped, you must rescue said person" plot line that crops up pretty often in these.  May or may not be a deal breaker for some if theyre looking for something new.
The only bugs I found were when I was doing a speed playthrough to complete an achievement I missed. If I cleared an area too quickly (picked up all the objects rapidly), the game wouldnt recognize that it was cleared and would let me keep opening that spot. Example off the top of my head being the crawfish cage and the toolbox in the boat house. When I played normally (and not spam clicking through), the game was perfect.
Overall, the puzzles were a bit same-y, but if youre into fantasy or folklore at all, the story was more than interesting enough to give this a big recommendation.

My recommendation comes with a caveat, I am only recommending this to people who enjoy turn-based cRPGs. I personally am not a fan of turn based combat, which is the reason I eventually gave up on finishing the game.
Visually and audibly, the game is nothing to write home about, being made by one person it is understanable and they are functional enough not to detract from the game in any major way.
Gameplay in my opinion is bland and uninspired, the turn based combat is quite slow and you are often faced with trash mobs that make the game stutter along at a slow pace. Later battles are frustratingly difficult, as you have to spend a long time clicking through the turns before you sometimes realise you haven't a hope of winning and have to reload. I eventually got sick of trying to beat a particular fight and called it quits.
Where the game shines is in its writing and story, I really enjoyed pouring over the descriptions of locations and the characterisation is pretty good in the people you meet. I find it a shame I couldn't bring myself to finish the game because I would have liked to know what happens.
So I will recommend this game to people who are into old school turn-based cRPGs, but if slow pacing and turn-based combat make you yawn you might want to check elsewhere.

This is an amazing old school RPG, with an atmosphere very reminiscent of Fallout. Combat is turn-based and very tactical: range, position and zones of control are important, as well as proper use of character abilities. The party composition will vary, the player will usually have the main character as well as two out of four NPCs in his party.
Additionally, this game is perfect for loot♥♥♥♥♥ players :P since there are no weight limits for the backpack. The weird isometric perspective takes about an hour to get used to, the controls are otherwise very intuitive.
The story is quite original, for a fantasy game, and the characters are well fleshed out. The game is fairly linear, but there are many choices and optional missions along the way, and the story does give you a choice during some important moments. I very much recommend this for anyone looking to play a classic and fun RPG

*I'd Rather Stay Dead*
SPOILERS AHEAD!
Before you read- I bought this game back when it was waaaay cheaper. Around the sixth or seventh update, if I believe. My opinion may not make a difference in your purchase!
As you can see, I've gone and sunk twenty seven hours into this game. And now, with 100% completion and the ending under my belt, I'm gonna have to leave it at that time.
This game costs £10. You need an honest review, and I'm happy to say that for £10 I got my milage, but my milage was found in the final run of the game, where I got my last achievement. You see, there's one main word I'd used to describe this game; Boring.
The game is quite clearly built to work as a sort of 'twin-stick shooter' deal, but I've only ever played with mouse and keyboard and was pleasantly suprised to find that this is one of the only games like this where this setup works. Unfortunately this is as far as the premise works, as random lag spikes and slow downs begin to chug this game to a crawl.
I'm gonna admit, I never followed the story of this game. I think you're dead, but it remains to be seen. The ending is my only reason I concluded with this, as the ending (spoilers) has all the playable characters find that the Earth is in shambles.
The theme of 'murderer' plays a big deal with this, too. You can enter two special areas in this game (They open randomly in the first/third area) and both have bosses who call you a 'murderer'. Now, I don't condone it, but if murdering the wizard and his daughter in the Forbidden Libary ends up giving me a craftable item which is quite clearly the best item in the game, I will happily murder (sarcasm). The murderer's ring is honestly overpowered, as it increases your damage and kills enemies at random. If you really want to find out, look up a tutorial or (If you care to spend £10) play it yourself.
The items are, in two words, insanely varied. You may find the best item on the first area, and the worst one at the end. There is no scale of difficulty, nor is there a sense of purpose as the final boss goes down as easy as the ones before it.
Speaking of bosses, KEEP THE VOICES OFF. I'm still sick of hearing 'RUN LITTLE DEMON' overlapping itself thirteen times in the matter of thirty seconds. The boss before the final boss is the worst, A horrid grating voice, albiet fitting for a demonic snake head. I think.
There are redeeming features, though! The cursed items actually feel like risk/reward, as they should, especially the Blind Sword which makes you occasionally miss a hit, while doubling your current damage. My favourite has to be The Frost Cloak, an item that doubles Freeze (one of the many status effects in the game) in order to allow you to deal freeze to others. This, admittably, doesn't matter, as Crafting comes into play around the time you may find it, and by then you'll find a recipe for one of the two varients of weaponary for each class- Fire and Ice. I won't go into crafting, mind, cause I only ever used it to craft the adforementioned Murderer's Ring, and it would be wrong to say anything about something I never used.
By the way, have you ever wanted to trial and error to unlock a character? There are multiple characters in this game, and I've no clue how I unlocked any of them, apart from the engineer (of which I never used). My goto ended up being the starting character, the Barbarian, as he was able to dish out and take damage amazingly so. Unless, of course, it was the Redeemer, and suddenly damage becomes speed and defence becomes flight.
The Redeemer is incredible! He is the only boss I actually like in this game. He's not orignal, sure; a bloodthirsty unkillable demon that hunts you down if you take too long has been used in many different games, but this one is special for being an amazing design with amazing attacks. Compared to the 'actual' bosses, he's genuinely interesting. Y'know, besides the Skeleton King, The Slime Monster, the Snow Witch, the Dark Knight...
All in all, I'm gonna admit, I'm not biased when it comes to this game. Like I said, now I've 100%'d it, I find no need to go back. So, be it as it may.
Thanks for reading!
-Joseph

LocoCycle is an insane game that that offers a fresh experience, but it remains interesting for only a couple of hours. Thankfully, the length of this game isn't very long as well, but it still manages to become tiresome before it's completely over.
So, the story is pretty crazy. Your motorcycle gets struck by lightning and breaks free while a mechanic is stuck to your rear wheel. The story is so over the top that I will just let you experience it yourself. That, and I don't want to talk about it in-depth, because it makes no sense in any kind of way. You'd only be confused, trust me.
Your motorcycle can also fight off enemies so while driving you'll regularly battle with enemies, and your stuck mechanic will help you with this. Add some QTEs, aerial combat, mini missions and boss fights to it (among some other things) and you have Lococycle. I know, it still doesn't make any sense.
The graphics are ok-ish. They're colorful and get the job done. The framerate regularly dips though (just for 1-2 seconds), and I have no idea why because it's no Crysis 3 and nothing spectacular is happening on-screen. Still, I can't complain here.
The voices are annoying as hell. Your motorcycle will talk, your mechanic will talk, and not just a few sentences, but the whole time. Basically non-stop. None of them are funny and it really just hurts the game when it comes to quality. I can't even remember what the music sounds like because of the constant chit chat. Annoying. Really.
LocoCycle is a fun game for the couple of hours that it lasts, but please don't ever make a sequel, Twisted Pixel. We don't need it. And I don't want it. It's just that it tries to do something different and I usually appreciate that. But it makes no damn sense if you think about it (or just play it).

tl;dr -  Clunky game coded by a single Russian guy.   It's bare bones, unoriginal, and has a penchant for hard crashes to desktop.  There are better options, even at this price point.
ts;wm - As far as I can tell, this is a clunky flash game coded by a single Russian guy.  The content is pretty much what you'd expect:  simple shuffle puzzles, a few seek/find-type rooms where you collect items, and a very basic plot.  You're dropped into the midst of things with effectively no instruction, clues, or backstory.  The options & controls are minimal, which is of particular interest since each "room" has its own 8-second loop of music that cannot be muted.  And if you're hoping for one of those seamless, "perfect gifs don't exi..." type loops, no - it isn't anywhere near that.
Frankly the game is boring, has a tendency to crash when you do things like click, or change rooms, or breathe, and plays like a flash movie because thats how it's coded (read: tiny screen, nothing but "video playback" settings).  There are far better options, even at this pricepoint.

When I first played this game I immediately became immersed in it's survival aspect, I just love it. But it can sure use some improvements.
-Difficulty.As it is now, I think the game if fairly easy, it would be nice to see a couple more difficulty levels or crank up the dangers that are in the enviroment.
-Music. I didn't really expect much in the music department in the first hour or so, but I came to realize that it could use some soft piano notes in those magical moments like looking at the sunset or such. Also, the music that plays when a shark is near is unnecesary and should be removed, as it removes the element of surprise that sharks have. I think it would be nice to give the player a false sense of security in these occasions, those are the scarier moments in games IMO.
-Bugs. Of course there are gonna be bugs, this is early acces, so not much point in bringing each bug I experienced as they have already been reported countless times and I'm sure they are on the works.
-Wildlife and Terrain. At the moment, wildlife and terrain are pretty much the same everywhere but then again it is early access and I know these are being worked on atm.
-Crafting. Crafting is good and all but it could use some work. Don't really have much to say other than it could be a bit more intuative.
-Items. I know this is an early build and items are limited and more are on the works but even so I have some ideas:
A writable map where you can record which island you've been to or compass to know where you are heading.
A journal.
A way to expand your inventory like a larger backpack or pouches to carry specific items.
CHESTS to store items in (Not really a fan of having everything on the floor)
A little radio to listen to some caribean tunes (Just for fun and to give a little more warm feel to your home)
Overall I think this game has great potential and I will continue to support Beam Team, they have done something with incredible value and I wuould like to see this game become one of the big indie games this year or the next!

Singularity is a fantastic singleplayer FPS. In the tradition of all the B-tier shooters in the 90's this game, like Bioshock, takes solid shooting mechanics, wraps in a unique gameplay twist and presents an interesting setting for the game to unfold.
The setting is an abandoned Russian facility that did experiments on a mysterious substance that affects time. That's the gameplay hook, you explore by dilating time and the age of objects around you. You can make enemies decay right in front of you. It's a fun experience.
Unfortunate for the developer Raven, Activision sent this solid gem to die at retail with no advertising support and so the game was religated to obscurity. I'm sure the multiplayer is dead at this point but the singleplayer alone is worth the price of admission.
Wonderful game. It should be in everyone's steam library.

Singularity, a 2008 release developed by Raven Software and published by Activision, is a good example of a game made with no intent other than to ‘follow the leader’: while the game incorporates gameplay ideas with some potential, it suffers from an incredibly flimsy plot and disconnected design choices.
Let’s start with the positives: some of the weapons, like the Seeker and the Dethex Launcher, offer some creative opportunities in combat, and combined with the TMD, combat gameplay almost never becomes a chore, which is good since it’s pretty much 95% of the game.
That’s where the positives end, though: the game lacks any creative thought outside of combat. For example, the TMD is a pretty see-through attempt at combining the Plasmids from BioShock and the Gravity Gun from Half-Life 2, with a gimmick that just adds one extra button press to crate-stacking sequences. The art design feels like a poorly made Soviet AU of Rapture, and the voice acting makes Hollywood Russian accents sound genuine.
The plot is the worst part of the game: I understand, time travel isn’t exactly an easy trope to work with. But even taking that into account, the story is horrendously full of plot holes, and is little more than a barely-connected series of events to get you from setpiece A to setpiece B through combat arena C.
Overall, I’d say: if you happen to own the game, give it a spin to play around with the combat mechanics, but don’t bother throwing away any money on it if you want a satisfying game experience.

Ship combat is really fun. Initially you are shooting blindly at enemy hoping to hit and do some damage. Over time you learn how to properly lead based  on your weapon and you will know where to hit to take out ship systems (reactors, engines, manuevering thrusters...). Cannons are reliable for close quarters combat, rockets are great for long range skirmishes (my favourite part). Missile tubes are really strong, easily disabling smaller ships in few hits. Beam weapons are still WIP, but are present in the game.
Ship designing is great, its complex but not difficult. You have put on lot of engines, fine now you need some reactors, now it flies forward but doesnt turn, slap on some thrusters. Dont forget to forget them to connect them to reactors (drawing little paths from power conduits is equivalent to high tech cable management :) ). The reactors will blow up easily without some armor. Now its good, but its not flying well, ah.. i forgot reactor cooling....
And then you add bridge, corridors, weapons and dont forget cargo space to hoard your loot somewhere.
Cons:
Occasional crash
Gameplay content is limited
AI is in its early stages (ship combat AI works well)
Simplistic infantry combat (for my taste)
People who like this game should suggest to the devs various missions and events which would happen in the world, because the game is currently lacking them (except the tutorial).
I would like to see improvements in the world desing: Station dwellers could do some meaningful tasks around stations, ships could come and go from and to stations. Ships in the world could have their destinations and tasks.
This game has big potential, hopefully the development will go well.

Disney Infinity may not be a great series of games, but even ignoring what has leaked about the would-have-been fourth installment, Disney Infinity 3.0 demonstrates that it was inching rather close. The combat is very engaging, there are plenty of collectibles to look around for, the characters are very distinct from one another, and the new side-content like farming, Toy Box Takeover, and Toy Box Speedway give the game further gameplay variety.
Perhaps if the series had been able to cross over characters between playsets a la Lego Dimensions, it would have lasted longer. The Toy Box Takeover mode and, to a lesser extent, Toy Box Speedway, scratch this itch to a small extent, but leaked footage of the fourth game indicate that there would have been a dedicated, seemingly full-featured crossover playset. However, just this one game on its own feels more varied than the entire Lego series I've played up to this point.
The port job is very good as well, but it's not quite perfect. Like the previous games, it lacks co-op and any sort of online play. More egregious, however, is the missing content. Gold Edition is missing two playsets (Marvel Battlegrounds and Finding Dory), ten playable charaters (First Avenger Captain America, Black Panther, Ant-Man, Vision, Dory, Nemo, Baloo, Alice, Mad Hatter, and Time), and their associated power discs. If you're looking for the complete Disney Infinity experience, even ignoring online features and multiplayer, you will not find it on Steam. However, if you want to enjoy the series at a low cost, the Gold Editions are an excellent way to get in.
As for the playsets, the three Star Wars playsets - Twilight of the Republic (The Clone Wars/prequel trilogy), Rise Against the Empire (original trilogy), and The Force Awakens - are all just light variations on one another. However, they are all among the best playsets in the series, offering a fun variety of combat, vehicle sections, and platforming. Additionally, unlike previous games, all Star Wars characters are playable in all Star Wars playsets if you find the right collectibles. If I had to rank them, Republic would come first, followed by Force and then Empire.
The Inside Out playset demonstrates the series' versatility. It's a solid mixture of 2D and 3D platforming, with a level select screen instead of a hub world and a Bejewled-esqued puzzle minigame. The controls aren't that great, to be honest, but the levels are quite varied in their use of mechanics. These lend the playset a very distinct feeling compared to the rest of the series, even if it drags on after a while.
It's not considered a playset, but I also have to give a special mention to Toy Box Speedway. It's no Mario Kart, nor is it even as good as Sonic & All Stars Racing Transformed, whose devs also developed this section of the game. However, the lessons from the Sonic & All-Stars series can definitely be seen here, between the driving that has improved considerably from the first Disney Infinity and the handful of solid racetracks. Bonus points for a Gravity Falls racetrack, even if there's no playable Gravity Falls characters.

as of right now, i would not recommend this game, even though the potential for greatness is there.
the game feels like a mix between the original stardrive and FTL. you have the option to explore an absolutely massive galaxy, all the while walking around your ship and repairing components in realtime, as youre fired upon. in theory, this seems awesome. in practice though, its another story. you cant pilot the ship and repair at the same time so repairing during combat is effectively impossible, unless youre willing to take hits for free as youre doing damage control. ive read that you can have another crew member, but he mostly sits in a station, and cant help. speaking of stations: the stations are actually environements you can walk into, complete with living quarters, reactors, storages and docking ares and whatnot. once again: in theory, exploring a massive space station sounds exhilerating. in theory, its a damn mess. the stations are absolutely massive and your character moves at maybe a brisk walking speed. there are no directions or maps, so finding things through the bland station is annoying at the least.
pros-
-massive galaxy
-interesting radar system
-combat feels interesting, with the possibility of destroying systems and systematicly crippling an enemy.
-ship building and designing
cons-
-stations are too big and empty
-no AI crew members to repair as you fight, or boost systems (this will come later but its a major problem now)
-no audio cues or UI elements indicating loss of systems. you can have a hull breach and lose air, yet no indication, and you suddenly die
-controls are clunky, yet manageable
-no multiplayer in a game that feels like MP would be amazing.
i would only recommend this game under these conditions:
-you are a hardcore space enthusiast and any amount of ship building/space exploration game satisfies you
-you wish to support the developers
-game is ridiculously cheap, like 5$
otherwise, just wait for more updates, especially the ones adding AI crew members, and more quests/storylines/jobs to do. as of right now, the game is too empty to be worth your time. theres definitely potential for an incredible game here, but a lot is still missing.

As a fan of twin stick shooters, and old-school arcade games, this was right up my alley.  After spending far too much time trying to reach the ending, the time has come to give up and write my 2 cents:
Like Gauntlet?  This is similar in some ways, though it does make for a better single-player experience.  You start out weak, and there are 2 levels of power up to help you along, along with scrolls that offer 1-use boost (destroy everything on-screen, make you invincible for a short period, etc).  Things start out promising for the first few levels, but around level 6 or so it becomes quite unbalanced and very grindy.  By the end, although I wanted to finish it, I had to eventually give up having reached the end-boss once only.  Maybe I'm playing it wrong.
The good:
- nice graphics
- good controls
- fun to figure out the map and hunt for your upgrades to help you along
- Not very long (at least to get to the late levels), so well suited to short game-play sessions
- Having end bosses is nice and adds to the sense of progression
- There are secrets to discover
The not-so-good:
- feels like your weapon could use a couple more levels of power up. Enemies become overwhelming in both speed and numbers in later levels, to the point where you basically have to keep restarting if you don't luck out and get a couple power-ups early.
- The randomly placed scrolls need to be "discovered" before they start to appear. Took me awhile to figure out "discover" means actually used. So if you are hanging onto a scroll (you can only carry one), and discover a new one but don't want to waste what you have, it basically is considered "not discovered".  To compound this, it can be sometimes hard to tell the colours apart so you end up wasting one only to discover your new scroll is something you've seen before.
- Hard to be certain, but it seems like the enemies become more difficult and faster as you acquire power ups like increased shot speed.  Basically you can never really even the odds.
- Some of the bosses are pretty cheap.
- Objects are random, and some things you destroy actually spawn enemies. Since you lose your powerups when you die, it makes restarting a bit of a crap-shoot.
A key thing in Gauntlet was the generators. If you could destroy one, you basically stopped enemies from spawning. There is no such machanic here, so basically there is nothing you can do to stop things from getting hard...nothing to really even the odds at all. Things just keep coming and coming until you are over-run.
In short, it is fun while it lasts, but unless your OCD kicks in like mine did it really runs its course pretty quickly.  The game is free now, so one can't complain too much but there are definitely more balanced games out there to spend your time on.  In the end, not a terrible game but one that I wanted to like more than I actually did.

( SPOILERS of Gameplay and game mechanics. )
I have decided to revise this review after every dozen or so hours of gameplay to provide as much info on what gameplay will be like as I can. Keep in mind I am slightly bias as this game is both of my favorite gernes combined ( Space Exploration and RPG/some sandbox elements), but I am still fair and wont leave out any cons I experience as I proceed to play the game. =)
Short Version  ;  Free form space sandbox with a semi-procedural universe and complete freedom to do whatever you'd like. There are unlimited enemies generated, and gameplay is enjoyable to the extent that it may quite literally provide endless hours of entertainment. There is space combat, mining etc
Rating: 8.7 / 10    Will be 9.5/10 if the dev's fix the bug that causes some crashes here and there.

Pro's and Cons
Pro's

* The game is massive. Look at the map and scroll out, you'll be surprised at the potential this game has.
* Research system that allows players to obtain blueprints and spend some resources to unlock new parts to use.
* Challenging AI  ( The ai will take advantage of your weak spots, and out manuever you if possible. Especially the flanking fighters. )
* Great soundtrack.   Sometimes I'll just explore new areas just to hear a new track.  ( btw, music is blusey with an outlaw vibe, perfect for exploring dangerous new areas and engaging in combat with tricky enemies that keep you on your toes.
* Great combat system.  I love using 220mm cannons to disable vital parts of ships ( Like engines and weapons ) to then move in for the kill when a ship is vulnerable. There is a major strategy element involved with combat. For the love of god please do no just rush in towards a bigger ship and hope to win xD Flanking and dodging are key. ( and shields, that works too)
* Not just a space game. You can walk around as a human player, mid combat, and repair damaged parts of your ship.. Put out raging fires before they suffocate you,.. Engage in combat with enemy crew and take their ship for yourself if you're successful... Explore your space station, or massive ships ( which are huge btw ).
* Humor .. Lol.   The Dev's have a great sense of humor, and know just how to balance jokes with useful information. Don't skip Dialog =P
* Great Visuals. Ships look great and the background nebula's/art have a really nice depth.
(The edits below are after another 15 hours of gameplay from the original review)
*EDIT*  - Some ships have a Mining bore. This allows players to mine asteroids via docking after launching the bore at one of the literally almost infinite asteroids within the game. You can also add a mining bore to custom designs of your own, I believe.
*EDIT*  - You can farm ( literally place plants in a garden of sorts ) and watch as they accumulate worth over time. I don't know too much about this game mechanic, It may still be a work in progress, but I do know that you can stumble upon new planting items on asteroids that you mine on.
I Could ramble on more but it's time for some cons
CONS
* Some bugs are prevalant in the game. One of these bugs can cause crashes once every hour or two of gameplay. Be sure to save frequently until this bug is fixed. ( watch the devlog incase the Dev's fix this and I forget to update my review) The other bugs are minor and is exactly what you'd expect from an Early Access Game.    ( Ex: fall out of your ship but still be alive without the graphic of your player ) Stuff like that.   =)
* Could use more items to build with at start. (Such as having Hallways and Corridors / the basic building blocks of a ship unlocked ) as well as maybe a tutorial on building ships. ( Could also use some smaller structural pieces but i'm not too experienced with the ship builder just yet. )
^^^^^ * EDIT * A Dev has mentioned they are planning on overhauling the research system eventually so that progress will be more streamlined and natural.
* Slight Delay when traveling at warp speed and entering a new section of the universe. The game universe is seamlessly connected but I think when enemies are spawned around your section of the universe, they freeze the game for a second or two. A very minor annoyance at worse.
*Game can be punishing to people who are careless. This can be taken as either a pro or con depending on a person, but the difficulty of the gameplay is entirely dependant upon the player and where they choose to go.
Conclusion and a Story/Glimpse of gameplay.
CONCLUSION: I was first introduced to this game 2 days ago and now have 15 hours.  *  EDIT*   (I now have around 28 hours of gameplay only a few days later, and I do not afk to gain hours. Still enjoying the game very much. ) I have a job and work 6-9 hours a day. To have 15 hours already tells you that this game delivers pretty well. There are some bugs in this game, but surprisingly not too many compared to many other early access games. This game is worth the money IF you know you like the space sandbox and combat / space exploration gerne. This game is perfect for the many of us out there that like the abstract feeling of being adrift in space, space combat with some elements of realism to it, and those of us with creative minds whom like to build and experiment with designs. This game has an extreme amount of potential, and I for one would very much like to see it reach it's peak.
I say give the game a chance if you are considering it. I know I wasn't disappointed.

I repaired what I could ( Thank god my suit had oxygen attributes, I would have suffocated otherwise.) and somehow managed to very slowly make my way back to my home station. A fun little fantasy twin-stick shooter. So far as I can tell, the classes aren't well balanced - range doesn't seem to be a major factor in the balance of attacks. As such, it's hard to beat the (free) unlimited range of the mage. You can kill things you can't even see, and with a high rate of fire, that really helps keep the screen clear in the direction you are moving.
The other classes seem to pale in comparison, but it is still a fun time.
The upgrades feel like a proper shmup, they are significant, but you lose them when you die. But the permanent upgrades give the game a slight RPG feel that is cool.
The game could use a couple of things that I think would have made it more fun:
1. A more gradual ramp-up of enemy difficulty and frequency. Basically you are getting random encounters with tons of monsters right out of the gate, and there doesn't seem to be anything stopping you from bumping into rather "nasty" monsters in the very first parts of the very first level.
This isn't a flaw, by itself, but it seems like a missed opportunity to feel like you are gradually ramping up, which is common in shmups.
2. The game could use some "sanctuaries". The shops seems like the obvious choice, but it would be nice to have somewhere to go to think, count, and just look at your map for a few seconds.
These flaws are all minor, though, and the game achieves its goal very well, overall, I think.

This game has a lot of potential but there's a couple of things that let it down. For example even when the enemy isn't in view or on the screen yet, you get shot at by the plants that spit things at you but how are you supposed to dodge them when you don't know that they are there? It leads to a very cheap kill system. It basically gives the AI an unfair advantage. In some parts you have to press the down arrow to get to certain places that aren't visable. How below some of these places are spikes but the problem with this is that the spikes aren't visable before hand, so you don't have a logical way of preparing to dodge the spikes. Instead, Cluckles just plumets towards the spikes and you have to redo the level, which isn't fair because it's not the players fault as they weren't actually physically able to see the spikes and plan a way of getting around them.
I do like the graphics and the combat with the sword and shield and would be interested to see these parts of the game develop. The amount of levels is just right and the platforming and parkour mechanisms such as clinging onto the walls is well thought out. The game lacks slightly when it comes to the tutorials. For example there are certain parts in the levels where you have to double jump and then use your sword to further extend the jump, otherwise you can't make the jump at all. When playing for the first time, it never once occurred to me that I could of used my sword to extend the jumps. With this in mind, I think it would be nice to see this included in the tutorial as it is clearly key to making certain jumps in the game. I'm sure this has been mentioned before also but the controller support in the menu isn't great but I'm sure the devs are already working on this, or at least I hope so.
Overall, this is a game with a lot of potential and visually looks very good with some great ideas and mechanics but does have room for a lot of improvement. I would definitely recommend if you like platformer games.

Edit: this was originally a negative review, but I've been on the fence about the game after completing it and have to conclude that my criticisms were not bad enough to warrant it. I'll leave it as a positive review that highlights the games weak points.
I am enjoying playing through Cluckles' Adventure, the controls are tight and movement and attacking feels very fluid. However as I have gotten to the third set of levels, its flaws are standing out more and more.
-When Cluckles falls, she plummets like a rock. This has lead to many deaths when I need to jump over a hazard and can't react before she falls to her death.
-There are several types of enemies and hazards that throw projectiles. Often they will attack the split second that the screen scrolls onto them leading to a cheap and unavoidable death.
-In the first two worlds, secret walls are hinted at by placement of a butterfly hovering around in the area. But in the third world, there are many secrets that have no butterfly which means I have to hump every wall, floor and ceiling until I find the one that leads to a hidden room.
-and finally a minor issue, the level select screen is very slow to navigate with a controller, it's far quicker to use the mouse to get to the level I want to play.

Eventide is a typical craftsmen work of a hidden object game. It uses well-known mechanics and story type (granddaughter saving grandma and cute creatures from evil demon), but it knows how to use them well.
One of the banes of hidden object games is that they all can feel relatively the same. For example, if you think about a typical modern HOG with all of the usual HOG elements, you think about a game like Eventide: Slavic Fable.
Not that it’s a bad thing; Eventide knows its trade well. With its great graphics and enjoyable hidden/fragmented object scenes, there isn’t much that can be said against it. Well, okay, the map system is barely useful and it really needs more puzzles over the point ‘n’ click style item management.
The story also likes to stay on known waters: our heroine has to go on a journey to save her grandmother from the clutches of an evil Slavic half-demon, and to do so, she gets help from other Slavic creatures. By the way, the game really wants to remind everyone that it is about Slavic folklore. Maybe a little too much…

A cute, fat chicken with a sword, a shield, and armor, out to save hundreds of stolen chicks from all sorts of monsters that normal chickens would usually stay away from. What could possibly go wrong? Absolutely nothing, there's respawn.
On a more serious note, I'm really impressed so far. The levels can be either extremly easy and mainly jump-and-dodge based, or they can be a bit trickier, requiring you to think outside of the box to find hidden areas for the lost chicks, or some buffs like a shield or armor.
The controls are very simple, the game doesn't really tell you the controls, but to players like me familiar with the genre it's easy to figure out, though for newer players button smashing till they find the controls might not be very pleasant. The only tricky part is the jump-dash timings. Failing is pretty easy, for me at least, but what I love is it doesn't seem to be that rage-inflicting as most games of the genre, and respawn in instant so there's no wasted time.
I can appreciate the fact that the dev bothered with achievements. Although they are not much, I can see a lot of other things in the game that could turn into some pretty fun achievements. Either way, I'm excited to get the ones that are already there.
Other than that, the graphics are simple and sweet, and the music is adorable and fitting. The price is very reasonable aswell, given the amount of content, it's not overpriced at all.
Overall I'm pretty happy with this, and would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a chill, addictive platformer. So, what are you waiting for? Grab your chicken, give it a sword, and start dashing.

Spiderwb Software is know for their old-school RPGs, and rightfully so.  Intersting NPCs, well thought out story, and a well designed world that feels alive. LocoCycle is a story about a newly-self-aware combat motorcycle, I.R.I.S. wanting to enjoy her newfound independence by taking a road trip with her best friend in the world, her mechanic, Pablo. It's actually kind of touching, in it's own way. Unfortunately, she's not exactly sane, and her translation software has been damaged, so Pablo can't get her to understand that he's not enjoying the trip.
"Arcadey" is the best word to describe the gameplay. Aside from the persistent upgrade system and game length, this would absolutely feel right at home in an arcade cabinet. It's a combination of Road Blasters style combat driving and shooting, God of War style combo-based brawling, and some (actually fun, not horrible) Dragon's Lair style follow-the-prompt events. There's a great variety of enemies and locations, stretching from the jungles of Nicaragua to the American midwest.
The intro and in-game cutscenes are all live-action bits in the best B-movie style. You're either going to love that or hate it, I expect. They're suprisingly well made and acted, funny, and exactly as cheesy as they should be. Robert Patrick (the T-1000) plays your equally unbalanced arch-nemesis, S.P.I.K.E., another motorcycle. Freddy Rodriguez plays the ace mechanic Pedro, being equal parts hapless victim of circumstance and quick-witted survivor. The legendary Lloyd Kaufman even gets a cameo in the opening movie.
If arcade-style fun is what you're in the mood for, I recommend it completely.

I really, really liked LocoCycle. It was a fun game. Clearly I'm in the minority based on the overall reception the game has got since release but I really liked it.
Just to get this out of the way -- I don't recommend the game to you or to anyone because I'm in the minority on it. A lot of people didn't like it. The core gameplay loop is pretty shallow (you get a shallow spy hunter clone, a button-mashing brawler element, some analogue stick rail shooter sequences, and then a few other surprises that I won't spoil here but they're similarly sort of shallow but still awesome and out of left field). So if you're looking for a deep, replayable game, it's not here. Despite per-level leaderboards and a score attack element, I don't think people will be coming back to this.
However, I found the game consistently funny (lots of puns, lots of deadpan humour, tons of reference humour, lots of great visual gags in the gameplay, it's so hilarious), it was always introducing new enemy types and patterns so that any shallowness in the gameplay was made up with sort of consistently new things, there are so many different gameplay genres including the second last boss fight which basically made me drop my jaw when it happened I couldn't even believe it. I thought the 30+ minute long B-movie that provides the game's live action scenes was funny and enjoyable. I thought the audio was excellent, with great performances by the Prague Symphony Orchestra. It ran well on my computer, it looked great in a cartoony way in motion (not so much in screenshots).
As with every Twisted Pixel game, there are hundreds of unlockable concept art bits, pitch videos, production shots from the live action movie, and historical stuff--including a sneak peak at their next game which seems to me to be ambitious.
I think the game succeeds at what it sets out to do. It took me about 4-4:15 to finish the game with all upgrades, A grades on most levels, all achievements, and look through all the concept art and stuff. This is not a long game. But I feel absolutely like I got my money worth out of it. I'd place it above Comic Jumper in execution, and personally I was pretty burned out by the end of Ms. Splosion Man. That being said, I liked Gunstringer and the Maw more. I continue to think that Twisted Pixel is an interesting studio doing interesting work and I'm glad they're around. While I think LocoCycle worked, I hope their next project manages to find the right balance between core gameplay that appeals to other people and their own unique style.

Bias Disclaimer: I have been playing this game for like 2 years, when the original "Wayward Terran Frontier" was nothing more than a ship editor, and only like 300 people in the world (or possibly far less) even knew it existed. I have been in contact with the developer many times, and helped provide input that helped change the games development with the many other people providing bugs and such. I have also played this on my channel, and continue to, claiming to be "Youtubes number 1 place for Wayward Terran Frontier Content", because to date I have played it the most out of anyone who is covering it on youtube. This is not a plug, it's part of the disclaimer bias. I am biased. I love this game. The copy is my own, I bought this game a long time ago, and was part of the Zero Falls kickstarter for whatever little I could offer. I was not paid in any way, nor will i ever be. Onto the actual review.
Wayward Terran Frontier, now known with an additonal Zero Falls, has come a long way. From constant crashes, and saves that don't carry over, to being controlled by the AI faction and having to delete your own save files and restart. This early access review is for the steam launch. Version 0.3.3.14.
With the 3.3.14 launch, many many many of these issues that persisted over the last few major updates have been fixed. We'll get to that.
What is Wayward Terran Frontier: Zero Falls? Other than a huge name i've come to enjoy quite a lot... It's a top-down space sandbox rpg.
You fly/ walk in 2 dimentions even though the game is rendered technically in 3, and play in a top-down perspective. Your only goal is to fly through the universe, fighting, mining and pillaging your way to loot. Lots of loot. From randomized stats on armor, clothes, nanite orbs, and other augmentations and most importantly... Blueprints.
Blueprints spawn as items known as "Data Cores". Data cores can contain any kind of blueprint, or garbage, depending on it's tier pool it draws from when opening 1 of 3 different tiers of Data Cores. Data cores are the reason no 2 blueprints will spawn twice, because the game now realizes what you are opening, and remoiving that from the pool once learned (hopefully this system works even if you die before learning a blueprint, but AFTER discovering it).
Features:
Blueprints- Contain modules, rooms, ship weapons, improvements to ship weapons, and many more things. Find blueprints to unlock the different components to building the interior of ships.
Player weapons - Rifles, SMGs, Machine Guns, Miniguns, etc. All with random stats. Explore the cosmos and kill for better loot, with a bit of luck.
Stations- Derelict stations to explore, raid, fight through, conquor. Currently no way to hack a station to make it usable for yourself. I know nothing of intended future features, so I'm just hopeful of this one someday.
Ships- Holy mother of pearl, there's lots of ships. You have 3 factions completely independent of you (no faction diplomacy or anything). I think they're civilian, military, and pirate. Ships can fly around in convoys protecting supply ships, some ships are neutral until provoked, most ships are immediately hostile - and ALL ships can be docked with, assuming you havent destroyed their air lock/ docking bay.
Speaking of ships, you can repair in the game, and if you repair a ship you fought and fly it back to your station, it can be reverse engineered to be built and modified for yourself, assuming your station reactor has enough energy to spawn it in. Every ship can be captured, and engineered for yourself. All of them. Some take far more skill than others.
The game can be punishing, whether it's because of some of the more... Quirky early access bugs, or because you don't have the knowledge of ship layouts to know where to strike them to disarm them or whatever. But if you trudge through it and take the time to learn as you play, the game is seriously rewarding. Editing existing ship designs to your liking through researching components/ weapons, and taking on ships that used to give you trouble with a little more knowledge and winning is such a nice feelings.
Oh, and did I mention asteroids? Those buggers will pop out at you in the middle of Travel Drive, and you'll be space toast. The burnt kind that smells like smoking metal, except there's no air in space and you're dead. This is a good thing. They're stationary, btw.
Mining- There IS a mining system, if you get a ship with a mining drill you can launch it at an asteroid and dock with it, allowing you to mine the inside of the rock like walking around a ship (you can't mine ships). This can give you means of expanding your farms, and growing crystals that can be thrown in the furnace for mass (the in-game currency), as well as finding ores which equal a LOT of mass when thrown int eh furnace. You also get mass from looting ships and stations in the form of 'Scrap'.
Idk what else I should say. This is whats in the game, with a side of sass because I personally enjoy it. Is the price steep? Sure, to some people I guess. The game is worth $29.99 USD, and george has gone on record to say that the game will be on various sales many times during development.
Whether you pick it up, or you follow the games development and get it down the road, it's super worth your time. And it only gets better as days pass. The small dev team updates the game once a month on average, if not sooner than that. They're also frequently patching bugs and letting you in on the development process, and frustrations.
Cons-
The only cons in my opinion are the bugs that comne with early access and the inconstancy of when the saves break. BUT supposedly this has been mostly fixed with the current steam version, because they wanted some persistance in their save files for steam. I do NOT have the time to play this at the time of writing the review, so I can't say with certanty that the issues are fixed. However my previous version successfully converted, and I can play the same file since the release, which is a good sign.
9/10 becuase I'm a critic.
10/10 because this small indie team is proving remarkable, compared to my many previous early access purchases.

Honestly, I don't even know where to begin with this title. I'll be honest when I say that my love for superbikes and motorcycles in general got in the way for me to pick this title right up with no initial reviews or expectations except that it had a bike in it... pretty much never having heard of it in development at all and simply saw it released today, I figured, "Why the hell not? It's got a slick looking bike in it...".
But boy lemme tell you, was I in for a surprise!
First and foremost, the game is a cinematic-spectacle with explosions going off in the game just about every 5 seconds (gameplay included) as you take command as I.R.I.S.: an extraordinarily advanced female-AI motorcycle. How advanced? You ever seen a motorcycle pull Brazilian jujitsu moves on a helicopter?! Yeah... THAT advanced! What a personality IRIS has got on her too... I imagine she must be some sort of distantly removed cousin of GLaDOS--the bubblier, more naive cousin who likes to talk about movies, wants to visit Scottsburg, Indiana, doesn't understand Spanish but pretends she does. Trust me, if and when you play this game, you'll completely understand what I mean...
The game itself borrows SO many different game mechanics, I don't even know where to begin with. If you've played Spyhunter, you've probably played this game before... except just as a motorcycle, that's it. As a motorcycle... wholly, the game plays like one of those oldschool arcade racers: Cruisin' USA, Ridge Racer, and Out Run come to mind. It even borrows elements from another unsung classic: ROAD RASH!! Yeah! It even copies bits of Road Rash at some point in the game! Yet further on in the game, I was constantly surprised by multiple other game mechanics that pop up. At times you're dodging things like in a Frogger game. Or button mashing like a beat 'em up--again, it's SO hard to say this game is ONE thing because it does ALOT of things at once or in various degrees throughout the game, and actually does them pretty well to make one hell of an experience.
FYI: there are quick time events in this game... ALOT of them, which also add into the rest of the expansive repertoire of game mechanics this game has got going on. And I'll be honest, I'm not that big a fan of QT-events, and I was all, "Ah man, REALLY??" When they first showed up, believing they'd be very gimmicky or add nothing to the game; I again was surprised as to how effective they felt and were implemented in the game. This of course could just be subjective and someone else could disagree with me, but in my experience, it was pretty solid.
There's nothing groundbreaking going on in the title except that it has a certain charm you can't dislike about. For instance, there's alot of pop culture references in this game, most of them based off movies. And I mean particularly old movies: Men In Black, Big Trouble in Little China, Ski School... oddly enough I've yet to hear a single reference from Short Circuit, but I haven't completed the game yet. Instead, what I got going on here is to let everyone know what I've experienced so far, and it's a pretty awesome game. Again, it's not THE GREATEST title you'll play, but it does what it does very well and you'll have a blast of a time watching all the action sequences which rival up to the likes of some Pixar movies.
In short, the game is charming, it has moments where its made me laugh out loud and it's one of the few motorcycle based games out there that puts a "CRANK IT TO 11!!!" Looney-Tunes type spin on some spectacular action sequences... I'm still wrapping my head around the fact I watched a motorcycle take down a chopper Zangief-style with its front wheel!!
Though I recommend this game, it definitely won't appeal to everyone and that's a shame because a game like this? Taken seriously? You're probably doing it wrong and seriously need to reassess your priorities in where they lie, because you can leave all your serious business at the door before stepping into LocoCycle's house. When you show up at this game's doorstep, prepare to leave reality behind and go back in time to that magical Saturday morning's cartoon weekend we've probably all lost touch with in this jaded age of ultra-competitive gaming going on these days. It's nice to know that a game like this is out there, because I couldn't imagine a world without LocoCycle; I mean I could, but it would probably be a little bit more boring.
I'd sit here and finish the game outright, but I got errands to run, a family to take care of--but once I've got some free time to myself again, I'm hopping right back in and see what else this fabulous little game has got to offer! And so should you!

Finally got around to finish the game and it takes about 4 hours give or take how fast you're able to get through some of the levels, though the pacing seems pretty consistent, so I'm sticking with my guns on this and saying 4 hours. Wow.

After 3ish years of waiting, I've finally got my hands on the 1.0 version of Starbound. After playing through the story, getting to the endgame, and playing the game to it's fullest, I think I can finally write a solid review.

+ Great potential for building structures
+ bajillions of decorations and blocks to use
+ Combat is good, with duel-wielding and various weapon classes
+ Randomly generated weapons, planets, and creatures for huge replayability
+Massive amount of vanity items and character customization options
+Colony system, where you can build houses (or small
boxes) to attract tenants that will pay you rent and give you quests
+You can capture creatures you find later in the game and become a Pokemon trainer
-Progression is dull, go to x planet, get x ore, make x thing that lets you go to the next planet
-story is meh; hero against evil thing with no twists or anything
-Everything is super easy, the only real danger in the end game is fall damage
-Developers are kinda iffy, they take out features and put them back in at random
Overall, I think this is a really good game that is absolutely worth $15. For those who liked building in Terraria, this game is a great buy. The combat and difficulty is hopefully something that will be looked at in the future, but until then mods are a great alternative.

Painted in shades of The Behemoth's colourful arcade multiplayer joys,
is a fun, cheap blaster that has you carving a path through thousands of zombies, werewolves, chickens, undead wrestlers and weeping tree stumps (I wish I knew) in order to conquer bosses and pour your subsequent loot into the game's upgrade tree.
With but two mouse buttons to control your guns and hand-to-hand weapons and a space bar to dodge, you'll get into countless scraps with the hungry dead by way of random encounters as you move from place to place on the world map, being dumped back in the safe confines of the church when you're inevitably overcome. The battles themselves are set in various arenas filled with crates that contain anything from a wheelbarrow load of coins to special limited super-weapons that can clear half a map out if you don't die getting to them.
The big issue here is the comical imbalance of the weapon system. You find new guns and melee items as random drops in encounters, all of which would traditionally have their own advantage/disadvantages but the minute you lay hands on the shotgun,
goes from beating your head in with a mob of corpses to standing helplessly by while you reduce that mob into red yoghurt with your double-barrelled death cannon. I can imagine that it becomes easier to roll with an automatic rifle in multiplayer with the mass of enemies split between more than one person but really, you'd just be handicapping yourself. None of the guns have any sort of ammo count so there's absolutely no reason to ever switch them out or even use a melee attack. Add to that a perk that turns the shotgun into a golden super-weapon after a killstreak and you're really just clicking to exercise your fingers after a while.
does start to feel inescapably repetitive after a couple of hours or so, by which point you should be well on your way to clearing out the majority of the bosses and grinding out the last few character perks but there's room to expand and tweak the parts that need it while it's in EA.

Attack of the Labyrinth is fun little arcade game. Sadly, it doesn't offer much depth, but it isn't an expensive title. This is first impressions of the game.
A peaceful kingdom is treathen by dark presence. A labyrinth of pure evil, with an army unlike any seen before. So, now it's up to four Champions to save the kingdom. Simple story.
This is 2D game, so the lacking of video options is understandable. So is the rebindable keys to ceratin degree. It would be nice to change them. The graphics are retro pixel art with a lot of colours
There is four classes to choose from. Those are the Champions. I only play with the Wizard. With him the gameplay is a twin-stick shooter. You have only one attack – a projectile and that's it. Well, there is more, but not much. In the levels you can find or buy upgrades. They change your projectile and your appearance. The wizard can be upgraded two times, I don't know about the others. The only other thing that can help you are scrolls. They are one time use magic spell. Health, Mace, Summon, Shield and Radiant. The last is extremely powerful clearing spell. You can carry one at a time. There is nothing more to the gameplay.
With the gold you collect from dead enemies, chests and everything that explodes, you can buy from a shop inside the level lives (yes, there are lives here), scrolls, health and upgrades and nothing more.
Dungeons or labyrinths are pretty diverce as layout. I saw ice cave, mines with tracks, grass, dirt or gold and so on. All levels are randomly generated, which add to the replayability. When you enter a labyrinth you have to find a key, then the exit. Also there is place with a map, that shows where those things are and the shop. There is no mini map and sometimes it's a little bit confusing. Before every boss you have to make it through series of levels. The first is small, but they get progressively larger. The labyrinth with the boss encounter are pretty big and without a mini map it can take you a while to find the key and the exit.
Enemies are okay. Different types of spiders, ghosts, archers, knights and so on. When they surround they are dangerous. The game is pretty intense and I like that. The bosses are creative and fun to fight.
Effects resemble 8-bit games from the past and they are nice. Music is okay, but not very memorable. I can't think of a single track.
The games is okay. It's very colorful with responsive controls and it's fun for a while. There is local co-op, but didn't try it. Probably it will be more fun with a friend, but I think it's a mistake not to have online multiplayer. Sadly, my biggest disappointment is the lack of gameplay depth. One projectile and scrolls. I played almost two hours and i'm already getting bored. It's just functional, fun little game. But when you consider the prise, I think the game is alright. Get the game on sale and find a friend to play with you.
What the story lacks in length, is made up for in the artwork and soundtrack. Wonderful game, and deserves top praise.

The maps are randomized each playthrough and there is a map stone on each level that can help you find the exit. I like the random maps because they are drawn like a classic maze, or a cornmaze, lots of winding corners and a dead end. If I pay attention it's not too hard but if I space out I find myself going in circles.
I didn't experience any bugs or stability issues and was glad to find that all features of the game and achievements worked fine.
Beautiful art, smooth gameplay, and an equally smooth narrator. The music too is wonderful. I'd recommend this game to anyone, especially if on sale.
