Dungeon Souls is a topdown action dungeon crawler highly comparable to
and other similarly styled games. You select a soul to play as (warrior, archer, thief etc.) and traverse dungeons filled with baddies and bosses to activate seals that progress you towards escape.
It embraces the perma-death feature found in Roguelites and encourages permanent upgrading of characters and equipment upgrades between each run, making future runs slightly easier. Each character has a few unique abilities, and dungeons are littered with items that modify or enhance character attritubes.
In order to play this game, I had to modify the properties of the game files. Consumers shouldn't have to do this to play something they've purchased, so this already gets a failing score from me. But there are other things that prevent me from recommending this to anyone.
For quick reference, I've played a lot of
and all but completed
, both of which I completely adore. Dungeon Souls just felt like an emptier, blander version of these games.
My main problem was the stale gameplay loop. Each floor has you running around touching seals to spawn a teleporter that brings you to the next floor. The issue is, every time you touch a seal, enemies spawn in a circle around the seal, and you need to kill them. But because you know it's going to happen, you can very easily wait until your AOE ability is off cooldown and then just obliterate everything. Move onto the next seal, do the same thing, rinse and repeat for every floor. It's monotonous and frankly unengaging. The obstacles between each seal are interesting the first time, but once you learn what they do and how to avoid them, they just become mild annoyances.
In addition, there are some questionable core gameplay mechanics. If you select a ranged character, you don't have complete control of where they shoot, and I mean this on two levels. First, you can really only aim in 16 directions, or at least it feels that way. And second, there's a "bullet spread" on your attacks that is so comically wide that you're often missing enemies that are right in front of you. I get that they were trying to incorporate accuracy as a stat to bring balance to ranged characters, but it eliminates skill and really just makes you sit there longer, begging for your character to RNG a hit.
And if you happen to die, which is highly likely, the dungeons aren't entirely procedural. What I mean is that the dungeon themes and bosses are all in a set order, and you'll have to slog through it all again before you can experience new content. The core gameplay isn't fun enough to warrant this suffering.
Simply put, this isn't a $13 game and you should really just stick to
, as it is superior in every way.

Adventures of Bertram FIddle: Episode 1: A Dreadly Business | Review
"Help me Fiddle, you're my only hope!"
Adventures of Bertram Fiddle Episode 1 is quite charming. Filled with puns, pop culture references, and all sorts of silliness, the game brings a kind of humour I haven't seen in a point and click before. You play as Bertram Fiddle, professional adventurer, hobbyist sleuth, and full-time pun enthusiast.
Best detective of all time.
Adventures of Bertram Fiddle is a 2D point and click story-driven game from Deck13 Interactive. The game offers a charming take on Victorian-era England's gritty, smog filled streets. You solve clues, combine items, and force your Peruvian/Cyclopsian manservant to do all your heavy lifting for you. Bumbling your way through the cobblestone paved roads you find yourself tossed into an adventure and murder mystery when you least expect it. While short, episode 1 offers more than enough puns and adventure for anyone looking for two to three hours worth of entertainment.
GAMEPLAY
Adventures of Bertram Fiddle is a traditional point and click. The game has some action sequences where you have to dodge incoming objects either to run away from or chase after something, and while these action sequences are easy, it offers a clear break in the sleuthing, and really ramps up the pace of the narrative.
WHAT'S IN THE BAG?
The game isn't very hard, but it's entertaining, and in a point and click I think that's mostly what matters. I only was stumped once, and it's because I didn't quite go far enough in a room for the camera to pan over to the object I needed. To get through the game you mostly have to click on everything, but Bertram is humorous enough in his commentary that you want to click on everything. I found myself laughing aloud at some of his funnier puns, although I was slightly disgusted with myself when I did. The mechanic of using your manservant Gavin to assist you with strength based puzzles is also quite clever, although I think it's a little too obvious when you need Gavin to help you.
Gavin has my goal body.
Like any good point and click, you run into roadblocks, but what makes Adventures of Bertram Fiddle so great is that you don't really mind when you run into them. Since you want to click on everything, and since everything you click offers such entertaining dialogue, you won't mind when you're stuck, and if you do ever get stuck, it won't be for long. The more you explore and the more you experiment with items, the easier the game becomes.
Click an item to use it, then click on the object.
The combination of incredibly funny dialogue mixed with interesting puzzles to solve really brings out Adventures of Bertram's charm.
STORY
The story is written well, and the voice acting is pretty spot on. The clues placed aren't obvious enough to make the story ridiculously easy, but easy enough not to spend hours searching for that one damn clue. The pacing of the narrative is good, and the action sequences help pump your adrenaline for when Bertram is in danger. Comedy is the main focal point of the story, as every other line or click has a joke intermixed with the dialogue. I thought the non-stop jokes would get tiresome, but the game is short enough and fast paced enough that you're still laughing by the end. Bertram is an endearing character, and you really want him to beat Sherlock Holmes in the race to find the identity of Geoff the Murderer.
Ever attentive, our Bertram.
USER INTERFACE AND ART STYLE
The interface for Adventures of Bertram is incredibly simple. You click to move anywhere on the screen, and clickable objects form a small circle when you hover over them. There are only ever two visible buttons on the screen; the pause button (a godsend when you need to pause but don't want to miss any story), and the inventory tab.
The inventory is simple and nice to look at. Also yes, that is a nose.
The inventory tab is easy to maneuver, and you just click and drag to combine any items. The art style is charmingly drawn, and the characters are goofy looking but not ridiculous. I figured out quite quickly that you could double click the next room arrow and you could skip the lengthy walk animation to the next room. This increased the speed of the games drastically, and combined with the skippable dialogue, you can breeze through the game no problem.
Such artistry. See how he captures the pain and suffering of the dodo?
FLAWS
Adventures of Bertram Fiddle doesn't have a great many flaws. Since this is a game for "casuals" listed on steam, you can't complain that it's too easy. It's a game for people who just want to experience a short story, or movie. Although, since it's episodic, I'm assuming there's going to be an $11.00 price point for each episode, which is too much. The game is fun, and entertaining, but I think its 40% off sale price of $6.59 is much more accurate as to what you are going to get. For an $11.00 game I expect more than two and a half hours of content. With being a point and click, there isn't much replayability, so that one experience through the story is all you're getting for that $11.00.  Besides the price, there isn't much I can think in the way of flaws. You know what you're going to get when it comes to Adventures of Bertram Fiddle, and it's a mostly fun experience.
CONCLUSION
I had fun. It didn't last crazy long, but that's almost a plus in my book. I paid less money than a movie rental, and got more entertainment time than one too. Bertram's love of puns and adventure really create a world that I want to dive into, and I can't wait for the next installment. An incredibly self-aware game, that doesn't take itself seriously at all, offers a fun and relaxing experience. If you are looking to spend your next couple hours laughing and solving mysteries, Adventures of Bertram Fiddle Episode 1: A Dreadly Business is the game for you.
8/10

A great upgrade from the old, webb-browser based form of the game. However, there are still issues as there were in the old version of the game. First of all, singleplayer mode is basically unplayable, which is a problem as the servers on this version are currently empty. All of the AI wants to kill you, and wants nothing else. If it sees you, it will chase and kill you, whether that would benefit it in any way or not. Without the errors of a human player, this means that you will die within minutes or starting the game, and this is unavoidable. AI will not stop chasing you unless you go somewhere that it can't (eg. rabbit/meerkat holes found in some maps.) Also, the game adjusts the amount of each animal in the map when you change at a totem, always putting in far more predators than you can handle, and potential mates will always try to kill you, as far as I can tell. Singleplayer needs to be fixed for it to be playable while not a lot of people have it.
PS: If people could not downvote the game just because they don't like its concept, that would help. We need more people who did enjoy the browser-based version to play it, not be scared off by your negative reviews. The game will be much better when there are more people.

I like this version much better over the Browser version which had too many hackers. The only problems that I see right now that can be easily fixed are these:
Too many aggressive animals:
Depending on the animal you are of course. That part is fine. I expect to be scared of attack all the time when I'm a rabbit or something small. But a large animal like a Wildebeast shouldn't have to be afraid of Meerkats. The only thing that should be aggressive to animals similar to the Wildebeast are the large predators.
The Fennic Fox is a different story. Why is the horse aggressive to me? While in the game you can hunt anything, horses, I don't think would instantly go for a fox.
Finally, the same gender. For males I can understand or females depending on the species. But there are too many. I don't care much for always being on constant attack by my own kind. Especially animals that live in groups.
The Controls:
Everything is done with 'ctrl' basically. This is a huge problem I think. Since I am always under attack when I try to fight, I end up eating (if I am prey this is usually where this becomes a problem) or drinking (if I am near water). It would be better if the attack button was a different button than the 'action' button. I am totally cool with eating/drinking/nuzzling being the same button. As those are specific and easy to go about than trying to fight while my head is down eating.
The scent button would also be better off as a different button as well. Same issue as with the attacking.
Animations:
I loved the animation of the tundra hare, and I think it would be great to add that to the hare in the forest. The new animals have some great animations and so I feel the older original animals need an upgrade to their models.
The Good Stuff:
I saw a lot of improvements. I was really impressed. I think the biggest problem were the hackers on multiplayer which, thankfully, are gone with the steam version.
The game has a lot of potential. The new animals and habitats are great. I look forward to seeing cool updates.
For $9-10 this is an okay game and not much of waste, especially since things are being updated.
Suggestions:
I saw someone had suggested homes for all the animals in the area. I support that idea.
A plains area would be cool. We have the Savanna, but I was thinking a North American plain with new animals like the Bison and mice.
A prehistoric map. Not dinosaurs, but more the ancient mammals like the Mammoth and Smilodon.

Makes me feel like an old nostalgic gamer.

I have a mixed relationship with this game.
On the positive side, I will say the idea is brilliant. What this amounts to is turn-based Mount&Blade, but with far more narrative capacity, more enemy types, and oh my god is it well-executed. As you can probably tell, I spent hours enthralled in this game. IT. IS. ADDICTING. Hats off to the developers for getting the game to the point it is now.
And, you know what? If that's all it ever had to offer, if the developers had given it mod support and left things otherwise the way they are, I would still be playing it and enthusiatically recommending it to everyone. But they didn't. And there is SO much wasted potential in this game because of it. Wanted new narrative events? Too bad, it'll never happen. Expanded classes and quests? Nothing. New weapons, armor, or battle sisters? Nada. Total conversion mods for Berserk or Game of Thrones? LOL nope.
I won't say it isn't worth the price, because IMHO it totally is. Trust me, the gameplay is enough to make you cancel your plans (if you have any) and spend a whole weekend engrossed in this game, then call into work sick just to keep living life as a mercenary commander. But what this really comes down to for me is my utter dissapointment, not in the game that is, but in the game that could have been.

Wow, that's pretty much the one word to describe Attack of the Labyrinth, this is of the most fun games I've had the pleasure of playing in a while. The gameplay is so simple, yet so addictive. This is a hard as nails arcade action dungeon crawling game. I'd also say it has a hint of rogue-like too.
There are plenty of classes to choose from as with most fantasy type games, my favorite here has to be the mage, his spells get so overpowered once you rank them up. I did also spend some time playing as an archer but I struggled to find my stride there.
As you roam around the dungeon killing the endless supply of enemies, you collect their coin and can upgrade your spells and weapons, along with buying additional lives and hearts. You have hearts per life, run out of lives and you have to start all over again. Thankfully there is some sort of gated progression here, each portal has three levels to it. As long as you beat the end boss in each portal, you'll only have to repeat one level, and not the whole game again.
I cannot wait to try out the local co-op here and can support up to four players! The controls are so responsive to your movements, it is almost perfect.  This is an absolute gem of a bargain at its current price as there is tons of gameplay and replay ability here.

This is a game that will likely catch you by surprise in more than one way in both of its main genres.  It creates as unique sandbox experience  with interesting lore and random or leaded events that make every playtrhough vastly different depending of which characters you recruit and what decisions you take. Very appealing to all RPG fans.  Its also presents a simple yet solid turn base strategy game, where every battle its filled with real danger for your party members, forcing the player to make very careful movements, positioning and pre-battle preparations.
The core essence of the game is your mercenary company and its struggles, hence the name. It will effort to level up and prepare your men to face the ever increasing difficulty of the game, this creates a bond between the player and its soldiers. You will want to keep the morale high and by this you will need to keep them well feed and with medical supplies, you will want them to have not only the best equipment but to also the tools to repair them after intense battles, you will need to measure which contracts your company can realistically undertake without suffering heavy losses. All this effort and rewards is where the game succedes in making something somewhat plain looking into something special
The game is very recommended to both strategy and rpg aficionados. I assure you this is a very unique experience.
If you like puzzles and hidden object games, you will probably like this game. It is not overly long, but it was definitely neat.

It's just not that good...
Pro:
_Looks good: The game looks simple, but vibrant. The character and attack animation all looks nice too. Wide variety of enemies sprites as well.
_Plays well: Controls exactly as you'd expect it. Feels precise.
_Co-op: The game has co-op, and co-op play should make almost any game better.
Cons:
_Bare-boned: This whole game feels like one level. The enemies, while varied in looks, mostly behave the same way. The levels are all the same too, with no set-pieces or events or anything interesting. The 4 chracters are basically only 2 characters: The melee type, and the ranged type. Chracters upgrade in a linear fashion twice, but there's no variety in term of how they're upgraded. There's no items that change the way you play. Shops only sell the same thing over and over. The list goes on.
_Short, really really short: I mean, it's really short. Might be a blessing, I suppose, if you're not having a good time. But it's hard to excuse a game that is THIS short, even on a $6 price tag.
_Co-op is only local: Minor point, really, but worth mentioning.
_WAY too easy, too.
Is it worth $6? I'm afraid not, and that's coming from the guy that gives every game the benefit of the doubt. It's simply too short, too shallow, too dumb, too easy, too simple. There's nothing here for you, the gamer. Game dev, if you're reading this, this is not a game, it's a level. It's a good start, but not enough is here.

If forced to point out flaws, I'd say that the developers could do with a thorough spell-check of the content; there are several phrases and words used that aren't quite right (in some puzzles the odd choice of words adds further depth). Apart from that, the program seems bug-free

My only change would be to make the map a better map--rooms are gathered into chunks so map-teleportation is handy but not as handy as it could be.

-One quest...yes. One quest in the entire game. The questboard is not available.
-No controller support (at least on my end. Used to work but doesn't now for some reason.)
-Weird keyboard and mouse controls. CTRL serves as the loot button instead of something more reasonable like F or E.
-Sound design is a bit quiet. You just hear the monotone background music and your characters attacks. It makes the game feel more empty than it should given there's always a group of enemies in an area.

I was trying to look for another local co-op rogue-like to play. During the Halloween Steam Sales I saw another game on my wishlist which was in a bundle with this one. Thinking it looked interesting and my small criteria was found in this game, I bought it.
Singleplayer actually works for me, so far. I've read alot of crashing problems but I've had none of those yet. It can get a little messy and confusing at some parts, in terms of not exactly being able to see what hurt you. I believe there was a halloween event as well, which just had this relic standing next to every portal to get to the next level. Sounds interesting, gets rather frustrating if you were just trying to pick up an item and then get teleported to a place that you can't possibly beat without having any of the upgrades. It would be amazing if there's a warning that you're about to go to "x" place before doing that. Would also help with all the other teleporters to other places. No, I didn't want to go anywhere, I just wanted to pick up that item/potion. That the game doesn't pause when you're trying to choose what skill you're using and stat you want to level up can get really frustrating, especially on controller in my oppinion. It's just painful to want to read through what every level up does exactly when suddendly a random opponent pops up in your face and hurts you. I can see how you wanted to add an extra challenge, yet like this you just constantly have to keep your eyes peeled and hope you found a good moment to level yourself up without getting hurt. At least have a save haven, like the shop for instance. Also it feels like the upgrades are necessary to just get past those points and I don't think it adds alot of fun.
It gets even worse on multiplayer though. I'm sure there's others but this is my first rogue-like where we had a split-screen. I guess there's the upside of just being able to do your own thing without having the worry of being stuck just because the camera doesn't go further, although I'm sure there's other ways of handling this. Not what I'm playing co-op for. Each screen is so small that we can't really see what's attacking us from afar. Suddendly getting rained down by a barrage of ranged units without a warning isn't exactly making the game harder, rather even more frustrating. It would be a great to have an option to choose one. Now for the worst part; When trying to read what skills do, what dmg boost they get from leveling up and even what items do exactly, text gets cut off because of the split screen. Not sure why this is still a thing while the game has been out for a while now.
It feels rather weird navigating through the forge, I can't even see the description of something I just created. It's another material to use for something else, I can still see the description of it on the recepie but why can't I hover over it? Having a mouse for non-gamepad users would be lovely.
Although I do still see alot of potential in this game, hence why I haven't refunded it. I am still a big fan of the art style and the music I heard in the different areas were really fitting. Leveling up happens at a fair pace and the items can add alot of fun. There's really interesting mechanics this game has touched on, which makes me keep the game and really hope the devs are going to work on these things.
I recommend buying it on sale, unless more of these frustrations get patched out or have options to get around them.

Dungeon Souls is fantastic.  It feels a lot like Binding of Isaac, but with a greater emphasis on strategy and reaction instead of timing and positioning (though those are still important).  The item diversity feels right - on par with Crypt of the Necrodancer.  Add to that a slew of different classes to choose from, and you've got yourself a great little adventure.
Unfortunately, it does a couple of things wrong, at least in my eyes.  Firstly is the character diversity.  Yes, I just complimented this, but unfortunately many of the characters tend to feel similar in nature and don't really offer a significant difference in terms of play style if you look past the surface.  This also partially has to do with the lack of a feeling of impact from enemies, especially in normal mode...
... Which is my second problem.  There are lots of enemies with lots of behavior patterns, but for the most part, it was rare that I felt like my interactions with an enemy in the game felt tangible.  This is due in part to the tendency to flood areas with action and lots of bodies, rather than opting for fewer but more intense encounters.  Even during boss fights, bosses are more or less just moving cannons that transform the game into a bullet hell temporarily.
With both of those points said, I still love the game.  These are problems that a lot of roguelikes suffer from, and DS otherwise is fun and well-executed.

Once the game is bug free, I'd definitely recommend it on a ~35% discount or more.

The different difficulties aren't exactly a difficulty increase/decrease, the increase in exp on impossible makes it really easy to become unstoppable on some characters, while others can have trouble on the early levels (until you craft items to start with), but still have the potential that other characters have. Things like boulders are terrifying on easy, but barely scratch you on impossible.
The only weapons worth crafting are the poltergiest weapons, that let ranged characters attacks penetrate multiple enemies, and melee characters don't have any weapons worth crafting. Crafting items to start with from a holiday event
All of the levels function exactly the same besides traps, enemies, and this one unique level where you fight the skeleton king boss 5 times, and a few of those levels could use a bit more enemy variation, for example the grove level that you get to from the strange tree, it only has 2 enemies and no traps besides boulders.
Some items that you find in the dungeon will actually make you deal less DPS on some characters (expecially the rogue), and in turn make it take longer to clear levels and kill bosses, however there is just enough item variation (or rarity), as I only had seen every item after ~16 hours (I think).
If I remember correctly, after the tutorial I was kinda left stumbling through the things that it didn't tell you about, but I actually enjoyed that quite a bit.
Overall, I think it's definitely worth your time if you've already played and enjoyed a lot of the indie games that share genres with this one.

I bought this game a long time ago for a decent amount of money, but since it's a long game, I postponed playing it... Until recently.
Many of the "recommended" reviews here are from people who spent a very, very short time playing Avadon. Had I written such a review when I was only a couple of hours into the game, it would have been positive, too. It was very fun at the start... but then it became profoundly NOT fun.
You see, early on, you have a couple of quests and a couple of locations. You have various characters, you find items, battles are nice, you get better loot, your characters work in synergy... And then the game suddenly becomes a chore. Quests pile up. The quest texts never get updated. There are no indicators anywhere about the people you need to visit or return to. No indicator of what you need to do. I spent a lot of time going around and talking to people, only to find out that a quest isn't over. The loot doesn't scale up. Your damage doesn't scale up. And the game difficulty (I played on "normal") suddenly switches to "most frustrating game ever". You die. You die a lot. You are too weak. You need luck with the RNG, and you need potions and scrolls in greater amounts that you can obtain. Your abilities are on a large cooldown. Again, not enough potions to alleviate that. To add insult to injury, you spend vitality on abilities and vitality *does not recharge by itself*. You need to basically go back to the Avadon fortress on a semi-regular basis. There's no real quick-travel system, so every time you want to do that, you're looking at about five wasted minutes.
About 15 hours in, I seriously contemplated quitting right there and then; but I said to myself "you spent more on this than on many other games, so you NEED to finish it". I had a quest to follow a warrior into the woods and clear out some spiders. "Some" turned out to be about four nests of four to five spiders each. They were teleporting spiders which cast corrupting spells and thus did a lot of damage-over-time. Took me an hour to finally win that sidequest. Okay, I said, this is one of the harder battles; let's continue. Then I found what was an almost unbeatable Shade. Somehow managed to get that done as well. Then I found an evil Drake that spawned minions *and* mind-controlled several tough soldiers (EDIT: forgot to mention that it was HEALING those soldiers, so every time you came close to killing one, it would be healed to max HP; repeat 4-5 times, while your characters die and you've spent all of your potions). That... that was unbeatable, and it was the turning point at which I resorted to cheats: bumped my characters to level 30, then constantly used healing, shields and ability cooldown reset.
I gave up on the sidequests. I have no idea where I found most of the people and what I needed to do next (again - the quest system is extremely rudimentary and doesn't tell you anything). Even with constant cheating, it took me a total of 40 hours to finish the main story line.
Disregard the "recommended" reviews, honestly, and check the achievements:
Only 1/3 of the total number of players met a certain NPC called Redbeard, and that happens *very* early into the game.
Only 1/50 (a measly 2%) of the players finished Avadon. Two percent. Wow.
You see all those <40hr reviews? Yeah, they recommended a game they never finished. If it's so fun and great and awesome, why did they stop playing? Because of the issues I mentioned here. Let's not even get into "OMG BEST GAME EVER!!11" reviews from people with 1-5 hours in.
Skip this. Honestly. Even if you get this in a bundle, it's just not worth playing. Get an RPG that's actually fun.
If you *do* feel masochistic and try to play without cheating, I'll give you a tip: in this game, Dexterity rules. Get it to a minimum of 25.
Highly not recommended.

Graphically, Avadon is very basic and quite primitive. The sounds also bear this same basic style, with the only music you will hear being from the main menu. All in-game sounds are done adequately though. You will hear your enemies roar and groan, coins, equipment, magic, and all other sounds you may come to expect from a fantasy setting. You should expect to do an immense amount of reading throughout the game. Because of this, the overall gameplay experience seems notably slow paced. While the story and gameplay are rudimentary, Avadon does flow, and there is fun to be had with the turn based combat, item looting, and enhancing the members of your party. Mouse clicking gets severely unresponsive as you play, causing the user to click each action three times or more. This is a major problem. To correct this, all one could do is play the game fresh from a system reboot. Within ten to fifteen minutes after the reboot, the mouse clicking and performance problems will return and stay. Very slowly, the game becomes more interesting and more challenging. The way quests are completed is somewhat awkward. You must go back to the exact place where the quest originated from, and go through the NPC dialog, exclaiming that whatever deed has been done. This would be okay if the map marked where these places are located, or where such NPCs are, but map markings are far from complete. Some quests are so ambiguous, that I found no other way to complete them other than looking at maps made available online. Several of the quests were created in such a way that they nitpick the player into minute details that are very difficult to discern. Avadon seems to drag itself most of the way, mostly because of its slow pace and repetitive game play, but also because of its drab visuals and minimal sounds. Some enemies can be challenging, and interesting to fight against. The variety in creatures is not expansive nor creative, but Avadon manages to keep the encounters enjoyable. The boss battles are difficult, exciting, and fun. The way abilities, spells, and vitality work together is both fair and balanced, providing for an appealing strategy between the usage of weapons and the rest of each character's repertoire. Ultimately, you will become acquainted with your character's powers, and you will eventually appreciate the game's subtle entertainment. The storyline is not very imaginative, nor is it very absorbing. It is conventional in every way imaginable. Also, once you defeat enemies located in a certain area, they will not respawn. Some of the keyboard shortcuts only allow you to activate their respective windows. Pressing the same keyboard shortcut does not deactivate the window. This is minor, but it is still a problem nonetheless. The quests are varied, but feel repetitive in execution. This is mostly because the environs and enemies look very similar from one to the next. Some of your adversaries are so arrogant that you will hate them and enjoy being the reason for their ultimate demise. The most rewarding part of Avadon involves leveling up your characters, equipping the discovered loot, and enhancing their specific abilities. The game often causes serious temporary problems with Windows if you Alt-Tab out of it. Performance issues are borderline ridiculous for a game with such a minimalist design and coarse implementation. In addition, the developer programmed the game to change the speakers' settings in Windows and not return them to the setup it was originally saved to. This is totally unacceptable. The performance problems in conjunction with the other developmental issues is proof of clearly awful programming, or at the very least inadequate porting from the original Mac version. There is basically no creativity whatsoever in Avadon. Every aspect of the game has been done before, for PC and consoles, even in the 80s. After a long while of repetitive, bland, and lackluster gameplay, you will hope for the game to end as soon as possible, but it doesn't. Avadon is clearly 50 hours too long. Much could have been condensed to save players from the tedium. After withstanding the exaggerated amount of hours, the final battle is incredibly frustrating, boring, and poorly implemented. In the end, I decided to quit trying and take a different dialogue path to complete the game. It is that bad. If you would like to read about how poorly designed the final battle is and how much players have complained, peruse the official forums. You won't have anything spoiled, as the ending could have been foreseen from the first half hour of play. This is all quite unfortunate. The finale left me with a feelings of time wasted and disappointment. I understand that the game was designed by one person, but with independent developers often excelling the multi-million Dollar studios, there is no excuse for poor execution anymore.

After having played the game for numerous hours I can testify, in all sincerity, that this is one of the finest rpgs ever crafted. Obsidian has taken what rpg lovers love, old rpgs, new rpgs, elements of surprise, crafting, scouting, searching, hunting, phenomenally written stories, well crafted and solid mates and a healthy dose of modern era graphics capabilities and put it all together in an amazing rpg called PoE.
Graphics are Unity pushed to the limits of what an isometric rpg can do. Fantastic spell effects, wonderful warrior abilities, The finest of gear to be had and worn, all fully displayed in wonderful 3D and customizable. Lazy fog wanders up a marshy area while springtime butterflies lazily meandor about, oblivious to your wanderings. The sun shines in the blue sky or you could be caught at night wandering a lonely road and the fog of war is tight around you.
Sound is equally impressive. Wandering (or sneaking) into a battle brings symphonic crashes and booming drums while exploration gives way to small flutes and nature's sounds of a bubbling brook. Voice acting is spot on. Your recruitable players that you control all have an interesting backstory, something they want to talk to you about sooner or later and it's all, pretty much, believable. Spell effects pop and sizzle and the warrior's mace hitting a shield is heard thudding away. Your controllable party grunts and echoes your orders all while leading the charge to the enemy you want to kill the quickest.
Running this on a dual R9 290 Xfire system with 16 GBs of RAM yields a constant 60fps with no micro-stuttering or visual shenanigans that could pop up without the use of Vsync. Everything cranked to High or Ultra yields a breathtaking world that has been handcrafted with a crazy amount of detail and an obvious love of the craft.
PoE plays like a spiritual predecessor of Baldur's Gate or IceWind Dale series. The similarities pretty much end there though. PoE takes its own path toward being an extremely well written and lovingly hand-crafted RPG that begs, yearns, for you to go and explore. Seek out new quests, do some side quests to discover what your party members need or want. Always, always be prepared though. On Normal difficulty PoE can test your mettle if you're not ready. Anything can happen and usually does in battle. Enemy spawns will pick and flank you, surround you and pummel you. Beat you to death with your own shoe and then walk away with a "Game Over" screen staring at you. On Harder difficulties, PoE will test everything you've ever known or learned over the years with games like Baldur's Gate or IceWind Dale and surprise you with the sheer amount of terror you will want to hide from. Harder difficulty is NOT for the faint of heart.
With the addition of a new main quest, The White March, parts 1 and 2, Obsidian has hand-crafted an amazing conclusion to the series and has, somehow, even made the original game that much better in releasing the DLCs. With each DLC containing about 10-15 hours of questing, fighting and talking, The White March is one of the best DLCs I've ever seen for a videogame. Think Neverwinter Nights 2's DLC, Mask of the Betrayer and you're on the same idea level. With multiple new party members and classes to get, new quest lines, new abilities, new added levels, new spells, new warrior abilities, etc, etc, right NOW is the time to play PoE and to pick up the extra content. It's on sale this week and you'd be playing one of the best rpgs released this past generation
In conclusion, with the Witcher 3's release and DLC program JUST getting started (part 2 coming out soon), Divinity: OS redux and Divinity: OS 2 being kickstarted and produced and Tides of Numenera right around the corner for release those that love rpgs are in for one hell of a year of gaming goodness. Enjoy!

If you have an itch for a Cold War themed game, this might scratch the surface. And by that I mean it's not a complex, grand-scale type of game, but a rather simple, yet fun and engaging little battle of world dominance which can be played in a single session. In fact it doesn't even have a save feature, so if you want to go all the way make sure you have an hour or two to spare. It plays sort of like a board game, you start with an equal score in January 1950 as either side (US or USSR) and you have to manage and juggle your resources and instruments (like spies) to influence and obtain new countries which add to your score. The game ends in 2000 when the side with the higher score wins.
It's not going to win any awards, but I find it enjoyable with some ambient music in the background (you can turn off the in-game soundtrack). Also, you can fortunately take actions while the game is paused, as sometimes things can get a little hectic and the game doesn't quite make it easy to follow all the events. You do get a news-feed and a country flag popping-up on the top-right of the screen when the AI does things in certain regions, but I found that this can be delayed and not very clear, although after a couple of sessions you'll probably get the hang of it. An event timeline would've been more handy here, but all in all for an indie title like this, it does the job well enough.
I can see why this won't appeal to anyone, it's a niche game, but if you have an affinity for these types of games you could give it a try. It's fair priced and offers enough replayability to make it worth it. Bonus points for the Steam Achievements, nice touch there! :)

I'm a Cold War junkie so I gave it a try but to be honest, this game is pretty boring, there really isn't much here. It consists basically of juggling three different buttons over a range of countries that you're currently trying to capture to get your influence up, recuit more military, and reduce their stability. You can pretty much see from the screenshots all that you have to do is summed up by those 'add' buttons in the lower hud. There are no historical events, no diplomacy, no nuclear weapons at all, and the space race consists entirely of paying to advance along a set of images that give you extra global influence. Oh, and there's no save and load function either so you have to finish your game in one go - it lasts a bit over an hour. Another thing that's missing is any progression of military technology, which they aim to add in a future (paid I assume) expansion, but as for what they're selling now it's pretty stripped down.
It's kind of like a board game, but not a very good one. If you want to play a game like this, you'd be much better off with Twilight Struggle, plus you can play it with a friend. I seriously doubt I'll ever play this game again.

The fact that having to start the mission over doesn't mean I could breeze over it, I still had to play out the clue finding. It's little things like that which make a great game, and it's only one example, there are many more like it in this game.

In short: Bastion rekindled my love of games. Don't get me wrong: I've always loved games. But, Bastion was so well crafted, it played like an homage that combined the best aspects of platformer-type games, story-based games, and experimental games.
The platformer aspect is solid:while it's not quite a run & jump, the level itself is still a mobile obstacle that must be considered during play. The story of the game is touching and interesting, and keeps a player that cares about said story on their toes, and possibly reaching for a box of tissues. It's hard to pull off a sympathetic villain and morally ambiguous hero in any story, but I find it's even harder to do in games, where the player (as the protagonist) is putting in tons of time and energy to work against the "villain." The experiemental bit was the Narrator. Cunningham's narration may be a fixture now, but when the game was released there were a TON of people who thought that it would never work. For most, though, those fears disappeared when his rich voice started, and you always wanted to hear more of what he had to say.
Supergiant Games have released just two games so far, but each of them have been gems. Bastion set them on the stage in a big way, and as their fans look forward to Pyre and beyond, it's good to recognize the game that brought the studio to us in the first place.

In a world of AAA games falling flat on their faces, Indie devs creating gems like Hand of Fate 2 (Henceforth HoF2) keeps me hopeful for the video game industry.
In their second iteration of HoF, Defiant Development manage to improve in every single way an incredible game.
If you played HoF before this review will be short: Buy it, hands down, no question.
If you didn't, as much as I'd love to delve into every single mechanic it would be a several hours endeavor which I don't feel like delving into.
I'll try to go superfically into it.
At it's core, HoF2, like its predessesors, revolves around D&D style gameplay, where you sit face to face with a card dealer   who generates card patterns on the board. You move your character on each of the face down card to reveal a litteral plathora of encounters. Encounters can vary from fighting a given faction (currupted[zombies], steel[imperial soldiers], undead, theifs, northerners etc.), to small scale scenarios to reap gold, health, equipment etc.
Fighting envolves an arkham style fighting system which also includes weapon abilities and consumable use.
Of course, encounters have fail states and there is a metric f*ck load of dice rolls, pendulum and card based minigames to determine wheather you get a huge success, success, failure or huge failure. The RNG may be the biggest turn off for most since it can f*ck you up, but the devs have improved your odds by adding in Companions
Companions can help you both out of fights and in fights. They can reduce RNG by giving you extra tries in minigames. In fights they can use special abilities and just default attack to take some aggro off you.
The game consists of a myriad of scenarios and in all the time I've played I've only just arrived near the end. They are, for all intentents and purpose, standalone ministories which require you to fufill sometimes one sometimes two objectives. Completing objectives gives you access to more cards, and more cards is definately what you want.
Because perhaps the most fun aspect of the game is that for any given scenario you get to choose encounters (from 6-15 so far I've encountered), your 1 companion, your equipments (or rather the equipment you can potentially gain throughout encounters in the scenario) and supplies (another new addition which gives your character a starting bonus which can be weapons, increased max health, +10 gold, +5 food etc.) As you play you'll have to learn which encounters, companion, equipments and supplies you need to beat any given scenarios.
Scenarios are in general easy to complete, although it is sometimes hard completing both objectives to gain all the cards, so you'll sometimes have to go back to replay throgh the scenarios to get all the cards.
As of writing this I believe I've uncovered all the scenarios, I believe there are 15ish scenarios give or take, all lasting at least an hour (certainly if you read all the text, without reading could take 30-45mins) you really get your money's worth.
As it stands, HoF2 should be a no brainer add to your library.
There are a few issues however.
Perhaps my biggest is that they decided to delay the release of endless mode. I understand why that is because idk how endless mode would work with all the new mechanics and the myriads of unique cards specific to scenarios. I'm the type of gamer who prefers having all content upon release, so I was kind of dissapointed when seeing that it wasn't offered off the bat. For this reason alone I'd recommend perhaps you wait for your unavoidable purchase of this game.
I did have a crash in the 30 odd hours of gameplay but it hasn't ever repeated, and the devs are super supportive and will offer tech support reliably.
There are audio clips, but I'm wondering how much of this is caused by the game itself, and how much of it is my s*it gaming laptop.
Perhaps the real infuriating thing is that, when you head into a fight, the loading times can be a tad long and (unlike the other game) the cutscene to head into a fight is unskippable. So it can take 2-3 mins before you get in combat. Thankfully I'm willing to be patient for this gem of a game, but it can obviously p*ss people off.
I don't really know how to conclude this...HoF2 is by far one of the greatest games I've ever played and this comes from a really green dev team (THIS IS ONLY THEIR 2ND GAME! AND IT'S SO DAMNED GREAT!). I call them Green but these guys know 100% what they are doing. They had a vision for a game and carried it out masterfully. HoF a good game, HoF2 is on a whole other level.

This game here was one of my first isometric, classic style RPGs. I guess you can say it opened the floodgates for a whole other realm of RPG gaming (hours have been lost, with even more still to vanish; time well spent!) at the time I was still being a great fan of RPGs all around (got heaps of them, even more now!!!), I picked up Avadon with caution, knowing that for it's price it wouldn't be a graphic breaking game.
I'd never even played a Spiderweb Software game either, for that matter, and it was an interesting experience.
The first thing I was surprised about was the epic soundtrack at the start. Unfortunately, this epic piece is the only real piece of sound in the game, plus some old audio files of swords swinging and animals growling, etc.
The first mission sets off the story well, and so far, having not completed it yet, it is a good story.
The graphics, as stated earlier, are nothing to go around shouting about. But they get the job done, and the writing is excellent, and though perhaps slightly less words are needed to state what exactly is going on, it feels mostly spot on. Even the side missions are fleshed out. They aren't (from my experience) about going around *kill X giant dingbats* and return to quest giver. The people have real problems.
Unfortunately, with said problems, come in game problems. The journal system is very poor, and records barely anything except the beginning and end of a quest. This becomes infuriating as many people ask you for help, and you jot down things in your journal, and eventually you become lost as what to do next, when you are part-way through one quest and stop to do another close by.
The combat is fine, with just the right amount of weaker foes spread between harder fights and opponents. It's a turn based, grid battle, but the grids need to be larger, as I clicked on the wrong thing, meaning a character fell in battle.
All in all, this game is recommended. If you are undecided, try out the demo. If you are a fan of RPGs, I am telling you now, this is a great game.

I was skeptical at first, but this is a really neat throwback.  The isometric graphic style reminds me of Ultima Online, but they're way crisper and look really clean.  The game runs smooth.
While the combat is turn-based, you're only stuck in those turns while in combat.  This means that you can wander around exploring and looting in real time but once you close to an enemy's proximity you switch to combat mode.  Even in combat it doesn't get overly complicated, which can be a tad disappointing, but it also allows the combat to be much faster paced than what you'd find in other turn-based combat games.
The storyline is engaging and interesting, and there have been many instances of dialogue that break the mold on RPGs only hours into the game.  No spoilers, but one example I could offer was talking to the warden of a prison and hearing him explain that treating the prisoners humanely and never torturing them was his policy.  There isn't a lot of cookie-cutter copy/paste generic archetype character development in this game, which is extremely refreshing.  I don't know how many RPGs I've started as a kid in a village that leaves to go fishing only to come back and find said village burned down, parents dead, princess / girl next door kidnapped, crystal stolen, etc.  This game makes an attempt to stray away from all of that when it can.  Even the flavor text seen when inspecting NPCs has had a good deal of thought put into it.  Another thing that's truly great is upon entering a new area you'll randomly get a written description akin to the old text-based games that helps flesh things out.
I've read that this game is long, and I'm talking Ultima 7 long, which is daunting, even off-putting, but in some ways it's refreshing.  These guys seem to have put their time in and this game feels like it would be right at home on the shelf next to any title in the Ultima series.  Even your NPC buddies that group up with you will randomly stop you to talk about things on their mind, so they don't feel like lifeless dolls filling a job requirement.
If I had one gripe, (I'm only allowing myself one because I'm still really early into the game) it would be that the characters don't change outfits when equipping new gear.  From a resource standpoint it makes sense... in a way.  You can have thousands of items and only a few outfit "classes" of graphics per each character, which makes sense for games like this made in 3D, but to have absolutely no changes at all in an isometric 2D game is a little disheartening.  Because of this you tend to overlook the icons of the new gear and find yourself only reading the stats, something I hate in an RPG.  I don't like items that boil down to numbers, plain and simple.
Overall it's a great buy and a rare find in this day and age where the majority of RPGs concentrate on action and graphics while letting the story slide.  Seeing this game's Steam page initially made me cringe and recoil from the connotation of similarities to all the generic crappy RPG Maker games out there, so I wasn't expecting much, but honestly the more I play this game the more I'm blown away by it.  These devs show that going retro doesn't mean the story goes retro with it.  This isn't some 14 year old kid's weekend project made as a free Android app.
Cheers.

Zombie Panic : Source is the sequel to the popular Zombie Panic game. As stated, it's a mod, so you'll need to download a Source game such as Half Life 2 or Team Fortress 2. Overally, the game is very interesting and in some degree, a 'realistic' representation of a zombie apocalypse. It puts you in the role of a Survivor or a Zombie, which you can choose at the start of the match, don't worry too much if you want to play as a zombie though, almost everyone will go survivor, meaning that someone will randomly be selected as the infected. If you volunteer to be Infected, you'll be the special zombie carrier, that has slightly more health compared to the default infected. He also has the ability to infect other survivors, who, if they don't find medicine, will become infected themselves. While becoming infected, the survivor will be unable to speak, and will hear heartbeats. Even if the survivor cures himself, he'll be greeted with a flash of colors that will last for a while, to be precise, he's blinded. If he's not protected by his teammates, he'll probably get killed. There are many maps, and most of them feature doing a certain objective or standing ground untill all the infected respawn counters are depleted. The goal of the infected is to kill survivors and turn them, nothing interesting.
Overally, the 'Game' is very good and get's a 9/10 from me. Just keep in mind that the community is dying right now due to the release of the sequel to this 'Game' called Contagion. But it's still worth playing this Mod though.

Impressions after 11 hours of gameplay. Will keep updating as I play more.
Pillars is Obsidian's best game to date, and a genuine masterpiece.
Visually stunning: incredibly detailed backgrounds, with plenty of environmental particle effects that add a lot of life to the scenery. The 3D character models fit perfectly into the scenes, and have smooth, weighty animations (far improved from the backer beta, from what I remember).
The audio is equally impressive. Everything sounds 'right', from footsteps to arrows hitting their mark. Music seems to be fairly standard fantasy stuff, with lots of flutes and such (Not a music expert, sorry.) Being 'fairly standard' is by no means bad. All the pieces I've heard have been very nice, and fit the scene and situation perfectly. The music is also not on a continuous loop: there are moments where all you'll hear are the ambient noises. Makes me appreciate the music even more, and has (thus far) prevented it from being overly repetitive.
The game's interface is great. It's modern and easy to use, but not minimalist. Wood and paper textures ties it to the world, but it avoids being old school clunky brilliantly. Fonts are clear, and the size can be adjusted in the settings. There's also a colourblind setting, for those who  need that.
Often in games like this, the story starts off very, very slow. Not the case in Pillars. In the 11 hours I played, the world has me absolutely hooked. The main storyline seems very interesting and highly personal. Side quests are mostly tied to the main story, and all offer a variety of choices along the way. I especially enjoyed a quest where the party is tasked with killing a lord. I figured out three distinct ways of disposing him:
1. Enter through the sewers and sneak into his throne room.
2. Scale the castle ramparts, enter through the top floor, disguise the party as priests and just walk to the throne room.
3. Storm the gates and murder everyone.
This specific quest also had an added layer of complexity, but I won't go into detail here; too many spoilers as it is.
As you would expect from Obsidian, there's a lot of well-written dialogue and every situation and character I've encountered has been described in great detail (made even better by the fact that the descriptions match the visuals, unlike in, say, Shadowrun Returns or Wasteland 2) Dialogue options are plentiful, with frequent skill / stat checks that do a great job of tying the RPG system into the conversations. Most characters also have at least one line of voiced dialogue, to give the player a better feel of the person. A nice touch.
The combat is solid, and reasonably challenging even on Normal difficulty. 11 hours in, my party consists of two fighters, two spellcasters and an archer. Even at low levels (2-4) my party composition offers great tactical depth. The casters both have ~12 extremely varied spells available, and the rest have 2 or 3 abilities each. Battles are quick and very dangerous; I find myself pausing after most actions.
Armour seems to play a huge role: my fighters wearing brigandine take significantly less damage than my archer, clad in padded cloth. The differences between weapon types are fairly noticeable as well (especially short vs. long weapons). As a whole, the combat is very fun and the interface for it is highly intuitive.
Character progression feels a tad slow, but every level up offers plenty of skill points to distribute, one or two abilities to pick and sometimes a perk as well. Leveling up feels meaningful, and it's immediately noticeable in the characters' performance.
The large variety of classes, races, backstories and cultures should offer plenty of replayability, when combined with the absolutely vast amount of different directions every conversation can go.

A game about the way of life.
The game is about being a fly and flying upwards.
In the beginning, you start out on the ground, with the dirt, grass, leaves surrounding you. You are right in front of the camera, with the details on your body very clear. You inquisitively explore your surronding, excited about its possibilities. Soon, you discover that up is the only way.
As you rise, what surronds you becomes less interesting, and you become fixated in your only goal -- rise up. The camera gradually zooms out.
On your way, winds make you tumble and blow you off course; falling leaves give you heavy blows and drag you down; worse even, spider webs encapture you, leaving you the choice between desparately struggle for freedom or fall prey of spiders.
You realize that this isn't a peaceful journey.
You become smaller and smaller in the screen, and now you are nothing but a dot. Eventually you rise high into the skies; the galaxies and the star clouds become your backdrop. You have finally, one again, began to appreciate the beauty around you.
The environment becomes peaceful and pure.
Something above emits a soft but bright light, casting a long shadow behind you, marking the journey you have embarked on.
At some point, you lose control. You don't fly up anymore, but it seems like something is pulling you up instead.
You rise up, and up, and up, and --
Zap ----
A red hot light bulb takes your life.
-----------------------------------

This is a fantastic turn-based party-oriented single player, story focused, old-school western-style RPG similar to the types of games that came out in the era just before Baldur's Gate (or very similar to BG if you play BG is auto-pause mode). The graphics are a little rough around the edges, but they have a unique charm. The story and choices that you make which have a lasting impact on the story branches available to you is really good. Characterization is not quite as good as, say, Planescape, or DAO, but still pretty good, you do get a feel for your companions and their unique personalities. I am probably only about 10 or 12 hours into this game but I've played it on a few different platforms at the same time, and I can verify that what class you choose and the companions you choose to take along with you can dramatically change the game play and even the story to some extent (choices available to you). I like the skill tree, it makes it so that even if you decide to be a shaman and also take the NPC shaman with you, you won't be carbon copies, you can be two distinctly different types of characters with their own role in the party dynamics. While I have not beat this, I've gotten far enough to easily recommend this to anyone. Besides, there is a free demo if you want to spend an hour or so to see if it is your bag.

Well, it is VERY early access but also very fun. As of my writing this review, I have approximately 6 hours clocked in playing this title. The premise is simple: Survive. The crafting is fun, but it gets kind of ridiculous to build sometimes. For example: Mass collecting sticks/rocks and palm tree leaves will really kill your framerate if you put them all in one pile. There should be some storage system implemented to help this problem. I'm dissapointed you can not craft a book bag to carry more items, it sucks to only be able to carry so little at times. The rock resource is very scarce and you'll have to travel between islands a lot to collect rocks if you choose to build a base on an island. You'll also need to cut down a LOT of trees. You can survive well only on coconuts so far, (My current gameplay I have 9 days survived) and I've only eaten coconuts the whole time.
Problems I've noticed with GAMEPLAY (Not bugs/glitches. THose will come later.)
1. All islands are WAY too small. You can walk across any island you come across in less than a minute. I think islands should be GREATLY expaned on. Please make them atleast 10x their current size. Sure, keep some islands these tiny little islands, but come on... THe current ones are way too small.
2. Sharks should be less common. It seems like there are sharks everywhere I go- not like they are a problem. (I have six hours in the game, 4 of which have probably been in the water, or on the water and I have yet to die by a shark. Maybe they are misunderstood creatures?) But I believe that sharks should be a lot less common in general, and instead they should be found in clusters in certain places.
3. Needs more animal wildlife. This one is probably obvious, and more wildlife is a guaruntee. Currently the only real animals are 2 sharks: The Great White, and The Tiger Shark. And crabs. There are OTHER animals, like the whale and starfish and various little fish around, but the world feels pretty dead. I wish I could find beautiful coral reefs filled with life, or maybe a strange encounter with eels, or an octopus... But at this stage in the game it's simply not possible.
4. Needs more animal wildlife on islands. This comes with point 1. Islands should be bigger with more animal wildlife. Currently, islands are small so it makes sense that there are no animals. But I think that should be changed.
5. Shipwreckes should be less common, and natural landmarks more common. Currently this game has about 2-3 ships wrecked on each island I visit. I've been to about 6-7 islands in my current playthrough, so you can assume ive plundered many ships. I have only found one skeleton arm, though. So where did those people go? It doesn't make sense that all the people aren't in the ships, or that there are so many. Surely this area is traveled through often to have so many boats. I think there should be less shipwrecks and more natural landmarks such as caves, coral reefs, natural volcanic vents, volcanos, trenches, canyons and so much more.
6. Needs more immersion! Maybe notes in bottles occasionally, maybe crewmembers bodies found on nearby islands. Maybe pirate ships or buried treasure? Who knows. A lot of potential, and I would hate it to go to waste!
Alright, those are all of the gameplay changes I hope to see as development goes on, I really hope somethings happen.
As for some bugs... There are many. I wont post them here, because that is not something that should really be included in a review.

With that out of the way, Battle Brothers is a turn based strategy game where you lead a mercenary group of up to 20 units (only 12 can fight on the battlefield). Every unit has a set of stats where you can specialise them into a melee fighter or a ranged fighter. You need to manage funds by accepting contracts with good pay, and use the money to buy equipment for your men and ensure your group's success.
Like the old X-COM, the game is brutal and unforgiving and punishes you for your mistakes. But that is the nature of all rogue-like games. You keep trying and dying until you get better.
Like the old X-COM, it pays attention to details. If you visit a coastal village, you will be able to buy fish as food. You can also buy nets as weapons. You are more likely to encounter fishermen to be recruited into your mercenary group.
After winning a battle, the loot you get isn't randomised, but based on what the enemies were using. If you had fought brigands, you would be able to use their equipment if they weren't broken. If you had fought orcs, you would get orc weapons.
After playing for over 100 hours, I understand why some people wish there was more. Things like being able to own your own castle or form your own kingdom. However, the game has been in development for 5 years already, and there is danger in adding too much and never finishing it. In my opinion, the game should rightfully stick to the basics of running a mercenary group. Being able to form your own kingdom would deviate from the core of the game, and that is to struggle in a cruel world where only the strong survive.
This game is very complete, and highly recommended for turn-based strategy lovers. However the price ($29.99 as of this review) may be too high, so wait for a sale.

If you are having trouble in the beggining here goes some tips:
1. Try to hire people of the right professions: caravan hands, ex-soldiers, hunters, farm hands, ... Do not hire taylors, bureaucrats, and other peaceful professions. The developers for sure read Vegetius manual.
2. Unzoom the map to find the current objective. It is much easier to find your objective this way.
3. To scroll the map, you have to unmark the follow the unit marker.
4. Hire at least 3 archers/missile brothers. Its is easier to win the battles with them.
5. Start with the objective of become friendly with a civil faction.
Have fun. It is a wonderful game to play while XCOM 3 has not arrived.

Since there's been a lot of negative reviews lately, i decided to express my opinion just in case.
Tl:dr would look like this: "the fact that the game could've been better doesn't mean that it's bad as it is".
Battle Brothers is not a bad game by any definition. It delivers
what it promises: tactical combat in a low-fantasy open world setting. It's not Mount & Blade, it's not a kingdom simulator, and it's not trying to be one. This game only does what it says on the store page, but it's really good at it.
The battles are fun and filled with suspense and tension, especially in the Ironman mode. You feel that every wrong move, every slight miscalculation could lead to grave consequences. Losing experienced mercs is really tough and it makes you actually care about your company. Those times when you've got to sacrifice your "young" guys in order to save a more valuable veteran - undescribable.
Enemies are quite diverse and each type requires different tactics, so there's no such thing as "best weapon" or "best build". There's always challenge, even on a successful lucky run. Sure, at the later stages of the game it's possible to transform your squad into an ultimate machine of destruction, but that requires a lot of skill and dedication, and even then there are situations when it just won't be enough to beat the odds.
There is room for roleplaying too. You could become a bandit, or a marauder, or a treasure hunter, or even go on your own crusade against the orcs, if you'd like. Hand of Fate 2 is a mixed bag, especially if you have played the first game.  For starters, yes, this game is MASSIVELY improved from the original, with different weapons, companions, and chance encounters like dice, wheels, and pendulum challenges which make it more about skill and helps to mitigate RNG.  However, it also has problems with creativity.  If we compare it to the original, the basic four types of enemies were bandits, rat men, skeletons, and lizard folk.  Variations of those and special monsters made that game feel like a true fantasy romp, but here...we get humans...but barbarians.  Humans...but in armor.  Humans...but thieves. And humans...but corpses.  We lack a lot of the interesting or imaginative monsters of yesteryear.
The quests in the game are much more varied and interesting, but they can wear on you, as some of the quests are unforgivably tedious and frustrating, especially if you want to get the true rewards. The story is more focused and if you are interested in worldbuilding and incremental storytelling, it's pretty interesting, as you learn about your history up to when you start the game...then go beyond it.  It's cool, but you lose some of the fun of making your own story about your life from the first game. Also, you have an insane amount of encounters, which is great for endless mode, but can be tedious for deck building, as you will wade through hundreds of cards to build a deck to help you with each challenge. Filters help, but only so much.
Notice how I'm not talking about the combat?  Because it's pretty meh.  It's Arkham counter, break block, attack rinse repeat over and over again.  It has a level of skill to it, but the storytelling is the draw here and the game is at its weakest when it forces you into encounter after encounter after encounter.
Despite my complaints, I had a good time with Hand of Fate 2.  It begins to fizzle out near the end, however I do appreciate the ending for what it is in relation to the story and also for not being a grindy slog, but a final boss battle that you can repeat easily if you wish and which is pretty bloody satisfying.  Gets rid of a real pet peeve of mine.  Do I recommend it?  Eh...yes.  Play the first Hand of Fate before this as you'll get more out of the story and mechanical improvements, but it is an interesting experience and fun...most of the time.

Beautiful color palette of earthy autumn tones to match an equally earthy game.  Slavic mythology centers around the hearth, the home, and the natural world.  This game does that extemely well in presentation, storyline and the creatures used, and is family friendly in theme.
Storyline: Dr. Mary Gilbert, botantist and saviour of endangered moss in Maple Creek (Maple Creek - omage to Enigmatis) has received a letter from her grandmother referred to as Baba (Yaga Baba reference) urgently requesting her help to save a rare and endangered plant in the Slavic Park, an educational outdoor museum centered around Slavic mythological creatures.  Upon arriving Mary is attacked by a creature and her car is shoved off a cliff.  Escaping the car begins the quest adventure of saving her soon to be kidnapped grandmother, meeting the mythology creatures who have taken refuge in the park, healing the rare and magical plant, and ultimately defeating the villian in an apropos way.
Gameplay:  This game is more point and click then hidden object but plays as a combination of both.  There are basically three main areas of the game, the Slavic Park, the abandoned village and the castle with side quests into other areas.  There is a fast travel map but the player can not return to the Slavic Park once they cross the lake to the abandoned village.  So make sure all the extras finds (notes, etc and bestiary cards) are found before crossing the lake.
Hidden Object:  The Hidden Object scenes are mostly fragmented HOs (find the pictured pieces to create a single object), find "X" amount of objects, and near the end of the game are list HO finds.  The list HOs have "ghost" puzzle pieces beneath them that the player clicks on to complete the 'extra' puzzle and the HO scene.
Puzzles: Nothing overly challenging and a variety of basic fun fare.  Sliders, pipe puzzle, picture puzzles, codes, telescope challenge, and a maze.
There are three extra find challenges in this game:
1) 30 bright pink purplish flowers that are very hard to miss.
2) Finding all the notes, posters, pictures, diplomas, signs, etc in the main game. Note: I am unsure exactly which ones are used to gain the achievement Bookworm, so do not be shy click on everything. Some are missable so click on notes, papers, etc first before any 'quest' object.
3) Collecting the bestiary cards scattered throughout the main game.  Note: some are missable such as the one at the end of the maze since if not taken at the time the player can not return to get it later.  These cards can be accessed during gameplay and the player can read about 30 different slavic mythological creatures.  I do believe the cards must be read to gain the achievement associated with them.
Achievements:  Most are gained through gameplay alone and all achievements can be earned in a single playthrough.
Fun game for the expert and beginner alike with three game modes to choose from.  If playing on expert mode the first time through here's a hint:  The list HO finds are found in the third part of the game (the castle and surrounding areas) these can be easy to miss so make sure to click on the background areas and places you have been before to find them.
Well worth full price for an easy romp through slavic mythology.

Almost everything in Hand of Fate 2 has been improved.
The character creation leads into a progessive story thats actually fleshed out this time around. You can have combat companions and the variables involved in combat scenarios have gone up. Chance cards are even more diverse.
Almost everything in Hand of Fate 2 is less fun.
New multi-stage events and intriguing character missions (there's an escort quest!) lead to many more opportunities for RNG to ruin your day.
Chance events don't feel nearly as fair this time around. The new chance minigames aren't explained well and don't read well. Boons resulting from chance are often more complicated, but overall have less of an impact on gameplay, making them feel unbalanced compared to the increased punishment dished out from the same events.
Map objectives are much more expanded, requiring things like certain number of blessings or other stats. However they don't make the game feel better either. Most of the time you'll find yourself knowing you're going to fail them very early on in a run because RNG just isn't in your favor.
Even from a technical standpoint, the game is still a net loss.
A month after release the game still has issues that were patched out of the first game long ago. Combat has weird slow-downs and input issues just like when the first was released.
Companion AI just doesn't work. They'll wonder into a corner and miss every swing they make.
The camera feels improved and has a much better feel, but because it doesn't show as much of the level, issues with the uncontrollable AI mean you will frequently be attacked from offscreen.
Overall, Hand of Fate 2 fixes quite a few things and brings a lot of new interesting mechanics to the table, but I don't want to return and play it again. Almost every run was tedious and included something that felt out of my control. It was painful and unrewarding even after I built my deck.
