After 300 hours of gameplay, I am ready to write a review
The game is, as advertised, an RPG game. Although level cap is 30 after level 30 there's still some stuff to do; You can get so much better gear than your average gear. To review this game it's important to explain how looting system works;
About looting:
While looting items there are a few things to look for -
1: Quality. That determines how good your damage/armor on your equipment you found is.
2: Level requirements. Stats scale with level requirements on items so you could have 2 legendary swords 100 quality and 1 is better because it has higher level requirement.
3: Prefix and suffix. Yellow items have a prefix and suffix while blue items only have a prefix.
with that being said, it can be extremely hard to find some really good items because it's all randomized so it leaves place for a good variety of weapon and armor range and endless possibilities. I think that's a plus because it makes a use to extensive farming. You don't just get to level 30 then it's over and you have nothing to do because it's near impossible to have perfect items so you are bound to have a lot of time to farm.
It's important to mention the game is in early access; Yes it has a few bugs but they are actively working on fixing them. The developpers are active and work hard to fix the bugs before bringing new contents (Which is what should always be done. Resolve issues first then add more stuff).
The game has a lot of potential - if the game gets enough attention and is developed properly it will turn out into an amazing game. As long as the developers keep pouring their heart in it we can expect something great out of it - Great game concept and infinite possibilities.
They are open to suggestions and they wish nothing but the best for their game. At first I was a bit perplex but in the end I noticed there wasn't much to worry about. The game's developement is going well and the developers are listening to their players feedback. When this game gets out of Early Access it'll be an epic game so get used to the game and get experience within the game before other players while you still can!
The community is nice for most part; Most of the people will be nice to you if you're nice to them. Of course it's not everyone but the vast majority of players are rather friendly.
Reality being told; All the rest of the reviews about leveling are accurate. Leveling will be a pain and there's no alternate way to level up than grinding and killing monsters - You can't get boosted - It'll take you hours (Yes, hours) just to get to level 10. The developers stick to the idea that they did this "so you can't power level in 1 hour" when my opinion is there's no reason since it's an unfinished product and if there was like 100 levels (Or at least 60-80 like in most online RPGs) things would be different. Although everything leads to believe no one is happy with the changes and leveling slower (Look forums and reviews, everyone will agree leveling is terribly long.), to this day the developpers still think they did the right thing by nerfing party experience along with adding a barrier that makes people lose experience for being in party. That's right, for each one level you are apart from the highest level in your party, you lose 10% experience, however for each party member close to you when you kill monsters you gain 20% more experience (Previously was a lot more than 20%). If it wasn't enough to add one measure to stop you from leveling, they added two. (Updated) As of lately they said they would look into the experience.
As of lately they have added the adventurer's guild; it's still in progress but it's worth mentioning they also announced they were working on a new end-game area (Which they announced new end-game content on the first weekend the game was released, yet nothing so far). They have hired additional people to their team which should make it easier for the game to progress. They have added one quest (Just one very very basic quest) as of lately. The truth is the game is progressing but really slowly, nothing wrong with that but it is a fact.
Most of the players who have the highest play time on this game don't sign in anymore for the following reasons:
1) After nerfing the rate you gain for honor(experience), no one wants to compete against the person who has 25m honor on the ladder leaderboards or even compete at all.
2) They all have stuff that is more than good-enough for now and are waiting for content that's worth playing.
3) The old school players don't sign in and a lot of people play to play with their friends so the interaction becomes dull / they have to make new friends and adapt.
4) Did I mention after grinding the same map for hundreds of hours/almost 2 months people get tired?
Although the game is not perfect and sometimes things seem to go in a strange way, I still recommend this game because overall it's a fun game and you can drop a lot of hours into it if you like grinding online RPG games. It's nice to play with friends and you can still go solo and have fun; People are rather friendly so it's usually easy to make friends. It is a very honest review, no candy coating and most people in the community will agree with 99% with what I wrote here and most of it is very positive so it's something to look foward to.
tl;dr
- Great game with unique and nice looting system.
- Early access game - Few bugs but getting fixed one by one
- Active and friendly developpers.
- Slow leveling.
- New content will probably get added as time goes.
- Friendly Community

This review might contain spoilers.
This review is not a "this game sucks" review, I actually liked the first game a lot and left an enthusiastic, positive review of the first game. I would give this sequel 6/10 overall, but if I ask myself whether I am happy with the direction the game moved from the first iteration, the answer is a sad NO, so the binary evaluation Steam demands must be regretfully negative.
While the game still retains some of the qualities of the first game, what was good was unfortunatelly diluted by "filler" content that while makes the game "bigger" by volume, does not necessarily makes the game better. If I used the booze analogy, it's like when a producer decides to replace his old, 0.7l solid whiskey blend with new 2 liters bottle of a new blend, where aged, flavorful components are cut back with raw, unaged distillate and neutral grain spirits to cut costs in order to "provide more" for the same price - and while 2l > 0.7l, the quality and thus enjoyment one draws from each glass will be significantly lower, so is it really such a good bargain?
In Hands of Fate, the good, aged, flavorful component was the atmosphere and the narrative - the mysterious figure of the dealer, his ambivalent attitude towards the player (he was a narrator, a mentor and a nemesis in one person in the first game), the tarot-resmbling card set that is an established cultural trope, pondering about fate, free will, luck and consequences of one's choices. Unfortunately, this premium component was severely scaled back in the sequel - the narration does not feel fresh and imaginative anymore, merely as a prop to various minigames that are supposed to be the core of the sequel's innovation. Also, many elements of the plot are poorly introduced/paced, so when we finally arrive to the much telegraphed conclusion, it does not bring shock, catharsis, conclusion nor meaningful answers, just a tired nod.
The main component of the game, where you will spend most of the time (and by that, I mean really a LOT of time) is the combat. Unfortunately, it's the weakest component of the game, and is very bad on its own. First of all, it always plays the same - there are no surprises, you always fight X enemies of Y type and Z enemies of Q type, and they are always the same, that means punching bags with lots of hit points that barely move around. Occassionally you are hesitantly attacked by one enemy, and you are required to respond with pressing the correct button according to a color-coded prompt - and that's really all there is. There is no precise dodging, no ranging, no specific tactics, the game chooses targets for you, if you are too far, you "slide" into position. Movement is imprecise, the controls are laggy, and the rules are full of counter-intuitive mechanics - for example, you interrupt "green" attacks by making a "block", but not by smacking your opponent with a hammer. Some things work, some don't, but there is little logic in the whole system. The "ripostes" look outright weird.
Besides combat, there are "gambits" - while the original had only shuffling card gambits, we now have three more types - the dice, the pendulum and the wheel of cards. While there is some skill component to every one of them - you can reroll dice according to probabilities, you can track the shuffling cards, and both wheel and pendulum must be stopped in the right moment, they can make you fail a critical quest and force you to replay the whole map, which results in tedium. There are soft "silver" victories for each map that allow you to advance in the game even if you fail some objectives, but completionists will want perfect, gold rewards, which is where a single failed gambit can cost you the game.
While I appreciate the attempts to innovate by constructing various minigames from the cards, I think it further dilutes what was good in the first game.
Probably the best level in the game is The Devil - if most maps were like this, I would probably not complain so much. But most maps require you to trudge around large maps where nothing important to the plot is happening.
The introduction of companions was a good attempt, each even has a narrative arc which is the best part of the feature, but outside of that arc, they resemble lifeless dolls, providing a passive gambit bonus (most useful), and participating in combat, where they perform as poorly as the AI.
I had great fun with the first game. I have mixed feelings about this second game that are mostly drowned in exhaustion. If there is a third game that continues in the same way as the second, I won't probably buy it. In my opinion, the game needs to rework its fundamentals - mainly the combat - so that the activity players spend most time participating it is worthwhile on its own.

I wouldn't recommend this game. It seems good at first through the gameplay footage, but when actually playing it at its current state is not quite what you'd expect.
A major turnoff is that currently you can only attack mobs if they are right near you, you cannot attack-move like in a lot of traditional dungeon crawlers, which is what you'd want to be able to do to avoid taking as much damage as possible.
I got stuck in a rock that was regenerating and it took maybe 30 seconds for the game to self-debug to get me out, which it then warped me to the starting town.

What makes this mod good? Well, the players. The game itself is quite basic, but the players make it worth it. There's not many of them, and the people who have stuck with the game are either terrible or amazing people which makes the game far better than it was a year ago.
Of course, it's not completely dead. The servers that have people (there are usually around 2-4 servers with people) have 1-8 players in them. If you want to just hang out with a random stranger, join the one with one player. If you want mayhem, join the one with eight players.
You'd think a massive map with scarce players would make it boring- but it doesn't. Either you have players all close together, or some spread out. When they're spread out, it's fun continuously trying to find them. If they're close together.. Well..
Anyway, that concludes this little thing that I'm currently typing. If you don't have the basegame and you're wondering if you should buy it, do it and make sure to check out this small community while it lasts, otherwise you might miss out.

Hand of Fate 2 is definitely a good game.  It includes some randomness from your deck building within chapters which contain a more structured story and their own cards outside your control, and these chapters have overall objectives and side quests besides "make it to the end and kill the boss." (Though you'll still be doing that too).  They vary from rescuing peasants from the corruption, building a fort, or evacuating villages from an approaching threat.
The deckbuilding is much more straightforward.  A card's effects will be unknown until you encounter it once, even if it is in a store's window, and from there you can see what each card's potential effects are when building your deck.  This is important thanks to the themed chapters, as sometimes you'll need encounters to help you see nearby tiles, more food, equipment, or so on.  Some cards are useless or significantly less useful than others, and you'll often only use them once to see what they do and never touch them again.
The combat is sleeker too, but it feels a bit at odds with itself at times.  Only one enemy will attack (including counterattacks) at a time unless you trigger a counterattack while someone else is in the middle of attacking you, which makes combat very tame.  This isn't helped by most enemies being hp balloons, bogging down the combat a bit as you do a lap around the arena smacking one guy around and avoiding their counterattacks.  It is further hurt by the fact each enemy only has one animation for each of their two different attacks.  Powerful artefacts and weapon abilities speed things along if you can string a combo together without getting hurt.  The most exciting battles involve team battles, where the NPC's are fighting each other and making the fight much more chaotic and interesting.
Overall Hand of Fate 2 is good, though combat often feels like the slowest part unless one has a power combo of equipment perfect for a certain situation (100+ damage to a frozen northerner with a flaming sword anyone?).  I look forward to seeing it get better as it is developed.

A Normal Lost Phone is such a good game, and for many reasons, the whole phone aspect to it is one that I absolutely love! (Even though I, myself, am not a big fan of smartphones). The game discusses identity not just
, but also identity in general. The game does have it's flaws though, although some of the flaws depend mostly on the player's taste in games.
The whole smartphone aspect of it is one that brings it a lot of charm. This makes the game more intimate, and more personal. This personal aspect to the game is to make the protagonist more sympathetic, and the whole point of the phone style. Having to figure out someone's passwords through understanding what they find the most important to themselves, listening to music that they made, and music that they enjoy, seeing the pictures on their phone, their private text messages, etc. these all create a sense of intimacy between the player and the protagonist. The person who has 'found' the missing phone, the one you are controlling is an empty vessel for you to insert yourself into, and the protagonist is out of your control, which can be very rare for a video game, especially a visual novel, where the protagonist's choices are made by you. But in this you can only make the choices that come in the aftermath of all the guts of the game.
A game that makes you experience the aftermath of the events, reminds you that you are not always the important one in the story, that other people have stories. Having to accept that your identity doesn't hinge around being the centre of attention, as it usually does in video games, can really put in perspective your impact on the world. Exploring the identity of the player, you. The identity of the player is more vague than the protagonist, in the end this game forces you to be yourself, instead of the protagonist. That is the main core of this game, being yourself. And the identity of the player is defined by being untouched, and unexplained. Sometimes people can be more interested in someone else's lives than their own, people can care about other people's lives than their own.
There could potentially be more flaws than I will mention, no game is perfect. This game has gotten criticism that it is written a bit too cold or unemotional, but within context, this can be explained, and only a part of the game can be said to be close to that. People have said that this game has bad grammar or a lot of mistakes in the dialogue, but another thing to remember is this game was translated, and a game's value should not be judged by spelling mistakes. A big flaw that I found is that the achievements were completely bugged for me! I had to do a second playthrough to get any of the achievements to work, but they do work after a second playthrough. I am unaware if the achievements are still bugged, because I can't test that, but be reassured that I was able to get them after another playthrough.
On the whole, this game is really worth getting. For some people it may not be their cup of tea, but it's a cup of tea that is important to drink, a cup of tea that is filled with important education, and great mysterious story, and great music! Even if you aren't a fan of the smartphone layout, I am really not either, this game can still be so enjoyable! And if you end up not liking the game, you wouldn't have wasted much time on it.

I have this game on my old iPad, and decided I wanted it on my computer as well. I have finished it before.
Avadon is an old school RPG, which means two things to keep in mind: 1. the combat is based on strategy, and 2. there's a lot of writing -- the game even describes the scenes you find, to make up for the lacking graphics. I'll elaborate on both of those.
The combat. It's turn based, so there's no rush. Take your time, think about your next move if you need to, and be efficient: no going forward to meet an enemy that's coming at you anyway, use that move to attack with your ranged weapon. The enemies are limited, so you won't be able to grind for levels. That said, the levelling system is quite a bit easier than older games of this developer -- there are four very defined classes, and you'll be able to choose your next abilities without too much time spent studying the possibilities and planning, making for a somewhat less stressful experience, in my opinion. Something to keep in mind: bonuses to probabilities make quite a difference.
As for the story: that's the focus of the game. You aren't here exclusively to combat enemies or plan the perfect warrior or finish the quest, you're here to read about a world and its characters. If you don't like to read much while you're playing, this isn't a good game for you. The story isn't action-based, either. It's a politically driven story, and your quests involve not saving the world, but keeping an empire stable and functioning. Of course, shades of grey and moral relativity abound. It's also an opportunity to get to know the characters in your party. They are well written and quite fascinating as a whole, representing distinct cultures of the fractured empire.
If you're just dipping your feet into this genre, and the story sounds interesting, this is a good game to start and see if you enjoy. If you do like this genre, this is a great story and the strategy is challenging enough. Also to keep in mind is that the whole game was written and coded by a single person, which is quite impressive indeed.

After playing this game for 20+ hours I only managed to finish the first act, and not because the main quest is long and boring, I was distracted by the great number of secondary quests which are as much interesting as the main story and less cliche. In this game you don't need to go and kill 10 rabbits to get a reputation from some guy. The story here is deep and catch you till the end. As you play you feel that you have much more freedom than in some of the modern RPG. Your choices aren't so evident, most of the times you can't say if it's going to add you the certain reputation or not. You choose by your concious (or your character's). I love how much of in control you feel.
It feels like Baldur's Gate by the look of it and it's game mechanics, but it also feels modern, bringing CRPG to the new level. Any character can equip any item, but some classes will handle those items better than others. I love how instead of DnD alignment system they added their own personality system that depends on your choices in game. Like punching people? People will call you aggressive. Or maybe your character prefers diplomatic solution. All those characteristics also open more choices during dialogs.
This game is not ideal, it still have some bugs, which I hope will be fixed soon. Your stronghold feels kinda useless, at first I was quite excited and spent much money to build it up, but then it almost gave me nothing and you want more from it. Your companions are great, they are interesting and each has their own story, but they don't have much impact on your story, and maybe I spoiled by BioWare games, but you don't feel so bound to them, they are your companions, not friends. There are no fightings between them like there was between Viconia and Keldorn. You can't romance them too.
Pros:
+ Freedom of choices
+ Great secondary quests
+ Huge beautiful and interesting world
+ Roleplay
+ The gameplay you know from BG series, but now it's even better!
Cons:
- Stronghold that you don't really need
- Your companions are interesting guys but they have almost no impact on the story
- Some minor bugs

This an extremely well made and excellent game, much better than it has any right to be. If you like games like Maount & Blade or XCOM this is a no-brainer pick. It's a gem. There are three things people complain about mainly:
* lack of modding support
* RNG
* Grind
The lack of modding support is an issue, it will hurt the logevity of the game (compared to Mount & Blade for example) but ultimately this a low budget indie title, the devs have the choice to continue supporting this game or making another even better one, and they've chosen to do the latter. As far as I'm concenred that's their choice and good luck to them.
The RNG in this game is pure - no quarter asked or given to either the player or the AI. As such it can be brutal. It's supposed to be. But just like XCOM the extent to which the RNG can wreck you is directly proportional to your skill and atteention to detail. It will casue you ro lose brothers occasionally but if you play well it won't cause you to lose battles or the game itself. It will merely amplify the consequences of bad decisions and losing your cool.
Finally to the question of grind. It is important to understand that this game is desinged to be played ironman. In ironman mode it is a test of skill, nerve and charcter. It is incredibly exiting and creates stories with intense highs and lows, joys and sorrows, successes and failures and also creates all sorts of different characters to colour the journeies.
But if you savescum the game loses all of that magic and becomes repetative, predictable, grindy and ultimnately pointless. You have been warned. Don't fire up this game and think you're going to win it first time out. Just play ironman and expect to last a few days and die horribly first time. Then try again and last a little longer maybe. That way you will learn to play so much better and get the real experience of Battle Brothers.
Not convinced? All you got to do is weatch a few LPs of even the best players. You will hear a constant litany of whining:
"Oh no. NOOOOOO!"
"You cannot be serious!"
"Why did I do that, Just WHY!"
"He missed again! OMG he missed again"
"OMG, they've got three marksmen. I think we've had it"
"I should have retreated. I know I should have retreated. Why didn't I retreat?"
When even the best players can be reduced to tears. you know you've got a really good game on your hands.

Yes it's early.  But whoa...    This game should be up for literary awards.  Only the written word can so easily, and completely, convey meaningful emotion and nuance.  Perfected along with the vibrant backgrounds, subtle yet solid soundtrack, and actually legible at high resolution text (adjustable font size in menu), this game will hold to be the test amongst all story based rpgs.  What little I have played of the combat engine has been intuitive.  Infinity engine perfected.  This game plays like a MUCH better written Baldur's Gate, except buttery as well, ...butter!   The extremely competent game mechanics hide away nicely, so that the immersion in environment and story stands unbroken for hours.  There have already been some large mood shifts and some mouth open gasps within the first 2 hours of gameplay.  I admit that I am already a huge fan of Obsidian, but it is with great reason.  I do not game for victory.  I do not game for competition.  I game to be entertained.  A 50-100 hour interactive book or movie is an immesurably better option than scrolling endlessly thru Facebook, or watching "reality" advervision.
Mr Sawyer, Avellone, Cain, Brennecke, Urquhart, and the rest of that team deserve an award.  Not an award given to shooters because of realistic ballistics.  No.  I am talking Pulitzer prize level descriptive writing..(in my opinion obviously).  Kickstarter gave them the freedom to be as flowery as they wanna be, and boy oh boy did it pay off.  AAA publishers and  mindless console drones, screw you and your multiplayer gib shot twitch muscle "e-sports".  No, not really, as that stuff has merit to you if you enjoy it.  But for me, THIS IS WHERE IT'S AT!  I have the butterflies like the first time I read LOTR, long before Elijah Wood supplanted my vision of what  Frodo looked like.  Bring your imagination and ENJOY!!
>>>>UPDATE<<<<
56 hours in and I love this game even more!  I have played thru some bad (mechanically) games just to see a decent story.  Not a worry here!  This story seems layered and rich, and even the game mechanics are amazing.  Anybody who doesn't like the way it plays are either looking for something specific (it does NOT play exactly like Baldur's Gate, despite similar appearance and mechanics), or they just haven't taken the time to learn the system.  If you choose to pass up an amazing artistic Tour de Force due to "mages not being as OP as in BG" or something along these lines, then you are very hard to please and I believe it to be a mistake.  If you like RPGs, and when you think of "RPG" you don't immediately think of skyrim, then this is worth a shot!!

Alternative history games I feel generally fall into two categories; absurdly grim alterno-dramas that take themselves too serviously, and the nonsensical cheese fests that know its a silly parody. Its a premise that can go both ways in quality. Singularity treads a good balance in melodrama and campiness, and offers up a decent shooter.
Story is your standard Cold War 'what would happened if'. 1950's Russians discover an all powerful, time distorting element E99 (not to be confused with Einsteinium) on a remote island, experiments go horribly wrong and left to stew for fifty years, and a botched American black ops mission changes the timeline and basically gives Russia the world, and you have to jump back and forth to fix the present/future. There have been better plots in games, but this isn't a totally laughable B movie. It is forunate that the games atmosphere saves it from B movie hilarity. Being trapped inside a decaying, direlict research complex greatly enhances the overall mood and plot of Singulariy, adding a mounting sense of dread and horror that; at least for me, was almost too much to handle.
Singularity's gameplay is pretty competent; starting off as your traditional FPS with generous doses of action survivor horror thrown in for good measure. It shortly becomes what I can only discribe as a 50's sci fi shooter with the introduction of the Time Manipulation Device, a powerful wristband that let you age and revert certain objects and enemies at will, it is perhaps not as solid as Half Life's Gravity Gun. But its still pretty fun. The guns you find throughout are varied and not half bad, but as you find your formula to fight Mutants and Russian soldiers, you'll find yourself using and upgrading only a combination of three or four for everything. Finally there is a lot of variety to them, some of them are not the smartest AI's I've seen; But some, like the mutants that shift in and out of the material world, are unnervingly tough to deal with.
Singularity is a little rough around the edges, but at the end of day its a very satisifing shooter. It does a worthly job of blending its story, atmosphere and game mechanics into something I found memorable and be more willing to replay some day. And in an Era of throw away military shooters, that is saying something.

Your grandmother needs your help to save a rare flower but you're attacked by a mythic creature. Unfortunately for you, this same creature kidnaps your grandmother and the friendly man that helped you betrayed you. Your only chance is to reach his castle in this park where slavic fables are honored....
Eventide: Slavic Fable is a nice story with elements from slavic fables: everyone around, apart for your Baba, is in reality part of the slavic folklore. Given the fact that you can collect cards about each creature in this culture, you can also learn about it.
The gameplay is quite common, though the hidden objects scenes are diversified: from rebuilding an object thanks to a list of pictures to a list of items to find, as they're hiding parts of a puzzle. The puzzles are also well-balanced and kinda easy when you're used to them. Even if the game isn't developed by Artifex Mundi, the gameplay is quite similar to their own games.
The ambiance is a surreal one and a nice one, even if the game is set during the night, in a dark forest but it's not the creepy type. The only thing that is weird is the grandmother's head: I don't know how to describe it but I think it's not as well done as the others.
The soundtrack is also correct and fitting to the story.
The bonus chapter seems to be out of the blue, however, you understand quickly that it's set in the past and that you'll meet again some characters. The bonus are also nice: minigames, soundtrack, etc...
Anyway, Eventide: Slavic Fable is a nice way to learn about slavic bestiary and belief. It's also a good game published by Artifex Mundi and almost as the same quality of their own games. As usual, don't hesitate!

Starbound had been rotting in early access hell for so long that it used to be held up as an example of how to do early access right. Somewhere along the way, a few things became obvious: Chucklefish is a horrible business with terrible business practices, and the devs lost their creative vision a long time ago.
What started out as a promissing game that needed some tweaking and more content, ended up as a disappointing game that needs so much tweaking its like it left early access in name only. I'm saying that Starbound is still in early access, no matter what anyone tries to tell you.
Long ago, in the age of myths when Starbound first entered early access there was a horrible monster known as "damage on contact". Everyone hated it and the devs rightly removed it. Then another set of devs got brain damage and decided that they wanted it back in because...I don't know, artistic vision? This is but one example of how its become clear that the devs have aboslutely no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what they are actually doing and what their vision for this game even is anymore.
Along the way, the toolbar was twisted every which way as the devs desperately attempted to find something that worked. As soon as they did find something that most fans were at least okay with, they'd decide that the fans were wrong and make it worse. As it stands now, its a hot mess that will probably get you killed at least once.
Planet and biome diversity has fluctuated over the course of the game, new biomes added, more dungeons added, and then a bunch of biomes and dungeons were removed for 1.0 because the devs knew better than those silly fans.
You might be noticing a trend here where the devs didn't actually want feedback for the game during early access, but just wanted people to pay to be beta testers. And they failed at that, because holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this game still buggy. Even if you could somehow ignore all the bugs, for there are many, the game is so horribly optimized that you will wonder how such a thing is even possible for a pixel graphics game. In my humble opinion, my PC setup is above average. I can run most AAA games with few problems if any. I can even get some of those up to 144fps! And then there is Starbound, a pixel graphic game where sometimes the fps dips down to 30 or less.
Its important you understand that the various races you could choose from used to matter, such as racial armor abilities, weapons, and more. As it stands now, the armor looks different and the ship is different and that's it.
I'm going to stop myself from listing every single thing that the devs "streamlined" from early access, because I'd run out of space here. I tell you about it so that you can know that this game really did have a lot more content at one point, but for reasons known only to the devs, its been removed with little reasoning. You could make an entirely new game with all that's been removed. So much has been removed it feels more "early access" than some points of its early access life.
Combat is awful, performance and optimization are awful, the "story" is homogenized and counter to promises made in early access, exploration is nearly pointless, the "quests" are repetitive to an insane degree, and the only thing that could possibly keep you interested is the colony system which I will admit is actually pretty good.
The only good thing to come from Chucklefish was Stardew Valley getting published. Go buy that instead. It is an infinitely better game that deserves your money far more than this massive letdown.

There is something inherently enjoyable to be able to build the deck that will be used in the upcoming adventure, carefully picking cards appropriate for the challenges ahead, and then during the adventure, playing the real-time combat with the items that you previously chose.
I highly appreciate the fact that in the later challenges, the difficulty is not only technical, but also mental: To get the best rewards, you sometimes need to think outside the box, and that is much appreciated.
The soundtrack must also be highlighted as it is excellent, and quite epic at times!
PS: Despite what some preview images might let you think, the RNG in this game is surprisingly sparce. Minigames truly are a game of precision and skill first and foremost.

A Normal Lost Phone is a terrific little game. The worst part of the game is the setup - you have found a phone and instead of handing it in to a security guard or a cop or something, you stalk your way through it like a creeper. This is the same kind of awkward setup as Gone Home, Firewatch and several other walking sims, so i guess it's just something we need to ignore for the sake of the story. It's worth it, because the game is very elegantly formed.
Essentially the story is played in two parts - the first part where you read through the messages and emails, then the second part when you hack into some password-protected parts of the phone to fill the gaps in the story. Aside from a bit of hokey dialog in the text messages, the rest of the communication feels pretty believable, and the main character's coming-of-age struggle is sympathetic. It's a compelling hour or two of gameplay that's well worth the purchase if you are into narrative games.

There are some other issues as well which I'll outline as feedback for the dev.
Terrible voice acting which repeats the same dialog in a loop constantly. Could honestly replace those out with just generic sounds and it'd be less jarring.
After completing an initial run with a character the progress occasionally gets reset after completion and getting sent back to a harder level 1.
If it doesn't get reset, the difficulty doesn't progress with you and there will come a point where you'll just be endlessly killing crap without any effort. There's no way to end the game outside of dying and if you build your character out enough it'll be pretty hard to kill your character. I played some of spiderweb software's earlier games when I was a kid, so I have some heavy nostalgia as I go into any of their products.  ...unfortunately, Avadon doesn't quite follow through.  Although it really really could, if it had been polished more.
The combat system is technically balanced and reasonable, but comes across as slow and plodding.  You have to sit through the entirety of every attack animation followed by a brief pause, for every action any character takes, before it will load the interface for the next character's turn -- which isn't so bad, the first hundred times you see the basic attack animation.  Combat also activates too soon, a lot of the time-- it can take several turns of walking before anyone is in range; and that walking may take you far out of your intended travel path...and into line of sight of more enemies, that can repeat the process.  It can also be difficult to tell at a glance whose turn it is, until you figure out what to look for, and sometimes the hitboxes of tightly grouped combatants overlap a bit (making it hard to select the right one).  Previous games also had a significantly more varied spell list -- the list has been easily halved, although the list of abilities for mundane combat characters has grown noticeably.  In short, there is nothing cripplingly wrong with the combat in this game, and it CAN be interesting and fun (particularly against named unique enemies) -- but it could have been so much better, so easily.
The game's story centers around being a new member of the secret police for a dubiously moral authoritarian medieval city-state, which keeps the peace for an alliance of five nations.  Which is excellent and unique.  All the characters are interesting, dialogue is interesting, and I will play this thing through to the end to see how it goes (..and then again with a ninja or sorceress; so I will have enough lockpicks to get through all the locked doors this time).  Unfortunately, that good dialogue and the interestingly-designed quests that go with it happen to be implemented as poorly as the combat system.  In one case, the only way to destroy a piece of evidence is to go talk to the local captain of the guards about it (and not the spymaster for your kingdom; only the local guardsman will do), and after bringing it up, choose "Never mind. [destroy evidence]".  How are you supposed to find that option, unless you've already decided to turn the evidence in instead?
The quests in this game are far, far too easy to break; and I find myself enjoying the story not because of their craftsmanship in game design...but in spite of it.  Even with that caveat, I can't deny that I AM largely enjoying it, and particularly the fact that even though they force too many situations to boil down to simple binary choices, it's often not "right" vs. "wrong".  It might be tradition vs. cultural innovation, freedom vs. security (vs. duty), or even just choosing whether or not to accept someone's offer to surrender/ flee.  ..I'm finding that a lot of my choices get overruled though, with circumstance forcing everyone into how the narrative WOULD have gone if I'd chosen the other way.  I'm not sure if this is a magician's choice scenario, or just bad luck on my part.  In any case...
If you want to play the secret police of a medieval magical mind-break-the-prisoners authoritarian citystate, with free reign to just do whatever you want to anyone you want, a reasonably complex and realistic political climate, and turn-based combat that is fine but slowish, give Avadon a try.  ...but expect to experience the story as they laid it out (with occasional breaks for mass-effect style Paragon/Renegage options), rather than actually control your path.

Yes it's early.  But whoa...    This game should be up for literary awards.  Only the written word can so easily, and completely, convey meaningful emotion and nuance.  Perfected along with the vibrant backgrounds, subtle yet solid soundtrack, and actually legible at high resolution text (adjustable font size in menu), this game will hold to be the test amongst all story based rpgs.  What little I have played of the combat engine has been intuitive.  Infinity engine perfected.  This game plays like a MUCH better written Baldur's Gate, except buttery as well, ...butter!   The extremely competent game mechanics hide away nicely, so that the immersion in environment and story stands unbroken for hours.  There have already been some large mood shifts and some mouth open gasps within the first 2 hours of gameplay.  I admit that I am already a huge fan of Obsidian, but it is with great reason.  I do not game for victory.  I do not game for competition.  I game to be entertained.  A 50-100 hour interactive book or movie is an immesurably better option than scrolling endlessly thru Facebook, or watching "reality" advervision.
Mr Sawyer, Avellone, Cain, Brennecke, Urquhart, and the rest of that team deserve an award.  Not an award given to shooters because of realistic ballistics.  No.  I am talking Pulitzer prize level descriptive writing..(in my opinion obviously).  Kickstarter gave them the freedom to be as flowery as they wanna be, and boy oh boy did it pay off.  AAA publishers and  mindless console drones, screw you and your multiplayer gib shot twitch muscle "e-sports".  No, not really, as that stuff has merit to you if you enjoy it.  But for me, THIS IS WHERE IT'S AT!  I have the butterflies like the first time I read LOTR, long before Elijah Wood supplanted my vision of what  Frodo looked like.  Bring your imagination and ENJOY!!
>>>>UPDATE<<<<
56 hours in and I love this game even more!  I have played thru some bad (mechanically) games just to see a decent story.  Not a worry here!  This story seems layered and rich, and even the game mechanics are amazing.  Anybody who doesn't like the way it plays are either looking for something specific (it does NOT play exactly like Baldur's Gate, despite similar appearance and mechanics), or they just haven't taken the time to learn the system.  If you choose to pass up an amazing artistic Tour de Force due to "mages not being as OP as in BG" or something along these lines, then you are very hard to please and I believe it to be a mistake.  If you like RPGs, and when you think of "RPG" you don't immediately think of skyrim, then this is worth a shot!!

A game that's really only worth it due to it's price tag, Please, Don't Touch Anything is a fairly challenging point-and-click puzzle game similar to some of the browser ARGs you may be familiar with.
The premise is simple, you're left at a button console, and your goal is to see how many of the 25 different "endings" you can achieve using only what's in front of you.  Different combinations and interactions with the things on screen can all combine in a ton of ways to get different endings.
It's pretty damn funny at times, and a decent amount of enjoyment for how small and simple it is, and the soundtrack is good.
That said, if you look up the puzzle solutions, this is a super quick game, but that should be obvious.  Some of the puzzles are fairly tedious and a bit repetitive, but in the end, for $5, it's pretty enjoyable overall.

With a flourish of his hands, a few fanciful words, and a flip of a card, my fate was decided by the cloaked man: I just starved to death in a burning city besieged by an undead plague.
Not exactly the most glorious of deaths.
With my character’s demise, the cloaked man offered me some patronizing advice, I easily envisioned his smirk beneath his cowl, and levitated all of the game pieces back to their proper places like he was some sort of creepy Mary Poppins.
Hand of Fate 2 is a game within a game within a game. Players take on the role of a traveler in a caravan wagon with the cloaked man. To pass the time he offers to let you play his card game. So you create a character for the card game and start his first scenario. The cloaked man’s game has a few rules to learn, but they’re nothing complex or abstruse. For the sake of time, I’m going to refrain from explaining the rules in much depth, however it’s important to understand that Hand of Fate 2 is not like a traditional card game video game. When it’s time for combat, the cards don’t just smack into one another as the game calculates the damage done; when it’s time for combat, you fight.
Let’s go back a few moments before my aforementioned demise. Across the gameboard were cards arranged in rows and columns. Each card represented a city block that I was traveling through, looking for survivors to save. Every turn cost me some of my food resource, and once I ran out of food, I would take damage with every turn. I ran out of food a few turns ago, so my health level was less-than-ideal at this point. I click on an uncovered card, signaling my character to move there for my next turn. The cloaked man flips the card and it’s an alley full of infected monstrosities.
The cloaked man mutters something hardly encouraging as the game warps me into a combat scenario.
Reality refocuses and I’m now in control of the actual character I’m playing the card game as. All of the weapons/equipment/companion cards that I held in my hand are now a tangible reality.  The monsters do not hesitate and they lurch forward to try and consume my companion and myself.
Using the WASD keys to move, and the mouse to attack/defend, I do a decent job of fending off the monsters’ attacks. As I take a few hits from the monsters, I regret not playing my reinforcements card before this battle scenario, as it would have spawned some city soldiers alongside my companion and I; not the best reinforcements, but it would have taken some of the pressure off of my companion and I.
Eventually, the monsters are slain and I am teleported out of the combat scenario and back to sitting in front of the cloaked man. Unfortunately, the few scrapes I sustained during combat were enough to put me below the threshold needed to survive my next turn. The moment I click to move to the next card, my health evaporates completely and I die. Whirling away all of the cards and game pieces, the cloaked man resets our card game and allows me to choose another scenario or to attempt that same one again.
Hand of Fate 2 is a tough game, but the combat is fluid and fun, reminiscent of early Assassin’s Creed games (I only played the first two), where icons indicate which enemy is about to attack, allowing you time to dodge out of the way or block/counter the attack. Enemy types are varied, so it’s not just hacking-and-slashing through hordes of monsters. Dodging, parrying, riposting, and chaining attacks are crucial for survival, and each action is easy to conduct and visually fluid to observe. Combat in Hand of Fate 2 is great.
The combat is complimented by the game’s easy-to-learn systems, and the ever-intriguing presence of the narrator/game master. I was surprised by how much I ended up enjoying Hand of Fate 2. I usually have little patience for learning a new card game, but the treat of actually getting to partake in the combat was enough to usher me through learning the basics, and then after that I was hooked.
RECOMMENDED: Hand of Fate 2 is great in every way. I’ve had no problem learning the game’s systems, the narrator is a great character to get to know, and the scenarios present enough of a challenge without being unfair or overly difficult.

I've been a long-time supporter and player of Kingdom of Loot, so I may be biased as I say this: I recommend this game wholeheartedly. I could have used the Steam Key they had given me so I could play for free; however, I wanted to support them and the game. I believe that the KoL Team will be able to make this game a big success, as they have great plans for KoL, and I can't wait to see the game bear fruit. But I'm writing this as a review, so let me review it:
The Team is constantly answering questions on the forums, as well as fixing bugs. The only issue that has made this game unplayable for me and many of the players were a CPU issue. HOWEVER, that has been patched, making the game so much more playable, and enjoyable. Everything is so much smoother and less laggy. They actually listen to the players of the game; leave a suggestion and more often than not, it will eventually be added to the game.
The visuals for the game is amazing; breathtaking even. It honestly reminds me when I played Sword of Mana on my Gameboy. Each dungeon, forest, or cave will have their own design to it and as of right now,  there's no big similarities for any of the current locations. So, each location will be unique and different. The animations are smooth and fluid as well.
There's currently five classes to choose from (sixth being the Cleric, and that will eventually be released); Knight, Mage, Gladiator, Rogue, and Archer. So if one does not match your play style, you can always change to a different one. However, as of writing this review, Rogue and Archer are lacking some skills, so beware.
The Community has been very kind, as they aid you in leveling, giving gear, or even money at times. They are also extremely friendly to one another, I have yet to see an arguement occur. You can easily make some good friends here (I know I have over the years).
Mining and Crafting is a thing in the game; except right now its currently just mining. Mining gives you the ability to mine for gems, and later down the line, materials for you to craft.
The Max level is currently only 30, but in that time there's a lot of things to do to occupy your time. Two forests to go to (Beginner Forest and a Level 10 Forest), a Lost Temple (Level 5 Dungeon) to explore and find loot, and a Cave full of crystals (Level 10 Dungeon). The dungeons have different settings; Normal, Medium, Hard, and Insane. The higher the difficulty, the better experience and loot you obtain. As well as that, the Lost Temple and Cave give you "Secrets" to find; those will take you awhile.
There are currently Trophies for killing enemies in the game under the "Achievement" tab in game, so if you're ever bored, you can do that. They are suppose to give out "Starcoins" per trophy rank, however that currently does not work. (There's three ranks for trophies, Bronze, Silver, Gold)
There is a leaderboard so if you're a competitive person, you can try to become rank 1 of you're current server.
I won't lie, the game has a lot of work to be done before it can be completed, there are no quests and bosses right now, which can bum some people out; however, their priorities lie elsewhere for now. But if you get this game, I don't think you'll be disappointed, as Presbyter (one of the Devs) mentioned they will try to release a new dungeon every month.
I hope this review, if you can even call it that, helpful.

A Normal Lost Phone blends novel game design with a meaningful story about a teenager coming to understand themself. I saw so many reminders of my digital past, from emotionally turbulent text messaging chains to bonding anonymously on forums. The gamification of exploring another's phone was quite clever, as well. The game goes beyond this, however, capturing in fragments that double as design mechanics the life of the phone's owner. You piece together major events, relationships, secrets... And if you choose to, learn a lot about a largely misunderstood group of people.
Give this short but important game your attention, and don't feel shame to look at the guide someone made that gives soft hints for a challenging password or two.

If you're familiar with Spiderweb Software's RPGs, it will come as no surprise that Avadon: The Black Fortress is another extensive old school party-based trek through areas full of nooks and crannies with unique encounters and secret loot caches to be had, as well as exciting set piece encounters and an intriguing overall narrative.  That's pretty much true of everything they put out. The big changes to the formula are: a new world; a significantly more linear progression than most of the other entries in their lineup, a class-and-skill-tree approach to character builds, and party members who are fully fledged NPCs that contribute insights and dialogue throughout the plot as you move through it, can be spoken to between missions, and have their own side agendas you will have to deal with.
The new world is an intriguing fantasy setting where five disparate and feuding lands have banded together in a defensive pact against pirates, invading empires, marauding humanoids and dragons, a blighted magical corruption, and other exterior threats. The pact is held together by the dictatorial enforcement of the Black Fortress Avadon, and they maintain a network of spies and enforcement agents to ensure compliance. The fairly unique conceit of this particular entry (and who knows, perhaps followup games in the series) is that you play Hands of Avadon, sent to enforce the laws of the pact and defend it from threats within and without. This gives you rather more authority and a much more fearsome reputation than your typical band of wandering adventurers, and this is used to good effect throughout, although alas you still have to contend with buying your own supplies, a tired RPG trope that seems even more out of place in this context (though they do attempt to explain it).
The linearity is somewhat unfortunate, but things do open up as you gain access to more of the areas and return to zones on new missions, and most of the sidequests can be done at your leisure. Still, the flipside of linearity is that you're always being sent into challenges that you should be equipped to handle, and it's always clear what you're expected to do next, neither of which are guaranteed in more open formats.
I am personally a big fan of Avadon's approach to skills and classes. I find the structure of new ability at rank 1, additional effect(s) at later ranks, and unlocking a secondary ability at a late rank very rewarding and I never feel like my points are wasted or that I have to save points from level to level just to advance at all, which have been issues I've historically had with the more freeform skill approach earlier Spiderweb games took (and other games with skill systems, for that matter). And Avernum in particular suffered from boring fighter syndrome where spellcasters got huge suites of spells to cast for a varied combat experience and fighters...got to hit things. Not here. The Blademaster class even passively is a blast, with heavy passive investment rewarding cleaves, a hilariously effective level of hit prevention, and the chance to riposte, curse enemies, or begin regenerating  if hit, and then on top of that gets group buffs and debuffs and attacks with additional secondary effects. The Shadowwalker hurls shurikens, teleports around, throws pots of acid and smoke bombs, backstabs and poisons, and is a huge fountain of damage in general.  (Needless to say, I was pleased when the Avernum remake cribbed from this system, albeit in a more Avernum-y way.)
As for the NPCs - there's one of every type, you get them all pretty nearly immediately, they stay levelled with you even if you're not using them, and they all have interesting personalities and backstories. I've never been a huge fan of the "party too large for everyone to simultaneously adventure with you" thing, but this is about as good as it gets considering that.
So all in all, another classic RPG. It's not quite as old school as previous series from Spiderweb, but the deviations from that formula mostly are in the vein of improvements in RPG design, in my book, not stepping away from the core appeal.

The game world is quite huge. Sadly, this just mean very, very long empty corridors and roads. The RPG elements feature a nice, if very simplified, skill tree, equipment and looting system. You can also recruit a few people in your party which you have full control over them. While the combat is turn-based, the rest of the game plays in real-time.
On the bright side, you can solve many encounters through dialogues, instead of fighting them. The game also has a well designed user interface and plenty of tool tips for about everything. Plus, for players who love hoarding stuff, you get to loot absolutely everything in the game, from trash lying on the floor, to bones and flesh from your fallen victims. Despite all my love for turn-based RPG's, I certainly can't recommend this game to anybody.

Avadon: The Black Fortress is a fine modern RPG made in the old-school style. Except better: no swapping floppy disks or CDs! But it makes me a little sad to say that it feels like a chore to play.
Visually, Avadon exists in a 1995 timewarp: Better looking than the SSI "Gold Box" D&D RPGs, but not as nice as the Baldur's Gate era games from Bioware/Black Isle.
But Avadon isn't so concerned about appearances. What makes this old-looking game work in 2013 is how fluid the experience is. It looks dated, but it streamlines gameplay, and adds modern features like skill trees, and the ability to scale the game difficulty if you want to move more quickly through the game's difficult bits. And your character speeds around the screen! No more waiting as your party trudges around the map; this game respects your time, as your characters hustle around in loose formation.
But this fast game pace brings me to the part that I don't like. Avadon is big on prose, like RPGs used to be. Avadon makes up for its stick-figure graphics by providing rich, descriptive storytelling. There's a lot of reading to be done, and no voice acting. So far, so good.
But in Avadon, your character moves so quickly from encounter to encounter, you find yourself reading constantly. There's no break. It's like reading a book. Frankly, I find myself resenting how much reading this game is asking me to do. And I kept nodding off as I was playing.
Baldur's Gate was probably a 80 hour game. Avadon makes me wonder how much of that time was just trudging around on the screen, revealing the dark parts. Walking from place to place. The pace was slow, but maybe that was an intentional break from all the reading we were asked to do back then. Walk a little, fight a little, walk a little, read a little. In Avadon, it feels like read-run-read-run-read-run. So... much... reading.
I recommend Avadon, because I respect how fine of a job Spiderweb has done to streamline old game mechanics, while still maintaining a flavorful, old-school feeling. And the story's good! But bring your spectacles; you're going to be doing a lot of reading as you play.
On a related note, I recently purchased a pack of classic Bioware RPGs from
. I plan to go back and finish the games from that era that I never played -- Baldur's Gate 2, Icewind Dale. I look forward to seeing how I feel about playing these games 15 years later. Will the pacing feel better than Avadon? Stay tuned to find out.

Battle Brothers could have been a classic. Instead, it's a moderately enjoyable but ultimately forgettable experience.
The game centers around rebuilding your very own depleted mercenary company into a vaunted fighting force. You do this in the usual way, by traveling from town to town and accepting contracts. These contracts range in difficulty from easy to very hard with the harder ones usually offering more reward. You the move on the map to the site of the quest, sometimes uncovering other encounters as you go.
The meat of the game is an almost chess-like tactical battle system. You position your forces on the varied terrain and with an array of skills and classes you commence combat. It's not dissimilar to Legend of Eisenwald or The Banner Saga in this regard. Success or failure will usually (see below) result on how well you manage your troops. If your guys live they might rank up and that allows you to choose certain perks though frankly these perks are often unbalanced and therefore the illusion of choice is removed since some are so superior to others. The rewards from successfully completing a contract will be spent hiring more troops and upgrading the armor / weapons of your merry little band. As you get stronger, events happen in the world that make the dangers more difficult in this low-magic world.
The game is well made, stable and you can tell care was put into it. The graphical style is one I don't particularly like but that's personal preference.
However....there's a few reasons why this won't be a classic. Fist of all, the RNG is a bear. In many games the RNG really isn't random or they do things to mitigate it (like Hard West's luck system). In this case you're really at the mercy of it in both your character leveling and your "to hit" numbers. One of the biggest complaints in games like these are that a run of bad rolls can cause you to lose. Battle Bros is probably worse in that regards because the potential consequences for just a single bad roll can be severe. When men flee in terror, or the damage can be so severe then just a couple of bad rolls can entirely overshadow your strategy. That's not good. It also extends to the randomization of getting recruits and leveling up. This is a game that rewards rubbing a rabbit's foot as much as a having a good tactical approach.
Worse, you often can't see the makeup or terrain prior to launching a battle. With terrain bonuses also being quite steep, you can accept a battle that should be winnable but simply is not because you're trying to fight while scaling the side of a mountain. It's incredible to me that the devs dropped the ball so badly on this that we're essentially thrust blindly into battles in often horrible tactical positions.
Then there's the grind. Fight a battle. Go to town. Get another quest. Fight another battle that is slightly more difficult. Battle Bros descends into a grind that e random stories can be fun but there aren't enough enjoyable events to prevent the game from devolving into a tedious grind. This doesn't happen all at once but after some time there doesn't seem to be much purpose in it. I have no idea how this game ends because, much like this review, the grind kept going and going.
Finally, there's the issue of development and mod support. The devs released this, put out a simple patch and then moved on. I have always supported the choice of a developer to move on to another project once the last one is done. But for cryin' out loud the corpse wasn't even stiff before they exited this scene. A game like Banished gets criticism for being "abandoned" after release, 6 months of patches, new buildings and mod support. Battle Bros didn't do any of that. So without any new content, DLC, mod support...what you see is what you get. I find that they moved on a bit too quickly for my tastes - almost like they realized that sales didn't explode when 1.0 came out so they packed their bags and left (even though sales were constant and decent).
If you like turn based strategy games, this one isn't a bad one to add to your library. Just buy it on sale so you don't feel ripped off after the drudgery sets in after 20 hours or so.

TLDR:  Excellent starting point for a brand new CRPG franchise.  This universe and engine proide the foundation on which future masterpieces will be built.
60 hours in and finished one full playthrough on Path of the Damned difficulty.  I can say for certain that this is nearly everything I had hoped it would be.  I'm just going to do a quick bulleted rundown of my thoughts.
Pros:
* Great story, with excellent flow and narrative
* Phenomenal art and asthetics
* Great set piece boss encounters
* Good interface and easy to understand controls
* Ditched D&D for a system much more suited to CRPGs
* Excellent, interesting and varied compaions
* For the most part providing a good level of challenge
* Good roleplaying opportunities
* Interesting and varied classes that feel distinct
* Excellent mod support for the community

At the time of typing this review I am sitting at 14 hours of gameplay. So long story short I recommend this game. It’s the type of masochistic experience my 17 year old edge lord self would really enjoy. It’s a roguelike turn based strategy rpg mashup with permadeath. So if you’re the type of person that gets off by sticking glass in your genitalia like myself then this is the game for you. Also if you see a Necrosavant for the love of god just run. Even if you’re guarding a caravan it is not worth it in the early levels. They have the ability to teleport and that makes guarding the caravan near impossible as they will just teleport next to the most undefended thing on the map and get a free hit every turn.
So I’m a big fan of this game but I’m going to start out with my criticism of this game before I get into what I like about it. First off the game world feels almost empty with a limited amount to do in it. The difficulty spikes can come out of nowhere and the only way to gauge it is by the amount you get paid per contract. It also has a terrible autosave feature. Just be sure to save after every city you come to and contract you complete because you can get ♥♥♥♥ed and be sent back days within a moment’s notice. I’ve actually accepted a caravan contract where I had to walk all the way across the map then accepted a contract out of the city I arrived at. Got near the target location and decided to camp up till morning, (all without saving). Got ambushed by Necrosavants apparently a new enemy type in the game. Having dealt with them before and having trouble with just 2 of them and now facing 9 of them I promptly hit ctrl+alt+delete shut of my computer, and moved to Brazil to teach History under the guise of a German named Hanz.
But other than the sharp and sometimes unforgivable difficulty I love everything else in this game. I can however understand why some people would not enjoy this game so if you actually decided to read this far in and don’t enjoy strategy rpg games then don’t buy it because you probably aren’t going to enjoy it. Also as a little side note I think the price is a little high for the quality of this game. While not as much as other games I have critiqued for the same reason it is still worth mentioning that a price $19 (£14.51) or even $25 (£19.09). Those would be more reasonable price ranges for the game but beside that it’s a great game if you’ve got a specific niche to scratch.
So the combat system is a top down strategy game basically like chess but with auto rolls per every attack you deal. Like chess with dice I guess is the simple way to put it. It’s frustrating and painful because it puts your enemies on the same level as you. But as I have said before I love pain so that might also be the reason I enjoy this game. I can’t fully explain why I think it’s fun other than it give you just the right level of challenge without being completely stupid, in most cases at least. You basically start out with your mercenary band in ruins after being ambushed. You are tasked with bringing your band back to its former glory and then some. Basically the tasks that you are asked to do are as follows; track down thieves, defend a village, track beasts that have been killing townsfolk, defend a caravan, or go to an ancient ruin to retrieve a valuable artifact. There are several weapons and weapon classes you can go with and several strategies you can use to defeat your opponents. So this is a game you will have to use your mind to play.
The enemy variety is a fresh of breath are and the medieval setting is something I quite fondly enjoy. The enemies are quite varied compared to similar games but most of them are the general run of the mill Tolkien rip off with orcs, goblins and undead. But there is enough difference in between the classes to still be enjoyable. And every play through is different because you can choose a random seed that spawns a random map that you can enjoy. I usually recommend end game events at random as to keep its fresh and interesting.
So all in all it’s a fun game and I am more than happy to recommend it. I hope this review has helped you in making a decision whether you bought it or not.

Once upon a time, you were a recruit at Starfleet Academy, when a super-powerful alien entity decided that reality is like a hentai visual novel - time for the kid gloves to come off, the tentacles to come on, and the Earth itself as the schoolgirl to be violated.  You were lucky enough to survive in a highly damaged ship.
Starbound is a 2D block-buildy game similar to Terraria set among the stars.  The scenario is that Earth was destroyed as noted above; you have to collect six Macguffins and defeat the final boss to avenge the Earth...regardless of your origin race.  Good times!
Starbound draws inspirations from
games and IPs - Terraria, Zelda, Metroid, Star Trek, and more are represented in some way or another.  And, to its credit, it does it well.
You can't talk about this game without noting that this is a controversial title due to things that happened during its lengthy, well-documented/discussed development.  I am going to intentionaly ignore those things and talk about the game we have in front of us, today.  The question I am answering is
The answer is yes...barely.
First, the general presentation is well-done.  The art style is effective, the music is tranquil and plays to the aesthetic of exploring an uncaring universe solo.  The nods to other IPs are done in a loving way.  The creative team on this game did great.
The static content is very well thought-out, to the point where I could comment that we could've had a great static game a lot more quickly than it took to get what we have now.  The first boss, the Erchius Horror, is a great puzzle boss that emphasizes mobility over brawn.  The various 'protected' mini-dungeons on planets are great parkour challenges that use the mobility mechanics in this game - including double-jumps, morph ball segments, and dashes - to great effect.  The story underlying this is a standard, but lovingly delivered B-movie plot that is cheesy, but sincere, while moving the player to take on greater challenges.
The construction aspect of the game is also good.  You can make your planetary colonies truly yours, and it's always nice when your colonists periodically give you gifts for keeping them safe and happy.  There's so many possible ways to build homes, it's ridiculous!
Before I begin, a relevant side-note: I find myself often griping about how Steam game developers don't seem to have a good grasp on good UX (user-experience).  UX is about using trends in how people actually use software, to make using
software easier and better to do.  Chucklefish: you're next on the gripe-list.
My specific problems with the UX begin with the 'hot key' setup that is used in release.  You can press buttons 1-6 to access a left-mouse/right-mouse item pair.  Does that sound unintuitive?  If you said 'yes', you summed up my thoughts.  A more standard 'press 1-0 to use a certain item' setup would suit the game a lot better.
Now, before anyone says, 'But...Asvarduil!  This game has a two-handed system where you can dual wield or use a shield with a 1 handed item, or all sorts of other stuff!'  Unfortunately, this game has some balance problems where there's no good reason to use 1-handed items - they do far less damage than their 2h counterparts, and using a 1h weapon means you give up the secondary ability that 2h weapons bring to the table.
Getting back to UX, a problem is that key bits of useful information are hidden or non-obvious.  In Survival difficulty, the hunger meter is unmarked - I didn't know I was hungry until my SAIL informed me that that dinging I heard meant I was hungry.  Your current pixel count is not obvious either, which is a problem when you need to go shopping for items.
Getting away from UX, a higher-level problem I have is that the world generation algorithm doesn't take into account the fact that this game gives you the double-jump, morph ball, and dash mechanics through an easily-accessible sidequest series.  The game would be more interesting if random worlds made it so that using those mechanics is easier than simply digging past obstacles.
This one was a hard one, but I do, barely recommend it.  The game in its release state has more good than bad in it.  The mechanics can be a bit repetitive when they're not under utilized, and the UI alternates between good and unhelpful, but there's a good game behind those two major flaws.
with the caveat that it will not be for everyone, possibly due to art style, possibly due to being yet another block-buildy survival game, and even due to this game's history.  Nonetheless, this is far from the worst game I've played on Steam -
has that "honor."

Enjoyable. Good replayability, random generated worlds for each campaign makes re-rolling fun. Never know what it'll turn out to be. A little bit of RNG but that never hurts (unless you're Gunnar the Thaumaturge/Flagellant who got one shot by a flipping crossbow bolt >.>) Don't get too attached to your people, they will die. Some will last for days, weeks or maybe months but they will die sooner or later.
All that considered, you can plan around certain things to give you a better edge.
~Out numbered? Look for terrain like trees, rocks or bushes that block movement so you can set up a choke point.
~Never, EVER, underestimate the value of the high ground.
~Keep some people in the back row with pikes or other 2 tile ranged melee weapons, they're life savers.
~Get some guys with kite shields and have them form a shield wall if you're dealing with a load of archers, then slowly advance. Seriously, fighting alot of archers sucks.
~Mix up weapon types. Axes for destroying enemy shields, Flails for getting around shields, Pikes for poking stuff
~Don't feel as if you HAVE to move everyone on their turn, sometimes it's better to let the enemy come to you or to give you guys a rest. Running out of stamina mid fight can be a death sentence.
If you like tactical games, this is worth it.

So, this game is pretty simple, right? You are climbing up a tower by doing a puzzle on each floor of the tower. It's not a very long game, nor is it like, dark souls or cuphead hard, but it's a hard game in its own right. There were many times on many floors that I had to stop playing and cool off for a bit cuz I was just having too hard a time to make it through; however, each level is indeed beatable. You will find that trying to rush through rapidly will lead to your death far too quickly, but you'll also find that taking too long will also lead you to your death. Also, not every level will kill you, it will simply "hurt" you, as you have a set amount of HP that you can see at all times. Once that HP is down to 0, you lose.
There are an infinite amount of lives and continues, so if you do find yourself dying often, don't worry, you can just keep retrying.
Now, as for the unforgiving part... There are some levels that you will have to try and try until you get each click, each movement, each timing absolutely perfect or else you die. You click to a spot too early, boom, dead, click to a spot too late, boom, dead, you accidentally click the wrong spot, boom, dead.
The game is fun and challenging, and for $1.99, it's definitely worth the buy.
Also, the music is really nice and fitting and changes every 10 levels.

HoF 2 is difficult to define, but its a mix of traditional table top card  games and RPG action games. Its a solid game, but like the adage jack of all trades  master  of none, it fails to impress. Among its chief shortcomings; the combat is shallow, controls are unresponsive and feel sluggish, it can get repetitive, and there is inevitable frustration from RNG.
The RNG is particularly annoying due to  the games nature. Even just a few bad RNG rolls can spell doom for your entire run. And if you fail in combat, you lose all progress in whichever "challenge" your doing. The structure of the game is very arcadey, with 21 different challenge missions. The game only takes 15 hours to complete which is very meager.
You could say this has high  replay value since it has a high degree of randomness, and each run will be different. Sadly, there are only so many different situation and event cards. Still, repitition sets in long before you get to that point. It  suffers from  the same issues from the first game, but it also improves upon the strengths it had.
Overall even  $30 seems pricey for this. Its a decent game, but falls short of excellence. A mere 10-15 hours of playtime  to beat it  also  effects its value,  and mileage may vary based on your tolerance to repetitive monotony and ragequit inducing RNG rolls.

I impulse bought this game for like 2 bucks because it said on the wiki Niko from Oneshot was a playable character. I couldn't find out how true this was because there wasn't much info out there, so I assumed the game was not known well enough, and bought it. Immediately, what stood out about the game was the poorly designed UI and how most of the characters displayed werent even playable and would never be because the game was cancelled. And of course, Niko wasn't even displayed. The game is just a grave of a project that never came to be.
I was then curious as to why this game got cancelled. If not for being cancelled, it probably would have become a really cool fighting game that everyone can play casually with friends. So that got me thinking quite a bit. Was it cancelled due to not having enough resources? Ran out of funds? Developers passing? No. They cancelled the game because they didn't have enough motivation.
When you are selling a product, motivation shouldn't be a factor. You were paid to make a product, and you have to make that commitment. Instead, they backed off and shut down the whole thing. I can only imagine how devastating this must have been to the fans of the game who put their hopes and money into this project, only to have it die before any good game was made out of it.
But devs, if you end up reading this, please continue development. It would make more people happier than you know, and you would get some good money out of it. Not to mention, it could fix your brand's image. I would personally love to see this game completed. It is too good of a concept to waste. Take your time if you have to. But as for now, I'm refunding so I can buy a different $2 game.

A Normal Lost Phone is a sweet little game with a lot of heart. The premise is simple: you find someone's phone, and have to dig through it to find out about the owner. It touches on themes of privacy and [spoler]LGBT issues[/spoiler]. It's got a simple interface as it literally operates like a normal phone. There's a decent amount of content in a short 2+ hour package, including some pretty nice songs.
The meat of the game, though, is finding out about the life of the owner, learning about their personal struggles and their relationships. There's a definite feeling of violation as you're going through, while your curiosity still gets the best of you and you keep going forward to see how the narrative unfolds.
The game was over quickly, but it will stick with me for quite awhile. Definitely worth $3 in my book.
