The idea behind Lif is a unique one. Playing as different animals in their natural habitat as you explore and stay alive can be a fun challenge. This Early Access version is (currently) pretty much the same as Gamevial's free-to-play version in the browser; by paying for the Early Access, you'll get updates that bring Lif closer to its realization as a more realistic animal simulator/survival game.
Lif is open-world, similar to Gamevial's Fly Like a Bird 3, but Lif takes survival to another level. Naturally the animals chase and kill each other constantly because Lif allows you to attack or befriend as you please, but we can expect improvements in gameplay as Lif evolves. There's fun in being able to roam around doing what you want anyway, and we'll be able to do more as the game gets better.
Lif has huge potential, and as with any game, the only way it will improve is by supporting its development.

This game is what happens if x-com was set in Westeros: a wonderful, turn based strategy game, soaked in blood and steel.  In this game you lead a band of mercenaries in a randomly generated map through adventures where, after slowly building your team, you face off against an epic randomly generated end-of-world type event.
Pros:
Amazing tactical gameplay with no overwhelming “meta” needed to beat the game; there are many different team builds that are all genuinely viable.
Combat is a wonderful medieval bloody mess.
Fun RPG choices for your group based on their background: My disgraced drunken noble lost his great sword so I had him flogged. Turns out he got a little mad about this and left my band.  Good riddance to Sigmaur I say!  My ex-Monk talked some children out of joining a crusade where they would almost certainly would have died: good work Torkel!
The random generation of events and missions builds in a ton a replay value.
Cons:
Most of the cons in this game are about presentation more than anything else.  Simply put the game is not flashy:
Graphics are not anything to write home about
To get story immersion you *gasp* have to read text instead being presented with voice acting.
Some folks may get peeved by the RNG nature of the game. (Random cross bow bolts to the head are an occasional downer)
Overall I highly recommend this game for the turn based strategy enthusiast.

Je n'aime pas la tournure de la réputation que prend ce jeu.
Ce n'est pas comme si le jeu avait été une catastrophe ou truffé de bugs., ou si le gameplay déplaisait fortement. Il y a là un long et beau travail, tant au niveau du gameplay, de l'écriture, des graphismes que du son. Les développeurs se font lyncher pour un soi-disant abandon de projet alors qu'ils ont bossé dessus durant 4 ou 5 ans pour nous pondre un bijou artistique.
Je comprends qu'on puisse être un peu déçu. Moi aussi, j'aurais aimé qu'ils le peaufinent davantage, qu'ils y ajoutent des armes, etc... Mais de là à dire qu'ils vous ont volé votre argent, vous êtes fous ! Arrêtez de croire que les développeurs sont à votre service, dévoués à faire évoluer le jeu encore pendant 10 ans. Le jeu vidéo est comme tous les arts, si les créateurs, et non les créanciers, car là, il s'agit d'indépendants, décident qu'il est complet et qu'il représente ce qu'ils voulaient transmettre, alors il est fini.
Quant au modding, pourquoi seraient-ils contraints de l'ajouter ? S'il n'ont pas envie qu'on modifie leur jeu et qu'il reste ainsi car ils veulent qu'on le perçoive ainsi, pourquoi ? Quand vous lisez un livre ou que vous regardez un film, quel intérêt y aurait-il à modifier la vision d'un auteur en remplaçant la description ou la tronche d'un acteur par une autre ?
Si vous aimez les jeux durs, réalistes et stratégiques, ce jeu pourrait vous intéresser. D'autant plus qu'il est plein de charmes.

As far as the game itself is concerned, it is an RNG heavy TBS in a very gritty low magic medieval world (reminds me of Warhammer, just without the magic). You move around on the main map (which is somewhat lacking in content, and this is the main gripe most people have), get contracts in towns and villages, and fight on hex based battle map. The art style seems very basic (there are no animations, hell, there are no legs), but it is stunningly beautiful (in a gritty way) and incredibly detailed. The battles are heavily reliant on RNG, but there is a lot of room for tactics both in combat (postioning, skill use) and before (equipment, leveling stats and getting traits), that most of the time you will feel that the RNG is tough but fair. Of course, there will be frustration, and a lot of it, so don't buy this if you dislike the outcome being random (although again, you can stack the deck in your favor with careful application of tactics).
All in all, this is my favourite buy this year, and I don't regret a cent.

There's three  very neat things about this game: 1) the art direction, a wacky combination of Soviet propaganda art plus steampunk; 2) the superpowers you get, which all have to do with time; my favorite is the sniper rifle with bullets you ride; 3) the various endings, all seemingly designed to mess wtih your mind.

Not to mention animations can't be skipped and some take a long time to complete. However the biggest gripe I have is the golden and silver tokens for every mission. It's a terrible design choice that adds nothing but mindless and unneeded grind to the game. I've found myself stuck for 2 hours doing a mission over and over again trying to get a gold token until I eventually just gave up. In the first game there was that sense of satisfaction, but on this one there is only that bad feeling because you know you could've acquired that golden token, but you didn't, because they want you to grind for cards so you can come back later (Which isn't fun, re-doing the same missions - some of them very long - with nothing new added just to get that golden token).

One example of this is the "Strength" mission. It is the definition of loading screens, as the board is filled with about 8 cards to go through, and 6 of them are combat cards. Once you reach the end, you go through some stairs and bam, guess what, 8 more cards with 6 combat ones. I'm all about showing off new and exciting fighting games—especially party/platform fighters—at our local tournaments back where I live. Even though our venue was originally Smash exclusive, we started appending things like Injustice 2, Skullgirls, and Rivals of Aether. Indie Game battle
have been that special next game, but it didn't happen for quite a few reasons.
Sure, maybe you have ~8 OCs that look like Tom from EddsWorld and stand taller than the rest of the cast, and maybe there are a handful of characters I can't vouch for simply because they're perma-placeholders for the characters they very clearly represent, whether that character may be another indie game or a Smash Bros inclusion. I, however, am not shy to admit that it is nothing short of satisfying to 4-stock someone as the Goat from Goat Simulator, or that Dust is probably one of— if not
— most fun character I've ever picked up in a platform fighter, or that the oddball Newgrounds inclusions sparked a hidden nostalgia that made me tear up a bit.
That aside, I'm going to be brutally honest: if there is one glaring reason I can't recommend this game, it's because of the
The notion that this game has full controller support, as indicated by Steam, is a blatant falsehood, although I
understand these things being a simple oversight. Allow me put things into perspective through anecdote.
Me and my friend usually play Super Smash Flash 2, Crusade, Rivals of Aether, etc. with 2 PS4 controllers key-mapped through Xpadder to make it easy on both the controller configuration and the game's processing itself. First time booting up IGB, we wanted to do similar to the above, but there was only support for a single player using the keyboard, which meant no Xpadder. Unfortunate, but since the game had native controller recognition, we thought we could shrug it off by configuring our controllers normally, but that wouldn't work because the game recognized both of our joypads as a singular controller, since they both registered as the same type of device according to Windows. So we had to begrudginly hand the keyboard (and sometimes his dusty Xbox 360 pad in place) back and forth because the game wouldn't let two players play with the same type of controller, which I feel is such an extreme thing to miss out on when talking about a local-multiplayer fighting game. All this and the fact that you
further configure controls outside of the Unity boot-up menu, which is just a total mess trying to navigate. I could go on about controls, but I know that it's a personal grudge above all, as most people who pick up this game are probably going to gravitate towards the keyboard anyways.
Moving on, the UI in this game is probably among some of the worst I've seen in a very long time. I'd be willing to bargain that if you showed any web/graphic designer your game's buttons/menu backgrounds, they would redesign them happily for free. There's no visual/audio feedback on menu selections, and some of the cursor detection feels really off-kilter. The roster layout is random, there is no better word for it. I can at least expect characters to be close to eachother if they're from the same series, but some of the unavailable/incomplete characters occupy the same slot positions that fully functioning characters do.
Although earlier I said I had fun experiences with this roster and the gameplay in general, I still can't let go of a few things. Some characters make me think as if they were only put in because you liked the game or because people asked for them. Poncho is a guest inclusion, and an interesting one at that, but he has one of the blandest movesets I've seen in a fighting game period. Characters differ vastly in quality and playability, and I really do mean it when I say that quite a few matchups in this game are 70:30 or likely worse. On that note I saw that you've also expressed interest in an appeal to the competitive scene for this game back before it was cancelled. I'll give my thoughts, as I'm technically part of that community. Why does G-canceling exist? Why do we need to wavedash into a tilt to be able to jump cancel it, why can't we just jump cancel tilts? This is an overcomplication, one that actually hurts newcommers because it comepletely negates the need for normal non-cancelable tilts, rather than acting as an option-select as you intended. Wavedashing on the other hand is fine, but it's so hard to execute one that actually carries your momentum and I couldn't tell you why. Above all, the average character's gravity makes recovery very difficult; I've died much too easily simply fumbling to keep myself on stage.
I still have to give credit where credit is due, and these are some of the things that make me stick around still. You and others put a lot of time into alternate pallete choice for characters, who all are 3D-modelled with striking resembalance to their respective characters on the most part, and even when some cases were a miss, like your first iteration of Niko, you strived to improve those characters and fit them into a game that had a level of visual consistency that surprised me, knowing that these were all from indie games with extreme variety in visual design. The stage choice, although sprinkled with a lot of hazards and random pit placement, are copious. To this day I still haven't played every stage (I'm close) but I still enjoyed more than half of them. The music composition, Visual FX, and sound design are actually pretty impressive for an indie come-up, and they look even better in the upcoming version of the game so stick to it.
Finally—and I'll try to keep this short since you probably haven't heard the end of this from ex-devs—I just wanna put out some thoughts about your decision to cancel the game, as well as the publicly disclosed/leaked events that led up to that point. I don't know if you were doing this game as a passion project, or as an actual opportunity for either yourself or the indie scene, but just relax man. Making a platform fighter is not an easy task to accomplish, no matter what tier of development you lie on. It's a proccess that takes a lot of blood, sweat, and tears. It's no wonder that even Sakurai himself continuously injured himself throughout the proccess of making Smash 4, as he really bore down to complete that project, and with that said, even with the entire team of Sora Ltd. on his side, collaborating with Namco as well it still took a good while to push the game out the door. Making a game in this genre simply as a hobby or as a wildcard is taxing, and I wouldn't be surprised if some of the people who you contacted for character inclusion thought you were reaching way out of your scope. This game feels like it was meant to be a fun platform fighter that pays homage to the indie scene that you've been part of and inspired by, but I think that started to get nudged aside for the sake of feature creep and status.
I, personally, wouldn't ask for a refund for this game, because I know I'm going to be breaking it out every now and then to remember how fun it felt, and that's all I really expect for 10 bucks earned over the summer anyways. It made itself up by far. As for people new to this game, who have no feelings attached to the characters, are on the fence about how it feels etc., I'd only really recommend it as an experimental title. Thanks for making as much as you did, and bless you and your team for what you've accomplished to date. Ambitious, yes, but even now it's still something me and my friends will play for a while. That's all that really matters to me at this point.

First and foremost, if you're looking for a fun indie fighting game, this is exactly where you should look.
While the game has been cancelled, more content is on it's way for a final update or two, which is exciting in it's own right. Indie Game Battle will make it's way out of the door, and out of early access.
I'll start by mentioning the controls, they're tight and responsive, which is important for a fighting game of course. I've never once had an issue with wrong button inputs or moves not working due to broken controls. When something happens it feels like the player's fault rather than the game's fault.
Next up; the colorful cast of characters. There's plenty to play as, and while they aren't very well known for the most part, that's part of what makes it special in my eyes. Rather than relying on Shovel Knight to carry the game or something, the cast is full of unique and colorful characters to play as. I found Matt, Bingo, Woodle Tree, Cpt. Viridian and Wizard to be the most fun, personally.
As for stages, while not many are there to choose from, the ones that are present are quite fun. I often find myself picking the Retrolands, The Sanctum, Final Rift, or the Poncho stage. Either way, I've never gotten bored playing through any of them, and they all look amazing too.
Overall, while I've received Indie Game Battle for free, I'd gladly pay 5 dollars for what's already there. It's truly an Indie Smash Bros, and a damn good one at that. While I wish Indie Game Battle could've grown more and more over the years, I support the developers decision to cancel the project, and I wish them luck.

First of all, I'll start with the fact that I used to work for Blob Games Studio since late 2014 on the team and left in August 2015, and was a third party from 2 May 2016 to 28 May 2016, so I know certain things that have happened behind the scenes. I am also not naming several individuals who I'm told want to be anonymous to avoid harassment by Blob Games Studio.
It began in autumn 2014. This was when I met Felix, at the time I was working on a game of my own (which in hindsight, was not that great) but okay. He gave feedback, some nice words, and we got talking. We agreed on making one project together (just one) called Delivery Boy Tale that later became Adventure Of Sol (which the Sol 1st party is from) but soon we had bigger plans so Blob Games Studio was formed. Another member soon joined (who created the Vanessa 1st party) and things went sort of well. The Legend Of The Artifact Remastered was in development, and I was to beta test his work and help with making some of the level designs. It was there that the darker side of Felix, or FelixBlobDev or Kirbypwnage started to emerge, as I left some honest, blunt but well-intentioned criticism on the mechanics. He got snappish and passive-aggressive and it became apparent how little tolerance he has for criticism and people who think different from him. He later also helped doing some spritework for my game (The Outbreak Story, but at the time it was named differently and had a wildly different concept) but often blackmailed me if I didn't do what he wanted or say what he wanted to hear by threatening to stop working, or postpone his work, put less effort in it and prioritize his own work, all because of criticism at his work and his behavior at the time. He twisted the things I said, he didn't talk to me for days when I said something he didn't like, then to turn it around.
At that time, the big project came. Indie Game Battle. It was to bring Smash Bros. to the indie scene and was to take the step of embracing both big indies such as Shovel Knight, Shantae and Quote as well as small gems like Tess and Clive & Wrench alike, to bring indies together and make everyone happy. That was the promise. A nice story to tell everyone was all it took for me to be sold on it. I was to get Alexia, one of The Outbreak Story's protags, in it as a 1st party. He was uncooperative about it and as he kept buffing his own characters, it made me a bit suspicious. Fearing he was to make my character less and less usable, I asked him to balance the game. Make each character powerful, so no one is OP, which he to this day seems to tell to people was me asking him to make Alexia OP, which isn't the case. I wanted every character to be powerful in their own right. I was working on the stage of Retrolands together with him, doing 8-bit assets for it.
As I grew increasingly weary of Felix's emotional manipulation, it showed. Along came Omar, a new team member and after a month or so, I was more or less forced to leave the team. He then erased my name from his project but kept the assets I mentioned before for Retrolands in.
Time skip to May 2016.
I was in a DM conversation on Twitter with the guy, where we sort of made up. Then I was allowed to join their Skype Group and have Alexia be a Third Party again, and we made a deal. She was to be released alongside a Greenlight for The Outbreak Story where I would also promote Indie Game Battle as a sort of both-sides-helping-each-other thing, but development on her reimplentation was never started, even though she nearly finished, Felix and I still had the 2015 assets so it'd be far easier than any other character that had to be made from scratch. I was suspicious, and asked Felix about it. He also confirmed to have never credited me for my contributions on the Retrolands stage.
I got closer to a member called Starturbo and a member called Bounty, both Third Parties as well (the developer of Superstar Technic and Nexum, two work-in-progress titles respectively) who also had lingering concerns but didn't state them at the time. Also, we found out that a few ex-members (a certain Rockto, and others who I am not sharing names of) were bullied out the server for criticizing IGB in a similar manner to me and Blob Games Studio had actively smeared their reputation using lies, fake accounts and wordplay. It can be said that some of them were harsh, but this is never a justification for such behavior. Also, the team had been asking people to write good reviews, upvote good ones and downvoting bad ones on Steam to keep the rating at Mostly Positive so people buy the game. Starturbo and likely (though I lack confirmation) others had their reviews censored by having to omit mentions of Rockto and other drama that would make them (rightfully) look bad in the customer's eyes.
The immaturity in the chat and Felix and another member (who has since left and has also been harassed and wants to stay out of it) being inconsiderate about their jokes rubbed off on us. We asked them, politely, to stop, only for us to mocked to hell.
This left to me and Starturbo both leaving at the end of May 2016. We were to leave them alone, as long as we were left out of it too.
Not that the calm remained for long. We started a Skype Group, later Discord server called Indie Game Utopia to create a hub for starting indie developers where everyone could have fun and speak their minds. A false, slandering article defaming me, Starturbo and other people was written by the aforementioned member that was at the time being immature and is now gone. I made a Twitter post debunking the article, and Blob Games Studio started to push the narrative that we were haters (which they still push and the Important Update refers to) and tried to essentially get us gone. That failed, as I started to expose more of what I had seen.
Now, at the end of 2016, things hit a boiling point. We were becoming increasingly weary of what was going on, and at the start of 2017, more Third Parties were getting removed for no good reason. Also, features that were promised (a Story Mode and an Online mode) were never created and work on a Story Mode was barely even started. All there seemed to be was a final boss and some stages.
Though at the same time, more and more 1st parties were added. The developers got worse over time in their disregard for the community and all forms of feedback they got and it was clear that this wasn't going to last.
And it didn't.
Cue the removal of my dear friend Ryan Silberman for an inexcusably pathetic reason. Add that to Blob Games Studio's morally bankrupt, sociopathic practices becoming more and more apparent and Felix becoming increasingly desperate to defend his spot, resorting to more insidious tactics and forms of manipulation, trying to kill Indie Game Utopia from the inside using a combination of manipulating mods, spam raids and spreading false information.
Now, Bounty has also been removed and his leaving was also spun in their favor. In truth, he was ran out of the server and had no choice, he was going to get kicked, but because he technically left himself that is the narrative.
Now, the project's cancelled, people ask for a refund (as they've been scammed).

Cheap and engrossing. It's a short game and hypothetically I could file for a refund after completing it, but even if that weren't a jerk move, A Normal Lost Phone was worth the time and money.
You find a phone. It's got some of its functionality. With enough prodding and poking through the mystery it contains, you can start digging deeper into the life of its former owner. It's a pretty well fleshed out story told through text messages, e-mails, message board postings and more and the light puzzle solving required to stitch together more and more of it keeps you involved rather than rapidly scrolling past everything.
People who are (or are close to) members of the LGBT community might find more to enjoy but this cisgendered hetero guy found it well worth the time anyway. It's well written enough to tug at the empathy of any decent person, I'd imagine.
A Normal Lost Phone delivers what it promsies but with more depth and care than you might expect. Pick up this phone.

You go down to the wateringhole and have yourself a nice drink. Time to relax? Nope. Now you're hungry. Time to go get food. So you bring down a wildebeast by chasing it around for a few minutes and biting it whenever you can. Eat the meat and now you're full. Time to relax yet? Nope. You're thirsty again. So, to the waterhole again. By the time you find a spot where there isn't a croc eyeing you and get a drink, well how about that, you're starving! Repeat this process two or three more times. Oh, but wouldn't you know it, a meerkat has ran up to you in the tall grass and you can't fricking see it. So you, one of the most deadly predators of the biome, has just been hunted and killed by a small animal that any lion could realistically rip the throat out of with little effort.
This game is horribly unbalanced. Pretty much any animal with an aggressive action can kill any other animal with little effort as long as the aggressor knows what to do. The meters for thirst and hunger run down way too quickly, so it's a constant struggle to keep from going thirsty or hungry that ends up being more frustrating than fun. As a carnivore, you don't feel the thrill of hunting, outwitting, and overpowering your prey, it's just a chore. As a herbivore, it's just a matter of running back and forth from a patch of edible plants and the river over and over again. It gets terribly repetative. The controls are awkward and the button to shift between aggressive and peaceful actions cycles way too quickly with anything more than the very slightest tap likely to land you on the same one you were already on.
If this game interests you, try the free version online first. Trust me, the two aren't all that different and you'll likely understand just how irritating this game is.

Serious review below:
I'll preface the following with that I'm not taking Chucklefish's questionable reputation among its community into account. I gave this game a good review while it was in Early Access. Thought it was a nice alternative to Terraria that had potential. But what we get in the end is not impressive.
The main story is cliche. Basically Earth gets destroyed by a Cthulhu monster, you meet a lady who you do chores for, wander space, scan villages (yes, all you do is scan furniture), get macguffin items to open a door and fight said Cthulhu monster in the end. That's pretty much it.
Mining feels unnecessarily harder and more tedious to do than in Terraria, especially if you're trying to mine some cobblestone out of the way in a tunnel with the first no upgrade mining tool. Seriously, cobblestone. Matter Manipulator upgrade modules are fortunately not so rare, but until the first few upgrades, you'll be relying on pickaxes most of the time. It feels clunkier than Terraria.
The universe seems vast, but in reality it's just the same content, same scenery with one lake and a watch tower and set scenery like that, the same villages and the same biomes repeated ad infinitum. Basically environment palette swaps. The more dangerous star systems (radioactive, frozen, volcanic) seem fun and interesting at first glance, but their dangers aren't really dangers, it's just a wall that gets resolved with a single item (EPP breathing module which you don't even have immediate access to in a game about space travel). And then it's no different from the rest of the planets you've been to. Also, if the dangerous stars are so dangerous, why are there civilizations? Aren't they supposed to be inhospitable, making them mysterious and scary? It kills the sense of danger and intrigue. I was expecting peaceful civilizations to be only on mild stars while the dangerous ones are reserved for the hardcore adventurers, bounty hunters and such hostile entities. Instead, dangerous planets are just another planet you've seen so far with stronger enemies. That said, if the game really wanted to differentiate itself from Terraria, it should have made space travel more meaningful than just hopping between insubstantially congruent settings. Is there really a reason to explore space? Aside from collecting ores, there's not much incentive otherwise. There's no real reason to explore space because there's such a lack of content. Again, refer to Terraria. It's just one world, but there's so much content. Content is key, which this game misses a lot of. So it misses pretty much everything good about the game that inspired this one.
Quests and monsters are equally boring and forgettable. Both are as generic as they come. When you arrive at your first village, it doesn't take long for the villagers to pummel you with repetitive and inane requests, more than you can handle if you take them all at once. The quests are not sorted by planets, so it becomes extremely difficult to track them all if you pile up quests from different parts of space. Also in the main story missions where you're basically scanning furniture and talking to people, leaving the planet or quitting resets the clues where you must speak to NPCs, so the progress bar drops when you come back, but that happens without explanation. It's mind-numbingly boring to search for that last clue to please the lady and move on with the story, worst case being that you have to find another village with the same race. Also, the delivery quests are just plain stupid. Deliver this note to the person literally standing a few blocks next to me, or even in the same house. It's pointless.
I've experienced noticable drops in performance sometimes, which I think is due to the lack of optimization in the game's code since it happens frequently. Doesn't look good for a pixelated 2D game.
NPC and enemy AI is absolutely brain-dead. Had an escort fall into a pit of spikes and just chill there till he died, failing my quest right next to the village I was to get him to. Conversely, an enemy did nothing but stand there or fidget around and stop again as I shoved rockets into his mouth.
For the default difficulty mode, you must eat to survive, but you probably already know that if you've read the very first thing in this review. So you get hungry very fast while food can only stay fresh for so long, and if exploration is your primary concern over survival and you're not paying attention, you'll be hearing those annoying hunger beeps in your sleep. Fortunately, there is no lack of consumables so it doesn't really make it a challenge to survive, it's just there to annoy you. It seems that the game is trying to be about survival and exploration but is mediocre at both; the survival mechanics feel like more of a nuisance than immersive or realistic, if that's what they were trying to go for. I don't know. Rather than actually difficult, it just feels like an added chore. One other thing to say is that nothing stops time in this game. Not opening the inventory or even hitting ESC. The only pause is saving and quitting. Going AFK while you think you're paused will kill you, which in this mode means 30% of money lost and most of your items dropped. Which is a giant waste of time to go back and get them.
Movement and combat is clunky at best. Movement feels awkward, like your character is stiff. Plain enemies might not be smart, but they are aggressive and try to ram into you. Combine that with bad movement (especially in caves, cramped space, etc.) and death happens frequently. Platforming is as pointless and frustrating as everything else in this game.
Really, the only positive thing I can say is that the soundtrack is great. It fits with the theme. Boss battles are okay, but they are nowhere near as fun as any of Terraria's bosses. It's always a closed space and lacks the freedom of movement that Terraria has.
Overall, for a final product, it leaves a lot to be desired. Especially considering that progress on the game's development has been unacceptably slow. I'm not counting mods, because that's asking others to do the developer's own work. As it stands, it's a linear, streamlined Terraria (contrary to what a sandbox is supposed to be) with inferior content using outer space as little more than a mere gimmick. I think the popular negative reviews cover all the constructive criticism about this game, more or less. Go read and consider those too before throwing a dime, or wait for a sale. It's a $5 game at best and even then I find it hard to recommend because Terraria is more worth your money than this.
This was once said about this game: Starbound is a game made by pixel artists, not game designers. And it's true. Also I'll say that there's nothing inherently wrong with taking inspiration from another game. But if this game really wanted to differentiate itself from Terraria, it failed on all accounts: replayability, challenge, creativity, variation and most important: content. I don't recommend it because as it stands, it's a tryhard Terraria that is way too over-ambitious and over its head which lacks the feel of true exploration, spirit and fun.

FIrst time writing a review because this is the only time I've been having lots of fun in one moment to no fun the next. Worst part is I love the concept but hate the execution of it. Not good at going on and on so I'll just make a good ol' pros and cons list.
Pros:
-Replay value of levels to unlock equipment and then doing companion and gear missions. Best part is if you achieved a token during a level, you keep that token whether you fail or succeed the level.
-New companion system with 4 possible options.
-New customization option compared to previous game.
-Card wheel and Pendulum, both skill-based test options as opposed to chance events which kinda tie in with cons (I'll get to that)
-Awesome equipment options and, like stated previously, gear missions to improve your equipment.
-Improvement, although very little, to the combat system since last game.
Cons:
-First and biggest con is the events where chance defines the outcome. No matter how good you are, there is still a slight chance (or huge chance as it sometimes seems to be the case) that you may die. Not because of your own mistake, but from a failed dice roll or card draw. The card wheel and pendulum do take a certain amount of skill which I love because if I lose, I know its my fault.
-Companions, though helpful, seem to be only helpful for their skills. They do little to moderate damage and the time between their strikes is too long. Hand of Fate 2 is a good example of how to make a sequel right. It's not overly ambitious or wildly different from the first one. It's just an all around solid improvement.
Most people mention how the combat is a bit of a hit-and-miss or somewhat shallow. I like it, although I think certain enemies could be way more difficult, like the
First few challenges aren't that hard to fight through but it ramps up considerably later on.
Combat isn't the game's strongest feature, but it's also not the only thing going for it. You're essentially playing a magical board game, which may not sound that interesting on paper but in-game it works beautifully. Each challenge is it's own, lovingly crafted experience. You won't learn or unlock everything easily, yet there isn't really much RNG involved. Most of the gambits can be mastered with skill and eased by companions or certain items.
All in all it's a good purchase, if you enjoy fantasy action RPGs and roguelites. It's reasonably priced for the amount of content and replay value you'll be getting. Endless Mode isn't implemented yet at the time I write this but they've done a lot of updates since launch and I bet there's plenty of stuff to come after it's added.

I've always wanted an indie fighting game like this, but as of version 2.07, IGB stands in the middle ground between decent and underwhelming.
The game has almost everything the basic Smash clone should have; customizable rules, compatibility for 4+ players, AI to play against, and plenty of stages and characters. There is no proper singleplayer mode yet, but at least the game itself can still be played solo.
I'm no expert at Smash, so I can't judge the gameplay much. I can say that the controls for the game are a bit wonky, especially with jumping; there is currently no option for you to flick the analong stick up to jump, instead you have to press a certain button for it. Additionally, you can hold the jump button to achieve distances much higher than should be possible, it feels like my character can fly at times...
My first gripe with the game is that there are so many "blank" or "grayed out" spots where finished characters/stages/features will eventually be. This makes certain menus, such as the character and stage selects, much more frustrating to navigate than they should be, as you have to spot out the character/stage you want over the sea of unplayable spots. Currently there's not much of an indication that something's not playable until you reach the select screens, so you could come in wanting to play a certain character (Hank for example) and be dissapointed to see that he's grayed out and unable to be selected. I hope the developers address this issue in version 2.1, by at least taking out the completely blank character/stage slots in the menu.
Secondly, I feel that there's a lack of familiarity and name power as of this version. Of all the 29 playable characters currently in the game, I can only truly recognize 8 of them. The entire first row of the character select screen is dedicated to first-party characters made by Blob Games Studio, so people who haven't played their other games are going to be very unfamilar with a huge chunk of the cast. This problem will be addressed in future versions of the game, as many more memorable characters (Brad, OFF Batter, Bullet Kin, SCP-049, Fancy Pants, etc.) have been announced as upcoming fighters.
I think my last true problem with IGB is the sound design... or lack of.  I have yet to fully experiment with all of the game's sounds, but I'm positive that some audio bits that should be in the game are missing at this time. Some characters I have played, such as Dust, do not seem to have voices yet, and a couple of them, such as Zee Tee, do not even have a jump sound currently. As this is an Early Access game, I'm expecting that proper sounds will be coming in the near future.
TLDR: The game at this state is quite playable, but its weird controls, missing aspects (characters, stages, sounds) and underepresentation of indie gaming diminishes its potential. I have faith in the developers that my problems with the game can be solved in the (hopefully) near future, so I wish them all the best of luck.

A Normal Lost Phone is a short game with an interesting story, the phone interface is merely a tool for the story to unfold. At first glance, it might look just like any other mystery-based game and appears very predictable. But the more you read and explore, the more you realize that the actual story has nothing to do with what you could have imagined.
As a very curious person, I had no trouble digging into someone else’s life, I was eager to click on all the app icons and read everything I could about the different characters and their personalities. The little riddles that must be solved in order to unlock new apps and the rest of the story required a little digging, but were easy enough in the end. If you read everything, even what looks like it has no use in the story, you’ll have no problem solving them.
The story itself is very gripping, I personally never had to deal with the issues the main character, Sam, is confronted with, but the way this sometimes-controversial subject was introduced was really smooth. It’s hard to understand exactly what he’s going through, but the story is well laid-out, so I think it’s something in which everyone can identify to some extent.
The way the phone is used as a means to tell the story is smart and I found it to give more depth to the narrative. The text messages for example are believable, and as you scroll up to read older messages it legitimately feels like you’re going through a stranger’s phone.
In conclusion, even if the game itself is short, it has a nice message and might change the way you think about certain things. It definitely provides food for thought.

Remember those weird ARG-style browser games where you go to a web page and scan it for clues hinting at the url of the next page, be it in the code, an image that needs to be photoshopped, or an obscure titbit to be googled? If you've spent a couple of nights on one, rejoice:
captures the spirit of those games perfectly.
The deal is simple: you have a panel, a button... and a lot of hints you're probably missing already. Any crack or blemish, any weirdness or irregularity can hold a clue as to how to reach one more ending. And there are 25 of those.
Do not mistake
for a regular puzzle game though; it is, first and foremost, a game for conspiracy theorists. Instead of a normal difficulty curve, it offers a bunch of clues and an even bigger bunch of red herrings for you to try out semi-randomly. You will likely find your first 4-5 endings quickly and easily; a couple more will require more experimenting; the rest though...
ARGs and those web-based games I mentioned have always leaned towards being community efforts. You were supposed to share your findings with other people.
, however, is a single-player game with no built-in option to fo that, meaning that you'll probably end up googling solutions, since some of the endings demand rather insane combinations or a lot of effort to check (the latter discouraging trial and error).
This is not necessarily a bad thing and makes discovering at least some endings on your own truly precious. The animation, music, and pop-cultural references the game offers are also great. I do believe it would have been better if it was either simpler and smoother for a better single-player experience or more insanely complex to reward community effort; but even as it is,
has a very particular charm to it.

tl;dr it's good for the reasons Mount and Blade are good (eg; its parts are all mediocre, but somehow it's addictive), but its RNG is ♥♥♥♥ing atrocious and it doesn't have modding support planned.
long; Battle Brothers is a tactical RPG that's a bit like Darkest Dungeon meets Mount and Blade with a bit of a stress-based heart attack mixed in there. The game's music is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic, the aesthetic - while I started iffy about it - grew on me, and while its mechanics are janky, unpolished, and collapsing under their own weight, much like the state of my heart after playing it and raging countless times, it has the same sort of roughshod charm that Mount and Blade does. Your role is to lead a mercenary company to glory and money in a world catching fire; build up from your motley crew of 3 up to as many as 20 men, controlling up to 12 at a time. You kit them out, take contracts, explore the world, kill orcs, fight noble houses, level your soldiers, and all in all, do what you can to get paid and not die, a lot like I am when the cardiac arrest kicks in.
The game's parts (not including the music) are all mediocre to some degree or another, but somehow, someway, they all form into a game that I could not stop playing after I picked it up. You can tell it was made with love, and considering how much of the game is randomly generated - from quests, to names, flags, maps, characters, fights, much like my erratic heartrate - that's an impressive feat. It wears its heart on its sleeve. "It's gonna get rough," it seems to warn you in the tutorial that you need to go out of your way to find, "and you're gonna get ♥♥♥♥ed up."
You might, at this point, be asking yourself two questions: Jackety, do you need to see a cardiologist? After playing this, yes, yes I do. The other question might be "well, what the ♥♥♥♥'s the problem? That sounds like any other TRPG."
Sadly, it's not. RNG is always a plague, but in most games, it's possible to get past it. You find ways to get around it. You learn how to pump numbers up so high that the randomness is mitigated, or you master other mechanics that make it possible to get out ahead. You're rewarded for learning the mechanics. Or, as you get better and better gear, some things are made easier, while others remain harder.
So what the ♥♥♥♥'s the problem, right? My impending heart attack. Other than that: the RNG. It's not just that the random number generator in this game - on any difficulty beyond Easy - feels weighted to the AI; it's that there is so ♥♥♥♥ing much of it. Each character has ten stats. (Each stating stat is randomized.) Each level, a character can upgrade three stats; you pick three stats, and the amount they go up is ... also a dice roll. A character has preference to higher rolls on a few different stats - each is different - but with a few exceptions, you can say "there's a dice roll" to just about ♥♥♥♥ing everything in the game. There's too much randomness, and it's too easy for five or six rolls to happen over the course of two actions that causes everything to sink to♥♥♥♥♥♥ a lot like my heart at the moment.
If you've got the mind for this sort of pain and suffering - straight up hard♥♥♥♥♥no-mercy tactical RPG slaughter - then go for it. The game won't treat you fairly. It'll make you cheese ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to survive for the first ten or so hours until you get some real gear, and even then, it'll ruin your day.
Even so, without mod support, it's just a pile of untapped potential that could be on the level of Mount and Blade in terms of time taken - but on top of the RNG (bad enough as it is), the game lacks so much polish in so many different ways, lacks so many basic quality-of-life things within its own framing, and has such a partial UI that♥♥♥♥♥♥just rolls down hill.
ps important context: the devs have stated their intent not to work on the game any longer. I probably would not have written this review if they hadn't; I'd be patiently waiting for mod support to come out. Know this: I cut my teeth on XCOM's Long War. I got mad. I stopped playing. I continued playing. But not once, not a single goddamn time, was I ever angry enough to outright uninstall the game.
So, short version again; game could be great, but there's too much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and it's no longer an active project. Don't buy unless it's on a 60% sale or something. (Never seen it on sale for more than 25% off), and be ready to be viciously, unproductively ♥♥♥♥ing angry.

Petite Games is specialised in the development of short, relaxing games. Midnight is one of them: our task is to shoot a square into the exit section of each level. The concept is similar to that of Angry Birds: the fewer shots you do to accomplish your task the better score you get (out of a maximum 3 stars).
The game looks simplistic in terms of graphics and the options available in the main menu but it is relaxing. It is a typical game used for pastime when you need something non-AAA and you want to get away from achievement hunting or multiplayer games that give you increased adrenaline. The game has an overall of 56 levels (a rather strange number) that get gradually more difficult.
Recommended if you like these short, atmospheric games; I recommend spending less than a euro, though. Your best bet is to purchase it when discounted.

Obsidian set the mandate from Day 1 of the Kickstarter that the game would be a spiritual successor to the Infinity engine games (Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment).
In all ways, Pillars of Eternity is a successful evolution of exactly that.  Where Infinity games were all based on Dungeons & Dragons, a system designed for turn-based combat, Pillars of Eternity maintains that same depth and feel, however built from the ground up for real time with pause combat.
Pillars allows the player a choice of 11 character classes, each are a very unique experience much like the Dungeons & Dragons classes they're inspired by.  Unlike a lot of modern games that follow the MMO-inspired holy trinity design (tank, support and healer classes), Pillars, like early Dungeons & Dragons ruleset have a lot more variety in their class design.  Sure, when you go into combat, you will still have your frontline, damage, support and healing characters, but it is not quite as cut and dry.  Additionally, there is no weapon or armor type limits on your character because of your character class, so a character could be a wizard in heavy armor and a blunderbuss, whether that is a good idea or not is up for debate but it is possible.
One of the biggest improvements to me over Infinity series as well as most RPG designs is the engagement system.  In most games, if a glass cannon character gets engaged by an enemy, their initial thought is to run and kite the enemy until a frontline character can reestablish engagement with the enemy.  However, if you attempt to run and kite in Pillars, you will suffer an automatic disengagement attack.  This system forces the combat to have more tactical value than what you see in most games with enemies just being kited around.
Of course, that is a lot of talk about combat, Pillars also has very deep and reactive story telling through conversations and choose your own adventure style cut scenes.  In both, you will have a variety of choices based on your characters attributes and skills.  Additionally, in conversations, there is a disposition system which tracks your character in 10 different personality types such as cleverness, cruelty, honesty, and more.  These will allow for some additional role-playing through the game as you develop your character.
With an unnamed expansion already announced, Pillars should have a lot of run time and with the variety of character classes and choices in the story, a lot of replayability as well.

Imagine you were playing a tabletop RPG with a friend.    Now, imagine this friend has the power to actually bring the various encounters and situations you get in to life.  Enter The Dealer, a powerful and mysterious mage who has spent the majority of his life on the Game of Life and Death.  After losing his position of power by the protagonist of the first game, he has bided his time and returned, albeit weaker than before and no longer the master of The Game.
You are a mercenary-adventurer, some how you have found yourself in the carriage of this mysterious man and have been tasked by him to master The Game and confront the usurper(the current master) on The Dealers behalf and bring balance and restore the world that has been corrupted by their influence.
The Dealer offers 22 challenges to the player, each with different requirements and strategies to conquer.  Side with the empire to make a peace treaty with northern tribe, do part-time work for the thieves guild to uncover a plot to assassinate a wealthy thief.  Each of the challenges presented to you are mostly different, and while some can be solved with sheer-force, will be unable to reap the full benefits of golden tokens doing so.
As you play the game, you earn more and more cards from the dealer. These range from 4 types.
Companion, in which you can choose one of four(must be unlocked) who each have their own abilities that give you an edge on each of The Dealers challenges.
Encounters.  Each of these cards represents a mini scenario, and the player is tasked with doing something to reach its conclusion.  Maybe a card has you enter a tavern, and a drunk soldier challenges you to a duel. Accepting, and besting this duel gives you more fame, which can be utilized for the rest of the challenge.  It is up to the player to learn these encounters for themselves, and stack the deck in their favor by adding favorable encounters that are largely beneficial to you to help you.
Equipment.   Every equipment item you find cannot be immediately used.  Say you find a super-rare sword card, and you put it in this deck. This causes that sword to appear as possible loot from favorable encounters that allow you to gain equipment cards.  There are many types of weapons, armor, enchanted rings and artefacts...however some have hefty requirements and simply rushing into a quest with 30 godly weapons equipped and being unable to buy them from shops or unable to equip them would be bad practice. Choose wisely.
And supplies. These are low-level cards that you bring with you to the start of an encounter. This usually ranges from ''start with +5 food'', or ''a slightly better than crap sword''.
While the player is able to stack the deck in their favor, The Dealer himself will add cards of his own to the overall deck.  Each of them relevant for the challenge you are facing, most of these cards are aimed at being an obstacle to you and far less rewarding than your own cards.    The Dealer does not do all of this to spite you though, at times many cards(including your own encounter cards) have special tokens on them, including all of his challenge cards.  The Dealer risks these tokens to you, so long as you're willing to risk failure in an encounter.    For example, there is a card where the player stumbles across a burning building.  They are asked by a villager to save people trapped inside. This is risky, as you can cause permanent damage to yourself, but should you succeed you will gain fame.  A token on this card is offered to a player who risks themselves multiple times, and succeeds every time.  These tokens are found on weapons, encounter cards, etc.   They bring a layer of risk and reward to the game, and persistent skill in mastering cards can often lead you to obtaining platinum cards.  These cards have almost no drawbacks at all and offer nothing but pure benefit to the player.
This game is incredibly atmospheric, The Dealer is an extremely charismatic person who has countless lines of dialogue.  He does not silently watch as you play the game. He knows every card in the game and will comment on the specifics of it, will comment on your failures and success.  You can really feel his wisdom and experience, and he even has his own opinions on cards.  He will often express disappointment when the player utilizes cards that are purely about violent encounters,  and he speaks very favorably of any cards where you deal with mages.  He pretty much sells the game on its own, and would be the perfect GM in any tabletop game if he ever existed in real life.  It is extremely rare for a player to hear him use the same quotes on matters multiple times, especially if you're the type of player to never re-do a challenge.
The music in this game is incredibly well-done.   There isn't much to say here.  You will probably find yourself idling during the game to listen to a good song(to which the dealer will scold you for wasting time, haha).
The biggest downside this game has is the combat system.  It has been vastly improved from the first game, but it's still very barebones. If you've played something like Assassin's Creed, or the Arkham style games, you'll know how this games combat generally is.   You mash buttons, and then wait for a prompt to appear over an enemies head and block it to parry, or dodge if it cannot be parried.    Thankfully, the mold is broken up in the later encounters when multiple enemies from different factions who have different queues you have to look out for at the same time start appearing.  The combat is definitely serviceable, but it's not a DMC game or anything.  You shouldn't really need to worry though, as combat definitely is not the main focus of the game.  All I can really say is the combat is ''good enough''.
I highly recommend this game. The feel of earning tokens after a difficult challenge, learning and mastering card encounters to benefit you, all of the Dealers quotes....it's just a magical experience and I don't think you'll regret it as long as you don't expect absurd amounts of depth in the combat system.

After playing Hand of Fate over 2 years ago, I was very happy to hear this game was in the works. I had high expectations for this game - I loved the theme, the idea behind the Dealer and his game. I had not expected a sequel and when I heard about it, I hoped that it would build upon the first game.
HoF 2 did not disappoint.
From the beginning you get hints as to the story: the Dealer is back, and somehow corrupted. Someone, I presume our character from HoF 1 is now in control, referred to by the dealer as the "Usurper". The Dealer is trying to train you to defeat the Usurper, and you are traveling to confront him as the game progresses and you look over your past.
All the old mechanics are here from HoF 1, with a couple alterations and a plethora of new mechanics and challenges. New suits of cards, new weaponry and a new way to improve your loadouts at the start of adventures. Rather than collecting the Dealer's relics of power (Chalice, etc) you gain better equipment by completing quests. You can select this equipment, along with extra food/life/gold when you set off on your quest, with a limited number of selections based on the quest.
Many of the quests have 2 tiers of success, granting much replay value as the gold standard of completion is often tough and more often than not requires multiple playthroughs of the quest. It, along with the classic token system lets the player hedge their bets and try to unlock more cards and equipment through the card/token system, or play it safe and optimise a deck to unlock the gold standard token for the quest.
With regard to the challenges, the classic card shuffle is back, forcing me to get fingerprints all over my monitor as I try to track the cards. To add to the game's arsenal there is a new dice rolling system, with rerolls and in-game items that give more power to the player - it does not feel like RNG has taken the wheel, in a game all about RNG that is quite a feat. There is also a spinning wheel of cards (named "the wheel"). Classic carnie game/wheel of fortune that feels perfect in HoF 2, I often forget that it was not in the original. Finally, we come to the pendulum. This beast of a challenge is often intense as it requires perfect timing (PERFECT needs emphasis) if you want the best results, and often it is all too easy to fail spectacularly with appropriate results. I will often either sit there saying "ding" to myself to try and get the timings, or hold my breath for the duration of the challenge. Success rates vary. Wildly.
One final gameplay change that I shall note is the inclusions of companions. They will aid you in battle, each with their own combat style and special ability, such as activating a protective shield on the player. Also, they each offer the player an advantage in one of the previously mentioned challenges, such as letting you re-spin the wheel once. They also each have their own storylines told through the classic card and token system. If you are familiar with any of the free DLC from the original game, it functions in the same way.
There are many other quality of life improvements, which I would list if I were not pressed up against the word limit!
I rate this game 10/10. The original game was great, this game is perfect, bar one sound effect that plays at the end of combat - it is a bit too discordant for me. That is my only issue and it is SUPER nitpicky. If you think you may like this game, or you are on the fence - pick it up. You will know if it is for you within the 2 hour timeframe for a refund. Or get the original, then this. Your call.
I want to make a special mention that the original was supported by lots of free DLC that provided new quest chains and storylines, the devs clearly love these games and go out of their way to provide us with more content. While we may not see free DLC for this game, don't be surprised if you do.

However, this game is not all that great. It's not unplayably bad, but it's not fun from a challenging perspective.
The bad
- Controller controls are bonkers. A pause function would make life easier rather than mapping every button for menu functions

It takes exactly six minutes and one second to be astonished.
The Plan ist about a fly doing nothing much except what lies in its nature – flying around and getting attracted by light.
That´s pretty much it.
It only takes a bit over six minutes to tell the entire story.
A rip-off, one could think, were the game not avaiable for free.

No, not at all.
In the simple elevation of a pixeled fly towards the light, The Plan finds a simple yet striking metaphor  for the circle of life, the strive and struggle of things and the ultimate catastrophe – death.
Fighting against sudden blasts of wind, the fly ascends higher and higher, leaving the green humming treetops behind and flying ever higher towards the light until it reaches transcendence.
We take a glimpse into eternity, flying among the stars and still escalating further.
Determined, blissful, the fly approaches the light at last, it being so bright that the fly´s shadow seems so dark and complete, that it might reach all the way down to the earthly ground which we have left so far behind us.
Like old Goethe on his deathbed, our little fly yearns for ever more light!
When at last we see it.
And the catastrophe runs its course.
It takes exactly six minutes and one second to be astonished.

Indie Game Battle. It's like Smash Bros, except instead of Mario characters taking up 1/8 of the roster, it's characters from Blob Games Studio's games that take up the 1/8 instead!
This game isn't good. Now, the game looks okay, and the controls are good, but this game has many problems that are pretty noticable once you play the game. I'll be comparing this game to Indie Assault in this review at times, because they are both indie fighters based off the same game.
So, like I mentioned, the game does have some okay graphics. Not the best graphics, but they work. Some characters are more detailed than others (Dust compared to Ness- I mean Matty) and it makes some moments in the game really clash with eachother. You could argue the same about some stages in Smash, like Flat Zone (and Game and Watch because of that), but that's one of the few exceptions. They really go out of their way to make everything fit into the same style.
The game also controls fine, but there have been moments where the shields have gotten stuck, and the AI has been able to hit me until it breaks as a result, and get a free hit. Though, I haven't replicated this in a while, so they may have taken it out. On the subject of shields, I discovered that shield + attack does not grab like in Smash Bros. In fact, there are NO grabs from what I've seen.
Now, the game's physics. They're really floaty and difficult to use at times. Jumping takes you 10 feet in the air, and yet I still stuggle to recover because 1) The gravity in this game is really, really heavy and you fall like a brick despite the high jumps, and 2) DI in this game seems to be either badly implemented or not put in at all. I've hit the AI with smash attacks way over 100% damage, and they can recover just fine. However, when they do that to me, It's pretty much a OHKO at that point, since I just fly off-stage, no DI helping me to reduce knockback and the cement attached to my feet that makes me fall faster than Metal Mario. Indie Assault had this problem too, and it actually seems to be a thing only Smash can get right. My suggestion is to make the characters not fall as fast, but also decrease their jump height.
The roster of characters and stages in the game does not help. The developers seem to be going for quantity > quality, approach, and it shows. Like I mentioned earlier, the character models are okay, not great. The game has more characters than Melee already, and it's only been out for a little less than two years. While there are exceptions (Dust), others don't have the luck of being as well modeled (just about anyone not named Dust). Oh, and the game has some very questionable character choices, with almost the entire first row of characters on the character select being first party, and The Kid from IWBTG in the game for some reason despite having like one attack in his origin game.
There's also an over-abundance of stages in the game, and a lot of these are not very interesting, forgettable stages as a result. The second page also has a bunch of placeholder stages that crash the game when selected for some reason. I found that out by accident. "Special" and "Funny" stages don't need to have their own categories and can be merged with the first two pages.
The game's AI is really poorly coded. The AI is frequently running in place, shielding for no reason, running into walls, and just constantly breaking. But when it's not buggy it is relentlessly chasing you and spamming attacks over and over. Despite this, I haven't had it try to gimp or spike me off stage before.
Finally... gimmicks. You don't need gimmicks like the PP or HP meters. Balance special moves out so they can be used without having a meter to be charged for them, and if I wanted to play Stamina Match, I'd play Stamina Match. You don't need both a damage counter and HP meter.
Overall, IGB was just not a fun experience. Indie Assault, while having less content, still felt like it had more effort put into it. Should I be so hard on a game in Early Access? Totally. Early Access is "okay we're kinda ready but not quite," not "We're not ready but let's put stuff up anyways."

You've just found a phone... You start digging around and looking at its contents. Many elements were thoughtfully designed, such as having to find the WiFi password so you can access more information on the phone. There's not much more I can detail, but you soon start to sleuth around for additional user passwords and piece together what happened.
With every additional account I unlocked and read (email, online profile etc.) I really started to worry for the previous owner of the phone and wanted to find out what happened.
It should be evident enough but "gameplay" only consists of clicking and reading. Definitely expect this to be a story-centric experience rather than a gameplay heavy one. I won't mention anything about the story - all I can say is let the phone take you along on the ride!
This game did a good job of immersing the player, and made me reflect on how our phones can reveal so much about ourselves. The intimacy of looking through someone's phone is especially relatable in this day and age.
Taking into consideration the short time to complete, but also the very low price, I would say purchasing at full price is reasonable. Of course, if you're getting it on discount that's never a bad thing! I enjoyed the experience and story for what it was, and it's given me an appetite for other games where you piece together intimate personal information, so I am going to check out
.

There are probably a lot of people angrily debating about whether A Normal Lost Phone is a game or not. It isn't particularly challenging. All the puzzles are easy to solve as long as you're reading what's in front of you. There's no end boss. It doesn't tell you your score. You can't jump. Don't even get me started on the lack of weapon choice!
So... is it a game? I don't care.
It's a story, told using games as a medium. If that disqualifies it from being a game, ok, but it's still a good story and I'm not going to stop calling it a game.
Personally, I found it emotionally compelling. The story is fairly sketched out, but it's probably about what you'd actually get out of someone's lost phone. Probably a bit more. I was brought close to tears at a couple of moments. Some might consider it heavy handed and preachy, as some reviews have stated, but I found it touching. (I suppose I can see the argument for heavy handed, although I honestly have no idea how it could be seen as preachy unless the idea that the targets of certain actions and attitudes wouldn't like those actions or attitudes and might say so is preachy?)
If you give a damn about the debate referred to in the first paragraph, and come down on the negative side, I'd give this a pass, but otherwise I think you'll find it's worth the hour or so it'll take of your time.

If the Devs ever end up reading this review, i've got a couple of suggestions for you:
-Larger Islands
While the Gary-Larson-Trademarked-Pile-of-Sand-with-Palm-Tree certainly has character, it's not very fun to explore. these islands are larger, but i've yet to see one larger that a tennis court.
-More craftable structures
these stick-and-palm buildings are charcterful, but i wouldn't expect them to stand up to a good storm - if we're in this for the long run, give us some more permanent structures (and maybe add in storm damage?)
-The dangers of loneliness
(At the risk of turning this into Don't Starve: Hawaiian Holiday Edition) isolation, and it's effects on the mind pose a serious hazard to disaster survivors and could be incorperated into this game as a danger when the sharks arn't around. in this game staving off despair could be performed by staying out of bad weather, sitting on furniture, eating a variety of foods (especialy cooked), finding luxuries and making progress towards the end goal (see below)
-Set peices & Island Chains
Islands periodilcy popping up as you travel is all fine and good, but islands that tell stories are even better, and make exploration far more worthwhile. things like; Atolls, Hawaii style volcanic island trails, the camps & bones of preceeding survivors, a reef filled with shiprecks, and abandoned Japanese military base (now that would be impressive) or tunnel network. these things add reasons to explore more
-An end goal
if it proves impossible to reverse the decline of the player's mental health in the game, then it becomes a gradual race-against-the-clock to be rescued before the player's mind breaks. a fairly complicated series of events, requiring materials taken from a variety of islands & wrecks, end the game with the player being rescued.

Gorglax the Destroyer, an orlan aristocratic ranger, was far from home. Hell, she was far from civilization. The nearest town was a day's walk, and she needed medical attention. Ever since that storm she hadn't felt herself. She stared for a while at the clearing ahead, a quiet meadow painted purple by wildflowers in bloom. Birds chirped, flitted and fluttered. Bugs droned, bumbled and buzzed. A symphony orchestra was blasting all around her, which was more than a little jarring. Finally she was jerked from her daze by her antelope companion, Gary. “We have to get to Gilded Vale,” she said, breaking the silence. “MRRABLURGHHBLURGH,” agreed Gary the antelope (that is an approximate onomatopoeia of antelope noises).
They set off to find the road when two young wolves, truants probably, attacked. Gorglax raised her arbalest, wound it, and loosed a bolt into one wolf. It whined and bled out on the soft blanket of wildflowers as the other closed in, bearing its canines. Gorglax was done for, she couldn't wind her arbalest fast enough. She shut her eyes and had all but accepted her fate when Gary the ♥♥♥♥ing antelope butted the beast, causing it to explode in a gory geyser. After acknowledging how metal that just was, the pair continued on their adventure.
I liken video games to baking. Yes, the recipes are frequently rigid and mostly unforgiving of experimental deviation (one such deviation I made while baking resulted in what I've coined as “bread soup”); but even the most structured recipe allots for the 'dash,' the mysterious magic that often defines the finished product.
“Oh, this is simply DELICIOUS. What did you put in this?”
“Oh, this old thing? It's pretty standard: egg, milk, flour... and just a dash of magic.”
“MAGIC ISN'T AN INGREDIENT, TED.”
And yet that douchey non-response best describes what makes Pillars of Eternity so excellent:  it's an original CRPG with the combined minds, bodies, and souls of its classic predecessors. It is, perhaps, greater than the sum of its parts.
So for the mildly spoiler sensitive crowd, let's revisit at the last paragraph. Everyone else keep your hands and feet inside the review at all times.
Pillars of Eternity has you, the hero, traveling the land of Dyrwood, a mystical realm filled with beings, creatures, ruins, and adra – a sort of organic rock jutting from the earth like jade claws from the depths. You are (shockingly!) the chosen one of sorts, a Watcher – beings capable of seeing the previous lives of the inhabitants of Dyrwood, speaking to the dead. Most that claim to be Watchers are hucksters, charlatans, and the rest are often driven positively batty by all of the intrusive soul fragmented former lives (theirs included).
There's mystery, intrigue, ancient civilizations and arcane magics, unique party members to drag along... pretty standard RPG fare. There are troubled hamlets, a large city, a ruined fortress, and natural wonders to gawk at, all lovingly prerendered. The world and those settled there feel alive, and for the first time in a while I felt compelled to listen to every bit of dialogue, read every bit of codex, flavor text, all just to familiarize myself with this fascinating new world.
Of course you'll have to do some killing, it is an RPG after all. And you'll kill 'em all: wolves, giant spiders, lizard men, ghosts, bandits, trolls, wizards, spooky skeletons, mushroom men and dragons... Pillars of Eternity doesn't exactly break the mold when it comes to mythical beasties and foes, but the combat does. When an enemy is spotted your party will pause and you'll be able to select a general attack or take the time to individually select special actions for each party member.
When you do engage you'll see their various defenses, strengths, and weaknesses of your foe – dependent on factors like weapon type, flanking, status effects, etc. It's thoroughly tactical and engaging, and even on lower difficulty settings I watched my entire party succumb to one or two enemies because I just tossed them into the fray all willy nilly. After dispatching enemies your bestiary will be updated with pertinent information. There's also often sweet, sweet corpse loot; loot can be equipped, used for crafting, or sold to vendors.
I'll also touch briefly on the travel/sleepy time mechanics. See, the Eastern Reach is pretty expansive, and you'll be hoofing it from the get go. Day and night cycles, and characters will become fatigued from travel (not to mention bogged down by negative status effects after lots of fights). You have one of two options: camping out “in it” while adventuring, or shacking up at a number of permanent locations. Camping should only be used as is necessary, since you only have so many supplies to set up camp with, and some of the longer adventures will require your party to get that much needed refreshing between combat.
The minor-est of complaints! Here they come, ready yourselves. Because the world is prerendered and mostly static, fights will sometimes break out behind solid objects, which is a little frustrating (if you zoom in on a solid object obscuring a character it will become semi-translucent, but it's still a pain). And when you have a full party attacking enemies the notifications fly by in a flurry of text, which can make optimizing attacks difficult on the fly. Other than these quibbles the game is great. I've encountered no bugs, no glitches, and it's just overall a delight to play. Anyone familiar with classic BioWare fare and CRPGs will find themselves very much at home.
Pillars of Eternity is, simply put, really really good. The scope of it is dizzying, your first hour ingame may very well be in the character creation menu (but in a good way!), the combat is deeply satisfying, the score is GoT/LotR/Souls Series/Elder Scrolls Series all wrapped up in one, and  the story is thoroughly captivating. I haven't completed this game (it looks like the first of many playthroughs may well take 60+ hours), but short of it ending with an about-face “it was all a dream” or an elaborate song and dance number my sentiment will remain unmoved: Pillars of Eternity is a spectacular game, proof that old-school done right is timeless... it certainly helps that I'm playing as a dwarf/elf with a wisecracking antelope sidekick that explodes wolves.
That's always a plus.

I wish steam would allow a mixed rating because that would more accurately relate to my review.
At a glance, which is the most, the vast majority of people will see, the developers seemed to have every intention to continue to develop the game as is common with indie titles. They took a 3 month break with almost zero communication shortly after release and came back to announce they are 100% finished with the game beyond patching bugs and small QoL features.
So yes, it has been abandoned if you consider no additional content is coming, in a game that although is generally good (and in my opinion had the potential to be a classic like XCOM), is sorely lacking in content and in fact plays like a beta. As it is still missing key features such as battle map generation, this is not a minor feature nor are camp followers and dungeon locations.
To put into the context of food service, if you had purchased a very delicious burger and had seen a picture of it on the menu, but had only recieved a partial burger, no matter how delicious it ended up being, most people will still feel a little bit cheated. Many would even offer to pay additional money in order to get the full burger because it was so good and this is what I believe to be the situation with BB. The burger was actually so good that the customers are begging to be able to go behind the counter into the kitchen and make their own burger (modding).
Don't get me wrong, I definitely got my money's worth in playtime and it was generally fun as I was not turned off by how repetitive the game is. However not everyone likes playing the same dozen of missions that all play fairly similiarly to each other. Nor does everyone think its acceptable for every single battle to take place in randomly generated wilderness, unless near a road in which case one is present on the map. What are supposed to be the 2 most difficult battles in the game, the Monolith and the Goblin city are both identical to any other battle, except for the part you fight approximately 50 enemies at the same time instead of the usual 20 or so. No cool goblin city assets, or towering obelisk as it is displayed on the campaign map, just randomized wilderness. I mean seriously, for a fight like an orc warlord's camp, which is described to be a sea of tents, how hard can it be include tents in the tileset? The only signs of civilization are broken carts alongside roads in the battle map, so clearly the basic system has been implemented, there just isn't any art to go along with it.
In conclusion, the game is fun and well made but it is unfinished and the developers have no intention to continue working on it nor have they shown any interest in allowing to modders to do it for them.
I can only recommend you pick up this game on sale for at least 15 dollars on account of it being unfinished.
