After a loooooooooooooooooooooooooooong long time, Starbound finally got out of the early access. Thankfully. Cause the only thing that really killed my motivatio was the fact, that every update deleted your entire progress.
Now officially released, Starbound is a blast. If you are fans of games like Terraria or Minecraft, Starbound is the game for you. You have an astounding amount of worlds you can discover, a wide variety of biomes you can explore above and under the planet or can even try to become familiar with the fauna and flora of one of these planets.
You have the possibility to enjoy a story and after the story is done, you still get tons of things to do. Build a colony, upgrade your ship, search for funny or awesome vanity items, try to find unique weapons (for example a worm-like bumerang), become an archeologist, a farmer, head-hunter or hero, who saves local residents.
Since this is a sandbox game, you can become creative in so many ways...
Try to build a copy of Rapture from Bioshock, a sky island, turn a barren planet into a living one, shape entire places like you want to. Thanks to certain mini-biomes (like an 'eye'-biome), you can farm hilarious blogs and pieces, combine them into more hilarious things and create things you never knew you would create someday.
You can expect a lot of fun. Yet you may guess, that this game has certain flaws and for me, there are some.
FIRST OF ALL THIS DUCKING GAME TOOK WAY TO LONG TO DEVELOPE THE THINGS THEY WERE PROMISING SINCE THE BEGINNING! YES, I AM STILL MAD ABOUT IT AND WON#T CALM MY♥♥♥♥♥♥
Then I want to stress out, that the colony and crew can be annoying at times. NPC's tend to crowd one place and if your luck is really bad, you end up cloning your crew or get people out of nowhere in your colony because.....gnarflik! I am not kidding, sometimes the NPC's are annoying and do things they shouldn't do!
I have to admit, that the biomes and mini-biomes ARE keeping up a certain motivation to explore and look around.....but after a while you can't help but thinking, that those places look ever so often the same. I was looking for a certain vanity item at the dessert planets and literally 3 PLANETS looked the same. First castle, then swamp, then tar, then a little bit special. I know it is hard to pick on THAT one, but you can't help but feel tired after a while of seeing the same things over and over again.
But other than that, I really have a blast playing it. Sure I would LOVE to see certain things like incredible huge monsters on some planets (like a giant kraken at the ocean biome or a antlion in the dessert region) or some mini-bosses. Also the other enemies seem to be very repetitive in terms of attack patterns: Tackle it......tackle it........tackle it......here and there is one animal that shoots energy and flames......more tackling. At the earlier stages, monsters had a more diverse way of attacking.
Maybe we could have those mechs back. There are mods around who provide other vehicles, but I'd really love to see them as an inherent part of the game. Some unique weapons like the gloves need a bit more polishing, since for the majorityof time, a two handed sword is the weapon of choice.
Aaaaaaaaand..... I would like to have some more ingredients, recipes and plants for farming and cooking.
Overall I think that Starbound belongs to the top sandbox games out there. They took there time, but the result is really worth it =)

Major points for me:
- Inventory/storage management is horrible. There is no way to bulk drop/delete/sell/store items. In a super sprawling game like this, it's not really acceptable. Paired with the low amount of storage per crate (or similar), it's impossible to keep a base tidy while expanding during the game.
- Teleporting is nice, illogical, and takes too long. Currently, I have had to find a flower biome, and pick up a plant-fiber-tree to re sew near my base to keep up with my flag-production needs. As well as, there's a hard cap on the speed of spinning fiber to material, meaning I'm basically walking away from my computer to let all the cloth be spun to make only a few flags each trip or three to a planet.
Upgrades seem tacked on, but that's fine for an ever-expanding game.
The Main quest line takes you logically through the planet progression, and ramps up combat pretty nicely so far (I'm up to the 3 weird ores, just past durasteel)
But world just doesn't feel like one I want to get immersed in. I don't know why.
Is it the fetch quests? Is it the hour of sorting to 20 minutes of exploring? Is it the difficulty of finding settlements that allow you to progress with the main quest, and therefore artificially hold progress back? I'm not quite sure.
Also, I still don't know how it'll work with multiplayer. Want to find out.
Edit: just finished the game, after expanding to rooms-worth of storage.
Bosses become pretty easy with grappling hook and healing +3 EPP upgrade (with a decent offhand weapon, like the craftable max-level wand)
And I've missed parts of the game, that just seem unimportant/not fitting in. Fossils, I didn't really know what was even going on until I googled it (would've been helpful at the very start but not as much later). Wires, I didn't find ANY good use for, except inspecting traps in fixed missions. Pets were a novelty at best, since they seemed really destructible (and therefore fairly useless in combat)
I still wouldn't recommend it full price. At £3-£5, it'd be worth it. As it feels fairly small in the "amount of stuff to do" category.

Stacking takes place in the early 1900s and follows a boy named Charlie. Charlie’s family is taken and enslaved by the Evil Baron and he goes on an adventure to save them. Stacking was a game made by Double Fine, the people who made the brilliant game, Psychonauts. I had a great experience playing Psychonauts so I got my hopes up when I saw the same people worked on this game.
This game like any game had some flaws. A big one was the camera. It was a touch to close to the character and was obnoxious throughout the game. The story was nothing special and the character development was almost non-existent. The interest of playing went down the farther and farther you got, and it began to feel tedious going through the levels. The music was repetitive and annoying except for the intro song which was fantastic. I ended this game listening to a podcast and wishing it had just played the intro song over and over. It would have felt less repetitive. The cutscenes lasted too long and felt intrusive, but without the cutscenes there would be no story at all. When the main way of telling a story feels intrusive in your game, something needs to change.
Other than that everything was unique and creative. The aesthetic while it didn’t really fit, was definitely something cool and new. The game was charming and the humor was ok. Nothing special and without the charm it wouldn’t have worked. Some of it actually fit into the puzzle solving aspect which is smart. The puzzles were mostly well done and hard to figure out and the hint system was done really well.
All in all this game is pleasing to the eyes and not much else. If you like puzzle games, pick this up while it's on sale and if you have a kid you need to distract for a while, this will also work. $9.99 seems reasonable but it is overall a mediocre game. 5/10.

Feist is a stylized, physics-based platformer. Because of the way it looks, moodily lit with silhouette-based graphics, Feist initially seems reminiscent of LIMBO. But this is misleading. At heart, Feist is a totally different sort of game. Its core is not meditative puzzle solving but a near-frantic brawl. This is not without charm, but the significant difficulty of the fight mechanics made the game very tense and kept me from enjoying the game as much as I hoped.
In Feist you play as the forest-dwelling fur-ball version of Rambo. (‘Feist’ in Geman means round and furry, while in English ‘Feisty’ means aggressive. Both fit.) A band of creatures somewhere between molls and trolls have locked you in a cage and abducted your kin. You are following their column on its march through the wilderness, confronting them one by one.  The terrain is filled with spikey, hostile creatures that make quick work of tiny fur-balls like you. You fight back with your superior agility and make-shift weapons: swinging sticks, throwing stones, even getting them to shoot one another with stingers.
These breathless fights with catch-as-catch-can armaments are the centerpiece of play. The enemies have decent AI, meaning that things actually aim at you effectively, dodge unpredictably, or form swarms which follow you when you try to engage too many at once. The weapons also pose a big challenge. Many are one use: sticks break easily and, once thrown, projectiles must be retrieved. One can improvise a sort of gun by wounding a stinging fly and then picking it up, but these too can easily be destroyed or, worse, escape mid-fight to attack you further. This means that battle is a constant flit from one armament to another, dodging all the while, hoping that your scant hit points see you through. Then there are the moll-trolls themselves, tough bosses who are faster on their feet than you and can absorb significant damage before going down.
I like this idea in principle. It brings a gritty bar-fight sensibility to a platformer. But in practice it is wicked hard; a bit too hard for my taste. Some encounters early in the game took a frustrating number of attempts before I was able to win through, and even then my victory felt lucky. Getting struck in a fight causes you to drop whatever weapon you are currently holding, and you can’t carry more than one, so when the fight starts to turn against you it’s hard to even fight back. Admittedly, this does make each fight you walk away from feel like a triumph—there is no perfunctory combat in Feist. This game is definitely not for those who aren’t already seasoned platformer veterans.
The aesthetics of the game, on the other hand, were immediately enjoyable. The almost-silhouette graphics are done in a limited color palate, mostly blacks, whites, and shades of green. Care has been taken to give the illusion of depth and with extras like the texture of reflections in rough water. The world of Feist is damp and moody, and the music compliments this atmosphere. Also worth noting are the wonderful designs of the moll-trolls (I find myself wishing they were good guys).
One stray complaint in this department is the odd way enemies explode into pine-needles when killed. Feist’s combat seems so staunchly grounded and then this adds to it a discordantly dreamy effect.
To sum up, Feist is pretty to look at, and challenging to play. For somebody looking for a gritty, combat-centric take on the platformer, it would be a very enjoyable game. To me, who struggled through the initial difficulty curve, it was a moderately enjoyable one.
[Disclosure: I received a review copy of Feist from the developer.]

Unfortunately FEIST suffers from unfair comparisons with Limbo, but apart from the somewhat similar artstyle, the game is completely different, whereas Limbo is a slow paced, thoughtful game full of platforming and physics based puzzles. Feist on the other hand is very fast paced game where everone and everything in this unique world tries to kill you. It's a thrilling ride right from the start to finish, but bear in mind that sometimes you might get stuck on some of the really intelligent bosses, I have never seen such an adaptive enemy Artificial intelligence in a computer game. The enemies are ruthless, visceral and highly intelligent. Not only the bosses but other fearsome creatures possess an incredibly aggressive AI, the most annoying of these are the so called spider ticks whose attacks are so vicious to the point the game can become quite frustrating.
I repeated some of the chapters multiple times due to merciless nature of the enemy foes. Prepare to die a lot in this game, this isn't a walk in the park, even for an experienced gamer like myself, you'll die and you'll die a lot, but with the death comes vengeance, you'll get better with each death, memorizing each step carefully and you'll eventually become victorious.
The game itself has a a simple storyline, but this game isn't about the story, it's strongest part is the ferocious gameplay and I have to say for nearly 14 euro Iam satisfied, it took me over 3 hours and 20 minutes to beat the game, I'll probably be playing through the game once again to earn some of the achievements I missed on my first playhhrough. Some of them are pretty hard to get too.
If you're a fan of fast paced 2D platformer in a pretty world with awesome atmospheric music and vicious, but highly intelligent enemy AI, then go for it.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
If you like games in the mold of classic's like 'Limbo' then you're in for a treat here... Feist is a savage survival experience full of stunning visuals, dynamic creatures, and a haunting soundtrack. Follow strange beasts through lonely forests, hazardous mountains, dark caves, and glowing swamps. Watch out for dangerous creatures that react to your movements and decisions, and cleverly concealed traps that will test your ability to survive. Over six years in the making, FEIST is a gorgeous hand-made adventure unlike anything else, with a cinematic presentation reminiscent of The Dark Crystal or Hedgehog in the Fog, and a tense original soundtrack by Tomek Kolczynski. - Highly Recommended!

10 Hours in.
Right off the bat, I love this game's approach to learn-as-you-go "crafting". The interface isn't overly cumbersome like most survival games out on the market. You must choose when to seek crafting recipes and slowly make room for new items as you hit crafting milestones. Crafting is both rewarding and fun. You'll find that searching for the right materials is more like a scavenger hunt than a chore, though you will need to grind wood and food.
Inventory management left me frustrated, yet adequately challenged. Having only six slots available in the beginning is the biggest challenge for me. Fumbling your items around the camp in clustered piles is a necessity, since the craftable camp-storage upgrade limits you to two small chests (10 slots per chest).
As you discover more about the game's "secret economy", you will find equipment that becomes hard-locked to your person, meaning it cannot be dropped. It is crucial that you craft the Palm Sack or you will eventually become too encumbered to continue. In my 2nd playthrough, I made it past day 40, with two hard-locked items and no Palm Sack, which meant 4 free spaces available at any given time. As a result, I met my demise, since I wasn't able to collect enough wood to keep from freezing at night.
The story so far has been very engaging, slightly creepy, and somewhat obscure. Overall it works in harmony with the gameplay and art design. The game doesn't rush you in the beginning, giving you ample time to wander around and discover things. However, you should work fast because as the season change, food becomes more scarce. If you are unprepared for Autumn, you may find yourself in a bad way.
The graphics are simplistic, yet beautiful. The pixelated sprites have just enough definition to be recognizable as their real-world counterparts. The art design is incredible all around, especially in the dreamlike sequences.
Having just binged two playthroughs in a 10 hours timespan, I would highly recommend this game to anyone interested in a semi-casual survival game without the typical gameplay tropes that plague the genre. Yes, there is thirst, hunger, and a day-night cycle. However, these elements serve the game well and do not detract from the enjoyment of the journey.

Hero-based Tower defense that has RPG elements mixed in. Something like a third-person POV Orcs Must Die (hero-based TD) mixed with Diablo/Path of Exile (RPG elements like loot, spells, crafting, skill point upgrades, etc.). There are three archetypes of a hero that you can play: Sorceress (spellcaster), Mercenary (melee) and Marksman (ranged). I mainly played as the sorceress.
13 (+6 bonus levels) levels that you complete then repeat in 4 tiers of difficulty (harder versions of the same levels, sometimes with conditions/level-unique towers/optional objectives). You can earn up to 3 stars per level if you complete them on the hardest difficulty without dying/letting enemies through.
There seems to be no real story besides the opening and ending parts; each stage just has flavor text of descriptions of the area. In the sorceress' path, you're a defender to stop creatures that spawn from portals from reaching a gate that leads to your world. You keep moving towards the Inkheart for some unclear reason. There's a connection to the Van Helsing series but I haven't played those games so that's as far as my world knowledge took me.
Perspective can be a little annoying. Because it's an overhead camera and there are
sometimes I clicked at an enemy with a ranged skill and it missed. Usually happened on inclines (like stairs). Best option was to click directly on the creature.
It was annoying to miss a lightning bolt and be forced to wait another cooldown cycle.
The first two tiers of difficulty allow you to experiment and find a playstyle you enjoy. I played a utility/cc style and was happy with that. But that gets thrown away in Tier 3, which is when the difficulty randomly skyrockets at the 4th level and you're forced to minmax and find specific builds that work for the level. It becomes quite a different experience; instead of an easygoing game, it becomes a hardcore minmax fail-unless-you-optimize game. I guess the developers figured that if you played the same levels 3 times already that you are looking for that hardcore experience with that steep difficulty curve.
I beat it by minmaxing certain skills, maximizing essence gain, and playing at 1/2 speed most of the time. Instead of essence multipliers being a bonus, it became pretty mandatory. Since every life mattered, I had to stare at the enemy bar to see when a new wave came (normal waves come silently) because they like to try and sneak in fliers while you slowly kill the tanky walkers. I ended up beating the stage with over half life left (missed some fliers because I stopped looking at the minimap/monsters-currently-on-map section while kiting) while my old build couldn't get past the first wave.
I think most people who like the idea of a Diablo-TD game can enjoy the first two difficulty tiers in this game. Then there's a sudden brick wall and hardcore gamers who like to optimize and figure out strategies will enjoy the challenge of the higher difficulty tiers.

Overhype Studios is a Hamburg-based game development outfit with only three employees. It may seem improbable that a game so engaging could be produced by such a small team but play the game they've made and you will come to realise a small band of brothers can go on to achieve great things despite fearful odds.
In Battle Brothers, you play the newly elected leader of a group of mercenaries who've barely survived a disastrous attempt to capture Hoggart the Weasel. You don’t have much of a reputation. You don't have much in the way of resources. The remnants of your old company number but three. You have a warchest of 2000 crowns -- just enough to hire those whose eagerness to join the ranks of
far outstrips their ability to wield a weapon. Can you rebuild your company? Can you earn the trust of the noble houses? Can you make Captain Bernhard and One-Eye proud?
There's certainly plenty of opportunity for those in the business of war to profit here. Brigands keep a keen eye on the roads waiting for easy pickings. Creatures of the night which can rip a man apart or swallow him whole roam the lands. And out there in the borderlands lie the greenskins, salivating at the opportunity to wipe out all of humanity. Caravans will need escorts; villages will need protection; venerated relics must be retrieved.
It's all easier said than done. Even experienced strategy gamers might be taken aback by the game's brutal and uncompromising nature. This is partly due to the complexity of the fantastic turn-based combat system. Morale, fatigue and positioning all come into play. One man surrounded by mere brigands might turn to flee while another might grip his warband firmly and grin wolfishly at the target-rich environment. The terrible worm may be safely ensconced in his iron cocoon but he'll not dance nimbly about the battlefield. The marksman perched on high ground will find it easier to put "the eye to the cord, the cord to the shaft, and the shaft to the mark."
You'll need every advantage you can get because the AI in the game is pretty damn good and reason enough to look askance at the efforts of larger game developers. Direwolves filled with bestial rage will throw themselves mindlessly at your spearwall and desperate thugs are little better but raiders display cunning and sense of self-preservation, wolfriders circle around your frontline seeking your vulnerable archers and fully-armoured orc warriors are flat out terrifying the first time you encounter them. This variety in AI behaviour makes a game that invites multiple playthroughs over multiple weeks or months a pleasure to replay.
And replay it you will because the game is marvellously compelling. Just one more contract. One more battle. One more hire. One more level up. One more ambition achieved. Expect hour after hour to quickly fly past as you rebuild your company, turning your riffraff of no import into sellswords of fabled renown.
As one historian noted, however, prowess was not easily bought. Life as a battle brother is nasty, brutish and decidedly short and your men's heads have a disconcerting tendency to fall off after several days of service. If your fishermen, farmhands, masons and miners are to survive their early skirmishes against brigands, they must have arms and armour, neither of which come cheap, both of which require regular maintenance. Hiring fees must be paid up front, wages must be paid daily and provisions must be procured. The lack of money and manpower will be acutely felt in the early stages of the campaign.
Ultimately, the challenge has less to do with the economy, the enemy AI, the RNG or the complexity of the combat and more to do with decision-making. Few games will punish terrible decisions as severely and as early as this one. One mistake is not likely to end a campaign but a succession of mistakes in short order will result in the death spiral of any company. Your numbers will be too few to take on more dangerous contracts and your treasury, too small to beef up your company, dwindles daily. Desperation sets in and you're forced to take a contract you would otherwise turn down. Your men are faced with overwhelming odds. Win and you return to the path to prosperity. Lose and it's all over. You now know what must have been going through Captain Bernhard's mind in his final moments.
With mistakes so heavily punished, retreat is no disgrace. You are no chivalric ideal, no virtuous avatar meant to bring enlightenment to the lands. You're a businessman, pure and simple, and you don't get paid if you're dead. Leave the heroic last stands to the gloryhound nobles and their lickspittle military. Learn when to hold and when to fold, when to fight and when to flee.
The imperious highborn and the fat-pursed merchants may think lowly of you but who is to say how you will be remembered? If history tells us a sellsword once deemed diabolical would be hailed by some as a secular saint at his career's end, which will you be: some misbegotten sons of malediction reviled and quickly forgotten or a company whose deeds are still remembered years later?

Hand of Fate 2, a rogue-like card collecting with rpg elements.
First, this is a great successor to a game I thought would be a one-shot. Some of the major inconvenience that would make the game less enjoyable to play (I look at you combat) were refined. Do I recommend it? Since you see the blue thumb, I will let you guess that part on your own...
But what does Hand of Fate 2 offer?
It offer a gameplay that I would consider rather unique. As a rpg, you don't level up your stats, but the events you will encounter. Hand of Fate 1 did have this system that will make the player go on cards, solve a solution to win more cards afterwards. This will make you gain other events/quests to do, but also equipment that will be available later on.  For what I have seen, you will win (or lose) these card's event by playing a few smaller games. For example, rolling dices/spinning the wheel/choosing the right card.
But does that mean that it is all random and that you need extreme luck to succed some tests? Well... Yes and no. Yes because, well, sometime you do need luck to have successes. No because there are many way to make your onw luck. Some items in game will make tests easier (wheel is slower, bad card is marked, etc). But for me, I simply watch the cards as they are shuffled and pick up the clues from what I see. The cards that are dealed in front of you aren't randomized, you can track a card! Many people didn't realized that.
You will start each mission without much, but you will find equipment cards to simple put on your character. Another thing that was changed from the first game was the mission type you would be doing. In the first game, you would explore a dungeon, get the cards, go beat a boss and you were done. In this new installement of the game, there are many different quests with different goals. It does give different gameplay options, so you don't get bored by replaying exactly the same mission, but it also impact the atmosphere in a great way. You feel involved in the story that is actualy your own. You will also meet companions that will aid you in battle, change dialogues in quests when they are with you and that will have their own sets of quests.
The combat in Hand of Fate 2 is better than the first game. It is, however, still a bit gimmicky for my taste. But, this isn't a dealbreaker in my opinion. The variety of the weapons and of enemies make each combat pretty entertaining. When you understand the battle system, it remains simple to play without being overly easy like the first game. If some people count this as a con, I personnaly really like the ragdoll effect on the ennemies.
But Hand of Fate 1 did something I really loved and I didn't think they would be able to reproduce the result another time. The main enjoyment in the first game was the narrator/the Dealer and the atmosphere that was produced. For those who finished the first game, you know how it ends. I was surprised and scared to see him back in a sequel. Surprised to see him back, scared that he wouldn't deliver as much as in the first game. I was glad that these risk were unfounded. Hand of Fate 2 is really acing the atmosphere while bringing the gameplay to new heights.
So, if I was to resume everything...
Pro:
-Atmosphere is great. May in be while you are with the narrator or in the battlefield, it just feel good.
-Music is done right. It never got on my nerve, I could actualy play it for hours. Really great for the atmosphere as well.
-Artwork is beautiful. On the cards at least. I'll come back for the models.
-The story progression feels right, the missions are all different and the event cards you bring always make these missions feel different.
-The Dealer. He was the reason I played the first game, he still takes the cake. That voice is amazing!
-Character customization. It isn't too much elaborated, but enough to give you the feeling of being your own character. More than in the first one!
-The Devs are doing so muh to improve the game. This is worth so much as a pro in these days.
Neutral:
-Combat is better, but still a bit weird. At least it's not too easy/laughable.
-There is some twitch integration. Not that I mind too much, but you can vote for things to happen in a streamer game if you are into that stuff. I saw someone get the dealer to put the ''deal-with-it'' glasses and I thought it was funny.
-The character models are neat. In battles, they are ok in my book. Beside, for a side-part of the game, I believe they did the right amount of work in there.
-Luck. I don't mind, but some people do care about this aspect. Just know that you can create your own luck in some ways.
Con:
-Combat gameplay is still a con for me. It is better than before, but it is still the part I enjoy the less. And the tokens for the weapon cards are so grindy... My least favorite aspect of the game to be honnest.
Conclusion
Hand of Fate 2 is better in everyway to the first game. If you like the first, buy it. If you didn't because of the gameplay, this may be the version to change your mind.

Bottom Line:
If you like Mega Man or enjoy classic 2D run and gun gameplay with excellent controlls (with a controller - Keyboard NOT reccomended), Mega Man Legacy Collection 2 provides a look at 4 of the more experimental games in the Mega Man franchise that should not be missed.
What I'm not going to talk about:
The overall contents or quality of each game - you can find that out in the product description, critic reviews, or dozens of other reviews on Steam.
What I am going to talk bout - Version Differences:
There were a bevy of questionable cuts between the Japanese and American versions of both Mega Man 7 (SNES 16-bit) and Mega Man 8 (Playstation/Saturn 32-bit). Thankfully you have the ability to play both versions in this collection regardless of region - and I've yet to read any review that shares why you should check out the Japanese versions of these two games. For the record, Mega Man 9 and 10 are largely the same between regions and I will not be covering those.
To enable the Japanese versions, simply switch the language option in the Options menu to Japanese. While it puts the entire game in Japanese language mode - just notice what the options are or take a quick screen shot with your phone. The organization of options and menu text is the same across versions.
Also, these games are largely playable in Japanese as much of the main text you'll need is already in english. For the item purchase section or story sections, the auto-save feature works on both region versions so you can hop back and forth between the two at any time if you need a refresher on the english text. Overall though, this isn't much of an issue as the story is largely unimportant and you can play through the games easily without any knowledge of Japanese. Okay, that out of the way...
Mega Man/Rock Man 7:
While the changes in region in this game are far less than Mega Man 8, there are some notable differences.
-Boss Select: After selecting your stage from the select screen you are greeted with the classic boss introduction sequence. In the English version only the boss' name is displayed along with their signature sprite animation. In the Japanese version you also get a fun little quip about the stage. For example: When you select Cloud Man, his intro sequence includes the text "Watch your step!" Why these fun little quips were removed are beyond be. They were already in English.
-Item Get Screen: After beating a boss you are taken to Dr. Light's lab where, in the English version, he tells you about the weapon's abilities. In the Japanese version you speak to either Roll or Auto instead of Dr. Light. Auto has some funny animation sequences durring these scenes that add some more personality to the game. Again, I'm unsure why this was cut from the english version, but interacting with the other characters is a fun addition.
-Secrets in both versions: [Shade Man's Music] As long as you have not yet defeated Shade Man, hold down the A button (XB One or 360 controller) on the controller after selecting him and you will hear the map screen music from Ghosts and Goblins (another classic Capcom platfomer) play instead of boss intro fanfare. When you enter the stage the music changes to the iconic first level music from Ghosts and Goblins. This is a great remix that should not be missed. [Fighting Game Code]: I won't post it here, but look up online the password to access this mode. You can choose Mega Man or Bass in a 1v1 mini fighting game. [Cloud Man Stage] If you shoot the second floating weather bot with the Ice Cracker the rain will turn into Snow - which makes a later section of this stage much easier as the snow accumulates on otherwise invisible platforms. [Junk Man Stage] You can freeze all flowing lava with Ice Cracker to reveal hidden paths. [Thunder Bolt Weapon] You can use Thunder Bolt to light dark paths as it will apply a - rather impressive for the time  - light source that follows the ball of electricity across the level. There is a section of Shade Man's stage where this is particularly useful.
Mega Man/Rock Man 8:
To preface, Mega Man 8 had two different editions: Playstation and Saturn. The PS version was released first so the developers had extra development time on the Saturn version which led to a few additions and changes - Sadly, only the PS version of the game is the one used in this collection. Before I get into region differences, here is what you are missing from the Saturn version:
-Cut Man and Wood Man Boss Battles: In the Robot Museum stage after you beat the first 4 Robot Masters you can find a secret room not far from the entrance where you encounter Cut Man - a Robot Master from Mega Man 1. This battle works much like his original from MM1 complete with a brand new, beautifully animated sprite and remixed stage music from his original level. In Search Man's level, Wood Man is an added mini-boss missing from the PS release. Like Cut Man, Wood Man has a beautifuly redrawn sprite and remixed stage music from MM2.
-Different Music: In Tengu Man's stage the PS version music does not fit well with the rest of the score. The Saturn version has a much more fleshed out redition of this song which is rather awesome if you've never heard it. Look it up on Youtube if you want to hear the differences without playing in-game. Some other music tracks are basically the same, but given hardware differences some of the music sounds richer overall on the Saturn version.
Region Differences:
Voice Acting: Mega Man 8 is known for it's notriously bad voice overs. While everyone should experience how bad these are for themselves, the Japanese version uses high quality voice overs that really add some pop to the bland English version. Much like anime dub's from the 90's, this game is no exception. Also, Mega Man still has a high voice - but it actually fits the character nicely instead of being jaring, high pitched mess.
Missing Voices: The English version also cut many of the voices from the boss encounters. In the Japanese version every boss has 2-3 different lines they use to introduce themselves when you enter their chamber - these are all but gone in the English release. There are also more voice samples overall durring the battle with the bosses. There are some other in-game quips that were cut from the English edition as well here and there. If you want the full voiced experieince, the Japanese edition is the way to go.
Wrap-Up:
There are some other subitle differences between versions like all Japanese versions of Mega Man (Rock Man) have a subtitle - Mega Man 8 is actually Rock Man 8: The Metal Heroes in Japan. Mega Man 7 is missing a screen when you boot it up that lists the first 6 games in the series and their release year - etc. There is one sad omission here: The Japanese version of MM8's animated intro was replaced with the English version due to an expired copywrite licence of the J-Pop song Electric Communication used in the original versions of the game. I highly reccomend looking up "Playstation Rock Man 8 OP" on Youtube to check out this awesome track. It is sorely missed from this collection and fit the action of the OP (opening) much better).
Overall, this is a more complete package than I was expecting, and the emulation is spot on. Sadly, there is no good way to play the definitive Saturn version of MM8 without having an actual Saturn and copy of the game. No Saturn emulator works 100%, and the most popular, SSF, is met with input latency that kills twitch heavy games like Mega Man.
Anyway, hope this breakdown of differences in versions was helpful!

Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe is a 2D puzzle platformer constructed around stealth mechanics with an elegant pixelated presentation. You take control of a clone trying to escape a deadly facility using merely planning and precise platforming skills, while “someone” gives you hints and snarky comments about your performance as you progress through each room.  Often as I failed to properly plan my course of action I was greeted with a “you really though that would work?”   from my mysterious watcher, or even a “I  like your thinking” as I realize the use of a puzzle piece. These comments not only serve as great tools to complement what can only be considered as great level design, but also set a humorous tone to the experience, turning many times a frustrating attempt into an amusing misstep.
Unlike several games in the stealth genre, Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe does not suffer from the “waiting syndrome”. Despite the fact that timing is key to  successfully traverse  many of the levels, you rarely find yourself simply waiting for an enemy to reach certain position or for a switch to active. This allowed a more fluid gameplay and also a higher difficulty without becoming punishing. This fluidity, coupled with the fact that every sector introduces a new element, which drastically alters the gameplay, gives this game a greatly satisfying pace.

Review edit: They've since fixed the "immediate crash on startup" issue, but many still persist. My review of gameplay will be below these. As such, I *still* can't recommend buying this game, due to these two major issues:
-Unable to put the game into fullscreen. If you do, the game blackscreens and/or immediately crashes
-Game randomly crashing in solo play. It's happened with lots of enemies on the screen, no enemies on the screen, lots of items/money on the screen, and with absolutely nothing else on the screen except yourself. Because of this, I haven't been able to get past level 5 because my game always crashes on or before it.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is actually pretty fun. Controls are responsive, the item system feels rewarding and exciting, and the classes bring diversity in a game that might grow stale fast. Connecting hits on enemies gives awesome visual and sound effect feedback, giving you that rewarding feeling every time you kill an enemy (and boy are there lots of enemies).
My biggest issue revolves around melee classes, and how underwhelming they are to ranged classes. Enemies deal damage on contact and immediately attack as soon as they get into range. Ranged enemies will fire at you from multiple screens away. Items that give passive health regen are few and far between, while your potion stock can become very scarce after getting hit by a trap or getting caught between a few enemies. Ranged classes, despite having less max health (the Barbarian class has 150 health and the Thief class has *40* health and I've always done significantly better as the latter), tend to just take less damage because of this.
I've only got a few hours on it as of this review (because of the crashing issue), but this game is genuinely a great time and I seriously hope that the devs keep working on and updating it.

Stacking was a brilliant game start to finish.  I played through the whole thing, including the DLC, and wasn't bored or getting fed up with it for a single minute.
Having played the incredible Psychonauts, I have no idea why I left it so long to play "Stacking".  I think it was because it seemed 'silly', which is odd, considering I loved their other game about a bunch of paranormal cadets in a cartoon universe.
As you can probably tell, the game is played in a universe where Russian matryoshka dolls live together.   The smallest dolls are "children", and the ever-larger dolls are grown-ups.   You play as a tiny child doll who has the rare ability to 'stack' inside other dolls.  You can only stack inside a doll one larger than yourself, but you can stack over and over until you're in the largest dolls.
The "levels" are set up with three things:
* A story plot, which you need to play through in order to win
* A set of dolls which you can use to play the game.  Some are 'special'.
* A set of challenges and other fun distractions to do while playing.
The story is that your family has been abducted, and you have to go rescue them.   You start off in a "hub" level, the Royal Train Station, which in typical DoubleFine fashion is host to a number of fun and interesting puzzles.    From the train station, you take trains to the various 'levels' where you play through the story to rescue your family, and ultimately win the day.
There are dozens (hundreds?) of dolls in each intricately crafted area.  some of the dolls are 'unique', while some are clones.  If you stack into unique dolls, you get an achievement, and a little trophy back at base.    Each of the dolls has an ability, which can be used on other dolls.  Some abilities work on a class of doll (all men, or all children), while some abilities work on specific dolls.  The key to winning is working out which doll to use when.
The puzzles are all relatively easy, and you can play through by solving the puzzles in the most obvious way.  Usually, just talking to the doll you need to get past is enough to tell you how to do it.  For example one doll might say "I am scared of clowns", so there's your clue how to get past.     However, each challenge has between 3 and 6 ways to defeat it, and some of the ways are downright devious.   They're mostly pretty logical though, and I only had to google two of them because the combinatorial number of options was scarily large.  However in both occasions, I should have just been more patient.
The add-on DLC, "The Lost Hobo King" is a great piece of DLC.  It uses the same style and puzzle format as the main game, but adds a few new bits and bobs to keep it fresh.   The usual tongue-in-cheek slightly adult humour shows through in the  add-on.
All the way through, the game tries to look "Victorian", with self-playing pianos, steam trains, zeppelins and monacled bad-guys.  The music is all twinkly piano music or violins, and the cut-scenes are shot in a style to evoke 1920s black and white movies.
This was a really fun, really nice little game. I really enjoyed playing it through.  Double-fine certainly know how to make a cute, fun game.

Edit:
The devs fixed part of the problem I was previously experiencing. The game now launches into a black screen but I can, at least, change the resolution in windowed mode and play normally.
As for the game itself, I think it's a very fun and interesting roguelike. The different classes and multitude of interesting items make the game fun and interesting with each playthrough. So far in the game, the hardest and most dangerous thing is not getting randomly murdered by a boulder that you accidentally triggered.
The classes have different strengths and weaknesses, with some of them feeling a little stronger than the others. Some will breeze through difficult parts and others will just have a tough time with the same situation.
The UI isn't perfect, story text is difficult to read due to the odd pixel font used. M&K controls seem to completely outclass gamepad controls, as it was difficult to get used to the camera movements when using my controller. It took me some time to figure out how to increase the level of my skills, as it isn't the same as an attribute upgrade.
Overall I think the game is a good time waster, well worth the money I spent on it and I hope the devs continue to improve some of the less appealing parts of the game.

I'm a fan of Double Fine and their creative style of game making. Unfortunately, Stacking isn't one of their finest games. It is, however, one of their most inventive. In this puzzler, you play as a Russian stacking doll who must save his family. Of course, you accomplish your goal by stacking into other stacking dolls, each with their own unique abilities. Each puzzle you're given has a few solutions, so the game encourages you to try out different ideas. It's most certainly very clever (and with a fun Lego style of humor to boot), but there's something missing here. The game feels too small and limited to really deliver on its premise effectively. Each puzzle only has a few set solutions, taking away the experimentation aspect of the game. It's also overloaded with cutscenes that take away from the flow of the game. Again, the premise is certainly there, but it seems better suited for a more open game more akin to Lego Worlds.
There's also such a weird disconnect between the gameplay and the game's style. It's a game about Russian nesting dolls that draws from old American silent films. There was a great opportunity here to play around with Russian culture, but instead we're treated to a somewhat arbitrary coal-era American setting. The stacking doll mechanic doesn't really connect to the game's themes or ideas in a terribly coherent manner, making the final product feel like a hodge-podge of mismatched ideas.
Despite it's flaws, this is still a very cute and clever idea from Double Fine, and as always, I tip my hat to their innovative thinking. But this isn't the best example of how great they are at making games. It's more so a fun example of how developers can think outside the box to make new experiences.
(Note: I received this as a gift from a friend.)

Just finished this game, took me the exact number of 111 minutes, and... the best way to describe it is "It only needs to be polished".
The game has a curious way of telling you where to go, and knows it has nothing to do with verbal storytelling, nor having a complicated argument. The far you go, the clearer it becomes you've gone the right or wrong path, and it just feels right to know you have sorted out every challenge without help from anyone. I think this is the message that the game is trying to say. As life goes on, bad and good decisions will be made. And when you make a bad one, it just doesn't work, no matter how hard you try to pull it out. But if you back up a bit and take a moment to think, that illogical trial that seemed to big to make it becomes a simple puzzle on which you just have to wait until the platform starts moving.
That being said, It's biggest flaw are the special phases. The main game is played as third-person open-world where you can run and search for the 8 golden stones. But some of them are only obtainable after defeating a special phase on which the game changes to present a different challenge, including racing, sword fighting and sky diving. And I really liked them. A lot, in fact. But they were just too short. Once I got my hands on how to drive the motorcicle,I finished it's level and never saw it again, and the same with the other two. I would really love to see more of them, and not just get limited to a short moment.
For the rest of the game, I don't really have anything to complain about. It's a game about realizing what to do, and it's confusing and low-poly aesthetic fits very well. The music is what you would expect it to be, and the camera and controls work nice if you learn how to use them. It just needs polishing: Exaggerating a bit the jump animations, working on some hitboxes and skins that don't work as they should...
Lastly, The only remainimg advice I can give is making the camera controllable by the mouse. It would help a lot making the game more intuitive

This game is very good... incredible actually. The gameplay captures many emotions at different times. The first time you light that makeshift bonfire... the fear and excitement when you find a sucken ship deep in the dark blue... and, in my case, buying a new mouse when I killed my first shark. Yep, so excited that I somehow broke my mouse. I am quite positive this game could go far. The exploration is intense. The weather can make or break you (good thing. No, really). The danger feels so real that I have to take breaks for fear of a heart attack. Bottom line: this game is fantastic and only getting better.
There are a few places that need tweaks that I've noticed since the last update a couple days ago. The ability to fly while carrying a shark is still there. Its better but still there. It would be loads of fun if gravity wasn't so... but sadly she is a harsh mistress. The sharks seem to be a main source of the lag spikes for me. The worst lag spikes seem to come when I get landsharks. This was a terrifying first experience. The cause of these seems to be the spawn points for sharks being too close to the ocean bottom. This causes some of them to clip into the sand and be able to follow you on land.
I would like to see more creatures in future updates. I have poked and cooked crabs and small fish. I have had ferocious battles with different types of overly-aggressive sharks. I have ridden on a whales back while slashing it to no avail (yet). While all this is exciting and fun, I would very much like to have the opportunity to make a bow with some arrows for some tropical birds or something. The bulk of the game happens underwater. While this might be the aim, I still think the land could use some more work. Not so much as to render the underwater useless, but enough to want to be on land at all.
All-in-all I would highly recommend this game to anyone seeking a thrill. It is still in developement, so you will have to be patient and wait for fixes and additions. However, I feel that it is worth the money as is. I am eagerly looking forward to further additions and updates. Keep up the great work guys!

It’s a different take on point and click adventure games but fails to live up to anything substantial.
Is there a story? Despite finishing the game, I’m really not sure at all. All I know is that you are a girl named Lilly who is searching for her brother who got kidnapped by a red cloth…. It’s kind of vague. I feel like there is supposed to be an underlying story by the fact that the ending hints at something but it’s literally a 3 second animation/dialogue so eh. Practically speaking, non-existent. AND IT ENDS ON A CLIFF HANGER.
It’s a twist on an adventure game. You don’t move the character by clicking on certain spots like in most adventure games but instead click on predetermined spots to move there/do something there. It’s a system that helps newcomers learn the basics and allows for a good hint menu but the problem is that there is no way to interact with the environment and learn more. I can’t learn the backstory about the other kid. I can’t talk to him, I don’t even know who I am. There is no narrative and thus, the world seems kind of dead. This is a damn shame because the world is beautifully crafted but utterly wasted.
The second gimmick is that you can switch between the future and the past. This allows for some interesting puzzles where you can (for example) create paths by moving where to plant an acorn. Those puzzles are nice but there are about 3-4 puzzles that use this gimmick at all before the game takes it away. I thought this would be the central element but overall, I didn’t understand the point of it and it seemed wasted.
The puzzles themselves followed some bizarre logic. The tree puzzle mentioned earlier made sense and was logical in its steps but later puzzles had you do color manipulation but you had to figure out what all of the buttons did and what the end goal was. It was adventure game logic to an amazingly bad degree and it completely killed any motivation I had to actually get into the puzzles. They were contrived as hell.
(with a 970, 4790K, 16GB of RAM, SSD)
The game is beautiful and looks like each scene was hand crafted but it chugs. Yes it’s pretty but not that pretty. The frame rate goes between 30-50 but I don’t know why. There isn’t an options menu where I can change my resolution so I had a weird scaled version that looked slightly off. The background music is pretty but the voice acting is extremely poor and I could barely hear it.
This seems like a proof of concept game. A place where people can try out making a game and seeing what works. Each area mentioned above shows promise but the execution is off. Play it if you really having nothing else to do but otherwise, it’s a pass

(The exclamation marks rank how much emphasis I put into the different topics I bring up here.)

- Intriguing and dynamic gameplay (!!)
- Always given a player's choice, as opposed to following scripted events constantly (!!)
- Gives you a fun experience by simulating how one would act in a similar situation (!!)

Overhype Studios is a Hamburg-based game development outfit with only three employees. It may seem improbable that a game so engaging could be produced by such a small team but play the game they've made and you will come to realise a small band of brothers can go on to achieve great things despite fearful odds.
In Battle Brothers, you play the newly elected leader of a group of mercenaries who've barely survived a disastrous attempt to capture Hoggart the Weasel. You don’t have much of a reputation. You don't have much in the way of resources. The remnants of your old company number but three. You have a warchest of 2000 crowns -- just enough to hire those whose eagerness to join the ranks of
far outstrips their ability to wield a weapon. Can you rebuild your company? Can you earn the trust of the noble houses? Can you make Captain Bernhard and One-Eye proud?
There's certainly plenty of opportunity for those in the business of war to profit here. Brigands keep a keen eye on the roads waiting for easy pickings. Creatures of the night which can rip a man apart or swallow him whole roam the lands. And out there in the borderlands lie the greenskins, salivating at the opportunity to wipe out all of humanity. Caravans will need escorts; villages will need protection; venerated relics must be retrieved.
It's all easier said than done. Even experienced strategy gamers might be taken aback by the game's brutal and uncompromising nature. This is partly due to the complexity of the fantastic turn-based combat system. Morale, fatigue and positioning all come into play. One man surrounded by mere brigands might turn to flee while another might grip his warband firmly and grin wolfishly at the target-rich environment. The terrible worm may be safely ensconced in his iron cocoon but he'll not dance nimbly about the battlefield. The marksman perched on high ground will find it easier to put "the eye to the cord, the cord to the shaft, and the shaft to the mark."
You'll need every advantage you can get because the AI in the game is pretty damn good and reason enough to look askance at the efforts of larger game developers. Direwolves filled with bestial rage will throw themselves mindlessly at your spearwall and desperate thugs are little better but raiders display cunning and sense of self-preservation, wolfriders circle around your frontline seeking your vulnerable archers and fully-armoured orc warriors are flat out terrifying the first time you encounter them. This variety in AI behaviour makes a game that invites multiple playthroughs over multiple weeks or months a pleasure to replay.
And replay it you will because the game is marvellously compelling. Just one more contract. One more battle. One more hire. One more level up. One more ambition achieved. Expect hour after hour to quickly fly past as you rebuild your company, turning your riffraff of no import into sellswords of fabled renown.
As one historian noted, however, prowess was not easily bought. Life as a battle brother is nasty, brutish and decidedly short and your men's heads have a disconcerting tendency to fall off after several days of service. If your fishermen, farmhands, masons and miners are to survive their early skirmishes against brigands, they must have arms and armour, neither of which come cheap, both of which require regular maintenance. Hiring fees must be paid up front, wages must be paid daily and provisions must be procured. The lack of money and manpower will be acutely felt in the early stages of the campaign.
Ultimately, the challenge has less to do with the economy, the enemy AI, the RNG or the complexity of the combat and more to do with decision-making. Few games will punish terrible decisions as severely and as early as this one. One mistake is not likely to end a campaign but a succession of mistakes in short order will result in the death spiral of any company. Your numbers will be too few to take on more dangerous contracts and your treasury, too small to beef up your company, dwindles daily. Desperation sets in and you're forced to take a contract you would otherwise turn down. Your men are faced with overwhelming odds. Win and you return to the path to prosperity. Lose and it's all over. You now know what must have been going through Captain Bernhard's mind in his final moments.
With mistakes so heavily punished, retreat is no disgrace. You are no chivalric ideal, no virtuous avatar meant to bring enlightenment to the lands. You're a businessman, pure and simple, and you don't get paid if you're dead. Leave the heroic last stands to the gloryhound nobles and their lickspittle military. Learn when to hold and when to fold, when to fight and when to flee.
The imperious highborn and the fat-pursed merchants may think lowly of you but who is to say how you will be remembered? If history tells us a sellsword once deemed diabolical would be hailed by some as a secular saint at his career's end, which will you be: some misbegotten sons of malediction reviled and quickly forgotten or a company whose deeds are still remembered years later?

This is honestly one of my favorite games. It's a great "wilderness survival game" with some roguelike and story elements. I like it's concept, it's graphics, it's music and it's depth. First the bad - There are some aspects of the game design that I find frustrating. Inventory space seems too limited. Areas you can remember also seems limited. Time in the day to do stuff also feels limiting. But while I find these limitations frustrating, it's these very things that make the game so darn challenging. It's not meant to be quickly played through once and forgotten. Rather - this is a game where you will likely die often. But each time you'll learn a bit more about yourself, these woods and the odd story that unfolds as you try to survive in the trippy wilds. I'm not a "HUGE" fan of modern pixel art games, however the implementation of such in this game is nothing short of beautiful. The abstract graphics somehow add to, rather than take from - the overall trippy atmosphere of the game/experience. I have yet to beat it. I doubt I've even come close. But I will keep coming back to these woods to discover how to survive them and eventualy get out of them. I honestly suspect that even when I do beat this game, I'll continue coming back to it just for the experience of living in this wonderful forest. Deathtrap is a tower defense ARPG based on the tower defense part of the Van Helsing series.  If you liked that part of Van Helsing, you'll probably like this.  The difference is that there is no open world here; the game is played in progressive stages where you get a set amount of essence (the main resource) at the beginning of each to build and upgrade towers, and you get more within each stage from killing enemies.  Also like Van Helsing, you still play a character of one of three classes, get gold, loot, experience at the end of each stage, and upgrade points for completing each stage depending on the difficulty and how well you did, as well as for completing quests within each stage.  The character development is fairly similar to Van Helsing; you get three skill points per level to spend on class skills.  The upgrade points are separate and upgrade your traps individually.  Both can be respecced for gold, and there is also a store in between levels.
Pros:
+There is a lot of content (13 stages x 4 tiers, the same map on a different tier isn't just higher level versions of the same stuff, but a completely different layout of traps, enemies, and quest objectives.)  There are also optional scenario-only maps and player-made maps.  Scenarios are stages where you are able to set certain difficulty modifiers in exchange for increased gold, exp, and loot.
+Decently interesting skill synergy between the character skill upgrade and trap upgrade points system.
+Relatively unique game; there aren't many tower defense games that have as much focus on character growth.  Dungeon defenders is the only similar game I can think of.
Cons:
-The experience system.  Any map more than a level or two below your current level gives no experience at all.  This is particularly annoying given that players will probably be going back to several stages because they were unable to complete it on hard, complete a quest, or otherwise get all the upgrade points initially.  Scenario mode gives almost no experience, even with the +90% exp difficulty modifiers on, regardless of which map you use.  Endless mode gives fair experience for the first few waves, but then exponentially too much experience after that.  Playing to wave 8 gave me about 60k xp.  To wave 25, gave me 700k exp (leveled from 81 to 90).  To wave 36, 1.8 million exp (leveled from 50 to 80).  The maximum level is 100.
-Some stages are just too long.  Earlier stages only take a few minutes, some later ones take 25-40+.  Endless mode should have an option to start at any wave you've reached before, as it takes several hours (even at x2 speed) of just waiting to reach the higher waves otherwise, or alternatively have a much higher speedup function.  A high level character can get all the essence they need to fully build out a map in one or two waves, and then do nothing for 20-30+ waves until the enemies get strong enough that they need to play.
TL;DR overall, I would rate 8/10.  Tweak the exp system so that lower level maps have maybe a penalty but not a strict 0% cutoff, make endless mode exp linear and not exponential, and make scenarios give a lot more exp (in line with doing a current level map + modifier), and it would be better.

I really want to love Starbound, I've been waiting for it for years...but I can't. It's a simple problem of control. I never appreciated just how tight and easy simply interacting with Terraria is until I'd spent only a few hours in Starbound, and all those minor problems add up to sheer frustration at why the hell Starbound doesn't just copy the best parts of the Terraria setup like anyone with sense would do. It's like making a Total War game but not wholesale copying the battlefield control scheme in favour of some different, crappier version.
For me, it can be boiled down to some important problems:
1) Field of view. Terraria has a generous field of view and Starbound doesn't. You can press CTRL to move it around, but that's nothing compared to simply pulling the view out and letting us actually SEE the world. Even if the underground were fully lit, you're still fumbling around blind compared to the original, and sadly far better implemented 2D survival craft-em-up Terraria.
2) Momentum. This creates the biggest point of utterly frustrating lack of control in Starbound. Your character controls like a heavy brick in the air, then the situation flips over when landing, where your character never seems to 'stick'. The result is that while you'll have fun spelunking around in Terraria because you have a generous field of view and slick, precise control of your character, in Starbound you're stuck in a claustrophobic postage stamp of space with a character that you can't feel entirely in control of.
3) Poor controls and UI setup. In Terraria you just tap down to drop through a platform. Quick, easy, affords you perfect control; Starbound has a duck seemingly just so they could have another pointless boondoggle for challenge rooms, and so to drop down you press down and jump. It makes a hell of a difference. On once hand you can move up and down the environment with two single button presses in an intuitive fashion, on the other, you're having to perform a button combo to move in one of the four cardinal directions....utilising one of the buttons you use to move up. And it's the cardinal direction that will instantly slaughter you with fall damage if you mess it up. Genius.
Then there's weirdly obtuse things like containers, which can be opened with E, but only closed by clicking on the X or hovering over the container which is now BEHIND the UI and pressing E again....instead of just pressing E again. Doesn't sound bad....until you want to get out of the UI quickly because of an enemy and can't, or if you've got lots of crates to go through.
4) Garbage early game. The early game of Starbound is unacceptably frustrating and boring. You've got a character that's needlessly imprecise to control, a characterless starting world, and then you potentially have to take that easily fall killed character all the way to the very bottom of that characterless world before you're allowed to progress. You literally have no other way to progress, you HAVE to go to the bottom of that world AND climb all the way back up.
This creates a game where there's no joy in exploring because simply interacting with my character and the environment is frustrating. There's no excuse for such problems when you're effectively a follow-up to Terraria which did these things better before you even existed.
Starbound has a lot of content, but the problem is that interacting with that content is clunky and frustrating. It doesn't matter how good the rest of the game is when simply moving around and interacting with the rest of the game is needlessly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.

Starbound is in many respects a lacking game.
I say this from the perspective of someone that plays sandbox type games with a focus on the combat, progression and exploration aspects of the experience. Therefore I will not comment on what it is like to build a settlement or how powerful your constructions tools are with regards to what you are capable of doing with them.
After an introductory part where you are introduced both to the different systems in the game and to the main storyline, Starbound establishes a persistent gameplay and progression loop. You will be given a quest to travel to a new type of planet, where you must discover and inspect the settlements of the world's inhabitants. After so doing, you will go through a short dungeon sequence and face off against a boss enemy. This process will then repeat - you will be directed to a new type of world and the loop starts over.
This type of gameplay loop can no doubt work. The problems I experienced with it lie in its surrounding systems. Difficulty-wise, each new planet represents a new tier of difficulty (which is indicated in the game itself when it gives you a risk assessment of the planet you are about to go to). This means that there will be one or two new types of materials that you are encouraged to gather in order to upgrade your armour and crafting stations. You are also sometimes required to upgrade a certain equipment piece in order to be able to live while visiting the next tier of planet.
The main factor that hampers enjoyment is the rigidness of the described loop. When you are playing, you can fairly accurately predict what you will be doing in an hour or two from now. This is not a problem if what the player is tasked to do is exciting, but it is not. The reason for this stems from several issues, namely:
Equipment variety is very limited. Each new armour you pick up will be a stat improvement in every aspect. But it will not have a special ability that is only tied to that set. This means that no matter what armour you pick up, they will not alter your playstyle in the slightest. It also means that you will never be making a choice between different special effects or raw stats. This makes armour upgrades very uninteresting.
The choice to treat armour in this way is perhaps surprising when comparing them to the available weapons. There are different types of weapons and within those types there are different abilities. Moreover, weapon statistics differ based on type and rarity. This means that you will have a lot more choices to make here than you did with your defensive equipment. As with most games it is relatively easy to figure out what does the most damage per second and will be the most efficent, but it should still be stressed that there is an excitement to discovering new weapons and testing their special abilities.
Unfortunately the crafting system sells the weapon variety short in a way. The weapons that you yourself have available to craft are very underwhelming in comparison to the weapons that you will find in the wild. There are some possible exceptions to this with a few legendary weapons that become available for crafting in the game's hub. For the early and middle parts of the game however, what comes out of your own crafting stations is laughable in comparison to whatever you will pick up out of random chests and boxes scattered all over the worlds. It is therefore not worth the resources to invest in offensive crafting most of the time.
What I described above comes together to be a problem once you've found the highest damage per second weapon available at your tier. You will be using the same armour as any other player and your weapons are unlikely to be much different. What this boils down to is that there is very little differentiation between player characters. The game does not support many different and effective playstyles. If you were to draw a comparison to similar games such as Terraria that allow you playstyle customisation in the form of many combinations of both armours, accessories and weapons then the variety on offer in Starbound falls short.
Previously I mentioned that the game is very rigid. This applied to the weapons and armour discussion, but it is also applicable to the environments. One of the reasons that you can predict what will happen after you reach a new planet is that the planets have a set, two-part layout. They have an overworld consisting of one or sometimes two different types of environments. There is also an underworld beneath the ground which holds a majority of the new materials you should gather. What this means is that one planet will not offer you many different experiences. I believe it is a design choice made to keep the player chasing after new worlds, but it does not work as well as it should when you have already experienced a large part of what a world has to offer the minute past your arrival. I do want to note that I have seen a few unique types of locations on different worlds, but they were usually the only unique thing about that world and did not force me to adjust my playstyle in any meaningful way.
Something else that came up as lacking was monster identity. Although the monsters are unique in their looks and sometimes their abilities, their impact on me as a player is not very big. As an example, there are several monsters that become invulnerable for a few seconds after being struck by a weapon. This did force me to wait around a little before being able to kill them, but it didn't bring moments of excitement. I wasn't holding my breath or asking myself if I could possibly evade a devastating incoming attack. The end effect is that because monsters didn't particularily stand out from one another in terms of what gameplay effect they had on me as a player, I felt them to be very identical to eachother.
I've already written a lot on what I believe are the most important things to mention. However I do want to say that there are other things that also could be improved on. Sidequests are uninteresting and generally unrewarding, controls feel slightly unresponsive and the weapon balance is somewhat off. For me there is definitely a feeling of a lack of polish in many aspects.
Lastly, I believe it's necessary to say that I have not experienced everything this game has to offer. Perhaps the gameplay loop will be altered later on. Maybe the armour and weapon variety increases. I do not know. What I mentioned in this review are my more negative thoughts as they stand close to 10 hours into the game. There were definitely positive aspects to the game, such as the random challenge doors that appeared in the underground. If anything, that's a feature that should be expanded upon even more.
As it stands however, I cannot recommend Starbound to someone who is looking for depth in the areas of combat, progression or exploration. As an alternate recommendation, I would definitely suggest Terraria if you have not already played it.
