Short Version:  If you liked Hand of Fate, you'll like Hand of Fate 2, though you might find yourself missing the old game while you play.  If you haven't played the first game, it's great - go play it.  If you like it, get the sequel, too.
Hand of Fate 2, like its predecessor, is an indie rogue-like RPG alternating between turn-based, card-themed strategy game and Arkham-style combat encounters.  Your object as player is to amass powerful cards representing not only your equipment and powers, but also the encounters themselves.  This means that you are basically deck-building the level you play against as well as the rewards you receive for overcoming obstacles - which leads to a wide variety of strategic decisions and opportunities, both as you plan for a level, and as you play through it.
The sequel is "bigger and better" in the sense that there are more challenges to anticipate, the levels are more structured and varied than in the first game, and there's a much greater emphasis on a scripted story rather than emergent storytelling.  Each level has its own new set of mechanics, its own new object, and a number of unique encounters - all of which escalate and contribute to the larger story.
The good news is that these new mechanics and new structures are all interesting and offer unique challenges to try and overcome with your gradually-growing collections of cards.  Each level is surprising and exciting as you learn to work with the new rules, and there are a few cases where you can "outsmart" the game, using combinations of cards to "break" the mechanics and solve challenges in interesting ways.
But the story is a bit lackluster, the dealer's lines aren't nearly as threatening as they were in the first game, and the diverse mechanics, while interesting, don't seem as "pure" as they were in the original Hand of Fate.  When you hit a combat encounter in the first game, you had no idea what you would encounter - a team of plague rats or a giant lizard king or a posse of bandits or a lich.  In this game, the combat encounters are much more scripted.  You ONLY encounter empire enemies with this card - only northerners with that one, etc.  The danger of the randomness has been largely sacrificed, and that's too bad.  It doesn't make the game bad - it's just more scripted.
And (if we're generous), the story in this game is, largely, about that loss - which makes it especially difficult to criticize.  The fact is that this was a well-thought-out sequel by a team who clearly cared about the game, carefully implemented the changes, and made another really great game, though it is great in a slightly different way.

I really, REALLY wanted to like this game. I kinda do, but I am so annoyed by the amount of cutscenes that it colors what would have been a really fun, quirky game without them. Here's the breakdown:
The story:
You play as the smallest of a family of Russian nesting doll chimney sweeps, in search of his missing family members who were taken by an evil baron. You're tiny and scrappy, and it's endearing. It's a little heavy-handed at times, since the villain is a baron who's profiting from child labor. There are characters you can play as that are clearly all the big stereotypes from the Progressive Era, like oil barons, union leaders, a black lung kid etc.
The Mechanics:
You solve puzzles by hopping into other nesting dolls, each of whom have a special power: digging things, hammering, drinking tea, flatulance, lighting things on fire, pouring soup, literally anything. The controls are tight, just WASD, Q for talk, E for your special ability, Left mouse to hop into someone else, right mouse to jump back out. There are multiple ways of solving each puzzle, and since areas are revisitable, you can do them all (and get achievements if you do!) but only one is necessary to progress the story. There are also collectible characters that you only get credit for if you actually hop into them, so people who like getting to 100% completion have a lot to do. There is a very fair progressive hint system as well, with three clues for each of the different variations of a puzzle, so if you just need a little clue or the full solution, you got it. That alone would have been perfect, but unfortunately the game ruined much of the mystery by telling you what to do at every stage, not just in the cut scenes, but also with screen popups and dialogue. So there's this whole mechanic of talking to different people, but frequently you don't have to, because the game already said, "Find this person, then go to this place and do this."
The music:
Fantastic. Lots of violin, kinda that small orchestra, lots of solo violin stuff and piano, very good turn of the century vibe.
The Art:
The art is, in fact, awesome. It's one of the reasons I bought the game despite negative reviews. All the characters really do look like Russian nesting dolls, you have large, revisitable areas with lots of detail. The aesthetics were good, with a silent movie era kind of vibe going during cutscenes, which brings us to....
The Pacing:
The pacing is ♥♥♥♥ing awful. There are SOOOOO many cutscenes to get the story across, unnecessarily long ones, too. For example, there are reactions cutscenes after EVERY SINGLE ONE of the times you injure the final boss. I'm not talking about a reaction animation, where the boss nesting doll gets blown apart, revealing another one of himself you now have to fight. That would be fine. But no, You have an unskippable cut scene where a group of the people come upon his discarded pieces, cheering each other on to "Get him!", then they pick up the pieces in a different way each time, then say something else, like "We got him!" then run off. AFTER EVERY ACTION AGAINST THE BOSS. Like, we got that he exploded. I mean, there are also huge, sweeping camera pans every time you entered a new area (sometimes 20-30 seconds long), as if to say "Oooo, isn't it pretty?" They gave a tiny bit of aid in showing you the general layout of where you're going, but since it was mostly in the 2D and you play in 3D, it's pretty useless. I mean, you don't get to play for the first 5 minutes or so of the game, and then when you finally get control, you go down one hallway, and there's another couple of minutes of cutscenes. It never ends. It's actually really sad because they were doing a silent movie thing with the cutscenes, and it looks great, but the devs clearly didn't understand that silent movies had hardly any dialogue in them FOR A REASON. It's like they wrote dialogue for the cutscenes and then said "Hey, what if it was like a silent movie?" and they did no changes to the script. Since the characters are wooden dolls, they can't move their lips, and have no visible emotions, so do we need to show them talking, then throw up an entirely too long paragraph, then have someone react to it while adding no new information (like to recap to another character the thing we just saw happen??)...WAY too long. If the dialogue had been spoken over the animation, the cutscenes would have been half as long and I'd have at least 30 minutes of my life back.
Overall:
By just inserting a skip function for the cutscenes, I would have given this game an 8 or 9 out of 10. But with the cutscenes...well, it burned me bad enough that I started the bonus mission and it started with another enormous cutscene and I just said "I'm out" and forcequit that thing hard. This game could have been wonderful, and if there was a way to skip the cutscenes it actually would be. I got it for $2 or something insane, and I DID like it during those few short bits between cutscenes, so I'd say I got my money's worth but I will not be replaying this.

This review won't deal about the games themselves and only talk about the Collection itself, its technical aspects and the new things it offers.
Pros:
-All 4 games play accurately without any noticeable input lag, except maybe a little bit in MM8.
- I honestly can't tell if 9 and 10 are emulated or actual ports.
-The aspect ratio is respected and the games aren't stretched to TV format like it was the case in the first Legacy Collection. Beatiful 1:1 sharp pixels are available. If your screen's native res isn't 1920*1080, things might be different though, as it seems it's the native res of the game and anything below is downscaling.
Stretching to widescreen and scanlines filter are also available if that's your thing.
- While I didn't like the challenges in MMLC1, the "new" challenges in this one are actually fun, especially if you want to train against a particular boss. In MM9 they allow you to battle Fake Man as Protoman, and in 10, you can battle all 3 MM Killers as Protoman and Bass, neither of which were originally possible in 9/10 so it's nice. Sadly, that summarizes anything "new" about those challenges, everything else is simply replaying parts of the games.
The previously existing challenges of MM9 and 10 are still there, including yes, Mr Perfect, though none of them are linked to actual Steam achievements.
- The only savestates available are checkpoints savestates, meaning you can only use them at a checkpoint or after you kill a boss. It's useful for MM7 if you don't wanna deal with the password system.
- The museum has a few new art pieces. Most of them could already be seen in the 25th Anniversary artbook, but a few of them are new.
Cons:
- "Full controller support" on the store page is a lie. The only controllers this game natively supports are the Steam controller and the XBOX360/ONE controllers. Anything else, you'll have to either go through Steam's Big Picture controller support or install a 360 pad emulator. I went for the later and it didn't add any input lag.
- MM9 has some sound issues. The music volume is too low, and some sounds get cancelled by others when they shouldn't (and didn't originally). Quite a few people in the forum also claim they have no music playing at all, but I didn't have this issue myself. Also a couple of sounds didn't play properly in 7, and in 8 the wrong music plays during the cutscene when meeting Wily before the final bossfight.
Hopefully these will be fixed in the future.

The game has nice background music, and is visually pleasant to look at.  The voice audio sounds fairly low quality, and they could have done with adding a few more variations.  The 'grunt as character falls on the ground' sound is a good example as you hear it fairly often, consist of just one sample, and sometimes is played multiple times in a row.   The characters say only a few words and dont emote that much.
All in all, I do not recommend this game.  It provides at most 2 hours of content with no replayability. Stacking is a unique puzzle game using Russian stacking dolls, of all things. You must solve various puzzles using the dolls unique abilities. The trick is, you can only stack to dolls that are one size bigger than you. Even further, there are multiple ways to solve every puzzle.
The puzzles themselves are not hard to figure out one solution to progress in the game. However, to find all the solutions was difficult and sometimes not logical. Luckily, you have 3 clues for each solution you can reveal.
The story unfolds using silent film cut-scenes. It adds a bit of extra charm. The environment and graphic design are well done. Dolls are uniquely stylized and the detail in the environment is more than expected for a game like this.  The whole game has a very Victorian, old style to it.
Along with the main story, there are “hi-jinks” you can perform and also collect all the unique dolls. Both of these feats are not too difficult to accomplish. The hi-jinks only hint is in the title of what they are. It takes some thinking to understand what they want. I’ll admit I had to look at a guide multiple times.
+60FPS (not a true 60fps, camera still feels like 30fps. Hard to explain)
+Unique gameplay mechanic
+Great art style
+Limited music tracks
+A few hard crashes to desktop late in the game
+Lengthy cut-scenes at times
Despite the last third of the game becoming repetitive and stale, I enjoyed playing Stacking. It can be a really short game if you choose to not find all the solutions and 100% the game. If you’re not a completionist, definitely grab this only on a sale.

has a disclaimer when you launch the game so it feels kinda natural to actually provide a disclaimer for this review.
The interactive story unfolding in
is heavy on LGBT-themes, a polarizing discussion both online and offline. Regardless of my irrelevant opinion on the matter, both sides of the aisle need to understand one another and actually discuss issues before resulting to name calling and blind hatred. We're all humans and we can work together to resolve our issues but this is a very touching matter for a lot of people, either on a personal aspect, a religious one, a principle one and societal one.
For better or for worse, judging the story of this game is an essential aspect of the review because as far as the actual gameplay elements go, there's very little to do and to say about.
The game begins with you, the player, finding a lost phone belonging to someone. There's a few apps, including messaging, dating and browser ones which are gonna be the crux of how the story is being
read by the player. There are a few progression puzzles involved which should not be too cryptic, if anything a couple are blatantly obvious, which basically are the only parts of the game you will actually play.
Now as I mentioned above and without spoiling the story, the central theme involves a LGBT person. As you 'pry' through their phone you'll uncover their secrets, their fears, their relationship with friends/strangers/family, their hopes and dreams, and for a good while you might empathize with the character. There are few nice reads here and there, there were some nice messages at times and some holier-than-thou preaching at others. Despite the
messages the game is trying to promote, there were moments where it made me reflect on the hardships some LGBT people face in their every day life. I want to believe that the developers were actually aiming for that and I have to say they succeeded in achieving that goal for the most part.
Nonetheless, the game attempts to also inform/educate non-LGBT people like a tumblr post at certain times. There are better ways to convey a message to people you want to influence, more subtlety does wonders and in my opinion is a huge way to actually find meaning, especially in an interactive medium, but
does not do subtle things. It just opens up and lets all the messages come in the most direct, albeit honest, way possible and for that I was kinda disappointed. There's no real mystery to unravel, they're no hints for the story and besides the main story, there's not really anything else interesting to learn about even though there a few alluring subplots that could have been developed.
Now do I recommend this game for everyone? Absolutely not. The game might appear to actually trying to push an agenda and you'll be partially correct. The game is also trying to promote tolerance and acceptance for LGBT people and you'll be partially correct. Different people and different opinions will react to this game on a whole different level. From a pure gameplay point of view, the game is incredibly short, ~2 hours, and there's very little to actually do. I did find it extremely fascinating to actually simulating prying into someone else's life through their social media platforms (sort of reminiscent of the game
) and the story despite being predictable and preachy at times, was for the most part interesting enough. The pricing on this game is also extremely accurate for its length. Finally, I cannot stress enough the fact that this is a very polarizing issue to have present in a narrative driven game and despite some of its nice messages buyer should be aware and beware of what they are getting into.

This game is a pretty good and brutal "tactics" game, with some overland elements that are similar to Mount&Blade.
POSITIVES:
- Battles are great. They are brutal, balanced, easy to understand, full of taking risks vs playing safe. They factor in fatigue, morale, various attacks vs various defenses (like flails VS shields), and all in all, great fun.
- Your units gain experience and get better and better equipment (hopefully), yet they won't turn into supermen. A few bad decisions and they just die like anyone else.
- The mood of the game is great, it is gritty and desperate, full of believable moments.
NEGATIVES:
- The game is mostly about battling. It is not really a sandbox in that sense that you cannot be a trader or merchant or slaver or anything else, like in Mount&Blade. Just a bunch of mercenaries, fighting.
All in all, a great game, recommended if you like the style and don't really want a true sandbox game.

Here's the 100,000th survival game, and it's pixeled! What else is new, right? WRONG. In Echo of the Wilds not only are you totally confused, excited and totally lost about what's happening, but you just want to keep going, you'll also work, HARD, for your bizarely-shaped character to stay alive through the night.
It's actually easy to understand, you'll know exactly where the needed items are to eat, drink, antidotes and such. But your daily limited time is going to make you choose, and believe me when I say your decisions matter. You could very easily die since it was too dark already to collect some wood because you just HAD to craft yourself that damn axe you wanted to use TO GET WOOD IN THE FIRST PLACE!!!...
I mean... Yeah, sometimes it's about getting through the night in one piece with as much health as possible, priviledges like storage or a hammer can wait... I don't know, 10 days? Even more?
And just so you know. You have limited inventory to 5 items, and since cutting down a three or getting stone takes 2-3 usable items to get, that means you have 2 to use freely, sometimes. Places? There are a few, but you can only memorize 15 of them meaning you'll have to decide which ones you want to leave to luck to stumble upon.
Don't get me wrong, though. It's hard in a very good way, it devours you. Nothing else matters for hours but this game, day after day, allucination after allucination.
Oh, did I mention the Save feature requires you to offer food? Yes, you're trying to survive and since you are about to die you'd want to save the game, just in case, right? Sure, just bring some food you don't have to Save a game you're going to lose anyway!...
In a few words. This is the most interesting, punishing and relaxing/rage inducing survival game you'll ever play, and it's worth every minute of your time even if it gets you NOWHERE!
I like the game, but there should be an Easy mode somewhere. Maybe with easier Save features or more space in your inventory.

TO SUM IT UP
A good turn based game sadly plagued by its un-generosity in everything it does and with no consideration whatsoever for the player's time.
The game is frustrating and an invitation for save scumming to most players while being appealing to a minority of hardcore masochists/fetichists (which is indeed a niche market for sure).
But it still definitely itches the turn base tactical genre as my playtime shows.
Too bad it is just so damn stingy in every aspect (poor loot and itemisation, hit chances jokes, enemy marksmen and their magical arrows, and a lack of content that calls for enrichment by DLC which i would gladly pay for).
--- WHY PUT A NEGATIVE REVIEW ?
It is a game not respectful of the player's time in the end. You need to invest lots of time for little rewards in a gritty to the point of frustrating system.
But if you have lots of time to kill like I do at the moment and are not prone to punching your desk, go for it.
It will take you more than a 100 hours to fully perceive how frustrating some mechanics can be, how the named loot is insanely rare and disapointing, how insanely slow the game speed is (hint : use cheat engine speed hack after the discovery phase), and just how repetitive this gets with such bothersome fatigue mechanics, conbat maps, or resolve stat, only used for 1 enemy but without which you can not do anything against them.
--- THE PERK SYSTEM
... is deeply flawed with some almost mandatory perks and far too many useless ones (or niche ones that the game over-gritiness does not let you explore anyway).
Below are a few gripes after spending a long time with the game (besides the lack of ANY generosity in design throughout).
--- THE INTERFACE
The interface is a bit too basic basic and in need of a an upgrade to more modern standards (buy/sell back, flexibility of repairs from any inventory display, buybacks, better retire system, load button available everywhere, autoloot not looting human flesh, have the activable option to see the recruits characteristics for those who want to).
--- ABOUT MAPS GENERATION
The map generations are pretty awful both for the main map randomly seed generated AND the battle maps and their characterictics :
- the main map generated at each start will have you start games over and over to get a decent map, with decent bros to start with if that matters to you. The main problem is the map generation which there again generates too many crappy maps lacking resources, lacking harbors, lacking missions somehow. This matters A LOT to the game you will experience and will probably have lots of players bouncing back from an awful start which happens 80% of the time just because of poor, then again un-generous, procedural algorithms.
- the battle maps have multiple biomes whichis good. But they are too often poor for battles not so much because of their characteritics but because of uninspired generation of the maps.
Let's say you attack a party roaming the land in the hills. Well the map will randomly put you in a position with enemies atop the hills. Not only will enemy marksmen or goblins will slaughter your troops from there, the pure slog to go through elevation with your bros is just an insanely boring game. I don't bother anymore with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ map battle and just reload the autosave to get a different configuration.
Why not have the enemy in a position of force when they sometimes ambush you, but the whole "sometimes you can't win battles" motto just to excuse for♥♥♥♥♥♥poor map settings is just awful. This aspect of the game is insanely poor compared to the more polished turn based fight system.

I will not reveal the narrative of the game, but some judgments of mine may be considered spoilers. So consider this as a spoiler alert.
You find a phone and dig through its contents to unravel the secrets of the owner.

As long as the truth is uncovered, the game reveals itself as ideological propaganda. The same themes have been treated by other games with more sensitivity... instead, "A normal lost phone" forces the player to hear just one side of the debate, without possibility of reply. This is exacerbated by the absence of choice: the game can be finished with a single action, that is even explicitly suggested by a message from a character. Apparently, the "positive" finale that the player could only passively accept involves ruining families, excluding any possibility of dialogue, and not-seeking help for an adolescent boy who (as far as we know) may simply suffer from mental health issues.
Independently from personal beliefs and ideologies, I cannot appreciate an interactive story that forces me to make immoral choices.

A 2D crafting/survival adventure/time-managment game with decent visuals and an okay theme/story. As a warning, I never finished the game (due to reasons below).
Days are split up into 4 time-sections and you choose where to explore each day until you run out of time. Any action that goes into the 4th time section will be limited as night approaches and the darkness stops your ability to interact with the environment (without a torch). One of the most important things you need to learn is that returning to camp costs no time so you need to drop off everything unnecessary in between areas (because inventory space is pretty limited).
Your only basic necessities are managing your hunger/thirst meters and gathering enough wood for the night's fire. Your goals beyond that are to tribute food/precious materials at the altars for more recipes, explore different areas, and learn more about the world's mechanics to survive into later seasons.
Personally, I would've liked a casual mode where you could save freely. It might go against the experience that the dev intended, but that experience isn't the kind I enjoy. Saving always seems like a waste of precious time because it takes up a quarter of the day and an offering. I think I read that the dev could 100% it before the end of summer (although he has added more things since then) so maybe time isn't an issue to someone who has mastered the game. However, that's not something you'd normally know and I've been a hoarder of rare consumables in RPGs and wasting a quarter of a day to save often is something I don't want to do.
My game locked up when I accidentally used reeds on a reed patch (no buttons responded except for the menu to quit the game) and I lost several in-game days of progress. On a x360 controller 'use' is mapped to B and 'cancel' is mapped to X (which was the opposite of what I'm used to) so that happened several times. Other than that, I didn't see any other bugs.
However, you might like that challenging/hardcore feel of needing to go through many playthroughs in order to learn, understand and get a little further in the game next time. This is a game that you need to get deeply invested in to do well at because there are a lot of little things you have to deal with.

If you expect a challenge from the games you play then this is a game for you - it's hard, but more of a challenge than being near impossible to play. I'd guess that a lot of people might submit to rage quits and hatred towards some aspects as the missions progress, but that's what's great about this game - you build your hero and invest in the traps you want to upgrade, and you should choose the right ones for specific situations. There's different ways to achieve victory, so it's also based on reflex and skill.
To those getting stuck, here's a few tips that are pretty much essential:
- the ice trap, although not very helpful damage-wise, is one of the most useful ground traps when upgraded (and you don't need to invest in nothing more than the slowing upgrade) - slowing your enemies down gives you a huge advantage in pretty much any situation.
- learn how to generate essense effectively (upgrade the essense floor trap and use it early to collect essense for later waves, invest in the skill that gives you more starting essense).
- the gun tower is OP, so keep it your main tower weapon until you get the Olympus Tower.
- you can respec your traps, and should do it when you run out of points for upgrade; some traps become obsolete and there's no point in keeping them upgraded. The purpose of the gold you collect in the game is pretty much mainly to allow you paying for respecing your skills and traps.
- improve skills wisely. Focus on lowering enemy defense to certain kinds of attacks (especially the main ones) so that big creatures lose their defense against getting hit. Make your main attacks more powerful and be sure to have mana regen set in a way that lets you use power skills without much delay.
- at some points you might find it that it's almost impossible to fight off waves of creatures or that they are too powerful for you to take them on. That's because your level is too low. You need to level up, which is fairly simple and becomes available once you get the "endless" option for completing levels. The more waves you take on in the levels that reward you with XP, the more XP you get. This way, you can get ridiculous amounts of XP - it can be a small amount for a few levels and over 100 000 for reaching wave 12 or so, but over a 1 000 000 XP (yes, MILLION) if you complete over 30 waves.
- The Olympus Tower is probably the most powerful direct damage trap in the game when you lower its cooldown. You can do it both directly in the trap upgrade page and also as an in-match upgrade. Combined with the +90% damage upgrade it's devastating at the highest upgrade level for damage and speed.
Deathtrap gives you an amazing experience of a very dynamic mix between tower defence and a hack and slash game.

So Feist is a good game in my opinion. Everyone compares it to limbo but honestly i find this better than Limbo. This doesnt require as much thought processing and more action and skill. The physics are amazingly realistic even though its a 3d platformer. Its about a small creature that got trapped by some beasts that are adventuring on. The aim is to kill all the beasts and save your friend and has a fun journey going through caves and forests and such, slowly picking the beasts off one by one. All the beasts have different abilities and are each unique and fun to killThough Feist does have its pros and cons so i will list them down and what to expect from the game.
Pros
- Incredible Physics
- Less thinking
- Amazing design
- A pretty game
- Good enemies
- Smooth
- Can fight back
- Small game size
The physics despite being a 3d platformer are realistic. The way rocks and sticks fall are actually fun and it was a big reason why i got the game. The game doesnt really require a smart brain and more skills like timing your hits and when to jump and stuff like that. The design of the game is nothing like Limbo, its in a forest and mainly nature and feels alot more peaceful, rather in Limbo it was alot of man made structures and figuring out puzzles. The enemies all are different and all have different ways of maneuvering past them. The game has a nice smooth feeling when you are jumping and you dont lose momentum of when you are running, jumping from branch to branch journeying through the forests and caves to kill the beasts. You can actually fight back unlike Limbo and pick up sticks, rocks, logs and push boulders to kill the creatures that try to stop your journey. You can also use the environment to kill creatures too. And the game size is like 300 mb
Cons
- Far Checkpoints
- Small max health
- Overpowered Enemys
- Small selection of weapons
- Overload of enemies
- Repetitive deaths
So first off the checkpoints in Feist are pretty far for the things you die loads from. You would have gone so far but then have to do it all over again because of how far the checkpoints are. Your max health doesnt help with that either. Its about 4 - 5 hits from anything to kill you. And the fact that any creature can do that and some of them are pretty overpowered with all those are pretty unfair. Also the selection of a couple items to use against creatures are pretty limited. Mostly its just a stick, log and rock. logs are like lighter versions of rocks and sticks only last one hit. Rocks slow you down and lower how high you jump. Sometimes theres times when there is far too many creatures attacking you at once. Fighting off all of those creatures can get pretty hard. Then with the overload of creatures constantly relentlessly attacking you, you have to worry about progression aswel. Killing enemies mainly helps you for most things. Not worrying about creatures is like doing homework early and not worrying about it.
Very likely a typo slipped my mind. There are plenty of more Pros that i couldnt think of at the time. Overall i suggest you get this if you like little adventures.

Starbound, the so waited 1.0 delivers what the developers promised. More or less.
As far as sandbox games go, this is one of the best around. You can explore a whole universe, meet different people and races, find hidden codexes and find out about the real story behind the game. But let's see what's good and what's bad about Starbound.
+addictive exploration system
+tons of content to see and witness
+different races with different equipments and ships
+codex books you can find on settlements give more insight in the inner workings the story won't elaborate upon
-ultimately the story feels rushed, as if the developers really wanted to get the game out of beta as soon as possible
-a big share of content (monsters, weapons, sidequests) was cut for no reason, 1.0 does feel a little empty compared to the beta.
-not a lot of incentive. You need to impose self-made goals if you want to keep playing after the story. Things like: 'I want to get the highest tier ship', or 'I want to colonize a new planet ad make a town of my own'.
Long story short, don't play Starbound for the story. Play it because you are curious and want to have a good time running across the stars.
Overall, I had a highly positive experience. I will say it again, the story feels rushed. And one of the races (Novakid) feels cut out from the universe (no settlements, no NPCs, no codex, no relevance to the story).
I still recommend the game, for its price. But the developers need to add more content, and some of what was cut between Glad Giraffe and 1.0, seriously.

After a loooooooooooooooooooooooooooong long time, Starbound finally got out of the early access. Thankfully. Cause the only thing that really killed my motivatio was the fact, that every update deleted your entire progress.
Now officially released, Starbound is a blast. If you are fans of games like Terraria or Minecraft, Starbound is the game for you. You have an astounding amount of worlds you can discover, a wide variety of biomes you can explore above and under the planet or can even try to become familiar with the fauna and flora of one of these planets.
You have the possibility to enjoy a story and after the story is done, you still get tons of things to do. Build a colony, upgrade your ship, search for funny or awesome vanity items, try to find unique weapons (for example a worm-like bumerang), become an archeologist, a farmer, head-hunter or hero, who saves local residents.
Since this is a sandbox game, you can become creative in so many ways...
Try to build a copy of Rapture from Bioshock, a sky island, turn a barren planet into a living one, shape entire places like you want to. Thanks to certain mini-biomes (like an 'eye'-biome), you can farm hilarious blogs and pieces, combine them into more hilarious things and create things you never knew you would create someday.
You can expect a lot of fun. Yet you may guess, that this game has certain flaws and for me, there are some.
FIRST OF ALL THIS DUCKING GAME TOOK WAY TO LONG TO DEVELOPE THE THINGS THEY WERE PROMISING SINCE THE BEGINNING! YES, I AM STILL MAD ABOUT IT AND WON#T CALM MY♥♥♥♥♥♥
Then I want to stress out, that the colony and crew can be annoying at times. NPC's tend to crowd one place and if your luck is really bad, you end up cloning your crew or get people out of nowhere in your colony because.....gnarflik! I am not kidding, sometimes the NPC's are annoying and do things they shouldn't do!
I have to admit, that the biomes and mini-biomes ARE keeping up a certain motivation to explore and look around.....but after a while you can't help but thinking, that those places look ever so often the same. I was looking for a certain vanity item at the dessert planets and literally 3 PLANETS looked the same. First castle, then swamp, then tar, then a little bit special. I know it is hard to pick on THAT one, but you can't help but feel tired after a while of seeing the same things over and over again.
But other than that, I really have a blast playing it. Sure I would LOVE to see certain things like incredible huge monsters on some planets (like a giant kraken at the ocean biome or a antlion in the dessert region) or some mini-bosses. Also the other enemies seem to be very repetitive in terms of attack patterns: Tackle it......tackle it........tackle it......here and there is one animal that shoots energy and flames......more tackling. At the earlier stages, monsters had a more diverse way of attacking.
Maybe we could have those mechs back. There are mods around who provide other vehicles, but I'd really love to see them as an inherent part of the game. Some unique weapons like the gloves need a bit more polishing, since for the majorityof time, a two handed sword is the weapon of choice.
Aaaaaaaaand..... I would like to have some more ingredients, recipes and plants for farming and cooking.
Overall I think that Starbound belongs to the top sandbox games out there. They took there time, but the result is really worth it =)

In addition the devs provided quite a lot of extra content post-launch. It may seem a bit strange then that what I liked most about the original was one of it's most understated features. The story. Hand of Fate's story was vauge and told through small hints that had to be patched together by guesswork. Hand of Fate 2 continues a hundred years later and makes the story much more concrete which I found to be very rewarding.
Everything else has also been improved. The beautiful presentation has only gotten better. The board mechanics are more fleshed out, the scenarios are more diverese and interesting. tl;dr: i rarely take the time to post steam reviews , and it's even rarer for me to buy a game so close to launch . That should give you an idea regarding how excited i was for this sequel , and how satisfied i am with the result. If you played the first one and liked it , this is a huge improvement in every aspect i can think of , that being said , if you didn't enjoy the core gameplay loop from HoF 1 , this is a skip . If you're starting with this one , this is a great jumping-on point , and a better product overall.
with that out of the way , here are the strong points:
+the combat has been improved with the addition of two-handed weapons and dual-wield type weapons . together with the improved enemy variety , the result is the fact that no piece of equipment is objectively better than another one , though there are some combinations which make a lot more sense than others ( like how there is a set of knives that looks like it's meant to fight Empire type enemies , when dual-wield weapons are weakest against them)
+the core gameplay loop has become a lot more varied and generally satisfying . While in the first game your goal was to beat the final boss of each chapter by any means necessary , here there are optional objectives for each mission , which reward you with extra cards . this makes each chapter more memorable , and the fact that you can choose which one you want to undertake first solves a problem the first one had , where losing over and over again would force you to repeat the same mission and make the experience feel stale .
+the introduction of whole new gameplay mechanics like camping , artefacts , new gamble type encounters as well as specific weapon effects make the game feel a lot more tactical . For example , you might try figure out how many hits an enemy takes to kill , in order to get him low , charge your weapon ability on another enemy only to activate it on the first and get a bonus . If you find yourself in a challange where you take constant damage , you could add more Food cards to your deck , and camp to replenish health whenever needed. As a result , losing always felt like it was my fault and there was some way to avoid it , which only made me want to switch my deck a bit and start over, making victory that much more rewarding .
+the new companion system is also welcome . On your journey , you will meet a set of characters who will help you both during combat , as well as outside , in gambits. Requesting their help in gambits can be a great help , by having them increase your odds of succes , or it can backfire horribly , taking them out of action for a while . This is all part of the fun since , even though they are great help during fights , you immediately feel the difference when you're fighting on your own.
+the story will be a nice callback to those who played the original , as the mysterious dealer tasks you on a quest that will see you resolving murder mysteries , building a fortress to fend off seemingly endless hordes of attackers , assassinating political targets and much more . And that's not even mentioning the stories your companions go through : with the corresponding companion , you can add an encounter card to the deck . At the end of this set of encounters , your companion will be upgraded with a new appearance and ability .
+the voice acting is stellar , as was the case with the first game , though you get quite a bit more here , as the companions also have their own voices .
that being said , the game is not perfect:
-the way you gain access to new cards can be frustrating to some . When a card is marked as new , you have no idea what it does . You need to put it in the deck and run into it to see its effects , and in some challanges , it's easy to skip over them without wanting to. Furthermore , the effect can be so bad as to warrant restarting the challange . It's quite possible to die on the first step on a challange that starts you with 10 health , because the first encounter you stepped on had a mandatory "take damage" effect. Again , you could plan for this in advance , too , so be careful what you choose. What's even worse is that one particular challange expected me to have a specific artefact , of which there are many , in order to get the token .
-many enouncter cards have the " screw this , i'm out" option , which makes it possible for you to see the outcomes in the card selection screen , even though you haven't run into them before.
-it's possible , even likely , that you can't complete the optional objetives the first time you try , as there simply aren't enough cards of the type you need to fill the requirement . One encounter in particular requires you to gain a certain number of blessings , however , this one is quite early , before you have access to that many blessing cards . While you can still score a silver token for just surviving , it can be frustrating to some .
-by the end of the campaign i only managed to complete one companion storyline , with varying degrees of completion for the other ones , which can be quite bothersome , seeing how the game expects you to have done them all of them by that point. You can chalk that up to me maybe using the same character too much , but aren't i supposed to do that , seeing how they're upgraded , or needing their specific ability ?
side notes :
*i finished the game at the 40 hour mark. This is more than the previous game , including a bit of endless mode and the DLC .
*endless mode has not been added as of the writing of this review
*the game only crashed two times for me , which weren't a big deal , as it seems to autosave after every encounter . patches have been constant since release , and i can't think of any other performance problems or bugs.
Conclusion:
While i may not have done a good job conveying how much i enjoyed this game , know that there are few games that i look forward to playing as much as HoF2, or ones that hold my attention as long as this , or ones as addictive as this one .A unique title from a dev that clearly listened to criticism , took notes , and actually solved the problems their first title had . If you're not completely sold yet , maybe check it out on a sale once endless mode is out .

This game makes me wish there was a "maybe" option rather than simply yes or no to recommend.
Although I adored the demo and really wanted the full game, I have to say that I don't feel it's worth the money - it has an extremely disappointing 'ending', if you can call it that.
While the game is - as many other reviewers have said - very short, that isn't always a bad thing if the game itself is a good one.  Lilly Looking Through is absolutely charming: beautiful to look at, completely non-violent (very suitable for children, although they may need help with the puzzles), includes an interesting mechanic with the goggles which should have been used more often, and has some scenes/events which are both lovely and a bit melancholy.  A couple of the puzzles (especially the colour-based ones) were frustrating because there seemed to be no clue what was required, but the majority of them were fun and not too challenging if you put a bit of thought into them and used what was available to you.
I could forgive the price and the length of the game if it had some kind of resolution at the end, but it has nothing.  There's sort of a hint, during the last 'chapter', that there'll be something more - perhaps the "unlocking the ultimate mystery" mentioned in the developer's description - but the ending is so abrupt and unexpected that it was a real let down.  Since people have been commenting on this even in the developer's own community discussion for at least a year and nothing seems to have changed, it looks like this 'ending' is all we'll get.
I waited months for a sale and never saw this reduced, so I eventually received it as a birthday gift.  Having finished it in less than 3 hours (my playtime includes the game being left running while I did other things) and been left feeling very let down, I can't help but feel sorry that my purchaser paid full price for the game!
In conclusion, then, I guess I can say I cautiously recommend this if you like the game's look and feel.  If you enjoy the demo, you'll likely enjoy the majority of the game - just be prepared for the fact that you'll be left hanging at the end with no resolution, and try to get it on sale if you can!

Lilly Looking Through is a point and click adventure game. You click on spots to move and items to interact. Pretty basic stuff. Everything you can click on is clear when you're in range because once you hover over it your cursor will change. The draw here is the art and the mystery. You get drawn in initially because you're just thrown into the world and start looking around at what to do and what effects your actions have on the world around you. You use these interactions to progress through the game. Also, part way through you get these goggles that switch between two versions of the world. It's a nice little twist. The art is pretty and some of the puzzles are neat. However, this game has a lot of issues.
For one, everything is very slow. The animations are interesting, but once you've seen it once you get the idea. So if you leave the game and start an area over or just have to run through a cycle of tasks to solve a puzzle, you'll be seeing the same slow animations a lot. The interface is also a bit vague. Some of the puzzles are confusing and... while I get that's the point, some of them want you to use colors as part of the problem solving which is hard for those who have issues differentiating colors... such as myself. While I didn't bother finishing the game, there was only one more section for me to do, and from the videos and posts I've seen... the game just kind of ends. So you'd better enjoy the art, the puzzles, and the mystery because there's not much of a story here at all. Plus, it's rather short, only about two to three hours long.
I know I didn't finish the game, but it just got too tedious for me. I entered into a giveaway for the game because... well... my last name is Lilly. So I got it for free. And honestly, it's not necessarily a genre I'm super fond of. I guess I might be being a bit harsh on it, but I can't recommend it for a simple reason... value. This game costs 10 bucks full price, but only last about 2 hours. While you might enjoy the experience, unless it really speaks to you on a deeper level, it's not really worth the price tag. Maybe look for a trade or a sale but... I really can't recommend it as is. I just didn't find enough enjoyment here to recommend it to anyone else. Lilly Looking Through gets a 3 out of 10 for having some redeeming qualities, but ultimately falling short of its potential.

There are too many imbalances, unpolished features, lack of information. And very little room for customization.
The game will not provide any information at all on enemies - their special abilities, physical immunities, hit points, gears. Same thing regarding ambitions, number of tiles a character may move, crisis development details, etc.
If you buy items for trading, you will not know where to get better prices. When you hire a character, you don't have a clue about what his background will do in practical terms. How may a historian, a caravan guide or a mason actually help you? They all look alike.
Furthermore, brawlers and butchers are much preferable to the very expensive nobles and mercenaries, since they cost very little to hire and maintain, and their stats are somewhat all similar.
Very poor documentation. There are no extensive tooltips for anything, ranging from battle information to campaign descriptions.
Some mechanics like food management, trading and party morale are not immersive or fun. Quests are not balanced and will not reward accordingly. Permanent injuries are not optional.
All in all, Battle Brothers is a nice little game, which unfortunately has not accomplished to fulfill its potential. Viking Reforged edition or Mount and Blade Warband are much better options, for sure.

Battle Brothers is set in a low-fantasy medieval world. That means you will encounter the occasional undead, orc and goblin horde, but magic has very little presence here and times are as rough as they can be. After a failed battle to kill a wanted criminal and his goons, you are left in charge of a small mercenary company. A tutorial that barely covers the basics will demonstrate how everything works, and then you are left to face the world and make a name for yourself and your men.
While there is no actual story in the form of main quests, there are countless other incidents happening across the world. You will have to participate in the nobles’ squabbles, or you will be called upon to protect the villages from a greeskin horde that ravages everything in its path. The world is full of misery and suffering, and this creates opportunities for a mercenary company, like yours. Only Game of Thrones portrays medieval suffering in such a fashion, and it’s really good.
The numerous quests are nice and all, but it’s dissapointing to see that in their core, are 10 different quests with altered text. It’s always the same, hunt the bandits, escort the merchants, find the relic etc. It would be nice to see a main questline, which will add some more depth in the game. The reason this feature is absent is understandable, the developers simply wanted to make the world feel «free». Still, it’s a minus.
This is where the fun begins. In Battle Brothers, the world is yours to explore. There are no limits to where you can go, provided you have enough provisions. Every town, village and city has quests, shops and potential recruits, and you can visit all of them, right from the start of the game. While wandering from settlement to settlement, you will notice the map is pretty busy. You will always encounter army patrols, other mercenary bands and trade caravans going about their business. On the other hand, if you wander too far from the road, it’s a death sentence. The wilderness is crawling with bandits, direwolves and abandoded towers, full of undead to explore. It’s a world that feels alive and makes you feel insignificant, especially in early levels. After all, you are just another mercenary company. The nobles can hire as many as they want.
Money is the reason you and your men walk, talk, breathe, eat and exist. That sweet, shiny substance is tough to obtain and even tougher to maintain. Your men must be paid, or else you face the danger of standing on the shield wall alone. Take as many jobs as you can and finish them as fast as you can, but keep in mind to always save some money for tough times. If you spend all your money in good equipment and the next quest is weeks away, don’t expect your men to feel happy about it. Get some basic armor and steel, hire a couple of drunk farmers and march. Don’t worry, any character can be shaped in a good warrior. Or die in the process.
Speaking of which, Battle Brothers is extremely deep and well structed, when it comes to your men. They are not just pawns in your grand scheme of greatness, they have actual lives and you will feel bad for them when they die. Based on their backgrounds, your men will have the appropriate traits, skills and preferences. For example, a farmer may have more resistance to damage, but he’s useless with a bow, while a thief is fast, good with a knife and a crossbow, but don’t expect him to face tougher enemies with heavy armor and an axe. Every character has unique stats, and keep an eye out for stats with stars. If a character has 1-3 stars above a certain stat, that means you have to level these up, since they will evolve your character to something better than a drunk farmer, covered in his own♥♥♥♥♥♥
In a similar fashion to characters, equipment has its own stats. Every weapon is good at something. Axes are great for smashing shields like firewood, hammers and pickaxes are ideal to tear the armor of your enemies apart, while spears are perfect for keeping enemies at bay, but good luck trying to kill an armored enemy with them. Keeping a good balance between the weapons your men have, means you will be able to deal with every situation. Keep that in mind.
All in all, Battle Brothers is like a board game. The terrain changes accordingly, based on where you where on the map. If you picked a fight with some pesky bandits in the mountains, prepare for a lot of hills, that give height advantage (IT’S OVER ANAKIN, I HAVE THE HIGH GROUND!). Use the terrain carefully to your advantage, since you can tire the enemy out faster and deal more damage with ranged weapons. Every character is portrayed like a chess piece, moving around as if an invisible hand is directing it. But we will leave that for the «graphics» sector.
One of the biggest drawbacks this game has, is the menu. Why, oh why, the developers did not throw somewhere a comparison screen? If you want to compare pieces of equipment, you have to open a screen, close another, open a sub-menu, and search each and every one of your men to see who’s carrying what. Would it be such a pain to add a screen when you select a weapon that says «the character you are hovering above has this weapon compared to this»? Jeez, it only ruins the fun, but not entirely.
One last warning: in this game, you are at the mercy of RNG. Prepare to witness failed shots with 90% success rate and your men getting mauled by orcs that are 10 times less experienced and well-equipped compared to you. Be patient, it’s just the way this game works.
This was one of the rare cases where a game surprised me in a good fashion. The whole minimalistic style was, at first, a bit dull and lacking detail. All I could see was characters like chess pieces, moving around without any worthy animation. Slowly, I started noticing the details. Necks snapped under the pressure of axes, heads flied in the air after a good swing of a greatsword and eyes went black with blood after many hits in the head with a club. The game has a surprisingly good amount of detail when it comes to gore. If one of your men permanently loses his nose to a spear, his portrait and «chess piece» will adjust accordingly. If a soldier is wounded in his arm, he will have some bandaged tied there until the wound heals. The pixelated violence is amazing, you won’t find anything like it anywhere.
Still, the lack of animations was dissapointing. I get the whole «board game» feel the game has, but an attack is just the «piece» shaking like a maniac and a couple of effects to top it off. I could not help but feel that this game has such a great caliber, it’s only appropriate to have detailed 3D models and animations. You can’t have it all, I guess.
The sound on the other hand, is flawless. The music tracks are incredible, with medieval-like tunes that amplify the atmosphere and pump you up for the battle ahead. Kudos to the team that composed the music and effects, they did an incredible work. I have a couple of tracks stuck in my head days now, and I’m close to making one a ringtone. The sound effects are also exquisite. When you visit a town, you will hear people selling their wares in the market, bells ringing and soldiers patrolling. The overall sound helps a lot with creating a medieval atmopshere, and you can’t have any complaints here.
What are you still doing here? You’re still thinking about it? Only once every 6 months a game of this caliber is released and it’s bloody worthy of every penny and cent you will spend for it. I reccomend it hands-down, I had tons of fun trying to keep my company alive and guide them to fame and riches. It’s realistic, it’s difficult, it’s merciless and it will make a man out of you. Go for it!

I got this game in a bundle, and was very excited to play it because of my love for survival/crafting-style games. Admittedly, I was a little turned off in my initial playthrough, however, after giving it another chance, I quickly dove into a refreshing, novel experience.
If you like survival/crafting-based gameplay, psychedelic-lite aesthetics, and an introspective storyline, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good - the detail in the environments and character models is well-done; the more psychedelic scenes are also great (and may take you aback if you haven't seen any screenshots). The ambient noises and sounds are good - in particular, I appreciate the change in tone whenever the vibe of the scene transforms (usually into a dream-like sequence). The story is very nice, and anyone who enjoys introspection and philosophical thinking should be satisfied with the game's message - I personally felt that the game was in no way pretentious or overly-aggressive in portraying said message(s).
I have a problem with the controls, and I think the main culprit is the poor optimization between controller and keyboard - when you edit the keybindings, it will only allow you to do this for the keyboard. Using a keyboard is okay - and perhaps even recommended - however, the controls are very counter-intuitive if you are used to playing videogames and choose to use a controller. I have played a lot of game throughout my life, and Western norm is for the right button (circle/B) to be the exit/cancel key, while the top button (triangle/Y) performs that action in many Japanese-based games. In Echo, the default gamepad controls are (in inventory management): x/A -> drop; circle/B -> Use; square/X -> exit. It takes a bit of getting used to, as I would constantly be dropping/using my items when I didn't intend to. The game makes an attempt to be ergonomic- the A, S, and D default keys are green, red, and blue in-game - however, when you rebind the keys, you will still see the letters A, S, and D inside the in-game keys (you can turn the key hints off to prevent confusion). A suggestion - having the three command keys spread out in the actual layout on a controller (if key hints are enabled)will take up space in-game, but will be much more ergonomic.
The controls will take a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial mini-mode will be extremely helpful in getting you familiarized with the gameplay. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with survival games - I will caution, however, that this game can be unforgiving if you do not plan your days in advance. Do not be surprised if you die during your first few playthroughs - once you understand what to prioritize and how (ex: "forgetting" initially useless areas), your games will last considerably longer.
Gameplay consist of you trying to survive each day/night while trying to progress the storyline. You usually have enough time to scout 2 new places on the map, however, you can only "remember" one area per day. Remembering a location will allow you to revisit it from then on. I recommend you do not remember places with one-time spawns (ex: an area with a LOT of fruit bushes), as only certain things respawn over time (like trees and shoots). You can also "forget" areas to clear up space on the map. If night time arrives, you will be unable to interact with any objects in the environment unless you have a torch. Your two main priorities are to secure a food/drink source (starving will decrease health over time) and a fire source (you will lose health if you sleep without an adequate fire).
During your journey, you will be treated to story elements that add a lot of interesting scenes. There will also be special structures that allow you to donate food in order to receive crafting recipes (extremely useful). Saving is fairly unique, and also requires a food donation. Note, you must locate these special structures first. Death offers you the slightest chance to continue, but you should never gamble on this chance (instead, focus on not dying). The goal of the game is to
. Endless mode has been taken out by the developer, which is something that I miss (although a new game+ is in the making).
Overall, Echo is a great game for any survival/crafting enthusiasts, and this game should definitely be given a try if you are interested in the genre.
Definitely recommend!

Several years after its original Flash release, The Binding of Isaac is still the top of its genre.
While the themes and aesthetics are certainly divisive (The lead developer, Edmund McMillen, has a preference for the crude and disturbing, as he uses game design as a sort of personal therapy to deal with childhood trauma), and not to my particular taste, you simply cannot argue against gameplay of this caliber.
What Binding of Isaac has, and other games in the genre, like Nuclear Throne, Enter the Gungeon and Risk of Rain, does not posses is a focus on really amazingly pickup interaction. The amount of work that must have gone into making each item work in synergy with almost all other times is amazing, and watching you huge "Brimstone" laser split into four when you pick up "Mutant Spider", and start bouncing off the walls after picking up "Rubber Cement" is simply just so much fun. Sure there are your run-of-the-mill stat upgrades, but they dwarved by the sheer amount of crazy items that will make you completely change your playstyle based on what items you find in a given run!
Any game session usually takes between 25-45 minutes depending on your skill level. The game is hard, but even when getting repeatedly stomped by The Bloat, you will still get lucky once in a while and find a particularly good item combination, making the entire thing worth it. I usually sit down for quick sessions to relax.
To quickly get better at the game I recommend watching Bisnap's video series on the game on Youtube.
If you are unsure which version to pick up, the original flash version gives a very good indication of what you can expect, and Rebirth and the following DLC basically just added a huge amount of new content and item interactions to the game. Rebirth is an objective enhancement of the original, but it might still be worth picking up the first game to check if you enjoy the gameplay before buying the full package.

Imagine a world that feels like Diablo in terms of look, loot, and character progression, but it's entirely a tower defense game. That's pretty much Deathtrap. This is kind of a lenghty and boring write up that goes into detail with my opinions on stuff; bottom line, it's a cool TD / ARPG game.
It's a 'pre-placed' tower build location type of TD game with predetermined paths. You can play single player, coop, or pvp, [though I had trouble connecting to a friend for coop, not sure if that was our setups or an issue with the game]. Aside from each TD level, there is no world to walk around in or towns to visit, just a menu map and tabs for crafting, the store, skills, bestiary and what not. Not much story except a few cutscenes but I skip em anyway.
There are 3 classes, and skill trees for player skills, traps, and world effects which are all fairly extensive. It has 25 different traps, split into 5 classes, and the build markers will be class specific so you can only choose from one of those 5 types of traps for that marker. This is pretty limiting and a bit of a buzz-kill but it's honestly balanced well. You'll be doing most of the killing with your skills, not your traps most of the time, but it's a pleasingly good balance.
There are something like 15 maps with 4 tiers of difficulty, and then scenarios with different difficulties and enemies mixed in for each map. Also this game has a level editor and is on the Workshop so you can find more player-friendly maps there where you can just stack up tons of traps and watch the chaos go down.
Item grinding is important, like any good diablo-esque game, and once you get the Godlike items it's quite fun adding a LOT of upgrade stats to them one at a time. Also, each trap has 2 slots (usually dmg & cooldown) which can be upgraded with tokens which drop along with other loot and are a major part of the customization. For better or worse most of time the best stuff you will buy instead of waiting for a good drop. There is magicfind and goldfind on items but it's kind of meh in my experience.
I've found the Sorc to be easy mode, the Merc to be pretty good, and the Marksman to be gimped. The marksman may be better for coop as he has some good traps buffing. I love trap-heavy builds, but unfortunately the marksman just can't succeed this way on his own, at least up to mid game where I got. in fact the only build I could find success with him is with his blue death beam thing, which is an awkward looking skill for a hunter type character. It shreds, but if you dont max out that one skill, he kind of sucks for solo play.
The graphics are great, once I got my 970 and turned everything to max, it looked even better, and the game runs well- alt tabbing and stuff is no problem. There is one crashing glitch where the game ctd if you try to craft something you dont have the blueprints for, something like that; it's been forever since that happened, it may have been patched anyway. Other than that, the game is entirely bug-free for me.
There are a couple of strong
which hurt the game. The game has a few points where difficulty spikes MASSIVELY. There arent a lot but when you get there, it could make you want to quit the game. The level designers seem to do what many (bad) tower defense level designers do - which is get bored, and force you to change your style & build entirely, in order to progress. And I hate that. There were a couple of points in the game that took a massive retooling, and were still SO hard,(that stupid one with the flyers, you know what I'm talking about devs) and what's more, there are very few places to increase your experience & trap levels along the way - you can grind gold & items but NOT experience & trap points, so you have to do the alternate Scenarios & Endless levels which are very few in number in some early - midgame spots. Also as mentioned before, it's a shame that the tower placements are pre-determined and pretty restricted in terms of what you can do, rarely can you concentrate them into a killing zone for instance. You can, but you have to do it -just so-.
If you can get past these few roadblocks, you should find a fun ARPG style grindfest to grind through at your leisure. Worth 50% off price, and would be worth full price if not for the couple of negatives.

Here's a game by Neocore, the creators of the Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing series. If you haven't played those, they're pretty decent hack and slash games in the vein of Diablo - and also the reason why Deathtrap exists. In the first game of the trilogy there were a few sidequests based around a tower defense minigame, where you used Van Helsing, his ghost companion Lady Katarina, and an outpost's arsenal of traps to defend your lair. They were a neat diversion, and proved popular enough to get expanded on in the sequels, and get its own spinoff title.
Deathtrap takes place in the same universe as Van Helsing, across a series of fortresses found in the Ink, a general otherwordly dimension you often visit for one reason or another. They were built to defend the human realm from the monsters found within, and you play as an adventurer who for whatever has decided to take up that task now. These are one of three classes: the close-quarters, tanky Mercenary, the fragile, spell-hurling Sorceress, or the ranged, hit-and-runner Marksman. All have their own skill trees, some of which are your standard ARPG stuff of passive bonuses and attacks, while others boost your traps. They also have their own dedicated upgrades, which are either unlockable boosts for them in the levels or passive stuff which is less potent but always active.
The levels play out largely the same as they do in Van Helsing, save for your character probably not having the array of skills he can. You're still able to contribute, but the towers will be the brunt of your offense. Most of them are lifted from their parent game, and include guns, spikes, burning floor tiles and even pits of monsters who fight for you. A lot of them enemies are also most of what you fight in Van Helsing, and have the same qualities such as resistances, auras that buff other enemies, and going berserk at low health.
This all makes sense given that you're in the same universe as the games that came before, but it still makes Deathtrap come across as a bit of a hand-me-down title. An expensive one, too, as it retails for twenty dollars when not discounted, five more than the Van Helsing games. Not that those games are bad or that this one is; I had fun playing them and so far Deathtrap is some decent fun. But it doesn't exactly stand on its own, and so far I haven't done much I didn't do in Final Cut. If there was anything you didn't like about the combat in that, such as the combat lacking a bit of punch, that would still apply here I think. Progression also seems to be about the same as in its big brother, which seems like a bit of a problem since you're only given new equipment, gold to buy it, or materials to craft things at the end of every level. You can get extra chests in some levels by killing optional enemies during waves, but it's not a huge boost.
Deathtrap also seems like it's a bit of a short game, with only thirteen levels, four of which I've finished in about two hours. There are higher difficulties for them the game encourages you to build your character up for, but it's overall not a grand adventure like Van Helsing was. It's probably a bit unfortunate they linked the two games together in so many ways, because this isn't a bad title at all, if you wanted more in that vein but wanted to take a break from Final Cut or whichever game you were on it'd be fine for that. But if you didn't like them, or don't much care for hack and slashes in general, this might not be the one to change your mind. Either way, I'd get it on sale.

Overview: 2D Puzzle Stealth Platformer
The Good:
+ The game does a fantastic job of mixing puzzle elements with platforming elements with stealth elements. All of this comes together in a complete package  designed to challenge you.
+80 levels across 8 sectors
+ Each Sector introduces a new gameplay mechanic that adds to the challenge and fun. As you progress through the levels these mechanics are put to more creative uses.
+ Each level contains a collectable, get all the collectables in a sector to unlock a new level.
+After completing a level you are graded based on three factors, time, deaths and number of times being spotted. S -Rank is the highest rank you can achieve. Achieving S Rank in all levels in a sector unlocks a new level. This provides plenty of replay ability to the game.
+ Different equipment to experiment with. Some equipment allows you become camouflaged, use a decoy, teleport etc. All of this is strictly optional, in fact to get an S-Rank you have to use no equipment, but it is nice they included these options for anybody who wants to try them out
+Level Editor to make your own levels and share.
+Lots of fan made levels that can easily extend your playtime
+ Game provides a cute story  that fits nicely with the game
+Great music
+Surprisingly addicting.
The Bad:
-Some minor glitches,
- Getting S-Rank in certain levels requires some luck
- The game can get frustrating at times, especially if you are trying to unlock everything
Conclusion:

Major points for me:
- Inventory/storage management is horrible. There is no way to bulk drop/delete/sell/store items. In a super sprawling game like this, it's not really acceptable. Paired with the low amount of storage per crate (or similar), it's impossible to keep a base tidy while expanding during the game.
- Teleporting is nice, illogical, and takes too long. Currently, I have had to find a flower biome, and pick up a plant-fiber-tree to re sew near my base to keep up with my flag-production needs. As well as, there's a hard cap on the speed of spinning fiber to material, meaning I'm basically walking away from my computer to let all the cloth be spun to make only a few flags each trip or three to a planet.
Upgrades seem tacked on, but that's fine for an ever-expanding game.
The Main quest line takes you logically through the planet progression, and ramps up combat pretty nicely so far (I'm up to the 3 weird ores, just past durasteel)
But world just doesn't feel like one I want to get immersed in. I don't know why.
Is it the fetch quests? Is it the hour of sorting to 20 minutes of exploring? Is it the difficulty of finding settlements that allow you to progress with the main quest, and therefore artificially hold progress back? I'm not quite sure.
Also, I still don't know how it'll work with multiplayer. Want to find out.
Edit: just finished the game, after expanding to rooms-worth of storage.
Bosses become pretty easy with grappling hook and healing +3 EPP upgrade (with a decent offhand weapon, like the craftable max-level wand)
And I've missed parts of the game, that just seem unimportant/not fitting in.
