There isn't much of a tutorial other than jumping in and telling you what your specific character does and what you must do to win. You'll feel lost and have no idea what's going on for the first few games, but that wears off once you understand a few roles, and what those roles want to accomplish. Like how characters are part of a faction or can act independently. There is some frustration because many of the game mechanics are poorly explained. Obviously the town people want to hang the mafia members, werewolf, serial killer, and arsonist, and vice versa. However some roles can take certain actions during the day or night, and the game doesn't show you what to click in order to take that action. You are left to figure that out on your own. This stuff isn't difficult to figure out at least.
The learning curve is the big obstacle in the game, but once past that the game becomes very enjoyable.

After about an hour of sitting on an island wishing I hadn't accidentally used all of my rocks to craft tools, I finally resigned myself to my plan of paddling out to a distant island to see if I could gather up some more. I paddled for ages and was incredibly excited to see the new shore. It was a small island with a wrecked ship on both it's east and west sides. After gathering a sizable pile of rocks to take back to my sad little home island, I decided to pull out my knife and explore the shipwrecks.
As I swam down into the tiny fishing trawler, I wondered how long I could hold my breath. Long enough to discover a hatchet stuffed away in a locker, and a fuel tank stored in the ship's console, and a spare lighter stored away in a toolbox. I excitedly tossed my treasure on the ground by my raft, eager to see what was located in the other ship.
This ship was much larger, maybe a crabbing boat or something. It had at least two decks. I couldn't discover the hidden gems in this thing. Oooh! Is that another hatchet? Yes! Awesome! Whoa, a machete?! Sweet, I should probably go up for air. Alright, air is sufficient. Let's go back down. Wait...what is this music? There hasn't been any music before...this sounds...ominous. Please tell me there aren't sharks in this game...OH CRAP, THAT'S A SHARK. SWIM DAMN YOU, SWIM.
After escaping what was certain death, I went back to my raft and settled on what to take back home with me. The rocks, the fuel tank, and my beautiful new machete. The rest, I left on the beach for easy access if I ever decided to grow a pair and finish exploring that boat.
As I began paddling back to my island, I reflected on my performance while I experienced extreme fear after spotting the shark, quite happy with myself. I escaped the wrath of a frightening creature while stupidly swimming around in his home turf. I can outperform sharks, man. I'm awesome.
It was at this moment of smug satisfaction that I heard the ominous music again and immediately reverted back to fear mode, and looked around my raft in a panic, trying to spot my tormentor. Suddenly my raft was violently pushed by something below me. I flipped out and started mashing buttons in an effort to pull out my new, prized machete treasure. In my panic, I managed to press Q instead, which resulted in my hurling the tiny plastic paddle I was using to transport myself home directly at the shark's head.
Realizing I was now stranded in a raft with no way to paddle back home, being circled by a large sea creature with enough teeth to completely ruin my day, I quit the game and decided to sit in bed for awhile wrapped in a cozy, warm blanket.
8/10 will most definitely play again.

Edit: Because I have been asked and the shop description isn't really telling much:
Luxor is from the same main principle then for example Zuma or Sparkle. Long lines of balls run along a track to a target (a pyramid in this case). By shooting balls to create rows of balls with the same colour, you can destroy them, before they get there. You get bonuses and powerups for creating especially long rows or for causing chain reactions. Powerups are things like explosive balls, special balls that match any colour or that change the colour of balls, static fields that collect bonuses for you or many different kinds of destructiv powers like the scorpion that kills those balls closest to their target. You'll have to kill a certain amount of balls/lines to pass a level and you'll lose the instant one of the balls touches it's target.
The best of all Luxor games. Quest for Afterlife features the original gameplay but is the only part of the series (I played so far) that has an upgrade-shop. With the Coins you collect in the game, you can buy upgrades for your power-ups such as making the scorpion smash another two orbs each time or increasing the fireball radius. Or you can personalize your wing and your balls with new designs.
And the game features unique game modes such as 'Crossing the River'.
If you just want to play along the standard Luxor-gameplay, you might not like this part of the series. But if you like to see a progress in your game and not just watch the levels get harder, Quest for Afterlife is the part of the series you are looking for. It even has some kind of story and sort of 'Open World'-map.
All other Luxor-Parts are just new graphics and some different power-ups and maps, but nothing new. I really don't understand why they removed all the innovative parts from QfA in the newer parts...

Thats all well and good but I get really tired of spending 20 minutes moving my characters to the edge of the map to avoid getting injuries when I retreat.
You can tell people are getting frustrated because after the most recent patch they started putting in helpful "tips" like "Mercs are paid to die" and "Losing is fun" to go with the actual gameplay related tips during the load screens.
The quest are your typical go to enemy base kill them and come back, follow enemy kill them then come back, watch a caravan crawl across the map kill what ever attacks you. The game is supposed to have replayability to go with its difficulty but you have to sit through the same starting fight every time and you don't get to see the map until after you've finished the first battle. I started 4 campaigns in a row before I got a map that was desirable.
Bottom line I won't be playing this game any longer, but I sunk 100+ hours into it so $.30 per hour of entertainment/frustration isn't as bad as some games I've purchased.  Pick up the game and maybe you'll like it, if you don't have rage issues like I do. Hopefully you won't end up randomly punching things as this game has inspired me to do.

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Isometric/ Action RPG/ Tower Defence
The Good:
+ One of the better looking tower defense games on Steam
+ 3 character classes; Sorcerer(Magic), Mercenary(Melee), Marksman (Range). Each one has their own skill trees. Some skills focus on making your character or traps stronger.
+ Scenario mode allows you to customize the difficulty by selecting from 9 different categories i.e. more monster health, faster monsters, less damage etc.
+ Endless mode
+ Each level has 4 different tiers. Each tier changes the tower placement or conditions of the map providing good incentive for replaying levels.
+ Completing levels, rewards you with experience and loot allowing you to upgrade your character and traps.
+ 25 different towers/ground traps between 5 different categories
The Average:
The game features controller support however for a much better and easier experience it is strongly recommended to play with a mouse. Certain functions can only be done with mouse.
The game does a poor job explain how certain things work in the game. I had to go online many times to check for answers that should have been explained in game.
In each level you can only place certain types of towers in predefined places. Unlike other tower defense games, this removes a lot of strategy associated with tower placement. This game is more about which skills and traps you invest experience points into rather than where to place towers which in my opinion takes a lot of the fun out of the game.
The Bad:
- Multiplayer is dead which is sad because some of the multiplayer modes seem really fun
- The game only has 13 campaign levels and 1 or 2 bonus levels. There just isn’t a whole lot of content here.
- glitchy achievements, some achievements will not unlock and the ones that do, require some grinding.
Conclusion:
A game that does a really decent job of combining action rpg elements with tower defense. The problem however is that the game is lacking content compared to other games in the genre. If you like tower defense games, I would recommend this game at a discount. I would love to see the ideas expanded upon in a sequel.

So I don't usually like writing reviews, but I was sort of blown away by this game.  First of all, the reason I bought it is because it's a tower defense game. I love tower defense, and the genre is getting pretty thin. Defense Grid, Kingdom Crashers, it just seems like nothing fresh has really happened td games in a while. So when I first played Deathtrap, I was very surprised.
First of all it looks great, the graphics are very nice. It has a very Gothic feel. There are some graphical glitches in the game, specifically when you kill some of the larger enemies, there is some screen tearing. I have yet to investigate how to fix that issue, but small issues are okay with me as long as they don't completely interrupt gameplay.
Speaking of gameplay, that's the strength of this game. It's sort of a mashup between Diablo and just about any other tower defense game. You have your character, you can choose from three, who can run around the battlefield and attack enemies, give power ups to towers, and they can also fight ghosts that appear on the battlefield to help you unlock better gear. Speaking of which, another cool part of the game is the leveling up of towers, and the equipment aspect. When you're in between levles, you can improve your equipment through crafting, finding equipment after fights, and purchasing items in the shop.
Perhaps one of the best things about the game is the towers themselves. It's very satisfying to watch these towers cut down a group of enemies as they walk along the predetermined path. I won't go into all the different trap types, suffice it to say, there are many, and they are all enjoyable to play.
The long and the short here is that these two elements brought together work beautifullly, seemlessly. It's like they were meant for each other and someone finally pulled it off well. If you like td games, you need to try this one. Worth every penny!

Feist is annoyingly hard to play. Trying to beat next checkpoint for ten or more times is a usual situation. Opponents appear ouf of nowhere. They fast, or tough, or attack in mass. And usually they are ridiculously precise in shooting.
On the opposite, for you, world's low gravity creates so much of a challenge itself that throwing or shooting becomes a frustrating experience. Consider the fact that you need to catch a fly of your own size and hold it to be able to shoot its stings. Just to discover that it can shoot only at most useless angle. And the fact that to catch the damn thing, you shoot beat it half to death first.  Spending a whole damn minute trying to jump and hit it with a stick. Dodging those very damn stings like crazy. And the fact that if you release the fly, which easily happens when you're hit, or have accidentally thrown it away yourself (due to struggle with controls, but as an adult you pretend that you did it intentionally), it shakes off and joins enemies surrounding you to take its revenge.
So, it makes close combat the best option. Which means running around with a stick. Which you need to find (strangely, beating it before taking is not required). There's only one little inconvenience with a stick. It breaks down after a single hit.  And nearest supply of sticks is left a couple screens ago. And is pretty limited (of course it is! hey, what did you expect? we're in a forest! what, do you think sticks will just lay around under you feet?). And, running back there usually rewarded with an immediate couple of spears in your sorry back (who would think that caterpillars are so impressive in throwing?).
Considering that your hero can take only around 3-5 hits, it makes combat a mix of chaotic running and jumping, counting much more on lucky circumstances rather than skill. The fighting takes around 95% of play time, and there's almost no other things to do. So, after first 1.5 hours of gameplay, I'm rather irritated than having fun.
For me, apart from bizarre visual style, there are no reasons to prefer Feist over a ton of other games, unless you're Dark Souls fan or dying over and over again is an integral part of your pleasure.

What I have learned playing Feist thus far:  The forest is full of treacherous beasties, but if you manage to seize hold of a dazed giant bumblebee, you can use his backside to fire stingers at the other treacherous beasties.  If you find yourself unable to scale some high terrain, find some things hanging from trees which resemble giant, hairy testes, and hurl them at the side of said cliff-face (they're sticky) to help you traverse said terrain.  And whatever you do, DON'T anger the gigantic, furry porcupine men...'cause gigantic, furry porcupine men will ♥♥♥♥ YOU UP.

Some even more surprising things which I've learned playing Feist thus far:  It is entirely possible for someone to make a game which superficially "looks" a bit like Limbo, and somehow make that game very nearly as GOOD as Limbo without replicating its gameplay too slavishly.  You can, for example, add quite a bit of "combat" to said game, whilst still replicating the highly believable physics and logical puzzle-solving of a game like Limbo.  Even more amazingly, you can make this new game seem oddly FRESH, in spite of the fact that it owes so much to not only Limbo, but indeed many a 2D, side-scrolling puzzle-platformer before it.  And all that's required to pull off this amazing feat is an extraordinary level of talent and an all-too-obvious "labour of love" work ethic evidenced only by the most dedicated of "artists".

I encountered several problems using the game in 4K (Ver. 1.0.6). Teleporters not working properly, monsters disappear from the screen and other small problems. I opened a ticket for one of these issue on the bug tracker Mantis (Ticket ID 0001265) and after several weeks without any feedback from developers, to my surprise, I find myself with the ticket canceled by this official explanation: "4k resolution is not supported, so there could be some side effects when set manually."
Unfortunately, 4K resolution is NOT CONFIGURED BY HAND but at the first start after the installation has been set AUTOMATICALLY from the game itself. The 2160p resolution (as several other higher to 1080p) is also available in the dropdown menu of settings. No hack or tweak was made to set the resolution.
A response of this kind is not acceptable.
Obviously the engine used on the game natively supports this resolution but the developer has not bothered to check what happened in the case was set to a resolution of this type by the user, or at least could have LOCK incorrect / unwanted settings.
It seems that the developer has decided not to further support this game and this is his right. But in my opinion does not make us look good in comparison to the thousands of INDIE games developers always available to deal with their users in order to refine and improve their products.

Dungeon Souls is an inoffensive but bland roguelike that feels like a mix between Nuclear Throne's and Risk of Rain, only less tight to control and not nearly as replayable.

You start by picking one of several classes: all of them have one basic attack along with a couple of unique skills such as temporary buffs, AoE attacks and so on. This is the game's greatest strength: each character feels unique and no matter what your playstyle is you're more than likely find a class that suits you.
You'll then be thrown into a randomly generated level where you'll need to find multiple summoning symbols. Activating these symbols will spawn a small amount of enemies, and once you've activated all of them you'll gain access to the next area.
This gameplay loop is simple but quickly shows its weak points:
-The level layouts will quickly appear similar to one another and you'll never encounter interesting combat scenarios like you would in Nuclear Throne.
-Fights quickly become samey since you always know when enemies will spawn, thus making you able to deal with them easily. Some of them are scattered throughout the level as well, but they're unlikely to cause much damage, unlike the traps scattered everywhere which can easily catch you off guard and eat away chunks of your health unless you manage to dodge them.
Eventually the only thing that breaks the monotony are the boss fights: while nothing special, they are different enough from one another to be challenging, although i felt their fights tended to drag on. Surprisingly they are voice acted, and while the audio quality and acting are both rather poor, i found it charming and appreciated the idea, even if it didn't really pay off in the end.
Finally the replayability: there isn't much of it.
Since Dungeon Souls shares Risk of Rain's progression system that consists only of picking up passive / active items that change the way the game plays (and occasionally level up one of your stats/skills), you won't really feel as though your character is different from one run to the next. Risk of Rain made up for that basic progression scheme by giving each character interesting synergies with specific items and through the use of artifacts that changed how you'd play the game as a whole. Since Dungeons Souls doesn't have anything like that, you're likely going to grow tired of the game fast once you've tried all of the classes.
To conclude: once more, the presence of a neutral rating would have been greatly appreciated.
Dungeon Souls, as the name might show, is unoriginal and doesn't play nearly as well as the games it was obviously inspired by. If you ever played Nuclear Throne while drunk, you've got a solid idea of how this game plays.
However i still had fun with it for the ten hours i have clocked in, whether or not that justifies the asking price is up to you, but i personally don't regret the time i spent with the game.
I guess Dungeon Souls earns a spot next to Neurovoider on the ever growing list of "okay" rogue likes on Steam.

TLDR For me this one of the best releases this year, an astonishing achievement for a tiny studio. For those who have played the previous game: This has improved from its predecessor in every possible aspect, a perfect sequel in my opinion, well worth the price. And just like with it's predecessor I'm sure the devs will add even more features over time.
For those who are new to the series: HOF is at it’s core a card game, but also much more; you build a deck of encounters (adventures) and items and then shuffle it with the cards the Dealer gives you to make a mission. It then plays out very much like a “chose your own adventure” type of game but it also has combat in it; the combat is similar to games like Batman AK, Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max etc, where you build a combo meter, dodge and counter your opponent and unleash abilities. It’s simple but highly versatile because of the huge number of factors that can modify how things play out (aka the cards you pick). The most noticeable difference between this game and the previous one is how much the game now relies on skill, instead of basing a huge part of the game on random chance ; this is also very much seen in how the missions are beautifully designed, the more you play one the more you discover that even what seemed unfair(rolling dice, card games etc) can actually be turned in your favor quite easily with the right cards.
Pros:
By far the thing that stands out the most as an improvement but also as a feature that takes the game to a whole other level is the
. It is magnificent…everything from the voice of the Dealer, one of the best written characters out there IMO, to the combat sounds and music that give a much bigger impact, a much deeper meaning to everything you do.
is improved much from HOF1. It’s now slower, far more impactful, precise and gives better visible queues to the player about what is happening. You have 3 types of weapons to choose from, a vast selection of armors/shields, artifacts and a wide array of enemies to fight, that are more or less effective because of what gear you’ve chosen. You also have companions that help you both in and out of combat, to make the journey far less lonely and give the game much needed charm.
The overall
is nearly flawless. Exploring the ins and outs of every mission is extremely fun, because unlike the previous game… where you basically played the same mission over and over but with different modifiers (which are fine, because they add replayability)… here you play a more linear but hand crafted mission that can be more engaging.
They’ve added multiple “game of chance” mechanics: dice, a pendulum/timing challenge and a wheel of fortune, which are all great additions brining much needed variety. Everything takes a bit of patience to learn to master and feels super satisfying when you do and like I’ve said these mechanics are NOT just RNG crap thrown in there, they take timing/skill and can be made easier or harder by different factors that you can influence.
. It is rare that a game grabs me so much that I want to unlock everything in it; I wanted to explore every single inch and then maybe even do a second run, but this does and I've enjoyed every minute of it.
The
is a bit more grounded then HOF1 and even if a bit predictable if you’ve played the 1st one, it’s still fascinating. Also the way it unfolds with side stories for each of your companions reminds me a lot of Mass effect 2 and that’s always a good thing in my book. It hard to make an overarching story in a game where the player makes so many of the choices, so I think they did a great job.
Things that can be improved:
The
have been a weakness in the first one as well, due to the low budget of the game, but here they are improved quite a bit. Still they need more special effects to go with the incredible sounds design; having no blood or particles really drags back the combat.The camera might need a bit of adjusting, considering the increased size of the arenas.
Also the
of the game is very bland and boring, pretty much anything you’ve seen before in any other fantasy game can be seen here. I wish the game could find its own style to stand out even more.
Cons:
NONE. This for me is a near pefect sequel, improving on everything and adding A LOT on top of it. Game runs great and had no bugs for me, while also having a VERY well balanced gameplay experience and that’s saying a lot for a card game that has multiple “game of chance” mechanics.
Congratulations and thank you to the devs, I had a blast.

I have not only survived on my island for 10 In-Game Days now, but I have prospured. Food and water is not an issue since I started coconut gathering, but I have three buckets of fresh water in-reserve incase I need them. And I have even begun traveling to other island for wood. My living quarters are nice for the island I've chosen as my home. I have a 3 by 2 hut with a roof and no walls (Who needs walls on your own island?) with stairs leading up to it.
Its a beautiful game, it has the potention to much better.
Here are some complaints about it:
I dont have any complaints about the graphics, the devs did a great job on that. But with placement when crafting solid objects and player interaction with the ship wrecks are what I have complaints about.
Crafting Placement:
My issue is that you cant place a bed on a foundation. In my current world, I have a 3 by 2 hut, soon to be larger, with the bed outside next to the stairs. Out of all things that should be on a foundation, a bed definitely should be one of them.
As for player interaction with ship wrecks I more specifically mean jumping over the rails and climbing on the ladders.
Jumping over the rails is a lot harder than it should be, I know in IRL, not everybody can clear a 3 foot tall rail in a second, but it doesn't take 30+ seconds to do so.
As for climbing ladders, you can't. Or atleast it doesn't work for me. If you see a hard box ontop of the beached ship, you have to jump on the rail and then the top of the ship to get to it.
Dev's, it you could fix those few issue, that would be great. :D
I do recommend this game for anyone who likes survival games.

While this game has many positives to it's name - the turn-based system, the action point costs, it suffers one major flaw in a game designed around replayability - it's so boring to restart.
Many games start players off slowly, adding in extra attack options, activated talents or simple squad size. Battle Brothers, unfortunately, allows you to start with a full complement of 12 members and punishes you if you don't do this (there seems to be no scaling of opponents based on your squad size). On top of this, you begin with so few hit points you're literally expecting troops to die at a time you cannot afford to replace them, because you are reliant on RNG when beginning instead of skill.
Ultimately if you can get past the initial tedium and horrible rng the game is absolutely fine... but that's a major if!

This is a mix of platform/puzzle/stealth games. With simple but  serviceable gfx.
The first time you play a level it is more like a steatlth and puzzle, as you try to figure how you can reach the exit avoiding all security systems and opening doors. Your receive a letter grade (A-D) for your performance which takes into account time/death/# times spotted. This part of the game is thoroughly enjoyable. Taking your time to explore the level and solve the puzzles is atmospheric and challenging.
Then the PROBLEM is that in order to achieve the best grade S (for stealth) you should complete the puzzle in a very short time without being spotted at all. And now  the game turn into a very tight timed platformer, where you must be very precise in your moves and jump. Hopefully the controls are quite good and the character is very agile and capable of changing direction in mid air. Yet getting a S grade on some level can be very hard and you may have to repeat the level many times to get a perfect result. BE WARNED that this part can be really nerves wrecking, and you'll realize why there is the B.....D word in the game title.
Note that each stage is mad of 8 levels and getting a S grade on the 8 level is not necessary to move to the next stage, it merely unlock a bonus 9th level on each stage.

I bought this game because it had positive reviews, it was cheap and I have no issue with reading a bunch of text/experiencing a story rather than playing a game. I also found the concept of unravelling a story through the use of looking through someone's phone to be an interesting one. If this also sounds like you, then go ahead and buy it. Now, onto the real part of the review.
SPOILERS AHEAD
I was really not expecting the story to take the turn it did. If you're observant, which I wasn't, you'll see the warning at the bottom about homophobic themes. When reading through everything, I expected the worst. I thought maybe Sam had been kidnapped or had genuinely gone missing. It's not until you start digging that you realise that Sam is actually a trans-woman. Maybe I'm exagurrating but I think the way the game reveals this is perfect and once you figure out what's going on, everything fits together really well. The game does a brilliant job of making you feel like a detective.
I know a lot of people will be turned away from the themes of this game, but ♥♥♥♥ 'em. Yeah sure, "SJW" themes are somewhat overdone in games these days, but I couldn't care less. This game does a brilliant job of highlighting the problems that trans people, or even just the LGBT community, go through and also the issue of coming out to a family that might not accept you for who you are.
That said, I have a few issues with the game that stop it from being perfect. The first issue is that the music player doesn't really serve a purpose and is honestly more destracting than anything. Trying to read large walls of text with music getting progressivly louder in the background is really difficult for me. It also served no purpose when it comes to puzzle solving. The second issue is that, while I apretiate it, a lot of the posts on the "Be You" forum seemed repetetive and not worth reading. Most of the posts there had nothing to do with the story, and while I do find it interesting to read about the LGBT community, a lot of the stuff there could've easily been compressed down. My thrid issue was the puzzles, some of them are a tad too cryptic. I feel like most people will need a walkthrough. And finally the ending. I'm not a fan of it. Maybe I'm bad for sympathising for Sam's parents... but I do. For all they know, their son/now daughter is completely missing. Possibly dead. But no. Sam just ran away from home without telling anyone. I know they are bigoted scumbags, but I feel like everyone should be treated with respect. Even bigoted scumbags. They have a right to know what happened to their child. In my eyes, Sam should've come out to them. The worst that could've happened would be them disowning her. Which, at the end of the day, is what she supposedly wanted anyway, because she ran away. I'm not sure how I feel about the ending. I'm usually a fan of bad endings, but this ending just makes the main character (Sam) unlikeable.
But honestly overall, I enjoyed this experience. While it has its shortcomings in polish and storytelling, I feel as though it does a great job of telling a story in an interesting way. Well worth the £2, heck I almost spent 3 solid hours playing this.

Feist is a little oddball of a game. It's rather Limbo-like but fails to capture the same atmosphere that made LIMBO special.
Even so FEIST is not a bad game per say, I rather enjoy it. The art style is lovely, the music and ambience great, and the backdrop and environment is actually rather nice.
It's a fun little platformer, where you play a feisty little furball that's recently escaped a trap and is now trying to escape this strange forest that's filled with hostile creatures. The AI is rather good, and certain enemies will relentlessly hunt you down, and even throw you against objects to try and kill you. You actually use the same method to try and defeat them, as you can pick up sticks to use as weapons. Although they break after contact with an enemy. Or you can pick up pine cones, and small logs to use as projectile weapons. At the same time the most irritating enemy I've ran into is the fly, they'll relentlessly pursue you, and fire projectiles at you.
They're also rather difficult to kill as a stick won't kill them with one hit. It will bring them down, and then you can pick them up and actually use them as a weapon.
While extremely annoying to face you can use them against other creatures, especially the large murderous furballs. Throw a fly against them and you'll turn the two against each other, and  you've done some damage to the large monstrosity. They are usually the bosses at the end of levels, so try with all your might to get past them.
The combat is entirely reliant on the games physics engine, and while it's not super complex it does a great job. Hitting enemies, moving boulders, and throwing objects all have decent velocity, impact and gravity attached to them, and without it the game would be horribly I feel.
The physics engine is also reliant on it, and you can move logs, stack rocks, or use these sticky plant seeds/pods to make little platforms.
So what's the main issue with FEIST? Well despite it being charming, and fun for a little platformer with physics based puzzles and combat; it's just too short. The game clocks in at 2.5 hours unless you've gotten stuck or died too many times. This makes it rather hard to justify the price tag of €15.
Add in that the game; while charming just doesn't capture you the way LIMBO did it makes it awfully hard to say whether it's really worth the price. Personally I enjoy the game, I actually find it somewhat relaxing. Even the combat is strangely relaxing. It's not intense, and the mood of the game; along with it's ambience and subtle music is rather soothing.

I would highly recommend this game if you have someone else to play with, it is a great couch co-op or online co-op (if you don't mind a bit of stream lag) or streaming puzzle game, if no one in the group has played the game before.
You basically are given a single button on a panel to start, and have to discover (currently, it keeps increasing!) 25 different endings based on various clues and experimentation. Some are very simple, some are deviously difficult, but most of them eventually make some sort of sense, and having multiple eyes looking at the puzzle really, really helps, as different people tend to see and think different ways.
You will probably eventually get stuck, and that's fine to do so, we got utterly stuck after finding 21 endings and with three half-puzzles left that we had no clue how to solve. From there, we had my partner look up the answers and start feeding clues instead, which helped direct the search and eventually finished the rest of the game that way.
As a single player game, I'd rate it decent but not great. I think a lot of the fun comes from being able to moan and sulk at a partner. :) I think solo, without external motivation or the enjoyment of being able to team up, a lot of people would discover maybe 10-15 of them, and then just give up or look the rest up. There tends to be some downtime in between ideas where you are just stuck and staring blankly at the wall, and having someone to bounce ideas off of during this time is enormously helpful.
Achievement wise, they're all fairly straightforward except for the last three, which become deviously difficult to do and requires a walkthrough (you basically have to replay the entire game without a single unneeded button press). Not a fan of that one. Still, the rest of the game was a pretty great co-op experience.
The music was great, perky and catchy without being too insidious. The graphics were decent and charming, I think some of the ending scenes could have been slightly better, but not complaining. Story? Not much of one. But that's okay!

A Land Fit For Heroes is a frustrating gamebook. I did enjoy the world, the characters, and the plot. I also appreciated the unapologetically mature tone. Regrettably, the drawbacks of this title outweigh those notable positives.
First and foremost, if a gamebook is promoted as having a connection to fantasy literature, that gamebook had better be written well, and this one is not, from a technical standpoint. It desperately needed a copy editor to fix a number of recurring problems:
* Improper punctuation, particularly the maddening tendency to omit ending punctuation (comma, period) in dialogue
* The insistence on using "There are"/"There is" in descriptions
* Comma splicing
* The frequent insertion of an unnecessary "would"
* Typos, missing words, repeated words, and other editing artifacts
As for the game portion of this gamebook, it also has technical, structural problems (aside from a significant number of irritating bugs, which I won't describe here):
* Combat is slow and clunky, and easily broken with certain feats
* A few choices don't make any difference
* A few choice sets seem to be assuming that the player will pick them in order

Starbound is a one-of-a-kind experience about exploration, the depths of solitude, and the limits of humanity (or perhaps I’m reading too much into it) that provides a unique atmosphere across a series of planets with near endless amounts of planets to explore, loot to collect, and places to see.
I think the only sensible spot to start with Starbound is in the darkness. Like many others, when I first started this game, I had a vague inkling of an idea of what I was getting into. Before there was an intro, there was silence. A vast void of darkness and I was alone; this is exactly what I want to highlight.
Starbound started in the dark (and if you choose to skip the intro, still starts in the dark but this isn’t about the main plot) where you’re left with absolutely no bearing. Your ship is offline, your Protectorate artificial intelligence S.A.I.L. demands a reboot, and otherwise you have no real idea of what’s actually going on. Earth is gone, and you’re alone in the abyss.
When you get down to your first planet, it’s typically a lush wonderland with green fields, huge forests, cascading waterfalls in the distance, and sizable mountains to scale. Your first instincts as a gamer will certainly recall Minecraft and lesser so Terraria but there’s no way to do this experience justice mentioning it.
The first time I ever saw this place, the game wasn’t finished. I was playing in Beta and it was some remarkable concept to me that this thing even felt so nice, it felt so polished for an unfinished product. I spent so long on my starting world that I felt as if there was no reason to continue any further in the game. The building took a bit getting used to but otherwise was rather conventional but done with the interesting Matter Manipulator in lieu of traditional tools. The crafting was simple, as you’d expect, with tables increasing your choices and just a decent amount of variety to be had.
I’d like to draw attention to the music as the primary inspiration here.
Something is... majestic and hopeful about it. It’s very well-made and composed, and the execution is done in such a way where if you really stop at the top of a mountain as the morning sun rises, you can feel the potential ahead of you. In time, however, I had exhausted all the novelty of my starting planet and I sought to see what the stars had to offer.
“What happened here?”
I know it doesn’t seem like a truly profound question but there are a multitude of ruins and towns alike that you will find on your journey through the stars that will make you truly ask yourself how things got to this point. Maybe it’s a ruined fortress on the surface or treasure-laden ruins in the depths of the world, but as time passes and you gain more knowledge of the universe you’re being put into, it creates a real sense of archaeological expertise when you can determine things such as, “Avians and Humans lived alongside each other on this planet thousands of years ago and were only small distances apart.”
Maybe it’s just the history lover in me, but I truly feel like each planet can tell a different story of how things evolved over time and how truly singular that you are as a person.
You might be a hero of legend who can save the galaxy, but you’re just one person.
I think the point where I truly became overwhelmed with emotional attachment to Starbound was the point where I discovered an old Hylotl (see: Space Japanese) castle in the middle of a quiet, unassuming planet and cleared it of monsters and spirits then proceeded to undertake a joint task of rebuilding it to make it suitable for colonization and turning a once-proud castle into what effectively was an indoor town. The sense of scale with buildings of this caliber is tangible, it truly juxtaposes the impact of your character being so much smaller than anyone before you.
Even further we continued to discover things in places I did not know there was anything to discover. An ancient Hylotl ruin in the depths of a planet with the only pocket of air being a half-submerged library as my companion sets up her cooking station on top of the bookshelves as we cook to survive the darkness with a full stomach. Each experience might come across similar structures and anomalies and surely the first time is the most breathtaking, but the experience will never be the same twice.
In total I absolutely love this game. I recommend it. I recommend it with friends, or alone, and I definitely think this is something you can play over and over again (and even more with mods) where you could surely have hundreds of hours of fun finding something that you particularly like about it and making it uniquely your own fun. This game is not like Minecraft or Terraria in any way but concept, but the execution and atmosphere are unmissable.

Hmm... this one's a hard one to review.
PROS:
—Beautiful, beautiful, BEAUTIFUL scenes/backgrounds. Absolutely magical art.
—A pair of magical goggles that transport you between past/present versions of the current scene (kinda like DOTT)
—At least one of the time-exploitation puzzles (the one involving trees) is very neat and clever
—Rather than inventory puzzles, LLT relies more on Myst-style machine-manipulation puzzles, which is a flavor I greatly enjoy and wish I could find in more games.
CONS:
—Every thing you click on plays a kinda slow/lengthy animation. Many puzzles require you to perform the same action over and over again, and it gets incredibly old watching these long, slow animations play out over and over again.
—The game’s coolest feature is the past/present time swapping goggles, but it is woefully, woefully underused.
—The game’s very first serious puzzle (i.e. the bubble pond) is one of the most frustrating puzzles in the game and may turn some people off right at the front door.
—Several puzzles in the game are based on color-swapping, but the puzzles don’t make sense. They end up being trial and error puzzles instead of puzzles where you work toward something that makes practical sense.
—The very last puzzle of the game is an illogical mess. You will most likely only solve it by guessing or by looking up a walkthrough.
—The game has no ending. Literally. It just abruptly ends with no apology or explanation. You solve the last puzzle, and then there is a short cutscene, and then Lilly finds herself in a new situation, and it appears as if this is a new room and a new puzzle is about to start, and then…. credits????? The ending is so painfully abrupt that it’s almost indistinguishable from a game crash. The barely-there story gets no resolution, no explanation, nothing.
--Very, very, very short. (About 2 hours, maybe a little less.)
This game is really beautiful, but it’s got some serious flaws that hold it back from being great. Here’s what it would need for true greatnesss:
+Some playtesting of the puzzles. A couple of them are painfully illogical/obtuse (especially that last one, holy hell).
+In fact, get rid of all of the silly color-based puzzles. Those puzzles are the worst offenders. The past/present time-swapping is the most interesting thing about this game and there is not nearly enough of it.
+Actually finish making the game.
I'm going to recommend this game to people who love point-and-click adventures, child-like wonder, and Myst-style machine-manipulation puzzles. However, I recommend it with a huge caveat, because I am not exaggerating in the least about the cons mentioned above. The gameplay is nicely composed one: you read the pages, you make choices and those choices affect the current or some future pages. As you advance, you gather items, information, you learn how to cast spells, solve some minigames, riddles and anagrams. Combat is pen-and-paper RPG style, turn-based and depicted on a grid. This game, man.

Earlier I was marveling at a herd of grazing antelope-like creatures on a little yellow paradise of a moon with a pink sky. I very much appreciate the technical and leveling aspects such as mining and trading, but most of all, this game has been an extremely emotional experience for me so far. Enjoy, everyone. And thank you, Sean and Hello Games. Jeez Louise.

While easily one of the more beautiful and aesthically pleasing games that I have played, Lilly Looking Through is definitely not worth $10. If you can get it in a bundle or for less than a buck or two, by all means - go ahead, purchase and play it. I, personally, did not buy it with physical money. I purchased it, from a friend who got it in a bundle, with virtual currency from another site that I play on. I almost (almost) feel cheated for how much I spent, even virtually.
Lilly Looking Through has less than two hours of gameplay to it. With only ten (or so) levels, it's definitely not a game that you want to sap time. The only thing that Lilly Looking Through has going for it, I think, is the fact that it is so absolutely beautiful and (kind of) relaxing. The puzzles do get tedious (as other players have mentioned), the solutions oft-times seem extremely arbitrary with no actual reason, and the game itself seems to be compiled of mostly filler play.
If I remember correctly, Lilly Looking Through was intended to be a short story. I think it should have been kept that way and not fashioned into a game. The ending is extremely abrupt, and I literally had no idea it was over until the credits started rolling and my boyfriend asked, "Is it over?" to which I responded that I think so.
There's absolutely no conclusion; the game appears to have been built on a cliffhanger, almost as if it was the end of one "part" and there is another part to follow. If there is, I do look forward to seeing the rest of the story. If not... well, I suppose that's that. For those of you who can't stand a lack of ending, don't play it until we know more.

So first of all, this is not the usual game you play if you wanted to blast dozens of soldiers into oblivion. A Land Fit For Heroes is based on Richard Morgan’s dark fantasy trilogy of books and like its ancestor, it is first and foremost: a book. You follow the narrative of three characters, all of them, ehm, damaged (to say the least) by reading. You start with Kirellin, a sad ex-soldier with massive ptsd, then you change to Calnar, who is a tribal warrior, abused by his father during his childhood years. Then you change to Ilaria, who is a rootless thief, trying to find herself. You can choose any of them to be homosexual or heterosexual, it does have an effect on the flavor of the story, but not on the main storyline. Lots of details depend on this, like Kirellin’s relationship with Ringil Eskiath, Richard’s main protagonist in the original novels. After reading Ilaria, you change back to Kirellin, and so on…
Your characters will have to cooperate by finding vital information (I’m not spoiling anything about how they communicate, etc) and as the story goes on, the three narratives get closer and closer to each other. Besides reading and making the usual gamebook choices (are you kind to barkeeper? do you kill the thugs?) which have consequences on the later pages, you get to fight battles. Previous reviewers said that the battle is “thin” – I kinda liked it, it reminded me of the old Pool of Radiance-type of games. But I’m above 35, so I like nostalgia, and I don’t have the fingers to click forty times a second, nor do I like FPS games. It is turn-based, you can roll virtual dice, you get to cast spell (after learning it), while learning and using Feats (special short-term powers) gives a small strategic element to each round.
Yes, you have to register to the publisher’s database in the game, to save your bookmarks to the cloud. I have no problem with this, though integrating the Steam’s cloud db would have been a lot more elegant.
There’s also some basic dungeon crawling, using an isometric approach for two characters, which I think is there to boost them before the final chapter, when you control all three of them and fight the Big Enemy together. It is fun, a bit rogue-like: some grinding, loot, some traps and locks to disable (with cool minigames) and then some more grinding.
Like I said, I like this game. It is unusual, the narrative is deep, and even disturbing at some points. The characters are very detailed, so you can easily find yourself liking the anti-heroes of the gamebook, like I did. This game is not for everyone, I guess, but I think it will find its audience!

You are Lilly, the first legally blind female to serve in the elite U.S. Navy SEALs. Guide your team through harrowing door-to-door urban combat and clear booby-trapped cave complexes across three different Middle Eastern countries that have been badly fictionalized by risk-averse developers. Wield your white cane and an awesome array of realistically-modeled weaponry (including the H&K® G36, the FN SCAR®-H and the Magnum Research® Desert Eagle) for a true Tier One experience. Lilly Looking Through is a touching story of honor, loss and redemption that has been hailed as "the best PTSD simulator since that level in Painkiller with the straitjacketed electroshock guys" (Game Informer), "a rollicking good time for the entire family" (IGN) and "a patriarchal, racist oppression of the disenfranchised minority diaspora" (Kotaku).

This ALMOST made it to the recommended pile, and I really wanted it to, but unfortunately the scales tipped the other way.
+ Art is beautiful and fun, animations very fluid
+ The goggles are fun to use
+ Many puzzles are quite clever, and pretty satisfying once you figure them out
+ Minimal UI makes the scenes more immersive
- No ending or closure
- No attempt to tell a real story
- No explanations of ANYTHING
- Animations between clicks are unacceptably slow
- Way too many clicks required to accomplish seemingly simple tasks
- Unclear puzzle goals
- Unintuitive puzzle mechanics (obscure hotspots, backward-thinking)
- Solutions require overly-repetitive actions
- No mid-chapter saving, so crashing means restarting the entire chapter
- Very short (~2 hours + more if you're forced to restart a chapter)
- Certain UI buttons don't do what you think they should
~ Not quite a con, but for such a dialogue-free game, the few spoken words detract from the atmosphere a bit
Let me start with a warning:
No, that's not a spoiler. I
I read about the lackluster (understatement) ending in reviews beforehand, because I felt robbed as a player. No closure, no satisfaction. I could maybe forgive that if the last scene made any sense, but it doesn't. And to make it worse, the final "reveal" is only shown for maybe 2 seconds before the credits roll, so you don't even get time to look around for visual hints.
I'm not even sure what the story is, to be honest. Nothing is explained. Other than the overarching "solve puzzles to find and save someone" umbrella plot, you get no hints about who or where these characters are, why the goggles do what they do, why Lilly can breathe underwater, etc etc etc.
But let's assume you don't care if a game has a story/plot.
I enjoyed the "swapping worlds" mechanic of the goggles. There are a couple of other games that involve a "magic lens" of some kind, so it's not a groundbreaking idea, but this is the first game I've played that makes it the main prop/power. Using it to progress through each scene and puzzle was a fun experience, and I wish there were more excuses to toggle it.
Moving around...oh dear. The animations are fluid and cute, but the timing is sooooo slow. It's not that big of a problem when the distances are short, but if you need to repeatedly run/swim across the entire screen, the wait time is simply too long. It gets absolutely excruciating in the last pipe scene, with jaw-grinding stop-and-go movement that has you clicking the same thing over and over and over just to achieve a single goal that could have easily been reached with 90% less clicks. (Then for all that work, you get no real ending.)
The puzzles are clever, yet simple enough to figure out with no direction. A bright kid would probably have a blast with them. However in several it's not really clear what the goal is. In more than a few cases I resorted to the help button (something I try to avoid), which highlighted hotspots I never would have guessed without more information. But once you know what you need to do, it's just a matter of completing the steps.
A note for the confusing color puzzles (bells/columns and berries):
The logic is there (and consistent across puzzles) - it's just poorly implemented.
Score: 4/10
Don't get me wrong - I did enjoy the game, and was very torn about giving it a thumbs down. But the lack of explanation across the board (story, puzzle goals/solutions, ending, everything) is a huge turnoff. The great aesthetics do soften a few of the cons, but don't expect more satisfaction than a handful of "a-ha!" moments during individual puzzles.
If you're a patient, laid back, and/or artsy person, I'd say give it a shot, but wait for a bundle or sale. Otherwise there are much more rewarding P&Cs to be found elsewhere.

Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is one of my favourite games and can be considered the one which induced my love for indie games. The game heavily relies on the rogue system and random items you are gifted with upon each run. Sometimes you might get a good run while other times you'll be having a hard time. Each run is new and different and not only does it rely on skills but also knowledge on certain secrets of the game that just makes it more of a master piece. Each run you might unlock new stuff that can be obtained in the next run and new levels after completing the the runs for a set amount. For some people Binding of Isaac: Rebirth also relies heavily on achievements so if you are a fan of achieving achievements then I would higly recommend it. All in all Binding of Isaac: Rebirth requires the player to have dedication, knowledge on certain aspects of the game (for a boost) and bullet hell dodging skills. As for its shortcomings there really are none unless you are the kind of guy that doesn't like the rogue genre itself (and maybe some offensive material such as different view on biblical depictions or feces but I personally like that it presents itself as it wants to.)

[This review was written on the original release: quite a few fixes have now been put in place by the developers in the time since then, and they've been good enough to comment below. Always a good sign :) ]
Richard Morgan's a talented writer when he's not having to string a plot around pretty lightshows like Crysis 2 & 3 or that empty-headed Syndicate FPS (his Black Widow stories are darn good), so I was intrigued when this appeared on the storefront and figured at the price it would be worth a go. Generally preferring his sci-fi novels like the 'Altered Carbon' trilogy or 'Thirteen', I had read 'The Steel Remains', his first fantasy book and found it actually pretty good, like it was written by a nihilistic Michael Moorcock, though didn't get around to reading the following ones.
So this game takes place in the same world as 'The Steel Remains', and is a choose-your-own-adventure gamebook with three characters you play in turn in their own parts of the story. It makes reference to TSR's hero Ringil, but you're not playing him so it doesn't mess up the canon. You can adjust their attributes and skills in a character creation screen before the game starts, interestingly picking their sexual orientation as either homosexual or heterosexual. I've not got far enough at this point to see how/if that affects gameplay. Doesn't seem to affect combat :)
The story starts intriguingly, and the prose is vivid. However, it's riddled with stupid mistakes. "You father", "a children have gone missing", "you suspects they are all fake", "your unable to make up your mind", "making his presence a cold and hard", "you have a clear view on their lips". This is pretty inexcusable for a game that lives and breathes by the text, but if you're willing to overlook it, the story flows well and the characters are better drawn than much of the multi-million polygon NPCs in some AAA games who still have the depth of cardboard cutouts. Some things are silly: the shop screen told me "You have 499 money". Really? Couldn't you have at least written 'Florins', the gameworld's currency? Lazy.
Oh, and the 'Exit' button doesn't let you exit. You just go straight back to the main menu. There's plenty of sloppily-left in clues that this was originally a mobile game too: prompts to "tap" and "rotate your device to landscape orientation". Ahh modern gaming, what are you doing to us?
So why recommend it? Because as shotgunned as it is with the kind of errors you have no right to make once you leave school, the text has a pull and interest that should keep fans of darker fantasy engaged. I already want to know where the plot is heading, and what repercussions my decisions may have. I can overlook subliterate developers for that.
(there's... morally questionable material here, admittedly. But nothing that'll shock you if you've ever watched Game Of Thrones)

I love this games creativity for the simple fact it attempted to put all the sports together into one game. This is not an easy challenge to overcome. How the heck do you put someone who dribbles a ball with their feet versus their hands in one game? Well, Super Slam Drunk Touchdown definitely will impact your perspective on what a sport can be.
The
is extremely simple and straightforward. There are a few buttons in the game that you will need to string together to win the game. As any sport game, pass and shoot are both there. Pass is very simple and straight forward. Basically wherever you point the joystick and press pass is where the ball will go. The shooting scheme is a little complicated - in a good way. There are three strengths of shots and possible variations. Your shooting style will depend on the type of player you choose. The players available are soccer players, football players, baseball players, hockey players, roller-derby players, and (not limited to) basketball players. So, for example, if you were to choose a soccer player, the soccer players first shot variation is a low short shot, the second shot is sort of a low power shot, while the third is a shot lob in the air. This means the soccer player can kick the ball in the net, kick the ball into the basketball net, and kick the ball over the football uprights (posts). The basketball player meanwhile might have a challenge throwing the ball into the net as he will go for the basket. The roller-derby player has no problem rifling shots on the ground, but cannot throw the ball up in the air. You are not stuck using one player and can switch players at any time during the game - so don't think you're stuck! There is a boost button that the players can use when it is not recharging. Tackling is straight forward and sort of goes by the system of who touched the ball last. Sometimes there will be full out brawls to determine who gets the ball.
The
follow a pixel/nintendo graphic art. I think it is suitable to the game, but can be a bit challenging at times. Throwing the ball into the basketball hoop sometimes is a bit difficult to do as the 3D is sort of there and not. It is fun to try and often the player is successful. The special effects (strobe lights) and other effects are in the game as well. Sometimes randomly, a zamboni, a streaker or even a band might start going across the field of play. The visuals are okay, but I think a little more could have been done to enhance the effects in the game. The
are not various, but are funny. You will know when the band starts marching across the field of play. I also think this domain could have used more bells and whistles.
Overall, the game is innovative, different and fun to play. The problem is the lack of content once you finish the challenges and play a few of the mini-games. Mind you, it is a fun local game you can play anywhere. For whatever reason though, it's not multiplayer. I think the game could benefit from having multiplayer features. I would recommend a purchase on sale.

I was heisetent to buy the game, I really enjoyed the first game and was thinking "what could they really change to the game formula to make it better without making it a different game?" The amount of changes and updates that have been made are well worth the asking price, they turned an already pretty damn good game to a great game.  The challenges are a lot more unique this time around and well themed, you get companions and there is more then just the 3 card monty game as far as the games of skill/luck during the card phases, the combat while still not the strong part of the game has been improved a lot, and there is a lot more enemy varriety with more enemy skills.
All in all, everything that was weak in the first game has been fixed in this one. My biggest complaint really is just how few cards you get to put into the decks this time around, but at the same time that also makes it much more likely for you to run into the event your trying to run into, and since the challenges are themed and have plenty of variety themselves it's not a big deal that you get to add so few random encounters to be drawn from. My only other complaint is that it seems a lot less percentage of cards have token events attatched to them, but again maybe there are more token events just a lot more cards so just seems like less at the start, but it seemed like almost every card in the first one had a token card for at least the first card in the chain, this one seems like maybe 25% of the intial cards have token events, but maybe that is just the early game, and at the same time there are also actual quests to do during the missions so maybe they focused more on the companion quests and mission quests leaving less focus on the one off token quests.
At the end of the day, if you enjoyed the first game, this one makes the first one feel like a demo in comparison, everything great about the first game is still here, and a lot of the poor things about the first game have been reworked to make them better.

A fun novelty - less than a game, but proficient at what it aims for.  It's essentially a "room escape" game, where you're scrutinising the environment for clues to a series of more or less arbitrary puzzles.  The catch here is that each "escape" takes a couple of minutes at most, after which you reset and look for another solution.  The aim is to find all the solutions.
It's the arrangement that makes it less than perfect.  Some solutions branch off other solutions, requiring you to repeat initial steps.  It's hard to tell when you've fully explored a branch, and each exploration may require repeating a number of steps.  At least one branch involves hundreds of clicks to reach multiple endings.
Still, fun for what it is.  Worth your time at any price point under $5 AUD.

Starbound was one of the first Early Access games a friend and I picked up. We played it a lot in the very early days and it was the first time we were burned by Early Access development: they changed the format of save data. We lost everything on our saves and we were legitimately bummed. It was in this moment we vowed to never again to become too time invested in an Early Access. For Starbound, it meant we removed the game and would occasionally install it for a day here and there to check out some updates.
We were excited again. The prospect of finally being able to enjoy the game that the developers envisioned made us giddy and impatient. We prepped the week of launch and when I returned from work, I dove straight into my server to get a dedicated Starbound server setup. And it was worth the wait.
Starbound is everything I had hoped it would be, especially following the massive successes that Terraria and Minecraft are. In so many ways it even surpasses both. It has the open world (or rather universe) feel we expect with hundreds of blocks to collect and make in order to build our own homes. But rather than emptiness, the worlds of Starbound's universe are filled with creatures, bandits, authoritarians, religious fanatics, violent tribes, savage lands, and towns full of merchants. It's a living universe.
And what's more is that you create a character that's part of it all. You choose 1 of 7 races to play as and then you take your ship from planet to planet, unraveling a story that's wonderfully told. Every animation is smooth and the style is fun, creepy, and inspiring. And even when you're done with the story, there's still tons of exploration to try and locate those elusive decorative pieces and amazing weapons. Speaking of weapons, combat is well balanced with players needing to keep track of terrain and combat style of enemies in mind at all times.
But you don't want to settle down you say? Then don't! Expand your ship through crew and/or purchased licenses and make a mobile base. The regular old game isn't challenging enough? With full Steam Workshop support you can find a mod to increase difficulty. Don't want to have to bother with anything? There's probably a mod for that too!
Starbound is hands down one of the best games I've played in 2016. If you're thinking about it, stop thinking and pick up a copy. It's worth every cent.

I can fully recommend this game, even if you didnt played the first title. I enjoyed the first title alot and even if many said they disliked the battle mechanics in the first one, i quite liked it.
They made the combat in the sequel much harder (no more riposte with only one button) and you have to play a bit more defensively when facing big groups of enemies. The variety in encounters and monsters was also improved and most of the different types are fun to fight against, once you understand their patterns.
The first few challenges are quite easy, but starting midgame they increase in difficulty and you have to think harder which cards you bring to the table, to beat the gold token. There are 22 challenges currently and the variety within the game mechanics is marvelous, i enjoyed nearly all challenges, even though i couldnt get gold in each encounter before moving on to the next one. But i guess thats intented, because you get more powerful cards towards the end, that make the hard challenges quite manageable. It's also fun to think how to tackle a challenge best, some require you to think outside the box.
Most encounters have some sort of gambit (a built in minigame) to determine what happens next, compareable to dice rolling in pen&paper rpgs. There are 4 types of gambit: a physics based dice rolling(the only random gambit), a pendulum where timing is crucial, a wheel of fortune(also timing based) and card shuffling, while you can track the cards to increase your chances. There are many equipments and blessings that improve the gambits and your chances at them, so dont get to frustrated too fast.
The developers are quite active in the forum aswell, i rarely see a topic, where they dont reply to help or fix some problems, i dont know many games, which such awesome developers.
Only downside in my eyes so far is the currently still missing endless mode, but im sure, that gets added soon. Even without the endless mode, you have about 40h playtime to get each token to gold, for all achievments maybe 45-50 hours.

Honestly couldn't recommend this game even though it has a lot going for it. There are too many problems to make this game an enjoyable experience.
Even after turning off most of the text and the screenshake, the fact you have to fight in tiny rooms with lots of projectile effects (plus all the bonus effects from items) means you literally cant see whats coming and you just have to hope not to be hit. I have died numerous times in my short playtime (I nearly made it to boss 3) to this.
One of the worst examples is the wizard. The wizard shoots 3 large fireballs; as well as this in one run I had upgrades that created fire on the floor, explosions and split my projectiles upon contact, as well as multiple orbitals flying around my character; if this wasn't bad enough there is also the addition of huge damage numbers that appear if you dont turn them off in the options, and all of the enemy projectiles and ground effects.
A lot of the damage you will take in the game is extremely cheap and doesn't really feel fun or skillful. All of the levels have traps, spikes that appear periodically from the floor and enemies that teleport or spawn ontop of you.
As well as this, you are nearly always forced to fight in tiny rooms with no real exit where there is no real choice to tank damage (or even die). The bosses are actually pretty easy because you have an open space to fight them in, and i rarely took much, if any damage from them.
Enemies randomly spawn around the map and you will get hit by projectiles from the room you just cleared seconds ago which is frustrating. I feel like the traps do way too much damage. I was playing as the necromancer and my skeleton stepped on a boulder trap that killed me from full hp. The ranger takes 1/2 his HP from a single spike trap and would probably be 1-shot by boulders too. constantly dodging annoying floor hazards isnt skillful; its just tedium!
Some enemies seem impossible to fight without taking hits. As a melee character you can rely on an extremely long cooldown ranged ability or charge straight into the enemy. In the ice zone there are enemies that literally fill a whole room with spikes that will destroy you as a melee character if you get anywhere near!
There are no warnings about low-hp; many enemies don't make significant (or any) noise as far as i could tell when they fired at you (or in the case of ghosts, teleporting directly ontop of you); and the warnings you get for stepping on floor traps arent nearly adequate enough for the danger they pose towards your character (i.e. immediate death). In a clustered fight, having a trap that can 1-shot you can be sometimes tricky to notice when dodging projectiles and dying immediately to a trap you didnt even notice is pretty annyoing.
I honestly feel that this game has many positives; but i'm not going to go into huge depth in this review; as this was mostly a complaint about the mechanics that I feel make the game worthy of a negative recommendation. If these features were amended then I feel like this game would be easily playable and fun.
Here is a short summarization of positives
I honestly think the game would benefit (in its current state) from the addition of some features.
Put the Runes (I'm sorry if I misremembered the name) that spawn enemies in much more open rooms, so there is room to manouver
Add a dodge/defence mechanic to the game so its much more possible to escape from a hairy situation
Remove constantly respawning enemies; or at least make them spawn from unexplored areas; since getting shot in the back is annoying
Reduce the huge amount of traps, and space them out. Running through a hallway with 8 spike traps is very annoying
Balance some creatures so there are combat options against them (such as melee characters vs the crystal spike things in the ice zone)

For those curious about the tactical combat, the best way I can describe the depth is:
First time through, nothing worked. My guys were getting slaughtered and I had no idea why.
Second: I figured out that some melee weapons can attack two squares. I start playing with a heavy front line holding shields, with pitchforks or polearms in the second line. This works well, so I give my front line guys all swords so they can shield wall AND riposte. Sadly, I learn they run out of fatigue very quickly when I do that. And even worse, I'm completely ineffective against anyone with a shield.
Third: I build a front line with shields and axes, 'cause I'm all about breaking shields. This works great! Well, against brigands at least. My back line of archers, crossbowmen and pitchforks can't do much against undead. And greenskins....I can't even fight them. I make it to the noble war and realize how bad it is to fight enemies in full plate when you have nothing but axes and pokey backline weapons....
Fourth: I'm gonna win a noble war, damnit! My front line focuses on hammers, and military picks are the weapon of choice. I mix an archer, 2 crossbowmen, a pike, and two axemen in the backline. This works great for the nobles war, but undead are tough and greenskins are so bad I can't win a fight against them.
Fifth: Three crossbowmen, two pike, and an axemen in the back line. Front line is all shields and spears, for spear wall. I give all my frontline guys quick hands, and equip them with an extra  shield and give each a different secondary weapon: Axe, Hammer, Mace, Sword. My spearwall really shuts down the greenskin charge/stun attacks, and after trying a variety of different formations, I'm able to effectively take them out. Undead still give me trouble since pokey things are worthless against them....
I'm sure that as I keep playing, I'll eventually figure out that I need a good mix of weapon types to be effective. I mostly run with a flat 12 man roster with no reserves, mainly because I have trouble enough paying the daily salary as it is. I suspect i'll also learn that I really need to have several bros in reserve, so I can swap them in for different situations, as it's probably pretty tough to build a single 12 man roster that can fight humans, undead, greenskins, and direwolves/nazguls.
This is all just the depth of the tactical battle side of the game. You also need to balance stats, like fatigue vs initiative vs armor vs mobility. In fact, fatigue and armor degradation are super important. It's not a question of IF you'll run out of fatigue, it's a question of WHEN. Sure, you can have a guy with amazing armor wade into a bunch of enemies without fear. But unless he's built properly, he's going to be unable to raise his shield in a few turns. And while he might take round after round of hits without losing a single hit point, all of sudden his armor is going to finally give out and.. POP...he goes from full health to dead in one hit.
If you like tactical turn-based games with character progression, you should defintely give BB a shot.

I'm a sucker for these you-against-the-world RPGs in the vein of Mount & Blade or Mordheim. Anything with a system that lets you slowly build out a team of your own design, with a little bit of randomization at recruitment, hooks me right away. Battle Brothers has that in spades.
- highly recommend for turn-based fans. General RPG fans should wait and see for mod support or DLC that makes the faction system more complex.
The writing and art is exceptional for a game from such a small team. Many different events crop up randomly but in a naturalistic way steaming from each character's background. There's lots of room here to try all sorts of builds with a wide variety of different weapons, all of which have their own advantages and disadvantages. Combat (the majority of the game) is satisfying and easy to understand, yet very challenging to maximize. You need to anticipate the most effective party set up ahead of challenging encounters. Exploration feels fresh in each new game due to the world map using a random seed.
Sticking with the characters you recruit and develop from the start of the game hurts you in the long-run. The most expensive men have higher base stats, and you'll need to begin rotating them in as the game goes on. There is a system to pay for exp boosters to help them catch up, but it's still an irritation. There's also no way to respec any characters. This can be especially frustrating if you find a unique weapon but have no one that was spec'ed to use it. There's no mod support at the time being, but if the developers are smart, they'll see how mod support could keep this game fresh (and sales coming in) for years to come. The world is detailed, but not quite as alive and changing as the world map in Mount & Blade.

I love this game so much I decided to write my first review ever... With almost 200 hours and counting I have to say the game is addictive and since I bought Battle Brothers I can't play any other games, they just don't seem to keep me interested. Starting with battle isle long time ago I always loved turn based hex strategy games. This one delivers a lot of tactical combat, with range of skills that are connected to the weapon your men use. Game is hard but rewarding. As your men gain experience and better equipment they become powerful. Enemies who would rip them apart in early game are just a meat to hack and slash... if you play smart. If you don't, you will end up losing your men.
I promise you, you will have your favorites. Some guys will be the core of your mercenary team. They will be your damage dealers with two handed swords, axes or hammers and you will send them to the front or flanks, so they might decapitate multiple enemies at once... and few turns later you will be swearing loud and brainstorming how to save them from certain death...
Couple advices:
1: Few guys with shield and spear can save you from swarms of "stupid" enemies. Zombies and beasts will kill themselves on your spear wall. "Smart" enemies won't go for that but you can learn to direct them to go where you want them to, with the right spear wall. Spears have low damage but still are useful because of that skill.
2: If you are strong enough to kill ancient legionaries, get few war scythes. Few guys armed with them can make short work of any swarm. They can hit 3 enemies at once if you set up your team properly.
3: Little stars next to your guy stats tell you if he is extra talented in that stat. That will give you more points to the stat every time he levels up. High starting value and 3 stars in melee( especially if guy has some good perks) make a great mercenary.
I have only few archers in my team. In late game I prefer 2-handed weapons, especially swords as they can hit 2 enemies in line or 3 around. Great axes can hit more enemies at once but the problem is you have to stand away from your guys or you will hit them too. Hammers are good in destroying armor, 2-handed hammer can hit 3 enemies like 2-handed sword. War scythes are great second line weapon. With long axe you can destroy shields from the second line.
If you don't play ironman mode, save your game often. Game auto saves before every combat so if something goes really bad for you, you can try again. You will notice that terrain in battle mode will be different each time, so if you really want you could chose one more favorable for you. You can also change your team setup after loading from auto save.
I didn't play ironman mode yet (no manual save). I believe its very hard. With ability to save you can check stats of men to hire and hire only those with better stats. And replay battles. On ironman you have to go through a lot of men to get highly talented group. And you will lose your best guys eventually.
Buy this game and have fun.
