TL;DR - Stranded Deep is an amazing island survival game. The gameplay is solid and offers several hours of playability right now. There are several bugs and polishing that could make the game play better, but are not essential to the gameplay experience. Right now, the system is very forgiving and makes it very easy to survive, but harder survival options may come at a later date.
PROS:
Unique crafting system
Underwater ecosystem (graphics)
Day/night cycle (graphics)
Shipwrecks for loot
Sharks (AI is curious)
Resource gathering
You can build an outboard motor for a wooden raft
Mods for creative or super speed
CONS:
Lack of harder survival options (yet)
No multiplayer (yet)
Shipwrecks are hard to climb on occasionally, and one shipwreck in particular you can't get out of. (fix by including vault button, or being able to jump out of the water)
When you sleep, the sun stutters for a few seconds.
Sharks run away from you most of the time.
Food bar runs out faster than water bar.
Plants regrow way too fast and coconuts spawn too numerously
No player shadow (game doesn't have character model, just hands)
Animations need polish and bug out in certain events
Sounds could be better
Building system has arbitrary "blocking" system so you can only place foundations on specific surfaces.
Can't cut down all trees.
Lack of ranged weaponry.
Lots of items are virtually useless (flare gun, whistle, binoculars)
You can only build a tiny raft
No endgame (yet)
No land predators (yet)
Many of the cons are nitpicking, or balancing bugs that will probably be sorted out by Beta.
All in all, the gameplay concept as of right now is solid and I've gotten a good amount of time out of it. Major gameplay changes won't happen until they add an end-game option or multiplayer (vs and coop).
Fun game, but very repetitive. I'd recommend it at the $15 price point or lower.

Easily one of the best games I've played. Bastion has a fantastic story set in a beautiful world full of wonder and mystery, backed by stellar voice acting and an unforgettable soundtrack. Everything in the game feels like it was crafted with an incredible amount of love and care.
You play as an unnamed kid, one of the few survivors of an apocalyptic event called the Calamity. As you explore and fight your way through the various levels, everything you do is narrated by the voice of a strange old man. The narration seems like a simple gimmick at first, but it ends up tying into the story in some very clever ways. The story itself touches on some interesting themes, takes quite a few unexpected turns (in a good way!), and kept me invested right up until the end.
The soundtrack really deserves a special mention. I can't begin to stress how good it is. From the main menu theme to the end credits, there wasn't a single track that failed to engross me. I had several songs stuck in my head for weeks after I finished the game. It's fanastic in its own right but, like the narration, the music also has a pretty big significance in the game's story. It's very rare for a video game soundtrack to tie in with the story in such a way, and Bastion's soundtrack is a testament to just how clever the game really is.
If there was one gripe I have, it would be with the combat. It's not bad at all; it's actually really good most of the time. However, some of the weapons you acquire end up being fairly useless and at times the controls for aiming ranged weapons (using a gamepad) feel a little awkward. That said, the combat is still great fun despite being a bit janky at times.
All in all, Bastion is a very special game. There is simply no other game in the world that's like it. No other game attempts to do what this game does, and few games can come close to looking or sounding as good as Bastion does. The story, the art direction, the voice work, the soundtrack, and the gameplay are all excellent, and these elements all come together to create a game that's so much more than the sum of its parts. I higly reccomend you experience this wonderful game.

This is what I call a perfectly executed puzzle game.
Ok, I don't get why this game has the title it has, as it does not have stealth (But puzzles involving remaining hidden) and there's no "b4stard" in the game (At least the main character isn't). It seems that the "DeLuxe" part is due this game being first developed as a free game. It also seems that it can't be "b4stards" in the review text, so sorry for the 4.
Anyway, title shenanigans aside, we have our little lovely clone, in the standard-post-aperture testing chambers, trying to get from A to B, where "B" is a closed door which usually has to be opened by "hacking" (Going to the terminal and press "B" for a small amount of time) some computers in points C,D, etc etc.
Here the meat and bones are in how is and what is in the path from point Whatever to point Wherever. And here is when Stealth B4stard DeLuxe shines.
There are several "worlds". Each world introduces a new mechanic (be it portals, platforms that move in a specific moment, new sentries that hunt you down in different ways...) and mix it with previously seen mechanics, adding new stuff just when you were starting to get tired of the old stuff and mixing it to get new original combinations. And it works, and its fun: There are maps in which you have to think, maps in which you have to be quick, maps in which you have to be smart and know where to crouch, maps in which you have to have iron reflexes... you have to pull boxes, to crouch behind turrets, to make NPC's work for you by moving parts of the map, to jump and crouch everywhere in the right moment to get the desired output... there's a lot of things to do and, as I said, there's always something new to add to the bag of tricks the game has each few maps. And also find the secret DNA sequences.
For better or worse, though, the difficulty of the puzzles isn't exactly top tier. I had to stop to think several times (After getting killed over and over in the same spot), and more times I got killed because I didn't jumped in the right moment, but still I hadn't to scratch my head a lot to go through the standard game. The game's easy, but not "The Ball" or "Portal 2" easy, just a bit less, enough to make it a decent light after work challenge. (And most of the DNA sequences are really well hidden).
But you will die. Lot of times. And you will even get angry at the game. And that's great, as you will not die too many times and the reason for your demise will be, almost always, your fault.
It also has standard issue scoreboards (Finish the level in the shorter time), some extra items to help you move for an already solved test chamber, and an editor with lots of communitty made maps that most of us will never use, but hey, is good to know it exists and maybe tomorrow I'll give a try to the editor.
Yeah, tomorrow.
In short, a great, fun, balanced and very well designed small puzzle game. Worth it.

At the end of January, you’re on your way home, in the dark – from work, from a party, from the shops. Something buzzes and you reflexively reach for your pocket, but your phone is minding its own business. A gleam of light makes you look down. On the ground by your right foot you can see the lit screen of a fancy new smartphone. It identifies itself as the culprit behind the disturbance by displaying a message: “4 new messages from Dad.” You pick it up, hit accept, and the phone immediately offers up the messages in question. Dad is worried. Mom wants to call the police. The phone’s owner, Sam, seems to be missing.
What’s going on with Sam? Some troubles are immediately apparent: a relationship in turmoil, friends revealing unsavoury character aspects, family secrets. Even though the game is short, playing it feels like settling in for the long haul as the player learns the names, relationships, and dates most important for Sam while trawling for a solution to a problem that has long since transcended the simple matter of returning a lost phone. Peeling back each layer by figuring out how to access and interpret all of the phone’s apps reveals Sam’s fleshed-out character nested in a web of complex social networks, acting and reacting like any of us would to events large and small.
What interested me most about ANLP is the meta-experience of playing. Statistically, most players will not have personal experience with the issues ANLP seeks to discuss, even though a slightly higher number might have encountered the topics through friends, and most will have engaged with some form of related media coverage. Many players will only have sparse, incomplete, or downright incorrect information on the topics discussed, but I would wager that some would relish a real-world opportunity to dig through the personal life of someone like Sam. This added an extra factor into the uncomfortable sensation of invading someone else’s privacy.

A Normal Lost Phone, developed by Accidental Queens, lets the player explore the contents of an unknown person’s phone. An intimate portrait of its owner is unravelled as obscured information is discovered that aid the unlocking of more of the phone’s features through various messages and apps. Starting with texts mostly devoid of context, a deep personal understanding of the character’s innermost emotions can be discovered over the game’s short play-time. These feelings derive mostly from subjects rather sensitive in nature, yet Accidental Queens deals with them in a mature and responsible way and isn’t afraid to do more than just hint at their involvement in the story. A Normal Lost Phone is not the most groundbreaking of experiences, but the way in which it reveals itself is extremely compelling and players are more than likely to walk away with a touch more empathy and understanding in life.

It seems as though there has been somewhat of a surge in popularity for reading-based games in recent years, such as Gone Home and Depression Quest. One big reason those games were so talked-about was that many gamers criticized them for not being “games,” but rather “interactive stories,” mainly focused on reading pages of text instead of “actually playing.” I feel that this, by itself, is an unfair criticism. I believe that these kinds of games cannot and should not be compared to more traditional titles that place a heavy focus on gameplay, since all kinds of games can offer unique experiences. Plus, there are some games out there that have amazing stories and weak gameplay, but are still considered to be great by most people. For example, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt was criticized for its mediocre combat and “stiff” gameplay, but ended up being widely considered one of the best games of all time (and a favorite of mine), mainly thanks to its astoundingly good writing, storytelling, and voice acting. Of course, story-focused games are not for everyone, and that’s okay.

Quite a fun casual game - plenty of puzzles and side things to do to, with light humour mixed in. It was entertaining to see what all the individual dolls did, and 100%ing the game was satisfying.
I loved the atmosphere of the game, the style of the era represented, the music choices, the silent film touches.
The Hobo King DLC delves into a much quirkier sense of humour with a splash of epic saga thrown in, with a nod to dungeon crawling that was pretty awesome. I'd love to see more DLC outside of the original game setting - I loved the original but actually loved the DLC even more, it felt like more creative licence/control was enabled than in the original game. That part at times felt like one of the Lego games (smelly meat hats, man. Stanky good time!)
The bonus art shows a museum  - I wish we could have seen that in the game, and I wish Hobo Yaga hadn't been cut!
All in all, fun, casual, play/explore at your own pace. 100%ing it is satisfying, but not at all a bummer if you prefer not to.  The hint system is handy - if you use it, you're not penalized for it nor does it feel like "dumbing down".  I hope to see more DLC in the future, I'd like to come back to this game, but 100%ing doesn't leave much replay value for me.  Note: game is kind of short but it didn't feel overly short. It told its story neatly and kept things moving without feeling abbreviated, but if length of game play is a value factor for you, you might want to pick this one up on sale.

Please, Don't Touch Anything should not be mistaken for the likes of Papers, Please or other games in that vein that use tone and setting to elevate otherwise simple gameplay. Please, Don't Touch Anything is, rather unfortunately, a game full of puzzles so obtuse I had flashbacks to Myst, and those flashbacks were still more intuitive. In this game, I hit a brick wall 2 minutes in. After using a walkthrough to go through every ending available, I feel confident in saying that if I had played it an hour without any help, I probably wouldn't have gotten more than three or so of them (if any at all.) The various endings are, for lack of a better phrase, "cutely nonsensical," similar to something like McPixel, but the next step getting to one of them is often so difficult to figure out that I wish I had just watched someone else show me every ending. For the price I paid, I don't have much to complain about, but between the gameplay being so easily stalled by confusion and the utter lack of any narrative or story, I can't recommend it.

I can fully recommend this game, even if you didnt played the first title. I enjoyed the first title alot and even if many said they disliked the battle mechanics in the first one, i quite liked it.
They made the combat in the sequel much harder (no more riposte with only one button) and you have to play a bit more defensively when facing big groups of enemies. The variety in encounters and monsters was also improved and most of the different types are fun to fight against, once you understand their patterns.
The first few challenges are quite easy, but starting midgame they increase in difficulty and you have to think harder which cards you bring to the table, to beat the gold token. There are 22 challenges currently and the variety within the game mechanics is marvelous, i enjoyed nearly all challenges, even though i couldnt get gold in each encounter before moving on to the next one. But i guess thats intented, because you get more powerful cards towards the end, that make the hard challenges quite manageable. It's also fun to think how to tackle a challenge best, some require you to think outside the box.
Most encounters have some sort of gambit (a built in minigame) to determine what happens next, compareable to dice rolling in pen&paper rpgs. There are 4 types of gambit: a physics based dice rolling(the only random gambit), a pendulum where timing is crucial, a wheel of fortune(also timing based) and card shuffling, while you can track the cards to increase your chances. There are many equipments and blessings that improve the gambits and your chances at them, so dont get to frustrated too fast.
The developers are quite active in the forum aswell, i rarely see a topic, where they dont reply to help or fix some problems, i dont know many games, which such awesome developers.
Only downside in my eyes so far is the currently still missing endless mode, but im sure, that gets added soon. Even without the endless mode, you have about 40h playtime to get each token to gold, for all achievments maybe 45-50 hours.

Ugh, what a mess.
A mess is a pretty good way to describe this game.
To start, I'm mixed about this game. While I'm infuriated by the amount of padding and poor design choices in this game, something kept me playing the game the whole way through.
To be fair, I'll start with the things I enjoyed with Starbound. The game aesthetically is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good looking. It's the kind of visuals that other garbage Indie titles with pixel graphics should try to do. This game's also decently fun when it tries to be. Specifically the third and fourth quest areas are pretty ♥♥♥♥ing fun. Some of the randomly generated buildings are pretty cool as well, at least until you see the same building for the fourth or fifth time. It's pretty fun to build things in this game and it's pretty simple to get furniture that you like when exploring settlements.
Oh but is there so much wrong with this game.
Firstly, this game should be called Space Grandma Scavenger Hunt. The whole game consists of some ♥♥♥♥ing Space Grandma sending you to go take a bunch of pictures of things so she can progress the plot. This is the least bad thing though since it's only really annoying if you get bad RNG and can't find whatever race she tells you to.
This game also took the stupid idea to have that awful Borderlands weapon system in which every weapon is boring and has no uniqueness at all except the ultra rare ones. Thanks for that Borderlands.
This game also has the same garbage that Stardew Valley had with the mining, in that it doesn't need to ♥♥♥♥ing be there. I'm sure there are people who enjoy mining and stuff, but this is a space exploration game. I mainly have a problem with it because I never actually had to do it. There are enough materials in boxes in the fun sections that you don't ever need to. I don't get why they didn't just cut out the horrid random underground and made more unique buildings and dungeons that actually have some level of creativity. And it pisses me off the most because I know that this had to be a feature that was put in because similar games had mining and not because they wanted to do something new with it.
Oddly enough, this game came from the same publisher as Stardew, so maybe it's their fault.
Speaking of which, they just imported the entirety of Stardew farming into this ♥♥♥♥ing game. And again it was just put in for no reason and has absolutely no depth whatsoever. It's just there because "Oh people liked fermin' in Stardew let's slap that♥♥♥♥♥♥in here."
This game also has boring space travel for a space game. It's obviously paying some level of "homage" to FTL but doesn't put in any space combat or space exploration, just clicking on a planet an taking a one minute loading screen to get to it.
I think the thing I hate the most is that it has those awful blocky worlds and buildings and no other geometric shapes. There are tons of cool platforming puzzles they could have done if the world had more shapes, especially with the morphball and jump types. It's a problem caused by the fact that they wanted to have these super "diverse" random terrain generation that just makes all terrains to look the same in a biome.
Overall, I still had fun playing this for sure. The modding for it makes it fun in that way the Skyrim is in which the game is garbage but there's always mods to have fun with. But overall this game is not complete, and I don't see it getting completed by the devs anytime soon. Definitely don't get it until you've looked into it and decided you'd enjoy the game.

Lilly Looking Through is a point and click adventure game that feels like it would be very suitable for a tablet.  Control over the character's position isn't allowed as movement only happens when interacting with objects, at which point the character will move by herself.  There's also panning and zooming which are done by dragging the mouse and double clicking, both similar to dragging and double tapping with the finger.  The tablet-like interaction isn't a detraction though, just an observation.
Overall it's an interesting game, but a couple of parts feels a bit off.  The minor one was the lighting inconsistencies.   When moving from a bright lit area to a darker place, the lighting on the ground and background would be different but the character would continue to have the same brightness on her.  This sometimes makes Lilly stand out in the environment more than I expected.  Maybe it's a stylistic choice and maybe it's a bit of nitpicking, but it was one of the first things I noticed.
The more major concern was the puzzles near the end where the method to reaching the goal of each scene and the reasons for doing the puzzles becomes more obscure.  Combine it with the trial and error method to discover what the puzzles are and the nice but long character animations, the later puzzles become more of a hassle.
For example, in one scene a bird steals her goggles and perches on top of a structure.  My first thought was to get it back and there was a mechanism nearby to fiddle around with which turned out to have an effect on the structure it's sitting on along with the nearby ones.  Maybe there was a way that I can scare the bird into dropping it if I played around with it.  I spent quite a while toying with it, watching her bounce back and forth between her idling position to her action movements.  Each trial was long to watch, and since I didn't know if this was the correct path, I could only try out the different combinations to see if there were any effects.  As it turns out the solution was to do something else and I only realized that after exhausting the possible combinations, but the mechanism was still needed to get to the next room, so I'm back again adjusting parameters and watching more animations.
The next few puzzles (except for one) after that are more or less the same style, a couple even worse.  For example, there's a mechanism that's clearly to be used to solve a puzzle but the puzzle and the desired solution is unknown.  It would be as if a stranger handed you a pen and blank paper and looked at you.  You know he wants you to do something but because he hasn't said or done anything, you're not sure what it is.  So you're left writing and drawing various things and looking at his reactions before you finally realize what he wants.  Maybe if it was clearer what the puzzles are and what was wanted out of each of them prior to interacting with the mechanisms that dealt with them I wouldn't feel as puffed about it but I felt these issues detracted from the magic the game presents.
I would recommend the game on the note that unless you're able to immediately determine what needs to be done to solve the puzzles, you'll most likely be fiddiling around with various combinations while watching Lilly slowly move about.

I have survived for 10 days and made trips to may close islands gathering resources.  Just a few more trips and I will have my engine built.  I have developed a great system to keep track of where I have been.  My first mistake was thinking this would be a routine trip to a neighboring island.  I set off with full reserves of cooked crab and a full water bottle.  This trip looks good.  Halfway to my target island I happen across a buoy!  What wonderful treasure awaits below.
I dive in full of expectation and begin my descent.  I quickly realize, to my terror, that this was a mistake.  I have no torch and the crushing darkness of the deep terrifies me.  I turn tail and barely make it back to my life boat when I have the ominous sense that I am not alone here.  I scan my surroundings to see that I am being visited by 2 great white sharks.
I furiously paddle to escape as the unthinkable happens, the sky darkens, lightning peels across the sky as thunder claps.  My visibility drops and I am now lost in a sea of gray.  I still have 2 great whites circling so I row furiously to escape, but I don't know where I am.  I try to continue rowing in a straight line but feel that I am going in circles.
When the clouds part I find what looks like my target island.  I come ashore harvest items and find a fuel tank for my engine!  Entering my raft I depart for what I hope is my home island, but alas, it was not, I have become lost in this wonderful paradise with no hope of finding my way home (or to my precious engine components).
Joy flows in as I realize the truth, I am playing a game with some of the best potential I have ever played.  I was sinceriously terrified, emotionally crushed, and stressed out at points in playing this game.  Great game and recommend it to anyone who wants a legitimate survival experience!

Super Slam Dunk Touchdown harkens back to the roots of arcade sports fun.  I would describe it as a combination between Ice Hockey for the NES and NBA Jam.  For anyone who has played either or both of those, you can probably stop reading now and just buy it.  If you haven't played those, imagine a 2 vs 2 or 3 vs 3 arcade sports mashup (of just about every sport) where you can pick different types of athletes with various strengths (e.g., speed, power, and shot types).  There are multiple ways to score, and you can attack opponents and use a short burst of turbo to break for the basket/goal/goal posts.  The matches are quick and frantic and there are plenty of wild distractions like banana peals and even streakers.
The sprites are well done and the game is funny in the way that Ice Hockey was.  There's just something about watching goofy sprites pummel one another while dribbling, kicking, and running with an ice hockey puck, and then bouncing the puck off the rim in a botched dunk.  The game doesn't resort to references memes or anything like that - it's just fun and humorous, particularly with a group of friends.
I suggest picking the game up and enjoying it with friends (or even alone - the AI is pretty competent) and hop on the forums to encourage the developers to continue to improve the game.  That's what early access is all about, and this game has great potential to be one of the better games to come out of the program.

In
, you are the one finding such an unprotected phone. It seems your ultimate desire is to find out what happened to its owner. Maybe you want to give it back or maybe you just enjoy snooping around in someone else’s private affairs. To do this, you will read the owner’s private messages, crack passwords, find secrets and listen to one of the best soundtracks in video games.
A
is another entry in a series of recently released phone simulators such as Sara Is Missing or Replica. Other than these examples, this game is not about scaring you to death or criticizing data privacy issues in general. This game tells you a story about the 18-year old owner of the phone. Basically, it’s a very well-written coming of age story that doesn’t shy away from tackling difficult and relevant topics such as puberty, homophobia, friendship and love. It is impressive how the developers
manage to pack so many compelling events in just text messages, photos and forum entries. The discussions feel natural most of the time, presenting the most accurate texts written by parents in video game history. These could have just been written by my own parents (except some political views) which feels quite scary at times. Here comes the time for a disclaimer: Although the game isn’t very long (about two hours) you will spend most of time reading. Not all of it is relevant to finish the game, but most of it is quite entertaining with little side stories here and there. So, players who don’t enjoy reading a lot in games might have some troubles with the game. The game basically simulates a phone interface with several apps such as a calendar, mail app, browser, weather app etc. It feels very much like using a real smartphone, although the software might be a bit outdated. It’s a voyeuristic experience and you will feel awkward from time to time violating someone’s privacy. Be prepared to question your own morals!
Nevertheless,
is a game that leaves you behind with a good feeling and with the urge to dig deeper into it’s themes. The story is compelling enough to drag you into the game (and the phone) but falls a little short towards the end once the big mystery is solved. The riddles are mostly logic and quite easy to solve for attentive readers. Overall,
can be considered one of the most beautifully designed games on the market. In it’s simplicity, the hand-drawn phone interface mixes very well with the stunning soundtrack that can carry all the right emotions. Everything is smooth and polished; I didn’t encounter any bugs. I absolutely recommend this trip into the emotional world of a young person’s phone and mind. And the music…!

Very critical of this game.  Here it is:  it's like mount and blade, only less equipment to choose from, less places to visit, less things to do, and well... just a lot less.  Next, it is top down view and turn based in combat.  Not that this is a bad thing, but I compared it to mount and blade so I figured I had to mention this critical difference.  Next, it is so aggrivatingly difficult I simply find myself happy to see my army go down one by one so the game will just end.  I never got too far into the game because your people die so easily, the enemy is almost never easy (there is no place to go or adventure to take on regularly to allow your people a chance to survive and get tougher), and you never have enough money to replace your dead with quality people and equipment because they die faster than you can make money.  OR you simply find yourself reloading the same save game over and over to try to come to a different resolution just to beat your head against a wall when you mistakenly forget to save the game before the next encounter beats the holy hell out of you.  The perk and points leveling system is pretty good.  However, your people "specialize" in certain skills, and unfortunately you don't know what those skills are until you have already paid to replace your prized archer just to find out that his replacement only increases in archery skill one point at a time per level gained (or insert some other scenario for some other type of character in your group).  I will be painfully honest.  This type of game is EXACTLY what type of game I grew up playing, and what kind of game I LOVE to play... and for a game that has gotten good reviews overall by the community, I was extremely disappointed.  In the end, it just made me want to put this game away and play mount and blade.

I am a very jaded gamer. Sick of fantasy/steampunk settings, and almost chronically unable to get into the narratives or plots of most games, even some of the great CRPGs. Hand of Fate 2, though set in a fairly run-of-the-mill setting, managed to capture my elusive heart with its story-telling, in words, gambits, and combat. It has been a long, long time since I've identified so closely with a game characted. I have completed the game yestersay, and I don't know what to say because I am overcome with love for this game.
This game takes tarot pretty seriously. It reflects on the meanings and implications of the different archetypes of fate and folly with which the tarot deck was conceived, and follows the cyclical trek of a harrowed protagonist's incredibly morally grey but constantly extraordinary life. I have always been a fan of writers who can draw out a tightly packed mythos into a concrete story that stays true to how that mythos has in turn drawn from reality.
The difficulty curve is strange and compelling. I am not much of an action gamer so it took me a long time to get into the flow of combat, so it felt incredibly rewarding once I got the hang of it, though I will admit that was after some hours of facepalming. One recurring stopping point in games for me is when I've overcome the bulk of challenges and difficulty a game has to offer, I am not a completionist, my brain will just shut down and forget why I was ever interested. But to the end of the journey of this game's story, it not only fed me new hurdles with more hectic and chaotic combat situations and demanding new clever ways to satisfy the needs of the maps, gold tokens, and really cheaty items for its gambits, it had me so locked in to the character's journey I could not stop thinking about it.
I finished this game like I often finish novels, which is well, well into the night with an almost evaporated sense of self, identifying or thinking solely of the story at hand. It was quite the experience. For me, it took around 50 hours, especially with trying to claw at each gold token victory with no spoilers. I will warn as far as replayability there is not a lot to do now, except perhaps build a strategy for speedrunning the game, until Endless Mode is released. Still even without the Endless Mode on the horizon 50 hours of such happiness is well worth it.

What to say about this game...
Well, first things first, I liked it. I don't know what sort of score I'd give it, maybe like a 7/10.
I kind of expected it to be like a detective game, with you going through someone's phone, gathering clues, learning about them and then solving the mystery, but instead, its more like a ~2 hour story, with a little bit of clue gathering and problem solving. There's a lot of reading, and the "puzzles" aren't that hard, it just depends on whether or not you were able to notice the clues.
The ending... I don't know if I can say whether it was satisfying or not, since as I said, it's not really that much of a mystery, but I will say that I only really predicted the ending right before I got to it, or almost as I was getting it, so it's not like you see it coming a mile away.
So! Good, interesting story (very socially "charged", but it didn't really bother me), it felt like it was meant to be a tool to educate a lot of people on the social issue it adresses. Gameplay seems dull since like I said, its mostly reading. Music is very good, I can recommend the soundtrack.
Overall, I recommend this game as a short, interesting story-experience.

Oh jeez, oh dang. With both this and The Lion's Song, 2017 seems to be coming right out the gate with those narrative-focused emotional games that hipster♥♥♥♥s like me love to obnoxiously recommend.
So the premise is that you've found a phone that contains clues relating to a missing person. In order to work out the mystery, you need to trawl through their social medias, connecting the dots that open up new clues. I like how subtly some of these dots are integrated, requiring you to really look hard over what you're given. There's also a really captivating, interesting story, as twists and turns are revealed which encourage you to reexamine things in a new context.
Also, because someone out there would probably yell at me for not bringing this up, yes, this is one of these 'ess-jay-dubya' games that have themes of race and LGBT life as part of the narrative. If that's something that'll turn you off the game, there you go, that's your warning.
To anyone else though, I really do recommend this game. It's not particularly long, but it's also only $3, which is worth it when you consider the rollercoaster of a ride you'll get as a result.

西方人总说“好奇心害死猫”，是因为传说猫有九条命，怎么都不会死去。但同时猫又是非常有好奇心的动物，总想去触碰或探究新奇的事物，最后可能因此遭祸。这句话常用来劝诫世人遇事别太好奇，否则会惹祸上身。而游戏 Please, Don't Touch Anything 就很好的诠释了因为好奇心所引发的连锁事件，颇有点讽刺意味。
游戏的故事围绕一台机器展开。你扮演一位实验员，在控制室和朋友聊天。恰巧朋友要去趟厕所，临走时对你千叮咛万嘱咐，不要碰周围任何东西。事实上，你除了面前的控制面板和红色按钮，也没什么其他东西好动的。手痒之下，你按了一下红色按钮，于是一段意想不到的挑战拉开帷幕。
作为一款解谜游戏，操作并没有特别的设计。你能做的就是在画面上可疑的地方点点戳戳，以找到所谓的线索。不过，场景实在过于简单，一台显示器，只有一个按钮的操控台，以及写着各类奇怪算式的备忘录就是全部。如果想看清备忘录里的文字，你可以双指捏合放大缩小画面。不过，并没有提供转动视角的功能。
复古风的画面配合悠远的背景音乐倒也烘托出了游戏的诡谲气氛，尤其是打击乐的节奏很到位，时刻拨动玩家的心弦，感觉随时都会出现奇怪的事情。
总的来说，Please, Don't Touch Anything 是一款很有意思的解谜游戏，风格迥异，虽然场景简单，但却能探索无限的可能性。25 种结局这样的设定着实雷人，估计要死不少脑细胞。聪明的你，有没有兴趣去挖掘背后的故事呢？
PS:这游戏的梗很多，如有不爽，请勿跨省，家无水表，不收快递~

Easily one of the best games I've played. Bastion has a fantastic story set in a beautiful world full of wonder and mystery, backed by stellar voice acting and an unforgettable soundtrack. Everything in the game feels like it was crafted with an incredible amount of love and care.
You play as an unnamed kid, one of the few survivors of an apocalyptic event called the Calamity. As you explore and fight your way through the various levels, everything you do is narrated by the voice of a strange old man. The narration seems like a simple gimmick at first, but it ends up tying into the story in some very clever ways. The story itself touches on some interesting themes, takes quite a few unexpected turns (in a good way!), and kept me invested right up until the end.
The soundtrack really deserves a special mention. I can't begin to stress how good it is. From the main menu theme to the end credits, there wasn't a single track that failed to engross me. I had several songs stuck in my head for weeks after I finished the game. It's fanastic in its own right but, like the narration, the music also has a pretty big significance in the game's story. It's very rare for a video game soundtrack to tie in with the story in such a way, and Bastion's soundtrack is a testament to just how clever the game really is.
If there was one gripe I have, it would be with the combat. It's not bad at all; it's actually really good most of the time. However, some of the weapons you acquire end up being fairly useless and at times the controls for aiming ranged weapons (using a gamepad) feel a little awkward. That said, the combat is still great fun despite being a bit janky at times.
All in all, Bastion is a very special game. There is simply no other game in the world that's like it. No other game attempts to do what this game does, and few games can come close to looking or sounding as good as Bastion does. The story, the art direction, the voice work, the soundtrack, and the gameplay are all excellent, and these elements all come together to create a game that's so much more than the sum of its parts. I higly reccomend you experience this wonderful game.

I thought this would satisfy some kind of strategic itch, but I found little strategy in the game. It is largely a choose your own adventure book with text that appears in the top left of the screen for the majority of the game.
There are three diffferent mini games for each "encounter" you move on top of.  Each is basically a different spin on randomness. You can choose one of 4 cards, you can roll some dice, or you can click on a pendulum as it swings over some breakout style bricks and try to hit the bottom one.
You've got food, coin, and a companion, along with equipment that aids you along the way. You build a "deck" of cards you've acquired which may reward you these resources and they appear along with other stock cards in your adventure path, which is just some cards layed out on the 2d play surface.
The game frequently cuts to combat, which will drive you insane. It is probably the most clunky interface and poorly responsive combat I've ever seen in a game. It feels completely amatuer beyond indie. You'll be screaming at the screen frequently, yelling things like "Move!" , "I hit block!" "Oh comeon! you piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥"
I suppose there are a few choices that matter, like throwing in food cards for a journey that is long or extra gold cards when you've got to buy or bribe something, but I fired 2or 3 nuerons for the duration of the play time. Overall, it felt mindless for a strategy game.

Deathtrap is a hybrid of Diablo style RPG and tower defense. Overall game-play is very enjoyable in single player. The campaign fits with what backstory there is and the overall atmosphere does have an appeal. The primary downside is the network/matchmaking code.
There are several instances with failures to route and failures to resolve (the match making server). Thus far I have experienced a 100% failure rate either as host or joining a game--where in at least one, if not more parties, could not sync and get in game.
This is not a UDP porting issue (although it could be for some individuals). I, and others, have tried various firewall settings and permission changes without success. While several people do seem to be able to enjoy CO-OP (I've not tried vs mode yet) there are far too many people experiencing issues in multiplayer for "everyone" to have UDP issues locally.
As it stands:
Deathtrap is very enjoyable as a single player game.
Multiplayer is not viable/stable and thus unplayable.
Recommended for single-player only--otherwise this is "coasterware".

First of all -> I'm a huge fan of the original HoF game.
I loved it, played it a lot, unlocked almost everything, and I consider it to be one of the best games I played. Mostly due to overal theme, atmosphere of mistycism created by The Dealer.
So what can i say about the sequell?
Well Holly carrots! This game is AWSOME! It trully is better in every aspect than original!
It is stil very much Hand of Fate game, and the spirit is retained. Developers had delivered what they promised! Creators took all the mechanics, they had from the original and refined it and improve them! They really knew what they are dooing and expanded very thoughtfully evry game mechanic!
The most welcomed, be me addition (or change) is new chalenge system. Those are highly themed missions that are really cool! Previously you were chossing one of the royalties and the goal was to kill it and survive the guntlet to get to them, unlocking some stuff along the way. Nothing wrong about it, itwas fine and all but got stale after a while - that is fundamental characterisic of rougelike type of game. Here in the second game it is wholly diffrent! Now you select a particullar "mission" and you have a set of objectives that are diffrent for each mission, also Due to more RPG like dilogue options it feels more like well rpg! XD
Misions have very clearly defined objectives which may vary from stage to stage, so when you reach a proverbial "lader" at the end of the stage you feel that a significant...part of the adventure was finished unlike the fell that original left you with after a while -> "we ran out of place on table and we have soooo much cards still to go".
I was concerend about changes to the interfeace. But From the very first moment my concernes were lifted - it is simply that good. It is rather minimalictic, but despite that I see everything I need to see and it doesn't get in the way of action!  Also description of items was very much standarised so now you know right away what an item does, how does it work, what are it's stats and so on. Also LEVELING WEAPONS XD Now equipment cards can heave tokens, which reuieres repeting, specific combat action set number of times to unlock a beter version of the weapon - briliant! I LOVE IT!
New system of very powerfull cards that are limited - very good! Deckbuilding now is much more important part of the game! Also those who played original game remember that along the progres of the game you were Stealing "items from the Dealer" and gained bonuses at the begining of the game - now you unlock said bonuses but you can choose only limited amout of them! So You have to chose betwen additional: food to start with? Gold? Max hp? Maybe a beter starting weapon! Sure! But you have to chose wiselly before each mission XD
Graphics are much beter: locations were combat takes place are pretty. The table where "the game" takes place (the "wagon") is much more dinamic that previous "crypt/dungeon" where the only change was baisicly the lighting.
Combat is improved - definietly more diversified, it took me a while to get used to new pace and tempo of it before I was able to actually survive very first scenario (not that it was particularly hard, but I had bad habits from the previous game).
I was initially woried becaouse of addition of new "chance games" (wheel, diece and pendullum), that I won't be able to control them but in the end they are not that "harsh" nor entierely luck based - there is both place for skill and preparations in order to play them around a little bit. Also it is welcomed that each set/suite of enemies have several types of enemies that fight difrently, have difrent characteristics and abilities - so even while facing only one faction you have to change your aproach between oponents.
In summarry Few quick questions and answers:
Would I recomend Hand of Fate 2? -> Absolutly yes!
Is sequell beter than original? - Yes definietly!
Does it has any major flaws? - If it does I haven't encoutered any. At lest nothing that wasn't present in original - namely some degre of luck in chance/gambit encounteres (i.e. rolling dice), and after playing insane amount of time repetivnes. But siriusly, I don't get the argument - try playing campaign to any FPS and check if it gets repetitive - I sure bet my sweet carrots it is! On the second run - since everything usually is scripted from tops to botom! In Hof 1 this crept after what? 20-30 h into the game? While trying to unlock particullar cards the 7th time. In HoF2 there is plenty to spice things up - difrent companions, difrent outcomes of encounters, many choices, many types of weapons - so far I'm like in 1/4 of "campaign" after 16h of gameplay and with every new scenario I'm astonished, exited, and suprised what developers had come up with! I'm trully happy with how this game turned out!
Trully a game one of a kind!

Cons:

Over all I really enjoyed the game. I liked the relaxed pace, the enchanting environments/art, and the puzzles were challenging but not maddeningly so (I used a guide on a few I couldn't figure out). The game provides little direction. You're trying to find your little brother, and solving each puzzle level brings you closer to finding him. The game is short, but that's part of its charm. The world is extremely colorful and vibrant, but in the end there's little substance to the world (as you learn nothing about it). Using the goggles to shift between (I assume) timelines is a really awesome idea, and the mechanic is part of the puzzle-solving. Still, it would have been cool to learn about the disparity between environments/timelines. The only real complaint (and a small one at that) was the open ending. Felt pretty abrupt and didn't offer any explanation for a strange twist in the last level. Perhaps it's leaving room for Lilly Looking Through 2? I'd certainly pick that game up, were that to be the case.

Starbound was one of the first Early Access games a friend and I picked up. We played it a lot in the very early days and it was the first time we were burned by Early Access development: they changed the format of save data. We lost everything on our saves and we were legitimately bummed. It was in this moment we vowed to never again to become too time invested in an Early Access. For Starbound, it meant we removed the game and would occasionally install it for a day here and there to check out some updates.
We were excited again. The prospect of finally being able to enjoy the game that the developers envisioned made us giddy and impatient. We prepped the week of launch and when I returned from work, I dove straight into my server to get a dedicated Starbound server setup. And it was worth the wait.
Starbound is everything I had hoped it would be, especially following the massive successes that Terraria and Minecraft are. In so many ways it even surpasses both. It has the open world (or rather universe) feel we expect with hundreds of blocks to collect and make in order to build our own homes. But rather than emptiness, the worlds of Starbound's universe are filled with creatures, bandits, authoritarians, religious fanatics, violent tribes, savage lands, and towns full of merchants. It's a living universe.
And what's more is that you create a character that's part of it all. You choose 1 of 7 races to play as and then you take your ship from planet to planet, unraveling a story that's wonderfully told. Every animation is smooth and the style is fun, creepy, and inspiring. And even when you're done with the story, there's still tons of exploration to try and locate those elusive decorative pieces and amazing weapons. Speaking of weapons, combat is well balanced with players needing to keep track of terrain and combat style of enemies in mind at all times.
But you don't want to settle down you say? Then don't! Expand your ship through crew and/or purchased licenses and make a mobile base. The regular old game isn't challenging enough? With full Steam Workshop support you can find a mod to increase difficulty. Don't want to have to bother with anything? There's probably a mod for that too!
Starbound is hands down one of the best games I've played in 2016. If you're thinking about it, stop thinking and pick up a copy. It's worth every cent.

Town of Salem is a game where your goal is to figure out what the roles of the other players are, convince the community to lynch the people you want lynched and try to survive till the end.
Pros:
- Every game is different because you're working with and against real people.
- This game is DEEP. I've never had a game make me try to get in the head of another player quite as often as Town of Salem.
- Town of Salem is very unique in many ways. It's like no other game I've ever played online.
- Death isn't always the end. The dead can still communicate with the town through a Medium or occasionally be brought back to life.
- Working as a team is incredibly satisfying most of the time.
- Adorable art style.
- The only in game purchases are cosmetic or irrelevant to the actual gameplay.
- It's fun to lie your♥♥♥♥♥off and see people hang for it!
- The community takes game throwing and harassment seriously.
Cons:
- There is a serious wall as far as getting knowledgable enough to play the game effectively. This is compounded by the reality that being a new player asking for help is immediately seen as a lie by most players, often making you a target.
- Many lessons can only be learned by doing something very stupid once, or several times in my case.
- It might seem like RNG is constantly killing you. Yes, RNG is a factor at times... but believe me, the more you play the more you realize it's rarely RNG but a mistake you're making that you don't even know is a mistake yet.
- The user interface is pretty basic. It's not hard to navigate but things aren't always clear from the beginning.
- This can be a surprisingly fast-paced game. Sometimes, it's a headache to get all the information to your team in the short time provided, but thats part of the challenge.
In summation, Town of Salem is a great game if you like to be cynical about the people you're playing with. Try it in the browser free first and after a few painful games you'll be hooked enough to support the company by buying the Steam version.

TL;DR: Arcade, fast paced, quite difficult action/puzzle game with little stealth emphasis.
TL:
: You probably won't get the stealth feeling you're looking for in this game, it's too fast paced and quite difficult, with emphasis on restarting levels until you get it right, rather than calculating a plan of action at first sight. You will repeat some levels so many times to unlock it fully, that it will become frustrating and stop being fun. After you restart a level a couple of times until you find the fastest course of action, you may become extremely volatile when you realise this game is not glitch/bug free and something won't just work on the 10th try (a switch may activate as you jump away from it, a robot may not move over a plain surface altough it should, etc.). Highscores are good and all but when each level is timed it will convey any other feeling but stealth.
: The music is retro arcade style, which is not to say it's bad, it's just not something to keep you around for long. The sounds as well.
: The visuals are fine, it's like a pixelated film-grain, this won't bother you, and it's good for the type of game SBD actually is.
: Almost non-existing, and since it's displayed briefly on the walls as you pass by, you might miss a few while trying to move fast.
: Don't get this game if you want a stealth game, but get it if you want a difficult platformer with fast paced action and some stealth nuances. The game is not bad, it's actually good for what it is, just don't be confused by the Stealth in the name since you'll regret paying for it. This ain't no Mark of the Ninja :P

You know, I really liked Terraria, and it's unfortunate that I discovered that game well after playing Starbound's earliest incarnations.  The sense of wonder and discovery in a brilliant new shiny thing (that is also charmingly retro) should have been reserved for the original.  However, Starbound still feels to me like an evolution of the subgenre that Terraria started - and although I much prefer fantasy to sci fi, Starbound will always have my preference.
I'm not going to nitpick on all the little things that have changed over this game's prolonged gestational period, like many of the other reviews I see from jaded vets.  I'm not going to wistfully conjecture on what could have been and honestly, the game is in 1.0 release with more to come. The fact that it's been out and playable for so long really muddies the waters in terms of approaching a review. With a fresh audience in mind I'm going to review it like I had never heard of it until today.
What this game is : is amazing.  A side scrolling, voxel based crafting/sandbox/metroidvania/building blast of fresh air that is insidiously addicting.  The comparison to minecraft/terraria are obvious but this game really stands on its own with a mix of great lore, amusing races, tons of weapons/gear and atmospheric planetary exploration all tied together by the amazing Terraria art style (in a more technically advanced form).  It is totally one of those broad-but-shallow, eclectic "jack of all trades" types of games, but the breadth is astounding and the variety makes it all worthwhile.
You are constantly being exposed to new mechanics and unlocking cool new things to geek out over as you blunder around the galaxy, and the pacing of such is quite well done.  The scripted dungeons/setpieces and boss fights are interesting and varied, and all the racial locations contain a satifsfying depth of background lore for the intrepid inspector and codex reader.  Your players character and crew members also make amusing comments on and criticisms of the others' civilizations. This game is full of flavor.
The variety of clothing/armor (with vanity slots!) and weapons is overwhelming and there are so many little distractions in the universe. I'm about halfway through the main story, as far as I can tell, but of course I keep getting sidetracked with giant colony building projects and exploration expeditions and crew recruiting and farming and monster capturing and dungeoneering and oh jesus it's already morning again and I have to go to work.
It has issues, of course.  The framerate gets a little wonky and the screen 'shimmers' in an annoying fashion when there's lots of stuff going on i.e dungeons and colonies.  Also, the actual movement and jumping mechanics (which are fairly important considering platforming apects of the game) are not as tight as they should be.
I have to say I am pleased with the direction chucklefish has taken in terms of tying all the game's sandbox elements together.  It provides vague long(er) term guidance; giving you purpose to exploration - as well as the breathing room necessary to allow the possibility of spending entire nights just screwing around with some Rube Goldberg-esque engineering project without feeling hurried along.
So I will update this review once (or if) I get to the 'endgame', assuming there is much of any at all and I can finish my aquatic city in time to squeeze out a few precious hours of sleep while praying my boss doesnt think I'm on drugs and fire me.

Battle Brothers is a game I've always wanted since I started playing Xcom. Medieval tactical game play done well. At it's core Battle Brothers is a low fantasy setting based around Germanic mythos and set in Medeival world. The game is essentially your attempt at running a mercenary company without having every one of your men torn apart by Direwolves, swallowed whole by ghouls, hacked to bits by Brigands, chomped on by Zombies and slaughted by Greenskins.
Like Xcom, Battle Brothers is unforgiving and relentless. Your men will die. You will lose. Your hopes and dreams will be crushed, and if you're into that sort of thing, you'll love every second of it. Battle Brothers excels at providing a solid game play experience that is simple, yet addictive. The art style is pleasing and the music is surprisingly catchy without becoming to repetive, even if the music is very samey. By far and large, Battle Brothers excels at its managing components, whether it be money, food or supplies to repair equipment.
However, there are two major flaws I find with the game. The first is: some times the game can be TOO punishing. If you don't dedicate time to understanding the game mechanics and min/maxing your recruits, you'll be punished once the late game rolls around. This is particularly frustrating, because once that point hits you could be in serious trouble. And this leads into my second complaint. Whether its management or tactical, Battle Brothers gives you few resources to help turn the odds in your favour. The battles in particular suffer this problem. A few bad rolls of the RNG can leave your company devestated. Once a situation turns on you, you have few means of turning it back. This is glaringly apparent when compared to a game like Xcom that allows you to, given skill and a little luck, turn bad situations around. Xcom rewards player skill and knowledge. In Battle Brothers, once the lines have clashed, only luck can save you if things turn sour.
I think the above could be mitigated if the late game wasn't on a Doom Clock that comes a lot faster than you expect or realize.
However, overall, Battle Brothers is a good game. It's flawed, but enjoyable. I hope the devs continue their hardwork and make this the best game they possibly can. Overall it's a 65/100 for me. Solid concept, addictive, but flawed with some less than ideal mechanics.

Hand of Fate is an odd one ... Part card game, part RPG with a dash of third person brawler.
You play as a nameless dude who is stuck riding in a caravan with a mage.   As it happens he is quite fond of cards, and the two of you while away the hours playing his favorite game - one that he originally created but which has been usurped by another mage.
He crafts 'challenges' for you which amount to short narratives that require you to complete a simple goal "Rescue a person",  "Kill a boss" , etc.  The twist is that each challenge is littered with randomized events of your choosing.  You get to pre-load each of these challenges with cards from your deck, so you can customize the types of situations you will encounter.  Since each card tends to have positives and negatives you can't just stack things in your favor.
One particularly interesting challenge has you attempting to solve a murder before it is committed.  You need to question NPCs and go on mini-quests with them to figure out who the murderer will be.  Others are much less interesting and simply amount to roaming around the board collecting buffs before facing a boss.
Probably the weakest aspect of the game is the combat.   It's a glorified button mash that borrows the 'counter attack' mechanics from the Arkham series.  It isn't terrible by any means, but it's pretty basic and once you get a rythmn down it becomes trivial to complete battles without taking a single hit.  This wouldn't be an issue if not for the fact that many of the 'event' cards treat combat like a punishment.  In reality, you'll often be *trying* to get into fights because of just how easy they are to win.  Add to this the fact that battles often yield spoils (Free Health, Gold, etc)  and it quickly becomes a case of throwing yourself at enemies whenever you can find them.
Another weakness is that the game relies heavily on text to sell the player's progress to him  (you're just moving a piece around a board after all).  Being told that you're in a dark forest and you can hear the sound of wolves is a lot less scary than it probably should be.  Particularly when the text isn't voiced, or especially well written.  I don't have a problem with text heavy adventure games, but if there's no voice acting to accompany the words, they need to be *really* comeplling to read,  and in this case .... they just aren't.
Final gripes would be that there is some element of RNG in many of the challenges which really just boils down to the order in which you encounter events, and some of the mini games feel overly punitive.  But these are small issues - generally speaking the game does a good job of steering clear of RNG and allowing you to control your "fate" through a combination of picking the right cards and playing the mini games well.
Overall I'd say it's worth a look if you're into card games and RPGs, and don't mind reading and using your imagination abit to immerse yourself.

My first game:
Day 1:
I land on my island, very pleased with the way it looked.
I collected enough materials to make an axe and a campfire. I chopped down a tree and took it's coconuts.
When night came upon me I sat by a fire drinking and eating coconuts.
I continued cutting the tree into bits until morning.
Day 2:
I construct a platform for my new house as soon as day hits.
I drink and eat more coconuts to fill my stomach.
I collect more materials and chop more trees to make a completed shelter!
After my shelter I looked off into the distance, I see some splashing or bubbles coming from the bottom of the sea.
I drag my raft into the water, whip out my padle and row towards the splashing. When I got there I looked down to see an old shipwreck. I dove into the dark mysterious water. I found a chest with an axe and a locker with some flares and duct tape. I swam to the surface, hopped in my raft and paddled back to my island. When I arrived it was night. I continued to expand my shelter while eating coconuts until morning.
Day 3:
I haven't slept in 3 days, yet I felt fine.
The amount of coconuts around me was scary.
I decided to sail to another island, I dragged my raft into the water and sailed off. I arrived as soon as it started to rain. I lifted my raft and layed it against a rock, I crawled under and waited for the rain to pass. It took a full day. I climbed out of my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ little raft shelter to see the moon just peaking out over the horizon. I collected some crabs and sticks to make a fire and have a meal. I didn't know how to cook them so I left them on the fire for about 1m. I grabbed the crab and ate it, my screen turned black and green and I puked all over my raft. I was now starving and thirsty. I put my raft back into the water and decided to sail off once more. All I had on me was my paddle and some duct tape, I left everything at my shelter. The sun began to rise.
The fourth and final day:
When the sun began to rise a thick layer of fog built up around me. I was scared and lost at see. I decided to paddle in the direction I thought my island was. I felt so alone. I looked at my wrist watch to see that I was going to die. I shed a tear. I sat in my raft alone, hoping something majestic would happen, but nothing did. Half awake I began to hear disturbing music, I thought I was going crazy. I look into the water to see a Great White shark swimming around my raft. I was so scared. I finally faced the truth, I was a dead man. I dropped my paddle and hammer into my raft and took one final breath before I jumped into the water. I swam as deep as I could, my ears began to pop. I looked up to see the sun shine through the waves...
I closed my eyes.

Deathtrap is one of those games that is good but not quite great.  While being a decent game in its own right you can't help but think that what it really constitutes is the potential foundation for something better and more polished. Maybe a sequel that improves on the formula in the event that this debut entry is supported enough to warrant one.
Just to get it out of the way I'll say straight up that I haven't experienced any technical issues with regards to the game not running, crashing, etc. I know that in the past others had complained about what sounded like really specific issues resulting in the game not running properly on their system. That hasn't been the case with me and at this point I've only encountered one very minor bug (twice).
Characters in Deathtrap control nicely, and by "nicely" I mean "exactly how you'd expected them to given that they represent the action rpg component of the game as advertised". Character specs are meaningful and interesting but not entirely pivotal which is probably as it should be.
The game's traps are pretty cool for the most part. Some are classics (spike floors, lava tiles, lightning towers, etc.) whereas others are a little more offbeat and serve to keep the tower defense aspect of the game fairly fresh. Traps have upgrades that must be spec'd into to utilize in combat and I think this is where Deathtrap really shines. The traps work like you'd expect them to and are devastatingly effective. Even while defending multiple chokepoints solo you won't feel like your arm is being twisted by artificial difficulty in an attempt to force you into multiplayer. The game gets harder, yes, but only as it ramps up naturally while your character and traps simultaneously gain strength. This alone makes Deathtrap worthy of attention in a development culture rife with micro-transactions fueled by nearly enforced group play. I paid a reasonable one time cover charge for the game and I'm having fun playing it. What more could an avid gamer ask for?
In the end I'm glad I supported this game and I hope others do too. I'll be looking forward to seeing where they go with it in the future.

Laconic Preface; This is not a glowing recommendation. But ultimately I can still say "yeah, I guess its worth getting if you like this sort of game and have already played your fill of Terraria".
The game falls into a space somewhere between Terreria and Minecraft. It's easer than the former, but harder than the latter. It's combat is worse/better respectively. A solid half of all the weapons in the game are garbage that can only be semi-effectively weilded by the AI, and almost everything that isn't a boss can be casually stunlocked to death with a pair of fast one handed swords/daggers. Hunger is an annoyance that doesn't add any enjoyment to the game; you will spend the first chunk of a survival game trying to collect enough food, and then spend the rest of the game trying to balance eating it as you have to with how quickly it all spoils.
You have four ways of healing yourself; eat food (at all in casual, when full in survival) to slowly regain it, throw a health regen mod into your survival backpack for likewise, or use one of two types of med kits, one of which regens health over 10 seconds, and the other which does it in one second, with the only limitations being that you can only use one at a time and however many you're carrying, so if you're stocked up, even when undergeared it's pretty trivial to outlast the bosses. Imagine Terraria if you could chug potions once per second, and there were only seven bosses, only two of which are particularly challenging. And The Big Ape is only really challenging because when you destroy one of his four orbiting projectors, /the others regain all of their health./
The one area it excels in is how intricately you can construct your homes and ships and soforth, though the absurd number of options it gives you can also be a drawback. Thankfully your inventory is fairly generous, but still not enough to handle the avalanche of material types. It's like having a lego kit where you have 128 different colors of blocks, great if you're feeling artsy but overwehelming otherwise.
The story... exists. Which I guess makes it more substantial than either of the other two. It's about as generic as you can get; I kept expecting a plot twist, but nope, it's entirely straightforwards with no surprises. Spoilers I guess? Scan the background junk from each of the non-human playable races (Except the Novakids, naturally, who apparently don't exist outside of being playable) followed by a mission where you're unable to place or destroy anything (including torches, annoyingly) to avoid sequence breaking, culminating in a simple boss fight. Each race goes in vague order to theoretically guide you to each star system type in order of difficulty but because starsystems and planets are procedurally generated, it's kind of a crapshoot. So, mission, scan stuff, mission, scan stuff, repeat five times, then dig to the core of the final boss planet and kill it in a disappointingly easy encounter.

-Day 9
I'm going to attempt to explore the nearby island.  Half way there, I dive to an old shipwreck down below. Found an engine part, nice! Resurfacing leaves me disoriented. As I try to find my bearings using the sun and my little knowledge of the existing islands nearby, fog rolls in and leaves me lost at sea.
-Day 10
I've discovered a buoy. Very large sharks seem to congregate around it, best leave it be. I make my way from two or three islands before passing the buoy again. Two great whites have taken interest in me and have begun to follow, I look back as I notice and begin to paddle for my life to the island just within reach. I make it. It's home.
One of the whites gave up and returned to the sea. I can still see him from time to time out on the water. The other managed to find its way into the geometry of my island. Thus begins the reign of the landsharks.
-Day 17
It's been a week since the event. I'm still haunted every day by the elusive beast. It hungers. I can't sleep, it may get me in the night. I've been hopping from rock to rock in attempts to skirmish the monster with me dulling machete. All attempts seem hopeless.
-Day 18
The rocks have saved me. The creature managed to lurch between two rocks and get stuck as I dealt the killing blow with my blade. As if by some unknown force, the shark launches from my island into the air, far and fast until it's no longer visable. Perhaps the same magic that braught such a creature into this world has taken it back.
I think I know now what hit my plane...

Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is one of my favourite games and can be considered the one which induced my love for indie games. The game heavily relies on the rogue system and random items you are gifted with upon each run. Sometimes you might get a good run while other times you'll be having a hard time. Each run is new and different and not only does it rely on skills but also knowledge on certain secrets of the game that just makes it more of a master piece. Each run you might unlock new stuff that can be obtained in the next run and new levels after completing the the runs for a set amount. For some people Binding of Isaac: Rebirth also relies heavily on achievements so if you are a fan of achieving achievements then I would higly recommend it. All in all Binding of Isaac: Rebirth requires the player to have dedication, knowledge on certain aspects of the game (for a boost) and bullet hell dodging skills. As for its shortcomings there really are none unless you are the kind of guy that doesn't like the rogue genre itself (and maybe some offensive material such as different view on biblical depictions or feces but I personally like that it presents itself as it wants to.)

Certainly not quite perfect, and has its fair share of development hell horrorstories, content cuts, pointless additions, disappointed early access players, etc...
But the spirit is still more than there from way back when, at least for me. And I can more than still give 1.0 a recommend for that.
I picked this thing up because I wanted to feel like a part-refugee-part-colonizer-part-spacecowboy, and Starbound still delivers this feeling in spades. Melancholy at times, sometimes hyper as hell, but always a beautiful (and often weirdly moving) experience.
Main Story Quest could use a little work. Your standard "Go Kill The Evil Tentacled God" story, but there's no real need for you to go follow it if you dont want to whatsoever.
When I want to feel like Im just a lonely runaway without a home, trying to make a peaceful home for myself among the stars, this is where I come first.
And really, the soundtrack just ties all that together...

Starbound.
The first thing that comes into your mind is "Terraria Clone."
The first thing that you experience is a whole new game.
No, this isn't a Terraria clone, even though it has some aspects that terraria does, but what it is, is a beautiful and well thought out game that makes you gaze in wonder and see just how infinite this game's worlds are.
There are possibly thousands upon thousands of unique planets each with their own aspects, and with the Frackin' Universe mod, there's even more to explore. You have Scorched Planets that you need a Cooling EPP for, Freezing Planets that you need a Heating EPP for, Moons you need a normal EPP for, Toxic Planets you need a Radiation EPP for, Mountainous Planets that can send you to death in a second if you're not careful, Barren Wastelands that are GREAT for building Bases on, since there are no Monsters, Weather, Plants, Trees, or anything else blocking your path unless you have problems leveling the surface to build your base. The vastness of things you can do in Starbound make for an amazing experience for all types of gamers, be it Laid Back or CS:GO Players (Harley)

This was given to me as a gift from my good friend D.H., so I never spent a penny on the game.
Pros: It's pretty fun, with a massive universe to explore and excellent mod support that fixes many of the problems the game has. . The combat system is alright, there's a pet system where you can capture wild animals pokemon style and have them fight for your amusement, you can build up a crew (slowly over time) and travel the cosmos and completely ignore the story if you so choose (once you finish the first two missions). You can farm and raise animals (specifically Fluffalo, your best friends if you want certain materials). There are randomly generated monsters and weapons also, so if that's your thing, there you go. You can terraform planets and build colonies (once you beat the first mission), and get quests from your colonists to eventually add them to your crew.
Cons: *See Update at bottom* THE LAG. JESUS CHRIST THE LAG. This thing will lag no matter what you do. I have a decent enough setup to run Gmod at 60 fps with a bunch of graphic ovehaul mods, and Starbound chugs at about 10 fps whenever I swing a sword or thrust a pike. The developers don't seem to care much about this problem, because it's been around since the beta. The story is really cobbled together with repetitive missions, so I wouldn't bother playing it. The only reason you would want to play the story is to complete the Floran Mission so you can upgrade your ship. Don't buy this game for the story, buy it for the exploration. Story missions are incredibly  formulaic, and follow the pattern of  "Scan Items, Talk to Old Lady, Get Instance Mission, Go To Dungeon, Kill Boss, Repeat until you reach Final Boss".  Crew building takes a friggin eternity as well, and the chances of being able to recruit someone after a quest is completely random. Also, you can't kill villagers anymore. That was a lot of fun, purging an entire planet of civilized life, then repopulating the empty homes with my colonists to make some easy profit. Now, you can't do that unless you break some pots and steal all the things you can in a settlement. Even then, they don't really try to fight at all. Really wish the devs would put in a setting or command or something where you can just go ham on the settlements.
Overall, Starbound is a decent game that i would reccommend to anyone who likes games like Terraria, but can tolerate a bit more bullsh*t. Mods will definitely fix a lot of what is wrong with the game and are a saving grace. I give it a 6.5/10. It's incredibly average, but has a lot of potential given time.
UPDATE: A new update recently launched which changed everything. The game is way more optimized, there are now fully customisable, modular Mechs that have been added to the game, players can build personal space stations and place them in orbit of any star system they choose and upgrade them to their hearts content. My major complaint, the lag, has been completely fixed. The story is still pretty boring and needs WAY more depth, as it's essentially still Mafia 3 levels of repetitive, and the "You can't kill non-hostile villagers. No, not even with that giant mech with a bloody chaingun and laser" thing still bothers me. I'm putting my final review (As of this update) at a solid 8/10. If the story were worked on more and better quests were added, this could be a 9 or even a 10/10.

The intro cutscene neatly sums up what the game is about and places a distinct emphasis on teamwork. This holds true during gameplay as well; stray too far away from the pack and you're almost surely a goner. Left 4 Dead is an arcade experience so don't expect much in the way of story. The cast members are basically walking one-liners but that doesn't stop them from oozing personality and being genuinely funny at times.
The premise is simple: team up with three other (preferably real) players and evacuate the zombie-infested lands or perish. Most of the zombies are of the regular fodder type but every so often the so-called special infected ones spawn somewhere nearby. These guys are especially nasty and demand an extra level of coordination to take out. Communication is essential for survival, watch each other's backs and decide when to use your items wisely.
Left 4 Dead is one of the few games that brilliantly blends RNG elements with handcrafted level design, without compromising the overall quality. This is done to create unpredictability in zombie spawn points and their attacking patterns which makes it difficult to plan beforehand and forces you to always stay alert. As such the game has a remarkably high replay value, which is important considering it only takes a few hours to beat the campaigns.
Crank up the grain filter and don't miss out on this co-op classic!

If you ever read John Keegan’s  “The First World War” or Heinz Guderian’s “Achtung Panzer”, this mod encapsulates the horror and tragedy of industrial age warfare that was World War 1.
What's great about this mod:
+Top-notch attention to detail.  Everything is meticulously modelled and historically accurate from machineguns to field guns.  Camo patterns of the tanks are correct, too.
+ Infantry combat shines.  As anything mechanized only appears late game,small unit tactics takes center stage during the early phases of the game. Infantry combat is more compelling than CoH 1 or 2, in my opinion.
+ Positional warfare.  This is the beauty of the game.  It forces the player to fight and win battles using inadequate means.  Tanks are slow and cumbersome. Infantry are cut to ribbons by automatic weapons, gas and shell easily.
+ Combined arms.  This was the era where the prototypical combined arms battle was developed.  You may find inspiration from the battles of Cambrai, Soissons and Amiens.  But, do not expect to recreate the deep battle theory or blitzkrieg as espoused by Tukhachevsky and Guderian, respectively.
Some criticisms:
-As mentioned, this is just a mod. So, the weaknesses of CoH 1 are present here as well like less than optimal unit pathing and poor AI
-Some bugs like units getting stuck.
-Some balancing issues. Doctrinal tank call-ins(Buetepanzer/MarkV/Whippets) should have fuel cost or caps.  Field guns should have better bombardment range than mortars.
-This game could use more units like the LK II and Medium B tanks.
-Absence of the foremost Entente nation:  the French
