Saying this game is a cross between Orcs Must Die and Diablo is misleading.  It is more like a mix between Defence Grid and Diablo.
Whereas Orcs Must Die 1 & 2 are fast, colourful games that give you a lot of freedom and choice in traps and placement,  this is not the case in Deathtrap.   This game lacks flexibility in both where you can place traps and what kind of traps can be placed, which makes this game even more restricted than Defence Grid.    The text is very small, so those playing on their TVs, watch out for that.   In one map, there is some kind of  temple, and the text is so small that even though I stood right in front of my HDTV, I still couldn't read the text so as to figure out what the temple was for.   Probably better to play this sitting at a monitor.   I wish game makers would always provide an option to increase text size.   The game is also quite slow and you can't run around fast, but they do provide portlals to help you get around.
The game does have depth to it - it's kind of like Diablo, with a screen where you equip armor, rings, amulets, weapons, upgrade skills - that part is interesting.
But if you are expecting the pace and feel of Orcs Must Die - look elsewhere.  Big BIG difference between the two games.   Watch youtube videos of this game first to get an idea of what you are getting.
The levels are also static, in that you can't rotate or move the level around.  Finally, the  graphics are not sharp, rather dark and lack-lustre - this is not a bright, colourful and vivid game like Orcs Must Die at all.
This is not necessarily a bad game, it is just really not my type of Tower Defence game.   Still, some people may really enjoy the game for the Diablo-like aspect of it.

I was so excited to see this game come out and more importantly the positive reviews it received.  I went ahead and bought it for 10% off and even gifted it to my father after playing it a bit.  He and I had both played HOF1 and enjoyed it a fair amount.  The original was incredibly unique, however I will admit that I stopped playing it for several reasons.  The main reasons were that I found it a bit frustrating to keep my food levels up and felt punished at times which is usually not fun in a game.  I generally felt "alone" in HOF1, which I guess is sort of the nature of the game, but I had wished I had allies.  Also, there really wasn't much of a "story" and you just selected "bosses" to go try to defeat.
Well, well, well...I must say that HOF2 is a significant improvement to many things missing in HOF1.  It is awesome to see the developers keep the great overall design from HOF1 and simply improve it in many different ways.  How often do you see developers improve a game in such a way that it seems like all of the improvements came from the end-users? So many times developers get it wrong and take away the good things and add things we don't want..well, not here!
Some examples are:
1) Story line/challenges - The game takes a more of a storyline approach and you embark on different challenges that are interesting and well thought out.  The challenges have "quests" within them in addition to the main focus of the challenge which is very cool.
2) Addition of Companions! So far I only have the first companion but it is awesome that I have someone in battle with me that can help fight, aid me with spells and distract enemies. Also, sometimes you find yourself fighting alongside some other temporary allies which makes it feel like a larger battle.
3) Camping - The camping functionality is probably the best part in my opinion for the simple fact that you can regularly get food and supplies without having to rely purely on luck.  You can buy food at the camp (though it is not unlimited) and also equipment as well as selling items. You can then cook food for 5 health each which is amazing! This is a HUGE improvement allowing a more likely survival. It is balanced however and so even at-times you will find that it is not going to save you (e.g. trader runs out of food or you have no gold to buy any).  Basically, the camp allows you to balance all of your resources and health. For example, you can sell some equipment to buy some food and then cook that food to gain some health, thus turning equipment into health!
4) Lots of little, but good, additions- There is the addition of dice and the wheel which is cool.  The dice is still mainly luck but you have the choice to re-roll and can also obtain boosts for your die rolls. The wheel is mainly skill as it requires you to line up a sort of laser as it goes back and forth on a pendulum. It feels like I'm taking one shot in Arcanoid.  Some other examples are using your companion for another type of benefit but at the cost of losing him for 3 turns. There are other little things like this along the way, and more being introduced as I go through the game, which is also a nice touch.
Overall, the game is very enjoyable.  The combat is good and very similar to HOF1 (which is fine, because this was fine the way it was).  I am finding it more forgiving overall and just balanced better.  I am not looking for an easy game, which it is not, but I am finding that I can apply much more strategy when I am playing that gives me a better chance of making it to the end.  I always felt like in HOF1 I would hit a point where I was just relying on pure luck to stay alive.  This game limits that much more.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone and especially those that played HOF1 because you will truly appreciate everything you loved from HOF1 but significantly improved upon in HOF2.
Oh, and of course, who can forget the awesome interaction with the game master guy. I like Tower Defence games.  Or, more accurate, I want to like them.  I keep buying them.  I keep trying to play them, but I inevitably get bored with them and quit after a few levels.  Only a few rare Tower Defence games can really keep my attention.  Both Orcs must die games and Defender's quest did it and kept me occupied for many fun hours, but I have not found anything I've like since.  Until now.
Deathtrap is a Tower Defence/Action RPG hybrid.  Like the later type of game, you have loot and lots of skills to choose from.  You also build and upgrade traps like in the former.  Unlike many games, hower, trap locations and types are fixed for a given level.  In other words, you will have locations pre-set that you can only build a specific category of trap in.  There are five types of traps for each, though, so you still have plenty of options.
While the main campaign only has 13 levels, you also have additional game modes, scenario only levels, and several New Game plus like modes that feature very diffent trap, entrance, exit, and moster waves for all the old levels.  There really is plenty to do and plenty of room for expansion for future DLCS.
If you like TD, ARPGs or both, check out this game.

Lilly Looking Through is a point and click atmospheric puzzle and (somewhat) adventure game. I’m a bit reluctant to call it an adventure game as the game itself has little to no story.
Now the artwork from screen to screen is adorable, beautiful even, the animation is great, however they can become a little bit out-drawn at times. The music on the other hand is simply stunning and ads a lot of mystery and whimsicality to the game.
When it comes to the puzzles, I had a hard time figuring out what I was supposed to do every once in a while, but at the same time I liked the challenge of solving them. As you often have to think outside of the box. I particularly liked the use of Lilly’s (or Lilly’s brother’s) goggles.
The characters don’t have any particular background story, which is a bit disappointing, but it is understandable, when you take into account the time you use to play through the game. Speaking of time. As the game is relatively short, I expected a closed ending at the least, but alas, that did not happen. The choice of ending confused me and made me think: “That’s the ending? That’s it?” The open ending made me think they’re planning a follow-up to this game, but in all honesty, if the next game is the same length as this one, I very much doubt I’ll buy it. The way the ending looked, it seemed that this is just ½ of a whole game. The latter is just speculation on my part though.
In the end, this is just an experience game made to set a mood and impression. Don’t get me wrong. By describing this is as just an experience game, I want to express that those wanting to play this game, and expect a plot and a story on the same level as the art, animation and sound will most likely be disappointed. Most of the short playtime is made up of puzzles that, once figured out are very easily solved the second time around.  Seeing as it's both short and without a story, all you’re really left with is a short time with a feeling of whimsy that's mostly filled by puzzles made somewhat tedious due to slow animations between motions.
When it comes to the price, I think that 9€ is a reasonable price for a game like this. I’ve seen games far worse than this going for a lot more, but I don’t think I’d go as far as paying extra for the “deluxe edition”.
Overall, I’d say this is a good game. What I’ve enjoyed the most in this game would be the underwater puzzles/ cave puzzle. Again, I really love the art, the music and last, but not least the puzzles plus the use of the goggles in the game. It definitely is worth a play-trough, but that is about it. As much as I’d love to recommend buying this game, I still feel something is lacking before you could actually say that it is a 100% finished product. I’d say the game is entitled to get ½ cookie out of 1 whole cookie :)

tl;dr: The game is just one endless grind to pay for replacement men and equipment, until your company eventually collapses and you lose.
Long Version:
The game describes itself as a tactical RPG. Forget the RPG part. In fact, playing this game as an RPG will get your men killed and you will lose.
Instead, this game could be described as a statistical simulator. Because that's what it all boils down to. Are your stats better than the enemies you're facing? I'm not kidding. People have published reams of spreadsheets on this game, because if you don't optimise your stats, your men will die and you will lose.
You're in charge of a mercenary company and it's up to you to decide who to hire, what to equip, and what contracts to take. But if you're not careful with your decisions, your men will die and you will lose.
When you hire someone, erase their name and rename them according to their role. Remember the part about ignoring the RPG aspect of this game? Suppose you hire Kurt the Farmer, who is down on his luck after watching his farm get destroyed by raiders. He also happens to have high HP and defense. Erase his identity and rename him "Tank #1", so you know his role when you click on him on the battlefield. Is Godfrey the Brawler excellent with damage? Good. Call him "DPS #1". Does Burton the Juggler have high initiative and resolve? Rename him "Sergeant #1". And so on and on. Because if you don't, and you forget the roles of each character, your men will die and you will lose.
Don't bother in creating a flavoured company, like a company of pikemen, or a company of rangers. The RPG part is non-existent, remember? The devs made the decision that certain foes can only be defeated with certain tactics, and nothing else. For example, zombies are best killed by decapitating them with cleavers. Try any other tactic, they will re-animate, your men will die and you will lose.
Dying in this game wouldn't be so much of a problem if hiring replacements was easier. Unfortunately, contracts tend to pay such little gold that you're often caught in a death spiral, unable to purchase new men, tools, food or equipment with the little gold that you're rewarded. Eventually all your men will die from attrition and you will lose.
The problem with this game is that a few deaths within your company can be catastrophic, especially during the early stages of the game when you have no gold or equipment. Turtling up and only accepting the easiest contracts is not an option as contracts pay little gold and you're faced with daily wages and food consumption. The devs have made that you MUST take on riskier contracts, or go bankrupt and run out of food, and watch your men die and lose the game.
Other games like Rimworld are reknown for their brutality, and yet they are still fun. It's because they are recoverable from catastrophic disasters. In Battle Brothers though, if you're caught in a death spiral, there is no recovery. If you can't pay your men, they leave. Or you can let them die and lose the game.
Ultimately, this game is not fun. Roleplaying is minimal. Yes, it is challenging, but in a statistical spreadsheet sort of way. And honestly, if I'm going to deal with spreadsheets and statistics, I would call it WORK, and prefer to be paid.

"Lilly Looking Through" is an adventure/puzzle game in a somewhat minimalistic approach, with a very relaxing and heart warming atmosphere. The presentation of the game is nothing short of magical. The art is beautiful, the music is dreamy and ethereal, and the characters' animations are most exquisite. The kids, Lilly and Row are so cute and animate so well that right from the start it was unbelievably endearing. The game immersed me in a feeling of childhood, with all that innocence, curiosity, cuteness and sense of awe and adventure, like I never have experienced before.
Speaking of the actual gameplay, it plays like a point and click puzzle adventure where one needs to figure out how to get past the obstacles of each screen to progress to the next. I can't spoil you, so I'll just say that along the way you pick up an item that not only serves as an excellent, original and creative device for the puzzling itself, but adds to the wonder and magic of the game and its world as well. Some of the puzzles are quite hard to figure out, but the hint system, which highlights items/actions you can click makes sure you're not missing out on where you can click, so you can focus on the puzzles themselves. If you have no patience for this genre (or in general), though, or you can't stand low tempo, relaxed games, I wouldn't recommend it.
Despite all that I loved about the game, which was, in a nutshell, that it provided me with a nostalgic reliving of the magical feelings of childhood, the game has some problems. Mainly, it's short, around 2-3 hours long, which is a pity and a little frustrating. Towards the end, the puzzles get a bit repetitive in "theme", and their mechanics get a bit more cryptic, thought one can argue that's the point of a puzzle game. But more importantly, and again, without spoiling, the end has little closure and feels more like a cliffhanger than an actual resolution it's surprisingly abrupt and open. Also, it creates the idea that there will be a "sequel"/continuation, one feels that there should be, that the game/story isn't quite finished.
It pains me to give such criticisms to this game, because, in spite of its failings, the it is so magical and endearing that I was really impressed. It was one the most memorable gaming experiences I ever had. I really hope that there will be more and longer "Lilly" in the future.

There are mainly two reasons a point and click game can survive this day of age. It needs to look beautiful, and it needs to have a story that keeps you interested long enough to not realize that all you really are doing is clicking on the left mouse button. Lilly Looking Through doesn’t exactly have both at the highest capacity until at the very end.
Looking through what?
At the beginning of the game a red scarf flies just right by you which will continue until getting caught on a tree branch. You go through a few tasks until a little boy pops up and eventually gets caught by loose red scarf and flies away to another. Lilly then cries out “Row”, it seems the little boy is Lilly’s little brother. While Row was picked up and dragged off he dropped a pair of goggles. When Lilly picks up the goggles and wears it over her eyes the world is different. The world has turned back in time when things were, much more refreshed, and clean. Throughout the game you must use the goggles to go back and forth through time to accomplish task and maneuver through obstacles while chasing your brother who is being carried away by a red scarf.
How is Lilly doing?
The controls are as simple as a point and click can be. You hover the mouse courser over an object, if the courser icon was to change, then it’s something you can interact with. At this point the game becomes, a searching game of what I can and can’t interact with that will actually be useful. There is a “Hint” button in the minor case that you do get stuck or just unable to find the right objects that is clickable. When you hit the “Hint” button, Interactive items will be surrounded with a circle that will increase in size to show you exactly where it is. The game is half 2D and half 3D with the 2D being the entire background and Lilly, Pow, and a few tiny objects being 3D. At firs the game utilizes a 2D object turning into 3D and back into 2D in the background. As far as I could tell it only really happened, noticeable, once.
Look over here!
Lilly Looking Through is a very short game, around the good 2 hour mark. The game did leave with an opening, and by the time it finally does open back up again, I’m not too sure if I want to come back and visit. The game is very casual at best. Some of the puzzles are near impossible to understand, that takes a lot of trail and errors. I would recommend playing the game the first time once the entire series is fully complete. At this point you can’t tell when the second part will come in and if there is even a third part. By that time you might not even care. It’s a shame, especially at the end when it finally showed a full story ready to be unfolded. I guess that’s what the cliff hanger is for though

Stacking is a game made by Double Fine Studio which produces classic which I will not name but you are probably familiar with. Anyways what is this game about? A lighthearted puzzle game set in a world where matryoshka dolls replaces humans and everything is shrunk down, scaled and done in a way that would make sense for a matryoshka doll. Since they also incorporated silent era film stuff what this means is that dialogue are not voiced but rather appear on screen to the tune of piano and violins and there is no such thing as facial expression since everybody have prepainted wooden faces and they all speak by flapping their midriffs. -sigh- Anyways,
It uses a third person perspective with a simple story and mechanic that I will describe later but do read the critique section to learn about some of its flaws.
Gameplay is really really simple to the point that even a child could finish the game provided they are age 8-12. Basically you press a button to possess a doll 1 size bigger than you so you can solve the objective at hand with the doll unique ability. Sometimes you need to possess a doll several time so you can grab the larger doll, also some dolls cannot be possess until you clear the challenge since they will either face you preventing you from possesing them since it only works when you are behind them or they are situated in out of reach places.
So with the power of the dolls you must then use it to clear the challenges aka mission objectives that ranges from reopening the train station to stopping the food services which is nothing complicated and they all have 3-5 ways to clear them and by finding all the solution you will earn a completion mark and a unique doll. Some of the solutions can be a bit obtuse but thankfully there is the hint system which after a short period of time will give you another one so you are never really stuck in a level.
So after you finish the level you can either do the side challenges like collecting all the dolls in a set, doing bonus challenges, collecting all the unique doll in a level or doing hi-jinks which are basically doing mean things using a doll's special ability a number of times.
All in all rather simple, good for some fun and one of solutions for any given challenges are often incredibly obvious. Once you are done with a level your hobo friend will draw a mural for you and display all the unique dolls you have possesed and all the challenges you have completed.
Very basic, you have options for controls, game effect, resolution, vsync, and a few other things but no sound, also what is the how to play section and credits doing here anyways. The option menu is rather empty for most parts.
I manage to get 60fps on the highest setting although it does stutters when loading a new section of the map.
Controls are pretty good but character tends to feel like they are sliding at times since they don't really have feets but after a few minutes I got used to it. I suggest  a keyboard since the game don't really support controller fully.
Graphics looks fine, all dolls have these sheen to them which suggest they have been applied with a layer of lacquer and dolls with soots and crayon don't have these sheen as expected. Enviroment are good, nothing of note.
Double Fine were aiming for a classical sound style and they succeded in that. Piano, violin and period style musics are used aplenty and dolls often grunts and do weird noises as oppose to speaking.
Now presentation. Double Fine really nailed the presentation, dolls have floating accesories since they don't really have any hands to hold things and everything else have been adapted masterfully. An example would be the animal which still uses the doll style and trains being made with pins and cardboards. Good point for immersion is what I am trying and failing to say.
It has a good premise, good gameplay and they really nailed the presentation so what went wrong in my opinion? Simple.
The game lacks depth. The whole game feels like one big challenge mode  with nothing else to break it with. While fps may have turret section or sniping mission that goes quiet and 3rd person games have stealth section but Stacking have only the power of using a doll's unique power and possesion to get through the whole thing.
So if you are not a fan of those I suggest you look elsewhere. But for what its for if you enjoy hearing about this premise I suppose you might enjoy it once this game goes on a sale.
Its short too, clocking at 5 hours for both the story and DLC with the story mission finished but not all the side challenges so there is that to consider.

Truly original ideas seem few and far between these days, with most games feeling like iterations on tried and true genre staples or else reinventions of the classics, but this feels like something genuinely new and unique that somehow manages to nail everything it tries on its very first attempt. The hook of this cute little puzzler is that every character is a matryoshka, a Russian nesting doll that can by climbed, or "stacked", into and controlled to command their specific ability, but you can only climb into a doll that's one size larger than the one you currently inhabit. This is where Charlie Blackwell comes in.
Charlie is the runt of the litter, the youngest and smallest of the chimney-sweeping Blackwell family, who've been tricked by the villainous Baron into hard labour across his various business ventures. Being unwanted in the workforce because he's considered too puny to be anything useful, Charles sets out to rescue his family and bring down the Baron and his empire, along with the help of his hobo friend, Levi. What follows is an epic adventure across land, air and sea as wee little Charlie stacks his way into a wealth of loveable characters and straight into our hearts.
Each of the four main locations has multiple challenges that can be solved in multiple ways using the abilities of various dolls. Abilities can range from shaking your tush as a beautiful widow to seduce and distract male dolls, to playing a flute as a pied piper and parading rats through kitchens or exhibits... or even just puking up cookies as a seasick child. There's a huge array of abilities, some useful or necessary, some serving no purpose other than to amuse and have fun with, but all are entertaining and encourage experimentation. I honestly had just as much fun using vital dolls to complete challenges as I did needlessly slapping some poor random waiter across the face with a glove for two minutes just because I could.
The characters are all incredibly loveable throughout (with even the bad guys being endearingly bumbling in their attempts to thwart our hero), but that's only one part of the wonderful presentation that manages to be so effortlessly charming in every way. Cutscenes are presented to us as a cross between a stage play and a silent movie and accompanied by some perfectly fitting ye olde piano music, all tying together the overall Victorian look and feel of every part of the game. The dolls themselves all have so much charming personality that's somehow amazingly conveyed through mostly static, shiny, painted-on faces, and the world around them largely assembled from everyday objects that stay true to scale next to the tiny little toy dolls. It all combines to an experience that has so much more warmth and heart than just about any other game I can think of and only adds to its already enchanting uniqueness.
If I had to criticise anything about the game it would be that the solutions to a small few challenges can be a tad, umm... "too imaginative" at times and the sense behind the answers feel a little stretched. But, unless you're a completionist, you only need to find one of the many ways to solve each problem and move forward, plus there are optional hints for each puzzle anyway, ranging from slight nudges to outright step-by-step guides, so no player should become too unstuck at any point. The free expansion, The Lost Hobo King, is perhaps a little less successful in winning us over, with its slightly more random feeling elements, but that's only in comparison to the phenomenal main game, and is still a fun hour or two either way, adding to the 10 or so hours to be had with the rest of the adventure.
Most of my time with Stacking felt like getting a great, big hug from a warm, fuzzy blanket and had me fawning over it with wide, glassy, wondering eyes for with just about every part of it. I really hope there are more games in the series to come and can't wait to see what kind of new characters and abilities we'll get to play with like dazzled kids rolling around with a new puppy on Christmas morning. Until then, the best present you can give yourself is a roll around with a cute little doll called Stacking.

Please Don’t Touch Anything is a small indie game where you’re filling in for a friend that has to go to the bathroom. It’s not clear what your friend’s tasks are, but his workspace contains a giant metal panel with a single red button and a monitor displaying a view of an anonymous city. His only instruction for you is to not touch anything until he returns. But that big red button is really hard to resist!
There are 25 different endings to Please Don’t Touch Anything, most of which do not do the city any good. It takes only a few steps to reach any of them. The first endings are quite easy to reach. You basically try stuff and see what happens (for examples, new buttons appear on the metal panel). But other endings are much more complex, requiring you to analyse small clues hidden within the scene.
I found half the endings before feeling helpless. Reading a walkthrough, there were maybe 3 additional endings that I could have figured out eventually, with more dedication. Although I understand the remaining ones, most are fairly gratuitous and it’s hard to imagine how players could stumble upon them on their own.
Graphics are entirely made of pixel art. A quick glance at the screenshots will confirm they’re functional but unspectacular. The soundtrack, on the other hand, is a perfect match for the game. It’s chiptune from start to finish, responds to your actions and instils a certain tension, giving the stakes an importance the gameplay alone wouldn’t allow.
Overall, Please Don’t Touch Anything is a decent curiosity that can entertain for a couple of hours, but it’s not an especially clever or polished design. I wouldn’t recommend it especially warmly but there are worse ways to spend 5 bucks and the best part of an evening.

Just played through the original Thief games for the first time.  This was my favorite, due to a lot of modernized systems, making for a better experience.
This is the height of the series, I feel.  It has enough modern advancements to be good, without getting into the sloppy side of modernization.  It's still very true to the originals, as well.  If you were to pick one Thief game to play, this one should be it.
-There's a hub world where you can fence, steal, and buy from.  It's also pretty hilarious to watch the townsfolk get into brawls on the street.
-No more 'one footstep alarms'.  I hated how a single footstep on marble in the original games would somehow mean a thief was present and everyone goes berserk trying to find me.
-Non-linear, to some extent.  You're given missions at the same time, so you can choose which ones to do first.
-Persistent inventory.  I feel better with an inventory that I can constantly monitor.  I'm more inclined to use it, because I know I can refill my supply.
-Quality of life improvements, like knowing how much treasure you've collected on the map and a lot less junk to cycle through in your inventory.
Some cons:
-Ducking is completely silent, no matter what.  This means moss arrows are nearly useless.  Still, it's better than the tap forward mechanic.
-Navigating the streets can be tedious, because of annoying guard placement.  You might end up throwing flashbombs all the time as a means to move quickly.
-There are some bugs.  Save often.
-I hear this game has compatibility issues.  Lucky for me, mine worked fine, aside from awkward, but functional, loading screens.  Playing on Windows 7 64 bit.

I've been playing video games since my family got a personal computer 24 years ago and all we had was Windows 3.1 and Killer Crayons. I've been a gamer most of my life, and of all the countless games I've played so far, this series is hands down my favorite. I love exploring forgotten dungeon, massive castles, palatial estates, haunted necropolis', forgotten tombs and so forth and this game series (thief 1,2,3) has all of them. Thief was the first game to use light and sound mechanics that allow the player to navigate the levels in a very realistic way. Splinter Cell and other stealth based games were influenced by this game.
As for the plot, it's actually pretty awesome. At first, you're just robbing wealthy homes and businesses for money. Then, inevitably, you draw the attention of somebody important who hires you to steal something much more valuable, a rare sword or artifact of some sort. This gets Garrett involved in a an intricate plot of power and betrayal that he has to get himself out of. There aren't very many cut scenes in the game. What happens when you decide to mix an isometric (or top-down) RPG with Tower Defense? Deathtrap happened.
From the same creators of The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, Neocore Games, brings you an incredible (no pun intended) Tower Defense game that mixes some of the best aspects of both genres into one great experience.
The game follows the same basic rule of Tower Defenses: protect the core element (the Gate) from the enemies (the Swarm). How you'll do it is completely and uniquely up to you.
It may or may not be relevant, but I've never been a huge fan of top-down RPGs. I've played ones like Diablo, Torchlight, Sacred 2, Titan Quest and even Adventures of Van Helsing, but none did capture my attention at all. So I decided to pick this game by the recommendation of a friend, and even then with doubtful thoughts.
My doubts were lifted after a couple of hours on single player and a bunch of co-op games. Deathtrap managed to catch my attention and focus and I stopped playing everything else I had to play it and test everything I could.
Deathtrap offers you three characters to play as: Mercenary, Marksman and Sorceress. Each of them plays considerably differently, and each one has their own skill tress (all characters may have one or two skills that the other has).
Mercenary is the one I recommend the most to play first. He's bulky, tough as nails and the easiest to learn the game since you don't have to worry too much about dying. You can use him to act as a wall to your traps and he only gets sturdier as you progress. Depending on your skill decision he can become a nigh unkillable juggernaut which can tank even the mightiest enemies.
Sorceress requires a lot more carefulness and attention. While she can dish some devastating spells and her skill tree is focused on offense, she is REALLY squishy and the bigger enemies can put her to sleep in two to four hits. She carries a wide array of spells either to move around or to attack at distance, a powerful easy to learn, but hard to master character.
Marksman is the most difficult character to learn and handle. He requires a while to cloak and regenerate his "mana" (which is called Focus) and that alone can be a hassle since if you attack or get too close to enemies your cloaking go away and so does your mana regeneration. Most of his abilities are very powerful, but he does focus more on trap rather than front line combats.
Deathtrap has things that most RPGs have: looting, leveling up and more looting. Something that is REALLY good about this game is that you will only get equipments for your current class when you finish a map, and even if you do get an accessory (which is universal) you can safely guard it in your Stash which is shared by all your characters.
Deathtrap is fairly short having only 13 levels in total in its main game, but each level has "Tiers" with each making the game progressively harder. And Deathtrap is unique among most games as it doesn't follow that sad, lazy idea of only increasing enemies and their health and damage. It changes the layout of trap settings and even add some other gimmicks to you.
Ever heard of a Tower Defense with side quests? Deathtrap has those which normally are challenges like "don't use a certain type of trap/tower" to "kill something that is away from the map".
After reaching Level 20 you'll gain access to Endless modes and Scenarios which allows you to customize the difficulty of the level you'll be playing. You can make the game fiendishly difficult by cutting your income, making enemies sturdier and even give them a chance to resurrect themselves. Such challenge is NOT to be taken by lightly armored players. Trust me on this one.
Deathtrap rewards your victories with experience points, but prevents players from grinding on the same map by cutting the exp to zero if the player is considered too strong for it. The only ways to earn experience if you want to level up more are via Endless or Scenarios, but even those are only unlocked after Level 20, probably when you are close to finish the game once.
Worry not, the first tier of maps are made for players and can be beaten even if you are rather under equipped.
Actually you don't have to worry about it.
You've read it right, Deathtrap doesn't clog your mind with attribute points, you'll have enough to worry about with your equipment, skills and trap upgrades, which are far more than enough to create characters from the same class but with different styles.
You have your fair share of tools to kill enemies: ground traps, towers that act as turrets, and even summon pits to bring creatures to your aid. All traps are divided by classes like Mechanical and Mystic for traps and towers and the unique Summoning for... Well, summons.
You'll earn traps as you beat the maps in the game, but that's not enough. You also need to earn your trap by completing a challenge like poisoning enemies, igniting them, pushing them or killing enemies on your own. Nothing is impossible as traps themselves gives you the tools to unlock other ones, but of course if your character is focused on a certain element it'll be much easier and faster to unlock another certain trap.
As it is with any good Tower Defense, there are tower which are better against small enemies (Horde) and deal extra damage to them, but if the enemy is resistant to it (Giants) it'll deal less damage. You must properly balance your traps unless you want to find yourself in a pinch.
Something some people will like and others will hate is the fact all places where you can set traps and towers are already set by the game. You can only build your Traps/Towers in pre-defined places reserved for Mystic, Mechanical and Summon classes (and Special towers not available for the players).
For me this was a miss. I really don't like this since it kills a ton of strategies and limits the player, sometimes forcing them to invest heavily in another tower.
Deathtrap features a very easy to use map editor and you can easily create them and share them via Steam Workshop.
Bear in mind that these maps WILL NOT REWARD EXPERIENCE. A smart decision by Neocore Games as the Workshop was filled with boring farming maps. You are still able to use them to unlock traps, however.
Deathtrap has a fair share of problems like any game does.
Some equipment like Rings are currently bugged and has a very noticeable writing glitch that makes the game look like it's still in Early Access.
Tier 2 onward may or may not force players to grind for better skills, equipment and trap upgrade points are limited by how many stars you've earned on each level with severely limits your choices on trap upgrades, specially when you get past a certain level.
The voice acting, while nice, it's a bit cheesy and not the best you'll hear around. Some people will like it, others will despise it.
Deathtrap is an amazing game. It gives you the satisfaction of crushing enemies alongside your defenses like a good Tower Defense game does and the pleasure of getting progressively stronger like a good RPG does. It's a mixture well crafted by Neocore Games and worth a shot for people that are fans of either genre.

*EDIT 12/11/2017*
After a few days thinking about this,  I now regret making a positive recommendation when there are so many things I dislike about this game. I wish there was a neutral or mixed recommendation button for cases like these. I'm still going to leave it positive because it's a decent video game asides from its flaws. Which are probably mostly subjective/opinion based anyway. However, I still don't like HOF2.
*END OF EDIT*
Anyway, this is definitely one of those cases where you have to had liked the first game to enjoy this one. I'd say it's better than the first, but... Well. I was super-drawn in to the first game when the idea of it was pitched to me, but I didn't end up liking it that much.
They did partially iron out some of the issues I had with the first game, but that's the thing though. Only partially.
Combat still feels a bit awkward and clunky, some enemies are also a bit too fast to handle which makes that even worse
The latter is especially noticeable when you get later into the game and start to fight multiple enemies who have unblockables that are fast, and their light attacks start to punish you for rolling instead of blocking.
The combat has weight unlike the first game and is a bit more fluid, however the character still moves around more like you're suggesting them to move in that direction rather than actually going directly there.
A good way to experience this in particular is the combat-free levels you can find where you have to weave through things like flamethrowers and timed floor spike traps. I had to get through spinning spike traps by running into a wall and awkwardly rubbing up against it while sprinting to have my character move in a way that felt natural.  Also kinda doesn't help that sprint and dodge/roll are assigned to the same button, that's gotten me screwed over in combat a few times.
Outside of combat hasn't changed much, you still have food, health, and gold as currencies.
I can't really remember if HOF1 had these but, with some events you have to roll dice and that's obviously based on RNG which I'm not entirely a fan of but I don't mind the existence of it. Especially considering now they added a swinging pendulum mechanic where you have to aim the laser for a sweet spot while avoiding fail spots. Though I can't say that I enjoy the card shuffles (You pick 1 of 4 cards, and they shuffle before you pick them) that much. Sometimes you can tell where the card you want is going to be, most of the time you can't though. Which is fair enough but personally I'm not a fan of that.
The wheel card thing annoys me in particular. You basically have a bunch of cards set in a circle, and it's like Wheel of Fortune where you have to try to land the 'pin' on the card that you want. It's frustrating though because the 'pin' does have RNG at times where sometimes it'll pick the one that you just missed or it'll pick the one you almost passed instead. It really sucks when you think you perfected the spin and it just decides to spit in your face by going forward by one, or when you think you got super lucky and just missed the bad card but then... It spits in your face by going back by one.
They did add character customisation to the game, which is sort of one of their selling points for this one?
It's
, it's about what you expect from an indie game with character customisation. Though I've noticed the devs for both games really love hairstyles where most of of your head is shaved. Even for the gals.
When you pick a male, I would just like to muse to you all that; with one hair style I looked like John Cena but as soon as I changed it I looked like Richard Spencer instead.
In all seriousness, all you can do is pick your race which also determines your face (IE: There's no variation in faces asides from picking a different race), and a hairstyle/colour. You can at the very least pick one of four super specific colour sets for your armor which is kinda nice. Not enough games do that.
TL;DR
It's basically the same game as the first from what I can kinda remember, you also need to enjoy rogue-lite gameplay with some RNG involved,
as well as fable/arkham-ish combat that in my opinion is very flawed. Character customisation is bland and extremely limited, but it's atleast there.
I'd say it's an okay game, but it's not for me. Probably shouldn't get it if you didn't like HoF1 though. Liked/loved the first one? Get it. It's probably great for ya.
*EDIT 12/11/2017*
There's one thing I had forgot to mention, that really bugs me about this game.
I wasn't sure if it was like this in the first game; but to unlock more weapons, events, and gear you have to gain tokens from doing campaigns, challenges, and getting the best result from an event.
This wouldn't be an issue if a lot of the events, some of the requirements to get gold on a campaign, and challenges weren't heavily based on both indirect and direct RNG.
Example: There's an event where you have 2 fail cards, one success card, and one huge success card.

Ok, So I have played this game a few months after its release, and I have played it since. Lots of reviews are complaining about the removal of things in the older versions. This review is only going to be based on the 1.0 full release, so things like temperature being removed etc. won't be counted. This review is based on my experiences in the game and not around a collection of pros and cons.
So the plot is pretty good, I liked the characters and I felt attachment to this universe. The Missions play out like this after you get your ship fixed: Find a specific race's structure or settlement, scan objects for clues until you fill up a bar, report back to outpost, complete a mission and fight a boss. Now the finding settlements and scanning can get a bit repetitive but it doesn't take long and you only have to do it 5 times but the missions are varied, fun and have great atmosphere. They are all different, One time you will be traversing a massive underwater library, next you will be assisting a group of rebels in an assault on an oppressive dictators compound or maybe defending a medieval castle from siege. Every one of them is fun.
So the main gameplay is kind of like terraria, except if terraria was set in space with an infinite universe to explore with an almost unlimited supply of incredibly varied planets to explore with 19 main biomes and 30 sub biomes above and bellow ground. There are so many things you can do from: Creating a massive farm and growing a large variety of unique crops (there are 35 crops in total) and looking after various farm animals, or you cound create a city filled with hundreds of NPCs that all have there own personality and uses. You can also grow your ships crew and create a sqad of soldiers, medics, janitors, chemists and tailors to assist you on missions or just traversing a planet. The Mining system can get a little bit annoying as it is very hard to get up to the surface after you have just dug a massive hole to the planets core but the underground exploration is amazing as there are so many unique underground and surface sub biomes and unique dungeons and mini dungeons. There is an infinite supply of unique randomly generated weapons meaning that you end never relying on one single weapon in combat. There are multiple combat styles and 3 branches of armor that match that from the high damage manipulators armors to the high defence separators armors or the high energy accelerators armor, there is room for many playthroughs.
The game has in my opinion one of the best pixelated art styles of all time, the environments look beautiful and when the game runs at 60fps (which is not hard at all) the animations are incredibly smooth. All over the universe there are over 60 sets of unique vanity armor to find all over the universe and nearly 200 unique hats to find as well.
The base game's sound is fine and it all fits in and works but the music, oh the music...
Possibly some of the best Sci-Fi music I have heard ever. It is beautiful and sets the atmosphere perfectly, One of those games that makes you want to go out and buy the soundtrack.
I enjoyed this game immensely, If you enjoyed games like Terraria, Minecraft or just sandbox or exploration games in general and love finding new secrets or customizing your character and base, if you enjoy going on adventures in video games then you will most likely enjoy this game a LOT and have a great time. So yes, you should buy it. 9.5/10

Ever wondered how would a Charles Dickens-esque story look like if all the characters were matryoshka dolls? You can stop wondering then, because this family-friendly action adventure game will give you the answer.
In Stacking, you play with dolls. Well, as dolls. Russian matryoshka dolls. And the funny thing is: this game is not just for little kids, adults will enjoy it just as much, if not even more.
Stacking is the name of the game and the main mechanic: your goal on each level is to solve a set of clever puzzles by jumping into other dolls, taking over their actions. All dolls have a unique ability that could be the key to one of the many solutions for each puzzle. If not, then it may be used to complete an optional challenge for added fun!
All of this puzzling is packaged into a story that reminded me of Charles Dickens: early industrialist world with steam engines everywhere, pompous factory owners who try to oppress the working class even more by introducing child (slave) labour, and a witty little protagonist, Charlie Blackmore, who starts on a quest to save his kidnapped family, following the advices of a friendly hobo he meets along the way.
The plot is divided into 4+1 stages (train station, ocean cruiser, zeppelin, luxury train, plus a DLC stage in a shanty town), all with increasing difficulty and maximum doll size. The first two stages start out especially memorable with their level and puzzle design, but the second half of the game is blander with darker levels and puzzles that share the same goal over and over: get rid of the next guard.
Luckily there is a DLC/expansion after it, the Hobo King quest, which brings back the creativity of the early levels, bumping this gem to “highly recommended” status for everyone who likes a good adventure.

When I was going into this game, I had high expectations because people were saying it's good, and that it's like Machinarium and so on. After finishing the game (yes, it was that short), I don't feel like it's really that great.
Lilly Looking Through is a story about a girl named Lilly, who has to rescue her brother Row, from a... magcial cloth who has appeard to taken Row away. Yeah. Anyway, let's start with pros. The pros are that the game is charming and whatever, and has a nice setting. You can switch between two worlds to solve puzzles in and the art style is really cool. The animation in this game is wonderful, and it just looks overall great. The game isn't too hard, and you'll have fun playing it. Maybe.
Now it's time for the long list of cons. Some are personal, some are obvious.
1. The game is waaay too short. After finishing a puzzle, I was thinking what would happen next to these two protagonists. Then the game ends. Seriously. On a cliffhanger. One second I'm partially enjoying myself and the next second the credits are rolling.
2. YOU CANNOT skip animations. So whenever you're doing a puzzle, you have to watch every slow animation Lilly makes. It looks nice, but not when you're sitting there for minutes watching Lilly shamble on. These long animations actually help lengthen the already short game time. It makes the game super tedious and I can't enjoy it if it's like that.
3. Variety. There were a lot of the same puzzles. Ones with color mixing. I no like colors. I never thought a really short game could get repetitive.
4. Random. There's an appearance from Lilly's Grandpa at the end that had nothing to do with anything and it baffled the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. Also, there's like 5 lines of voice acting that randomly appear and I don't get it.
Overall, I wanted to like this game, but I just couldn't bring myself to enjoy it. There were a lot of cool things, but when you stop and look at it, you'll realize that there's problems abound. With that said, I wouldn't mind a sequel with some improvements or a new game from these guys. There's still a lot of potential here.

I have heard a lot about the Thief series, considered to be some of the best stealth games out there. As someone who loves the Arkham series and is enjoying Stealth Inc I have wanted to try this out.
When the opportunity came up for me to buy one of the Thief games I opted for the 3rd entry under the small fear that the older (and from what I have heard slightly better) instalments might not run very well on modern machines. I will not deny that I had to mod it(please get the Sneaky thief update from Nexus Mods if you  want to buy this) it still ran fairly well.
Thief 3, as someone who has never played a Thief game before is a game that I have really enjoyed. I think the stealth mechanics are extremely well defined and fun to use, you have to use and create spots of shadow sneak past  your enemies while stealing everything that is not nailed down; combat is there if you need it and it does the job but I felt better knocking people out or not being spotted as being the best way to play the game. I loved the atmosphere; a game that makes you wait on the edge of your seat to see if guards spot you is something to be applauded for by any means (I will give a small gush to the Robbing the Cradle mission later).
The story is decently written for the most part but nothing special, Garrett is a master thief who just wants to meet his payments and keeps getting dragged into intercity conflict between the Hammerrites and pagans or between keepers and an evil hag who wants to become an invincible world destroyer because why not?.
Voice acting as par for the course of late 1999 and early 2000’s voice acting, which means it is a mixed bag, Garrett is voiced wonderfully by Stephen Russell and some of the supporting cast (I cannot find the names of them sadly) are done pretty well, however some namely the guards, pagans and some of the shop owners have really bad line delivery that make their darkly humorous lines come off very flat at best and cringe worthy at worst.
Now for that Robbing the Cradle mission, without giving too much away I think it is a masterpiece in creating a horror atmosphere, the way the lights brighten and dim like a heartbeat to the distant howls of long suffering ghosts make it one of the best levels I have ever played, get this if you just want to experience that one mission, trust me it is worth the rest of the game!
Overall despite uneven voice acting and a starting struggle to run well, Thief 3 is well worth a look at!

It's a really cool web app, but I'm not sure I respect it as a retail game. It's hard to see any sort of logic in the puzzles - the game is really just a series of locks that you find the combinations to, all of which are typically hidden in plain sight. You gather these combinations by messing with components of the machine in varying orders, and from there it's a lot of brute force as you try out combinations to see the results. It's fun at first to experiment with everything in front of you and get different endings, but after a certain point it gets entirely too abstract and effectively forces you to use a guide to see everything, especially since there are a ton of red herrings that just waste your time. There are parts to this game that didn't make a lick of logical sense even when I checked a guide (for example, how does the clock puzzle hint at it's solution at all?) It's fun to screw around with, but I can't take this seriously as a retail puzzle game.

First off let me say I am somewhat of a NeocoreGames fanboy I will admit it.  I really have enjoyed their TIAoVH series and loved the tower defense game within it.  At first I didn't think I would like it but it grew on me so when I found out about Deathtrap I was like oh cool they took one of the coolest things that made TIAoVH a unique ARPG into it's own game.  Some people seem to have taken that as laziness or a cash grab for some reason, I think it was a good idea.  I don't see it as lazy, it is a is a tried and tested idea for within the other game and they have fully fleshed it out into it's own game.
Currently I have just over an hour invested in the game and so far it is well worth the money invested even if I don't play another minute, though I am sure I will certainly play a great deal more.   Neocore is very good about spreading out achievements in their games making it one of those games that is fun to keep playing because you know that any minute you may stumble across just one more unlock.  It works.    As far as the game games if it is a fun tower defense but it doesn't get too stressful unless you play at the harder levels so if you just want to relax and plan some fun traps and sit back and have fun it is that type of game.  You can play as actively or as inactively as you want depending on the level you set the game.   I like to play actively myself.
All in all it is a great game and at the asking price of $20 it is worth every penny, I have plenty of $60 games that I haven't gotten near the enjoyment out of as I already have out of Deathtrap.

Bastion is what makes me never fully lose hope on the videogame industry. Where most famous videogame developers release and publish a popular IP with many installments that differ very little from one another, or focus too much on low quality casual games, comes a developer out of the blue with a videogame played on an isometric point of view, solid gameplay mechanics, a beautifully written (and most importantly, beautifully narrated) story, a cute and mind blowingly beatiful art style and the most perfect soundtrack to ever grace your ears and I can't help but weep at the beauty and perfection that is this game, this...EXPERIENCE. There will never be a game that makes me nearly as much as emotional as Bastion. I can never suggest this game hard enough to all my friends, as a "once in a lifetime experience that you MUST have" and will probably still do for the rest of my days.
I thank you so much, Supergiant Games, for bringing this masterpiece of video gaming to life, and I thank my friend Joshua aka "Zetadar" for insisting so much time and time again that I should play this game that he got it for me as a gift. After playing it the least I can say is that I wish I would've payed full price for this magnum opus myself. But I still have the chance to purchase the soundtrack and most probably will once I receive my next paycheck, Darren Korb definitely deserves a lot more recognition than just an OST purchase.
And for Mother's sake, do save Zulf. Every time. No weapon is worth sparing the life of someone who made a mistake out of anger. We all made mistakes once.

First impressions after six missions (5–6 hours)
While not without some minor flaws, HoF 2 improves on just about everything I enjoyed about the original. More cards, new mechanics, greater enemy variety, and a *far* better narrative. While there is a level of RNG, most of it can be augmented in your favor in some way — success/failure cards can be followed if you're quick, blessings and equipment can be seeked out to improve die rolls, and new mechanics like the wheel and pendulum require skill more than luck (some practice in precision).
Some other thoughts:
– While gamepad controls are excellent, M&K is pretty rough. This isn't much of an issue for me, as I'm happy to use either depending on the game I'm playing — M&K "purists" will struggle however.
– Combat has been improved, though it is a slower more methodical process. Don't button mash and you'll be a-okay.
– Some difficulty modes or modifiers would be nice as I find the current one-and-only a bit too easy for too long in the early game. I'm six missions in (out of 22...?) and have barely struggled.
– Endless mode was one of my favorite features of the original, and it is temporarily absent here (there is a placeholder on the main menu). While there is plenty of game and replayability in story mode, I'm greatly anticipating Endless mode's arrival.
If you thoroughly enjoyed the first game, Hand of Fate 2 is a no-brainer purchase. If not, there's still a lot to like, though I wouldn't blame you for waiting for a demo or sale.

Hand of Fate 2 tries to improve upon the first one's premise but feels more like a hardcore mode that takes away alot of the enjoyment.
While the original had some unforgiving events, its combat was simple - and its "gambling" minigames (the one minigame, the card shuffle) was made in such a way as to give the player the abillity to guess quite well where the successes were. The new minigames range from being completely random (stuff like the roulette) to what basically can only be called a rhythm puzzle, and while the added minigames do break the pace from the same card shuffle, I didn't feel they were ever needed.
Part of what makes the game less enjoyable is the new mission layout:
unlike the original, Hands of Fate 2 aims to have every mission unique with its objectives.
For example where the original only had you killing bounties, the second game gives me a mission to stop an assassination, while gathering clues from suspects.
Those new missions does take away from the monotonous grind that is jumping into missions and just fighting your way through everything inorder to complete the game, but it also makes each one strech longer - with more dialog choices, more checks, and more missable objectives.
When you died in the first Hand of Fate, you could jump into the level like nothing, the only difference would be having to fight your way through it again. But when you die now, you have to click through a bunch of mission introduction, and repeat specific steps in the mission inorder to complete it, which makes the mission much more frustrating to play through again.
The game also feels like it have less variety of cards than the first one (including the expansions), although having alot of returing cards from the original game which begs the question if some of them were kept just to be resold as DLC later down the line.
Hand of Fate 2 also added a new companion system to you loadout, which lets you take along an npc to fight along side you. The companions are pretty unique, each having his own set of attacks, passive benefits and can buff you during battle, and each comes with its own set of cards that deepen their relationship with the player as dive into their backstory and the events that made them join you on your travels.
Overall, Hand of Fate 2 is a fantastic game. So I had seen this game on sale and was interested in the concept.  Hell, I think I've boughten most of every RPG + Tower Defense hybrid, it's a genre that I'm glad is exploding haha.  With that said; this is seriously one of my favorite games for the hours I've already put in.  The balance is so great it's almost painful to see so many other ARPGs struggle, including the title The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing.
I think a lot of this stems from the fact that you're constantly upgrading gear, but it's never a huge leap like in other aRPGs.  As an example, I'm doing about 400 damage with my weapon at level 1 and nearing 500 around 20.  This...is so smart, seriously it feels great and makes it so you do get more powerful, but not trampled by over powered monsters and not so strong that previous levels are necessarly easy.  On top of this, the skills are interesting and varied, with the classes playing quite different from one another.
Another fantastic aspect of this game is the level design and how the NG+ works.  There's 13 levels including in the game, each having endless waves, scenarios and 4 different approaches to how they're done.  The levels are pretty standard right away, but they start throwing curve balls in the game as it progresses, with new mechanics and level specific traps, not to mention all the levels are fun, I never got overly frustrated with any of them, and they're all challenging, but manageable, you are legitmately able to 3 star these levels on your first go, but it won't be easy.  I feel if I can do it with the melee class, it's got a good balance.
Now I have heard that later tiers of levels are a wall in difficulty, but so far, for the 20 hours I've put in, it's been smooth and awesome, I can't recommend this game enough, I truly hope this concept gets expanded upon.

While the gameplay is fun, what really sticks with me is the fantastic music and the brilliant in-game narration by Logan Cunningham. That keeps me playing more than anything else. Always worth a replay.

Loving the game. Keep up the good work. Content. It's going to need more content to be successful though. I see this being played a few weeks and then dropped because it's the same thing over and over. I am, however; very excited for it's continued development.

A worthy sequel that expands on the ideas and mechanics of the first game while still being very familiar.
The combat was the weakest aspect of the first game, and it remains the weakest aspect in this game as well. The equipment is more varied and interesting and the multiple weapon styles are a welcome addition. Despite this, the combat is still the simple bamham style from the first game, though it is slightly improved. Combat feels better and the varied weapons and companions make it more fun, but I think the enemies in this game are easier and less interesting than the first game (except the Mages, which are much stronger in this game). So far, I have only ever lost from not completing a challenge's objectives. I have never died in combat. Maybe the later challenges will be harder (I've done about 2/3 of the challenges so far), but I think the combat is too easy.
The deckbuilding in this game is much more precise, allowing you to really tailor the deck to each encounter. The boss-focused story in the first game was cool, but the challenges that replace it in this game are much more varied and interesting. Each one has a unique mechanic that changes how you have to play the game. The new "chance" games are also pretty great and there is a slew of items that help mitigate bad RNG.
The one great dissapointment to me are the types of enemies. The first game had humans, ratmen, lizardmen, undead, mages, molten golems and sometimes a minotaur. This game has humans, big humans, sick humans, quick humans, mages, undead and sometimes an ogre. I love that the weapons and equipment are more closely tailored to fight these specific enemy types, but I miss the fantasy enemies from the first game.
The first game had a great development cycle, so I have a lot of faith that this game will have the same great support from the devs. Maybe they can even add an enemy that isn't a human.
EDIT: After playing a little more, I think I've specifically identified my gripes with the enemy types in this game. HoF1 was focused on the progression of bosses, leading that progression to making you fight those bosses in regular encounters later. Each boss was unique and memorable. In HoF2, many of the enemies of the same tribe look alike and fight similarly. Some of the bosses in this game are reskins and don't use the "Jack, Queen, King" tags of the first game, making them much less memorable and identifiable. I don't really see bosses in regular encounters very much, and it's becoming apparent that this game's difficulty ramp is more focused on more enemies, rather than harder enemies like the first game.

If being Robinson Crusoe or even Tom Hanks from "Castaway" is your thing, then this game is for you. You play as someone surviving a plane crash in the Pacific Ocean. You can paddle from island to island in your dinghy and explore or simply just build your own small camp on the first island you get to. In order to do this you'll need to build some basic tools of course, and naturally you will have to scavenge for food an water to stay alive.
There are also shipwrecks that you can swim to and dive to in order to get loot from which will hopefully aid in your survival. But watch out, the water may look gorgeous and be populated with all kinds of wildlife, but remember there are tiger sharks and great whites roaming around.
The environment and sun sky effects are gorgeous, the water/underwater is very nice too. It also rains, but i haven't seen or heard any thunder and lightining yet. But i'm hoping that some real storms can whip up eventually as the game gets developed more. The crafting is pretty basic for now, and a few things like campfires, tools and shelters can be constructed. Again i expect this to expand quite alot in the non too distant future. Not too many bugs to speak of to be honest, which is pretty refreshing for early access games. Bring on bigger islands with waterfalls and maybe more wildlife deer, boar, snakes etc...that would be great.
All in all for £11 this is a bargain, especially if you're into survival games without the zombies/mutants, it's just you against nature.

This is a great buy, the game itself is absolutely brimming with potential and I'm excited to see where they go with it. The graphics are exceptional and the dev's have done a really good job in terms of making sure that resources are scarce enough that you can't have a comfy life forever.
Now that the disappearing raft bug is gone too, I can play this game without needing a spare set of underwear on hand. There is nothing nice about trying to quietly scoot by a pair of sharks in the dead of night and then hearing a splash as your raft quite literally vanishes from underneath you and you end up having a meet and greet with Jaws and his bigger brother. On that note, if you're one of those people who get freaked out in water that's too deep for you to see to the bottom, move along - this is not the droid you are looking for. That's the norm here and not only that, but there's almost certainly a shark below you. They're everywhere.
The tension throughout this game is good and there's a lot to be said about being careful with your resources. Some are definitely a little too abundant and others a little too scarce. But if you're pretty happy sat in paradise eating crab and coconut all day, throw your money at Beam Team now!
Given it's early access, this is a good enough taster to warrant buying the game. I'm going to make an effort to not rinse too much time into this for a little while and give the devs some time to iron some things out and inevitably add some things in.
In terms of what I'd like to see, or see amended, I've made a list below:
Improvements:
* ROCKS - we need more. I get incensed when I break the tool that I was using to cut down the last tree to keep my fire going so I can cook that last crab and I no longer have any rocks, despite the fact that when I pan the camera around, there are rocks goddamn everywhere, but I can't have any of them because they aren't....well I don't know. But come on, rocks are everywhere yet, there's only 7 - 8 per island you can actually pick up. 6 of which go on a fire pit. Maybe include the options to break down larger ones?
* Fast travel to islands you've already visited (OR access to improve your storage capacity in lieu of this), if this were to be incorporated, perhaps add in an increased hunger/thirst penalty to balance it out?
* Along similar lines, perhaps have the option to generate a makeshift map of sorts as you explore? This could be done through crafting a sheet of wood and a rock shard acting as chalk or something?
* You should be able to make food spits without having to upgrade to a fire pit. (Those six rocks are far more useful for other things, but manual cooking is a real bore too so it's a bit damned if you do, damned if you don't.)
* It'd be nice to put my bed in a shelter, pretty sure this is just a bug though and I expect this to be fixed asap.
* Larger islands with access to more resources - balanced by having hostile natives/animals perhaps?
* Flotsam - I saw on a survival doc once that there's always lots of things literally washing up on shore - cans, bottles, rope etc. This would be a good addition. Have 90% of it be useless, 9% be sort of useful (burnable for example, or rope etc.) and then every now and again, have the final 1% being something really useful like a backpack, harpoon or something - basically a set of items that would be unique to flotsam only, not obtainable at dive sites etc. Balance it out by never guaranteeing that an island might have one of those "1%" items.
* Sharks hostile to those f'ing Marlins. I've been knocked out of rafty more times than I can remember by bloody Marlins, once straight into the path of a great white. Throw us a rope if the two happen to meet?
* Shark music - I think it should be an option in the menu. I can see a solid argument for having it, and an equally solid one for not. Perhaps meet in the middle and have it something that can be turned on or off?
* Other ways to die - the list is endless - sea snakes, stone fish, jelly fish etc etc.
* Storage - crates out of sticks and rope. Even better have some that can attach to your raft, who doesn't like a picnic at sea?
* Variety of wrecks - airplanes, larger ships with air pockets in etc. This one might be wishful thinking, but it would be cool.
* Shark sizes - Great Whites are way bigger than Tiger Sharks, easy fix.
* Digging! Have some islands that aren't just sand so you can dig in, what if some had caves for example? Even if they were only big enough to have yourself plus a fire in, it'd add a bit of variety.
A few people have mentioned PVP, but I'm dead against it here, multiplayer could definitely work, trying to survive as a group is much harder as you need so much more food etc. but hostile options will ruin this game, I'm certain of it. Imagine logging in to find some ballbag has stolen all of your stuff or broken your shelter etc.
There's a lot of other stuff, but it's all things that I'm 100% certain that it's already going to be sorted, things like having to stay warm in the rain, sickness, an end game etc. I can't see how they won't address any of that, so I'm leaving it out. Oh and this game is screaming for an Easter Egg, something crazy like a kraken, giant shark or pirates or something equally stupid, make it happen!
Really happy that I bought this and looking forward to seeing where it goes!

I'll start from afar. You can as well skip to the "All in all" paragraph at the end.
There was that article on RPS or some other Internet game press site about playing the old Xcom with a lot of attachment and devotion to the characters as a child. The man put a lot of imagination to it (up to the point where two of the characters would be "kissing" every fifth round - and by kissing that guy meant crouching by each other).
Well, Battle Brothers
.
What you might have had to do in other open-world games yourself - like setting up a long-term goal - here is done before you even think of it. Characters have their colorfully-described backgrounds - and these backgrounds count when it comes to characteristics of fresh-hired men - and to the random events (which happen unfrequently yet, thanks to that, don't get repetitive).
At the same time this game - as many negative reviewers justly remark - is utterly simplistic in terms of gameflow. It consists of:
1.finding contracts
2.accomplishing\failing contracts
3.getting reward for them
Plus
which includes:
1.food'n'equipment-management
2.medical issues when your men suffer from battle-acquired wounds
3.risk-management, because at any given time you will have to make decisions on how much risk you are willing to take
4.reputation system which helps in money-making (although the reputation could have a bit more economical impact, it still works pretty well)
5.trade-management, because sometimes you acquire costly goods in battles that you can sell for a good price - but where exactly? In big towns, not just anywhere. Hence -
6.route management, because every day you pay your men their fee, so you won't want to make pointless journeys.
Hmmm... If I'm being honest, that doesn't look all too simplistic to me anymore.
is hard'n'heavy'n'fun. A lot has been said about it in other reviews, I'll dwell on one particular issue. Some negative reviewers have been saying that there's no tactical depth to the battle system because there's no cover system which makes you shift constantly.
Well, first off, it's not modern-day fluid combat, it's a medieval one, where the solidity of the line is over all.
But even putting that fact aside: there's the height-system. Occupying the overlooking position while keeping enemy below is extremely important and makes you constantly shift (yes, constantly shift) your men when the action is taking place somewhere in the hills. Add random-generated maps to it, and you will get the picture.
An example out of my own experience. A battle agains orcs in the snowy hills. we started on the slope of a plateu.
We had a choice
1.to climb up the slope to the top  thus gripping the equal ground-level with our enemies but we wouldn't able to form the line before they attacked.
2.stay where we were. Thus we would keep our fine defensive line intact but inferior in terms of ground-level.
3.retreat a few tiles back and get off the slope - would cost us some fatigue, but maybe we could form our defence-line before the orcs caught up with us plus the ground-level would be the same.
I'll leave it up to you to think what the best decision here is. I didn't take the best one, unfortunately, so this battle cost me some good men.

I'll start by saying that the game is fun and addicting, it's the most basic Tower Defense game you can get and play for hours, and it looks and sounds freaking amazing. You definitely know when your Howitzers are shooting. For what it costs it's a great buy.
However, that's about it. Beyond basic arrow/cannon/flame/frost/lightning towers, it brings nothing to the genre, and is not even the best at being a basic TD game.
On to the bad parts...
1. The placement grid is awful, it feels like someone used a spray tool for the grid, but then left a lot of rubbish in the way to prevent you from placing towers. I legit had to turn down the mouse to 300dpi to place a tower in tighter spots.
Placement aside, the grid does not feel thought out, maybe it is, you couldn't tell because it wastes a lot of space.
2. The tower sell option is questionable, the value is so low you could just rename it to "Destroy".
3. Easy difficulty means nothing, started playing on Normal and by level 16 the game felt more like Hard, switched to easy and saw no actual difference.
4. No reasignable hotkeys for game speed. Normal mode is very slow, and "turbo" is a speed adjusted from the menu which you toggle ingame.
5. Towers are boring. Plain and simple, boring. Besides the enrage mode after Tier 2 there is nothing more to them. Upgrades are just color and stat changes, and visually inconsistent. Some towers get more guns/bigger, others just get a new color.
6. The creep movement overlay could be color coded or something, it's impossible to distinguish how the units will move until you actually play the map.
7. To quote the description of the game "virtually endless tactical options". Not really. Your endless tactical options are just restarting the game 10 times until you figure out how not to lose lives on level 1.
8. Abilities have the most annoying sounds possible, and the targetting for the fire strike is impossible to aim consistently.
9. Back to the boring towers part, there is no progression to the game. You get past a couple of maps, have all your towers and abilities "unlocked" , and every map after is the same. Figure out where enemies come/go > place lightning tower to start > fill map with frost and Howitzers/Tornado. Which is expected for a TD game, but gets boring after a while.
10. Needs a sandbox mode or map creation mode.
So yeah, pretty long negative list, but maybe I just expect more from TD games. Don't let this sway you away, it's still a good game for the money if you like TD.
