This is a little addictive gem, the kind of game that keeps you awake until 3 AM, while you still think it's 11PM. At the core is a turn based tactical battle game, where your squad of mercenaries has to battle wolves, goblins, orcs, brigands etc; the ruleset is pretty simple (albeit not very well documented) and offers you several possibilities for customization (so, the typical easy to learn, hard to master gameplay).
When you are not in battle, you are roaming the random generated map in search for contracts, points of interest or good trade deals. The world is a live entity (think at Sid Meier's Pirates, but on land)  where cities can spawn caravans directed to other cities; you can ambush them if you want, but if you leave them reach the destination, then you can eventually watch the town grow. It's a nice system but I believe it's a bit simplicistic, I wish the simulation would be more "vibrant".
This game has a lot to offer, the sandbox approach works well, but it amplifies the main issue of Battle Brothers: repetitiveness. Eventually you'll start asking yourself what's the point of all this loop (roam to city, accept contract, reach destination, battle, go back for payment); however the game is very challenging, so this is one of those few cases where repetitiveness doesn't lead to boredom.
I can see myself playing this game for 40-50 hours before going back to Panzer Corps, so I'd say it's definitely worth the price tag

This is the 3rd game in the thief franchise, following Garrett exploits who always for some reason unwillingly getting himself involved in some world ending event that he accidently help to start and now must stop it.
I have played the previous thief games in the series and I have entered this game with low expectations since I heard that this game is not a proper/good thief game and that this game is a step backward but I got to tell you that this game actually a very good and a proper thief game. Yes, it's flawed and feel rushed but it's still a good game.
The graphics are very beautiful and aged very well and although I personally prefer the artstyle of thief 1 and 2 cutscenes, the cutscenes of this game have their own charm which I approve.
Lockpicking is now a minigame....finally, you can climb down ladders safely without falling to your death now, new interesting gear to use like the gas bombs and the oil and the most important thing - you got a loot tracker where you can see how much loot you got in the middle of mission and how much still left around waiting for you to steal it.
There are very serious problem and flaws with this game and I feel that they are as a result of a rushed release:
The way Garrett move in this game is very sluggish compare to how he moved in the previous games, it feels like he moves in molasses,  and for some reason you can get stuck on the terrain and in some instances you will start to skate on the floor because it appears that you got stuck on the falling animation.
The concept of the city is cool, you can go to other people houses, some stores and pubs and steal their stuff.
There are also handlers that you can visit sell them your ill-gotten loot and blackmarket shops that will sell you equipment for your next missions and items for your house (this is instead of the starting menu before each mission in the previous game)...but again it feels like it was rushed and poorly implemented.
The problem with the city is not the thing that I mentioned before, no, those work as they were intended....
it’s the city guards....not the other hostile NPC in the area......it’s the annoying stupid city guards.
It becomes tiresome to evade every time those guards in order to get from one section of the city to the other, these guys are everywhere, and it becomes more of a nuisance then a challenge as you continue to play.
I get the factions that can be hostile to you, but those have their special areas where you know you want to stay away from there unless you need something specific there…but the guards, there are just too many of them for the sizes of each quarter.
I get it if the city would have shortcuts and more hidden routes to get around the guard problem but there aren't any.
The difficulty adjustment is not well implemented, for example in the original thief games you were forbidden to kill anyone(because a true master thief don’t need to kill) but here on expert you are allowed to do so.
Also to those who did the mission with the captain's widow: on that mission you need to get 90% of the loot on expert and you reach a point in the game were it is told that the widow will need the money in the specific chest to survive which is worth 12% of the total loot in the mission and you can see the problem…so on the other difficulties I would not have taken it...but apparently the devs didn’t playtest this part at the time and rushed it out.
Other than that I have really enjoyed the game; the funny dialogues are still there…though I miss the Hammerites funny voice acting.
Each mission feels different, especially the Shalebridge Cradle one, and the main villain and its minions are very unnerving.
Final words? it's not a perfect thief game but still a good one.

OH, WE'RE NOT DONE YET, MY FRIENDS!!! What happened next was the REAL icing on the cake, something that will keep me awake for many nights to come, staring up at the ceiling from my bed. As soon as I quit out of the game, I noticed something a tad... off about my computer's display. Somehow, simply playing this game changed my display settings. No, not like one detail, that sort of thing happens on rare occasions with games. No, it changed ALL my display settings to random sizes and resolutions because... Well, I don't know, but if I ever DO figure out the 'because', I'm sure I'll be doing so from a secure wing of some mental hospital, most likely staring at the door lock helpless to do anything about it similarly to how I did so playing this game, but I digress... My resolution was zoomed WAY in, the icons were changed to be tiny and oddly vertically stretched  and menus and text were MASSIVE to the point where you could read words on my screen from a neighboring county.
Needless to say, I had a real blast working out exactly what my original settings were! Played that longer than I played 'Thief: Deadly Shadows', actually! So there's that, at least! tl;dr: High Action Stealth 2D puzzle platformer that's so much fun you'll have trouble setting it down. (Requires a controller with analog input)
I must admit that I wasn't expecting this to be so good. Nor was I expecting it to be so HARD.
SBD is a great game but it's not what one would describe as a true "stealth" game. Sure, it has stealth "elements" in it but it is essentially a well executed 2D puzzle platformer. Not that being a 2D puzzle platformer is a Bad Thing; on the contrary, a well executed 2D platformer is one of those rare things that still makes me smile.
SBD's main draw is in how it tackles the biggest issue with stealth games: it takes all the slowness and waiting and completely removes it all. The remaining stealth elements (props like lasers and cameras. game mechanics such as visibility, sound travel, and patrol paths) are then taken, distilled, and subsequently shoved in your face in a fun yet comically brutal manner. Gameplay and level-wise, it has well designed bite-sized levels that can take minutes to conquer but hours to master.
My only real "gripe" about SBD comes from the lack of story; the "Why am I here? What's going on?" kind of stuff that never really got answered. However, this genre hasn't exactly been known for great story telling so it's par for the course on that point. What little narration there is comes in the form of sarcastically encouraging snippets found throughout a level. It is a little strange but it works. I did on more than one occassion push through a difficult section just to see what smarmy comment the game could throw at me next.
On a final note, only those of you in possession of some analog method of controller input should get this game. Keyboard or d-pad won't cut it for some of the parts and you should Definitely avoid playing this on a touch screen unless you're looking for an excuse to upgrade your phone/tablet. But if you've got a controller lying about and a couple crumpled Washington's in your wallet definitely give this little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a try.

Trimmer Tycoon is a pleasant surprise that is - sadly - marred by a glaring technical issue (at least for me?) at the later parts of a playthrough.
The gameplay is simple:
1. Click on a Customer.
2. Erase (Cut) and Re-colour (Dye) Pixels to match Customer's desired Pixel Beard.
3. Repeat 1. and 2. in order to (a) Pay for Rent and (b) Upgrade Shop.
4. When you can’t pay your rent, you lose.
Erasing Pixels involves two tools (shaver and scissors, which both erase pixels based on their respective tool shapes) and the usage of the left mouse button, where you swap between tools with the right mouse button.
Re-colouring Pixels involves the usage of the Red, Green and Blue tint bars, where you click-and-drag to make the colour match; over here, the challenge is the combination of all three bars to achieve the colour that matches closely/exactly to the Customer's desired colour for his/her Pixel Beard. Re-colouring affects the entire beard and not individual pixels.
The more accurate you are in erasing and re-colouring, the more money you get, which either has to go to your rent or can be used for shop upgrades.
The goal of this game is to see how far you can keep paying your rent as your rent cost goes up every time you are charged for it; when you can't pay your rent as it’s due, you lose.
The amount of time you are given before your rent is due each time is based on your shop upgrades, but the base time of the rent cycle you start with is 1 minute and 30 seconds.
Shop upgrades stretches the gameplay along with your ability to keep paying your rent as you (1) hire beard barbers and train them, (2) buy furniture and (3) expand your shop. In fact - in order to survive beyond the 30 minutes mark of your rent cost, - you need to upgrade your shop, especially having furniture to provide you bonuses to keep paying your rent considerably.
(1) Beard barbers (employees) are basically automatons to help you cut the beards of your waiting customers because customers who wait too long will leave. Upgrading your beard barbers makes them cut faster and increases the revenue gained from them cutting. You can have up to two (2) beard barbers max - based on expanding your shop. Though, I might be missing something because the trailer shows that you can have three beard barbers whereas I could only have two at most after expanding.
(2) Furniture provides passive bonuses, which will help in the long-run (either by spawning more customers through popularity, by increasing their waiting times, by increasing the general revenue, etc.).
(3) Expanding your shop allows you to hire more beard barbers (up to 2 max) and to own more furniture, and - also - shop expansion provides passive bonuses similar to furniture but also provides one setback based on the type of expansion you choose. You can only expand your shop twice and - for each expansion - you only have two choices, which both have differing bonuses and setback.
Basically,
This game is a time trial pixel art tycoon, and it's hilariously more fun than you would expect as - together - the simple mechanics of erasing, re-colouring and shop upgrading starts off excitingly and manages to keep the pace of adrenaline in wanting to paying your rent to see how far you can get.
Despite the average pixel art,
This is a good game in its simplicity, and the music keeps a fun mood.
There's a Leaderboards too if you're into competing scores, which I have no idea how 'Time Survived' and 'Beards Shaved' scores are calculated since only the 'Money Earned' score follows the exact value you earned in total via revenue.
In regards to the thumbs-down reviews,
Majority of their complaints are based on the difficulty that comes from the lack of using shop upgrades to keep paying rent, which leaves them losing earlier in their playthroughs in comparison to players who do utilise shop upgrades.
However, what is deserving of a thumbs-down is the glaring technical issue of this game.
The glaring technical issue of this game is that the spawning of customers - along with the playtime of your playthrough - eventually reduces the consistent framerate; I started off at a very stable and smooth framerate, but, after 40 minutes into my first playthrough, I started losing framerate to a point where - at my 60 minutes mark - I couldn't properly erase nor re-colour my customers' beards to match properly (with 7 frames per second then) so I had to depend on my beard barbers, which led me to being unable to pay for my rent since my 2 beard barbers (both of them at skill level 31) couldn't generate enough revenue to pay off my rent, which had become around 70,000$ by the 87 minute mark.

Much of the enjoyment comes from strictly-unnecessary "cute" features such as petting the dogs, silly hero-shot close-up portraits of the dogs when they level up, cute sound effects, and the dog happiness system. If you have ever wanted to upgrade a dog's happiness from "good" to "great" by petting it, this is your chance. The automatic name generator won me over immediately when it named one of my first dogs "Trashboat."
The dogs each have their own personalities and quirks, but whereas a normal game might revolve around discarding characters with bad traits and hiring new ones with good traits to maximize team effectiveness, here they serve as just more fun flavor, as they aren't make-or-break in any given race.
tl;dr: Dog Petting Simulator 2016, 11/10 would pet again

An intense fun active Tower Defense game with action RPG elements. I'm a tower defense addict and this game is on the top for me.
The plus :
- The game doesn't hold your hand too much, yet mechanics are very clear.
- A lot of freedom how to approach the game, especially after the initial levels. You can spend skill point and trap points to suit your style of play.
- You won't finish the game fast, the game has 3 classes, the 13 levels have 4 tiers, customisable scenario modes and endless mode and there are some additional separate scenarios as well when you finish the game on tier 1. And if you still can't get enough you can make your own levels or download some from the steam workshop.
- The loot and craft system add another layer on top of everything.
- You can play the game at three speeds (50%, 100% and 200%) to save time or get through harder parts easier.
- The battle music is awesome and intense.
- Level design is really good, the levels feels very balanced.
The minus :
- Although the music is awesome there is only one track for menu and one for battle.
- There are three difficulties but you actually need to play on hard if you want 3 stars, that renders the difficulty levels and stars system kind of redundant. The game feels like it needs to be played on hard. Normal is pretty easy, especially if you are used playing ARPG's.
- 'Sidequests' are pretty mandatory because you get a lot of trap points from them which you will need, and in many cases they feel like a waste of time. This is a pretty minor complaint though, some of the sidequests are a good learning experience.
Conclusion :
This game is very well put together, both tower defense and APRG fans will find very big value for money in this game. It's the best Neocore game in my humble opinion.

I have personally never played Hand of Fate 1, so I have no particular basis for this review beyond HoF 2. However, Hand of Fate 2 has been a very fun experience for me due to the variety available, as well as the combat.
The Combat, while rudimentary in nature and being largely a Batman styled attack-counter-attack ordeal, is still dangerous enough to be entertaining, especially when larger numbers of combatants hit the field. Your efficacy in combat is influenced by the equipment you both sort into the playing deck for that particular mission, but also if you even find it through play in the first place. This leads to some serious moments of concentration and deliberation as you think on what cards to enter into your deck, as it may be a series of easy encounters, but should your equipment be lacking you may find yourself in peril.
The Game is varied, and pretty entertaining to play, due to the RNG at play, and almost all gambits, save for the dice, are influenced by some skill or another. Certain gambits (IE the little skill minigames, such as Shuffle, the Wheel, or the Pendulum) require patience, and a careful eye, but can be influenced by certain pieces of equipment to ensure an even easier go at them. Blitzing through some of them will be met with failure, and that is something that I find to be quite gratifying, that the game rewards careful planning and perception.
Overall HoF 2, with the much needed updates courtesy of the staff, is a very entertaining game, and I look forward to perhaps seeing more content for this game, or indeed any content from the developers themselves.

I LOVE THIS GAME!
I got the first one years ago through Xbox Games with Gold and loved it, so I bought this 10 minutes after it was released, and a few hours in I can confidently say that this game is an improvement in every way.
I'll start with the styling: The music, art style, and general feel of the game are incredible. The dealer's voice is creepy, and his slow drawl portrays him as this awesome foreboding figure. The shuffling of the cards, blowing of the wind, and ambient sounds of your environment are immersive and wonderful. I absolutely love everything about how the game looks, especially when your in the top world (i.e. not in combat). The cards have real weight to them and I absolutely love the addition of the map with several different challenge locations - each with their own unique playstyles.
I am so impressed by the ways in which Defiant amplified the board game aspect of Hand of Fate - from varied challenge types (I won't spoil any because I haven'y seen them all yet and uncovering a new minigame is such a pleasant surprise), to new styles of maps through which you must traverse (again, I don't want to say too much but there's a challenge pretty early on that fundamentally rearranges how you move through the over world and it's just so awesome), the board game is engrossing and fantastic.
Defiant already established themselves as master stroytellers in the first Hand of Fate (in my opinion), and that only continues in this new iteration. Awesome tales about the people you meet and the environments you spend time in are plentiful.
The combat has been reworked too, and is super fun and there are so many options that you're playstyle won't get stale. It's similar combat to the Arkham games, but I've found it to be a bit slower paced, which has caused me to approach fights with a more methodical approach rather than button mashing.
Hand of Fate 1 was an awesome roguelite card-based dungeon crawler (or something along those lines, I can't keep up with all the genres these days). Hand of Fate 2 takes that formula and breathes life into it - I'm only a few challenges in, but already I've seen side challenges and alternative navigation methods that weren't in the first game and just add such a pleasant degree of complexity to an amazing style of gameplay.
THANK YOU DEFIANT DEVELOPMENT FOR RELEASING ANOTHER AWESOME GAME!

I started out really liking this game, and sunk quite a few hours into it.  But, sadly, it's not holding me.  I think a negative review is a bit harsh, I'd rather give neutral - with the emphasis being that it's a great concept, and is exciting to start with as you see the potential - but after a while you realise the things that usually draw you to a TD/RPG style game are done very plainly.
Pain points:
- Towers can only be built on specific locations in each map - and of those set locations, only certain types of towers can be built there.  This is part of the strategic element - but it feels very constrictive.  The best tower defense games allow creativity, being able to mix/match towers and put them anywhere along the route - this game doesn't allow for that.   Want to place an ice trap that makes creeps susceptible to ice damage, and put a frost tower nearby to exploit that vulnerability?  Well, only if the level designer lets you by having put the "right" tiles for you to build those types of traps/tower in that area.  Given that the traps/towers inherently complement each other, restricting the use of these combos is really annoying.
- No mazing, no ability to divert waves whatsoever.  This is part of the game design and intentional, but something I don't really like, as you don't get to maximize damage tactically by funneling creeps through your carefully built deathtrap.  Creeps will stick to their set paths always, so the only strategy open to you is to build different traps on each route, and again only where the level designer allows you to do so.
- Item drops - this game is mimicking a Diablo-esque / Van Helsing style, yet there are no item drops from creeps.  Only at the end of each level a chest drops, with a handful of (generally rubbish) items.  The items in the game are largely indistinguishable in their variety; there is no excitement in item drops, everything is some slight variation in resistance or damage type to the last 50 drops that you sold at the shop or melted for crafting materials.  The shop sells equally dull items; nothing ever appears 'awesome' or 'too expensive but I'd love to save up and get that'.  There is no "wow" factor in any item I've seen.  Money is not an issue, before long you have more than you'll ever need or use, yet there's rarely anything good or different to buy.
There are other small annoyances, but these are the main ones.  Again I emphasize I did get quite some enjoyment out of it, it's not a bad game, but just disappointing that the core elements of creative TD and RPG the game really skimps on.  If they improve the loot drops and flexibility in tower setup, it would be heaps better.

I really liked Hand of Fate (The previous game). It's a fun single-player card game that was challenging and had lots of cards to collect. The expansion was also fun as it introduced classes which made the endless mode even more fun. However, I always felt that the first game lacked polish and felt a bit clunky.
I've been waiting on the sequel (this game) for well over a year and boy did they deliver. While this obviously uses the same formula from the first game, it almost feels like something completely new. Hand of Fate 2 has a much more compelling story and each "level" feels different and unique from the last as well as different from the first game. There are also new mini-games which are fun to learn and break up the game-play...it's not just the same "shell-game" from the previous game.
My favorite aspect of Hand of Fate 2 is the difficulty. It feels challenging enough to complete a quest or level to earn a silver coin, but the levels also offer a gold coin with better rewards. In order to earn the gold coins you have to complete a secondary objective that is more difficult and not always obvious.
I highly recommend this game and feel that $30 is a great price.

There's a certain childhood wonder and curiosity that at some point we all loose, as we gain knowledge of the world and realize that our magical fantasies we once imagined possible were just that; figments of our imaginations that will never actually come into existence. Nevertheless through books, movies, games and other art forms we can still visit the enchanting worlds of our dreams, carrying ourselves away for a few hours to a place that can only be described as extraordinary.
is a lovely, imaginative journey that captures that childish awe and spirit of discovery exceptionally well; placing it under an adventure game guise and a gorgeous presentation which carries you on your way sidestepping the many pitfalls games of the genre often fall into. With very little in the way of story Lily is a game that is largely about spectacle over plot, but personally I didn't think it needed anything more than what was here. The simple opening of your brother being taken away by a magic scarf sets off the adventure, and I was more than happy to continue on it without anymore development up until the very end.
This is the point that I was disappointed with where the developer took the game. Instead of ending with the heartfelt reunion I think many will expect from the start, you are left with something that feels entirely misplaced among the rest of the game which makes no sense and left me feeling a bit empty inside, almost as if the developers themselves had no clue what it was intended to mean. I'm perfectly fine with having to decipher an ending for myself, but when it comes so out of left field as it does here, I have to wonder if it was intended for any reason than to confuse the player.
While I disliked the conclusion, the joy I had traversing the rest of the game certainly made up for it. Lily is about as simple an expression of the point and click adventure game formula, but it works wonderfully in this instance. Instead of collecting items, talking to characters, or solving obtuse puzzles, in Lily you simply progress and explore the world. Puzzles come in the form of interacting with objects, pulling levers, and using Lily's goggles to see the world in a new light, all of which formed logical and satisfying solutions which were enjoyable to solve but didn't exasperate me by being too challenging. While I wouldn't call it easy per say, this isn't a game that should give many people trouble, which I feel is admirable in a genre that is so full of alienating game design. If you are looking to flex your cortex intellect this may not be the best way to do so, but as a mellow and relaxing experience Lily succeeds beyond doubt.
Easily Lily's biggest asset is it's artwork. Each vibrant scene is full of lush colors and beautiful detail, mixing pseudo-3D character models with hand-drawn 2D backgrounds. Seeing the environments come to life is a sight to behold, and the top notch animation flows with impeccable grace and fluidity. If the interaction was removed this could easily pass as an animated movie, something I don't say likely and intend as a great compliment taking into account the great strides animation has made in the last few years.
My only "complaint" if I have one, is that everything moves at a very slow pace. Doing anything traps you in an animation that you then must watch to completion before being able to interact with anything again. This isn't a huge deal for the most part, but when you are at times required to repeat the same task several times in a row it can become a bit frustrating that there is no way to speed up or skip through an animation. I got used to it after playing for a bit, but it wouldn't have hurt if the world moved just a little bit faster.
Clocking in at about 2 hours,
is a decidedly brief experience but one worth having. I loved every second of being in Lily's world, from the amazing art to the delightful puzzles, right up to the regrettably unsatisfying end. While its simple nature may put off some, it was a pleasantly mellow surprise for me and one I would wholeheartedly recommend for anyone looking for a pleasant game to relax with.

How I Played
Stacking is a clever, colorful, family oriented little game, that is easy to understand and quite simple to work through.  I mean, hell, it comes with it's own cheats.. err, hints, even.
In fact, it seems that if one were to do only the main objectives, one could easily complete this game in about 90 minutes. But then, one would be stupid, because Stacking is, actually, not a game, at all.. it's a toy.. to be played with.  More precisely, it's a toy box full of animated old wooden dolls.  Robust characters, diverse in size and personalities (though, not ethnicity, as everyone seems to be white.)
But, wait a minute.. they're not just dolls, but vehicles, too! They're easy to jump in and outa, and speed around in, and take screenshots from.  And, as if all that isn't fun enough, each doll type possesses a talent or skill (from gross bodily functions to amusing cartoon antics) to be mixed and matched, and otherwise, experimented with, and giggled at.
Frankly, the only reason I ever moved on to the next level was to get more dolls, and different places to ride em around in.

How You'll Probably Play
In Stacking, you'll play Charlie, the youngest member in a family of old-world themed nesting dolls. They're poor (of course), but happy (of course), until one day when Charlie's dad goes out for a pack of smokes, or something, and doesn't come back. Eventually, and mysteriously, all of Charlie's older siblings disappear, leaving young Charlie the task of rescuing them, all.
"Don't worry, I'll bring them home." He tells his mother, then bravely bobs off in search of family.. and adventure.
No Matter How You Play
I think there's 5 levels, each with a main challenge, as well as some optional side trips. In general, the challenges are simple, and puzzle-ish (unless you're crazy enough to set it on hard), which allows for a stress free, laid back gaming experience.
Well, that is, until Charlie's last challenge..
You'll probably need to sit up a bit, to get through that one.
Notes:
I got my copy as part of a bundle, so paid about 1/4th Steam's retail price of $9.99.
This copy of Stacking also included The Lost Hobo King DLC,  which I have not, yet, played.

You can't review this game without comparing it to Thief 2 if you've ever played it, so this is my fair warning that this review will be full of that.  Let's get started!
The Good:
-Thief 2 quality gameplay in high quality graphics.  I played using the John P Reily texture pack and the sneaky thief patch thingy.  Everything looked lovely (possibly excluding cutscenes).
-Shalebridge Cradle is noteworthy.  If you haven't played the game and intend to, don't google that.  But it deserves mentioning.
-Climbing claws helped to make things feel organic.
-World building.  There was a time I broke in the same house twice and the owner of the house wrote in his diary about me breaking in previously.  The game is just showing off by that point.
-Story was grand.  Voice acting was great as it was in the previous game.
-The final chapter.  Many games that focus less on action have a terrible time trying to make the end feel climatic.  I remember the first Assassin's Creed had this problem.  This game, however, pulled it off wonderfully.  I won't spoil anything but the developers very successfully made an ending that felt epic without throwing out the great gameplay that the rest of the game was based on.
The less good:
-Thief 2 had a much more interesting system for when you can knock people out in one hit.  Dumbing it down to simply "aware or unaware" only hurt the game.  It ended in situations where I was smacking a skinny noble woman in the face and all she did was make fun of me.
-Faction system seemed a lil unnecessary.  It was easy to stay in good standing with both factions, but all that did was make it seem even more pointless.  There's no reason why you wouldn't want to be in good standing with one or the other.  So why bother?
-Thief is a really hard word to spell and I keep messing it up, so the game is going to lose points for that.
-The levels are smaller than Thief 2 and they're broken up with loading screens.  Apparently there's a mod to address this annoyance, but I didn't play with it.  The loading screens were especially obnoxious when there was apparently a guard chasing you so the next time you come back he immediately attacks you.
I don't know where to put this:
-There was a time where an NPC attacked me and apparently hit another NPC.  I think what happened is at some point this happened again.  And then guards got involved.  Long story short, every time I walked into the district this all occurred in from then on, there were constantly NPCs murdering each other and there were bodies everywhere.  It was amazing.
So to sum it up:  Is Thief 3 a good game?  Yes.  Is it better than Thief 2?  No.  Should you buy it if you enjoy this sorta thing?  Yes.

There is a limited variation of quests and although the devs try to rotate them (including some of the lore text), it just becomes a grind.

for short review, yes Deadly Shadows is a good game despite its flaws. One thing that i think Ion Storm certainly does get in Deadly Shadows is that they experiment it further without losing many of Thief's characteristics. new engine makes for great graphic and great atmosphere, great soundtrack and gameplay, good story, good lockpicking segments, changable POV from 1st person to 3rd person seamlessly is quite useful and fresh, it makes the players can easily see the environment more clearly and our Master Thief as more of his own character. but the annoying double system .exe which makes Steam Overlay doesn't work (just like in Deus Ex Invicible Wars), cramped level design & environment, unchangable FOV, small maps that are divided into many parts makes Deadly Shadows a decent enough Thief game but not an excellent one.
sure, level design in Shalebridge Cradle is an awesome one. for a few minutes into Shalebridge Cradle, there are no enemies but the atmosphere really strikes me and it makes me anxious and scared and prepared for anything that comes up. unfortunately, Shalebridge Cradle great level design is the only great level design in Deadly Shadows. other level designs are just OK, even the anticlimatic battle with The Hag isn't well designed. Deadly Shadows really forces you to stealth and while it's probably a good thing for a thief, it doesn't really adds up because once you're spotted by enemies you can only run and hide. if you try to fight them head-on,you'll be dead because you only have a dagger and you can't defend which makes combat quite stressful.
on a good side, i like its stylized cinematic cut-scenes which gives an impression of a book. it's like i'm reading a book about Garrett and really dive into his story. its lore and background stories such as Kurshok, Pagan, Hammerites and civilian's some backstory through letters are great to further expand the world of Thief. i often found myself really immersed with these background stories even though they don't really add anything to main storyline but it successfully makes me into the world and its environment. one thing that i often had a very good time with Deadly Shadows is when i, for example: open/close door, steal loots etc and NPCs react to what i do. they don't really do anything extraordinary, except telling guards, but it delivers a believable NPCs that some video games ignore.
Thief Deadly Shadows is good game, it's probably not the best Thief game and it's good over its flaws which you can easily fix them up with a few patches. i, myself, use Thief Sneaker Upgrade and Texture Pack and it fixes almost everything annoying in Deadly Shadows.

Defense Zone 3 is a standard tower defense game.  Enemies try to cross the map (usually with numerous paths available to them), and you try to stop them by building and upgrading defensive towers, and by using a handful of special attacks (like mines and aerial strikes).  You can only place towers in special build areas, and these build areas don't include the paths enemies take, so you can't adjust their routes in any way.  Towers include things like machine guns, rocket launchers, flamethrowers, and howitzers.  Enemies include ground forces (soldiers, tanks, and mechs), air forces (a variety of planes), and even ships (but only on a few of the maps).
The main strategy for the enemy is to throw a horde of enemies at you in 30 or more waves.  The sheer number of enemies involved mean that the missions tend to take well over an hour to complete, even if you use one of the fast forward options to speed up the action.  Luckily, the game saves your progress at the start of every wave, so if a wave goes poorly, you can repeat it without losing anything.
I found the game to be reasonably tough even on the "normal" setting.  But there are also "hard" and "nightmare" settings if you want something more difficult.  Sort of annoyingly, you don't get credit for completing the easier settings when winning one of the tougher settings, so you have to play each of the 15 available missions four times to earn all of the achievements.
This was my first Defense Zone game, and I was sort of iffy about it.  There isn't anything really creative about the game.  It's just a horde of enemies in each mission, and once you figure out how to deal with them, the same strategies work all the time.  If Steam had a "sideways thumb" option, I'd give it that, but since that's not available, and since the game is fully functional and priced favorably, I'm giving it a recommendation.

Spoiler-Free Review
Thief: Deadly Shadows was a game that I went into with high standards but low expectations. I loved the first two Thief games. The third I expected to be consolized, watered-down experience that wouldn't do the series justice.
I'm happy to say that I was pleasantly surprised, and as the game went on, familiarly exhilarated. Everything I loved about Thief was intact. The mechanics are smooth, the AI is just as familiar. The oppressive, dark atmosphere still hangs over all locales. The graphics liven up the settings, as well as the inhabitants of the City. The stylized cut-scenes are again present, the story fits the series lore, and even many sound effects are taken from the other Thief games.
What I was most impressed with, however, was how the game still controlled like the first two games. The Dark Engine used for the first two games is a beautiful, wonky, archaic, one-of-a-kind engine. Thief 1 and 2, and System Shock 2 as well, have a distinct control and floatiness to them. I thought the simple fact that Thief: Deadly Shadows wouldn't be using the Dark Engine would massively take away from what made playing Thief feel like playing Thief. But to my surprise, Thief: Deadly Shadows runs on the only engine that rivals the Dark Engine's wonkiness: Unreal Engine 2.
Unreal 2 is the only engine in 2004 that would've been capable of preserving the feel of Thief. Those Havok physics that don't quite make sense, leaving everything a tad slow and floaty, end up perfectly, if even unintentionally, preserving Thief's feel perfectly. I loved it.
There are a few new features in Thief: Deadly Shadows. I don't want to spoil anything, but there are items old and new. The world sits more like a hub, with places to sell stolen loot and buy items and arrows between missions. While some may find the hub hard to get used to, I ended up likening the hub to its own mission, familiar and simple, between the more unique missions in other locations. The last big feature worth mentioning is the third-person view. It is a toggle and completely ignorable for the purists, but I found it unintrusive and useful. I preferred to play in first-person the way that I was used to, but being able to look around corners, get better views, and even just ground Garrett in the world around him I found very enjoyable. To be able to see Garrett in more than just cut-scenes helped me more connect with the character as he mumbled his comments throughout the gameplay.
Altogether, this game is a very worthy entry in the series. It upholds all that makes Thief great, and successfully makes the experience fresh. I recommend it to all Thief fans. If you've never played any Thief games, I highly, highly suggest starting the series chronologically. While I believe you'd still appreciate the game without playing the first two, Thief: Deadly Shadows is in fact the third game in the original Thief trilogy. The game treats itself that way as well. The game, in form, mechanics, and especially story, is very noticeably built atop its predecessors, and it should be appreciated that way.
Happy Playing.

Guide made during update #14.2
To give a brief summary of what this game is I'll compare certain elements to other games with similar elements thn give pros and cons.
The comparison:
Dungeon Souls is similar to Nuclear Throne in the base game mechanics of run around and kill things while getting hit as little as possible by the multiple projectiles/opponents on each floor. Your character also dies forever and you must start over when that happens. The items found in the game on each floor all give effects to your character, mostly only give you buffs but some give nerfs as well. You can find these item in chests, shops, after you kill a boss, or as rare drops from enemies. (you need a specific item for the last one) Certain chests require specific types of keys to open, every shop has 3 items but you can only buy 1, and every boss drops multiple items with a higher chance of uncommon items. These items can stack to a limited number (examples include max stacks of 1, 5, or 10) but if you pick up an item that you have the max number of it gets turned into gold, materials for crafting, or xp to level up your character. Every level your character increases you get points to spend in specific skills that increase your health, damage dealt, and resistance to damage. However the higher level the character is the more xp you'll need to get to the next level. From my experiences both the leveling and item systems (mostly the items) are similar to Risk of Rain. Also similar to Risk of Rain you can loop through the previous floors with increased difficulty, however unlike Risk of Rain you can only loop through prior levels after beating the final boss. Some things that I have not found in other games is the crafting system this game has and the permanent levels that give buffs to stats on specific characters
PROS
+ Multiple unique character classes
+ Randomly generated floors to keep the game varied from run to run
+ Multiple unique items that can be found in various ways
+ Some items can be stacked (to a limited number) to increase the effect
+ Crafting system including weapons that add effects to your attacks
+ Good amount of content for the price
+ Early Access game that already has a good amount of content
+ Has a developer team that seems to care about the game instead of money
CONS
- Some classes seem much more powerful than others to me, specifically ranged classes over melee
- Use items have rediculously low drop rates
- Can be a bit grindy to get specific crafting materials/gold required for crafting new weapons
Upcoming Features to look forward to:
+ Multiplayer
+ More characters to play as
+ More items
+ More weapons that will be able to crafted
+ More that I don't really fel like listing

Comic Book Hero: The Greatest Cape is, in many ways, my dream game. I've always wanted to make comic books and am currently studying the medium. When I decided to boot this game up after owning it but never playing it, I decided to role-play as the hero I've been wanting to write for some time day, "The Silver Sword". Sort of like Blue Beatle mixed with Power Rangers. I created my hero, wrote his biography, designed his personality, upgraded his stats to what he would be like in character and...nothing. I spent no less then 30 minutes looking for something to do. I tried looking for crime to fight, civilians to save, heroics to do and nothing would appear. I looked for heroes to maybe get some advice from or team up with, or at least become friends with and nothing. I moved around cities and finally I found a villain to fight...and he decked on the ground within a few turns. I went back to my home town, healed myself and started to train, maybe I was just really low leveled and needed to increase by abilities, right?
Training in this game is miserably slow. Training seemed to net me anywhere from 2-11 "Hero Points", which are basically the in-game experience points, but they have other uses too. For context, even cheap powers cost around 1,000 Hero Points, with more expensive ones being anywhere from 10,000 to 50,000, if not more. Needless to say, this was a slow venture. Oddly enough, I discovered doing civil services yielded more Hero Points, but it was still low payloads, anywhere from 2 to 40 in my experiences. I was fine with this at first, because doing charity work was within Silver Sword's (who lets just by his real name, Noah, for now) personality, but it was still so slow. Without me realizing it, my "Sanity" began to slip the more charity work I did. I desperately tried to find friends to hang out with, or villains to fight, but nothing worked. Noah was getting miserable and unhappy and I hadn't had a clue what to do. After my desperate attempt to find a friend, Noah was to depressed to continue his superhero career and quietly retired to no fan fair. Needless to say, I was confused and annoyed, but I enjoyed what little role-playing I had to do.
The following day, I read some threads on the game and discovered I had to put points in the "Cunning" stat to actually do stuff in the game. Already, I'm annoyed. Let's put it like this, Noah was more of a Gryffindor, not a Slytherin and so being cunning isn't his personality, meaning I had to compromise my role-playing experience for the sake of actually being able to play the game. Regardless, I sucked up my pride and changed Noah's personality a bit to be more "functional" (I wonder if this is how actual comic creators feel?). This new game went much better than the last. I managed to get a superhero on my side and we stopped a few robberies. I managed to nab a few powers that actually dealt good damage and could hold my own against street level crooks by my lonesome. It was going pretty well, until me and my partner came across a trap. Now, I thought I put a good amount of points into my "Reasoning" stat (which sounds more diplomatic then problem solving, but whatever) and thought I could solve some basic puzzle...
...Wrong. I failed it each roll. When the puzzle was over and the villain got away, I lost all of my Hero Points. All of my hard earned Hero Points. I immediately started to train and do civil service, but it was so slow. I wanted to unlock Noah's actual powers, like time-travel, spacefight and teleportation, but those cost well in the tens-of-thousands of points, no way I was going to get anywhere close to them even if I massed those options for an hour straight. Eventually I came across a street level villain named "Miss Sin", and after barely defeating up, I only got a measly 40 Hero Points. My partner was nowhere to be seen and no other heroes wanted to give me the light of day. An hour of trying to befriend any of the superheroes in my town with nothing to show for it. It was at that moment that I simply gave up the will to play. I could forgive the slow pacing, steep learning curve, weird combat system and butt ugly visuals, hell I could even forgive compromising my role-playing a bit, but all of those complains meshed into one game with a terrible GUI and garish colorscheme is just to much for me. It's a shame too, I really, really wanted to like this game.
All in all, amazing concept, awful execution. I can see people getting into it and I almost did, but it falls short in to many regards for me to keep up with it.

This game is a twinstick-roguelike that is truly a gem.
Think Isaac and Nuclear Throne had a gorgeous baby.
Every item in this game will make you feel powerful and satisfied. There are very few times I did not feel significantly more powerful when I got an item.
That's the beauty of this game.
The items.
Most are things boosting your stats or adding little extra effects but when you get one it's a feeling of satisfaction that few other games can make me feel.
The RNG can make something beautiful.
I was so strong one time that the game actually crashed when I died.
Don't let that fool you though.
The difficulty options can suit everyone.
If you're a casual gamer and just looking to have a good time, easy mode is for you.
If you're the type of person who enjoys an extreme challenge Nightmare difficulty is for you.
If you enjoy something in the middle Normal or Hard is for you.
Every character is fun to play as and they are fairly hard to unlock.
This game is much more replayable, polished, fun, and overall better than many more finished projects these days.
The only bug I've encountered was not unlocking a character when I beat the boss needed to unlock them.
There's a little bit of lore if you look enough, and while it's nothing special, it's interesting nonetheless.
The soundtrack is nothing special either but there are a few good tracks.
This game is overall a pleasure to play and I can recommend it to ANYONE.

I was about to name this game the greatest tower defense game of all time, until I hit the Tier 3 version of the fourth level, Bottomless Pit. That means I've played through all the main maps twice and was on my third run through when I hit this shame of a level. This game was an enjoyable and often challenging experience. Losing was irritating but there was something I could tweak just a little in my tower layout or even my character's skills to make it all work out.
Then came the aforementioned level. In it, you start with virtually no building resources, and they put large enemies with tons of HP close to small enemies. Any time you hit the big enemies, they put a shield on the small enemies. The best part? The SHIELD STACKS. When you have damage resistant small lizard enemies you have something like 80% damage reduction and already take a while to kill, having multiple shields on top of these enemies makes them virtually impossible to kill before they get to your core and you lose lives. This is on the first of four waves.
I've watched a Youtube video and read a lengthy Steam forum debate about this level. It appears that you cannot beat it with the Sorceress unless you use a specific skill and trap (Essence Trap and some essence-boosting time-based spell you cast on a single gun tower). This goes against the principles of the game before this level, which is the 60-something hours I put into it before then, completing every main level on the highest difficulty and all the side quests up to this point, so I have a pretty good understanding of what this game was all about until this level ruined the game for me. I even grinded myself up from level 39 to level 44 by playing endless for several hours then tried using the setup the Youtube video used by wasting a lot of my hard-earned gold to respec, but did even worse than before. The Youtube video doesn't show the player's level, though he claims to be level 50 or so in the description. I doubt his level was that low, as he never actually showed his character screen in the video and did tons of damage without traps most of the time.
Also, this is not something the developer is likely going to patch because one of their representatives dismissively replied to someone's forum post 3.5 months before I'm posting this review, stating their tester had played through all the levels on all the tiers and difficulties with all the classes. So obviously, because -someone- can beat it, there's nothing wrong with it. There are people who can do a lot of things you cannot and never will be able to. The difficulty spiked up astronomically, people pointed it out, and because some folks are able to beat it as a Sorceress, it's allegedly fine as is. This level is not fun and it has blocked my progress. There is no legitimate reason for me to be giving it all I've got for several hours, brainstorming about the level, using an overpowered character, trying to mimic someone on Youtube doing it, and still failing on an epic scale despite having aced every main level before it.
I have gone from loving this game to obsessively angered at the thought of it. I suspect preventing the stacking of shields on the armored enemies would turn this level into a challenge rather than a brutal beating of the player, but with the developer's disinterest in making the game fun and well-balanced on this level, I am left disgusted with their attitude.  All the TLC that went into the many levels before it ceases to exist on this level. Of course, why should the developer care? Players who got this far will say they had "enough fun" earlier in the game and give it a positive review, while those who only played it a little and reviewed it, will be giving a false impression of the game based on their lack of knowledge of this travesty of a level. They have their money and they've indicated the level is fine since their tester beat it. Nothing else matters to them but profits and positive reviews which perpetuate further profits.
The developer could insult my intelligence or (lack of) skills in primitive or eloquent fashion, or offer "advice" as they did on the forum which I used and which did not help at all, or they could even go the good PR route and apologize for me not enjoying the level, but none of these are a solution to rectifying the legitimate problems with the level itself. This was almost a great game, but this level has made me wish I never played it at all.
UPDATE: I played the entire game through as the sorceress again this week, because I liked the first part two playthroughs and the first three levels of the third playthrough, hoping that perhaps I misjudged this game, because I had such fond memories of the game's first half (and some change). This time, I got better magic find so I had superior gear dropping, ended up with a level 38 weapon with 12% armor penetration and a 10% armor penetration amulet, to help with the enemies that make the aforementioned level a living hell.
Not only that, but I used a variety of strategies to try and snipe the armored enemies without hitting the shield-stacking jerks and making the level unwinnable at a low level, while using towers that claimed to boost the damage of all allies in range by 30%...with two of them side by side. I thought "AHA! I was just being an idiot before, and didn't realize I should be standing here to shoot, and that will take care of my damage problem. The damage stacks when using similar towers that boost tower damage, so it should double up my damage boost! I tried it, and as far as I can tell, my damage was not boosted
by these towers. When that didn't work, I tried the twirling towers the pre-mission briefing recommends. The results? It didn't help.
I have given this level a genuine benefit of the doubt, and am practically begging the game to not go down the crapper on mission 4 of the third playthrough, but it does. The only way to beat the level is to use a very specific setup that betrays the freedom of variety the rest of the game before it offers, OR to level up to max or close to max, just steamrolling everything in your path with superior firepower and no real strategy, which ruins the balance of the rest of the third playthrough and the fourth.
I desperately want to love this game, and I do...until this level, at which point I absolutely detest it. I am mentally throwing my hands up in the air in confusion at why the developer would let such a terribly designed level remain as such in a game that offered such strategic freedom and amazing fun prior to that moment. The easy answer seems like "money," but then, they are also making Warhammer 40,000: Inquisitor - Martyr, and after seeing how the last chunk of this game and that latter portions of the Van Helsing series turned out, I'm losing faith in Martyr being good...

Played the first game and loved it, so I had to try the second one. I'm only a few hours in but loving it just as much. They added a few nice features but kept the core game in tact (mostly). The new combat system takes a little getting used to but it works perfectly fine.

- The new pendulum responsiveness can be improved

Overal very good indie game that is well worth its price

You're flying over the Pacific Ocean in what appears to be a high-class private jet. You seem distressed, no doubt business is taking its toll on you and the plane going through turbulence doesn't exactly help, luckily you are the only passenger. You decide to ease your sorrows with a martini. As you return to your seat to go through some more spreadsheets the plane starts shaking violently until suddenly, you come to realise you might not make this trip. Your fears quickly become reality.
The jet's fuselage is getting torn to shreds, the inside becomes a tornado of clutter as all sorts of objects start getting vacuumed outside. You're pressed against the back of your seat, gasping for air, as the plane loses altitude... until it crashes into the sea. As you recover from the trauma, you start swimming toward the cockpit, only to find the two pilots dead. Wasting no time, you escape the wreck and climb into a life raft. You make for the nearest bit of land as to not get dragged down with what used to be your only way back to civilisation. You are stranded. Deep.
With this introduction, I hope the scenery is set for Stranded Deep, a survival game in Early Access now available on Steam. The scenery is important here, because it is all the story we get at this point in time. You know you're in trouble and have to make the best of it for as long as you can. You start with nothing more than a lighter, a pocket knife, a bottle of water and your life raft (plus paddle). To survive, you will need to stay well-fed and hydrated. Eating crabs, fish or native potatoes and drinking from a coconut or boiling seawater over a fire should keep you covered. There is also a crafting-system ingame, which lets you craft primitive tools for when your metal ones break.
Perhaps most interestingly, the island you are stranded on is tiny, not much more than a pile of sand and rock with a few palm trees here and there. This means that you will only have access to a very finite pool of ressources like wood. To find more, you must inevitably climb back into your life raft (or a wooden one you've built) and start exploring the ocean around you. The world is potentially huge, depending on how far out you're willing to go, with more and more small islands appearing on the horizon. Exploration doesn't end there, though, as the ocean floor holds more secrets for you to discover. Ship-wrecks scatter the landscape below and do have loot for you to find, like proper tools or other useful items like goggles or a ship motor to stick on your raft.
Carelessly bathing in the rough seas can be dangerous, though, as a very hungry shark might start thinking about making you part of his dietary plans. Shark AI seems very much unfinished at this point, though personally, sharks really freak me out so just their presence is enough to at the very least be very unsettling.
It's not just the sharks that need some more polish, as Early Access suggests. Surviving by doing the same few tasks over and over is all you can really do in Stranded Deep at this point and exploring will just reward you with more of the same. Building shelter has no real purpose and, sadly, there is no way of getting rescued yet, though plans are to include more end-game as development goes on. The two things that Stranded Deep has going for it are its unique setting and the stunning graphics, inviting you to forget about your dire situation and just bask in the tropical sun.
Stranded Deep is worthy of at least being followed by survival-fans. Probably not a purchase just yet.

This game is immersive and thrilling, combining the tranquility of an island escape with the terror of the deep unknown. After approximately 10 hours of play I have experienced a lot of what the game has to offer such as the overwhelming sense of isolation, the desperation that pushes you to be resourceful and frugal with your supplies, and the great atmosphere created in the presence of wildlife such as sharks.
On a more technical note, there are many bugs (which is to be expected of an alpha) which do cause minor frustration. Many have been rectified since the update (28/1/15) however mechanics such as climbing and jumping do become troublesome, especially when your character is trapped within a ship wreck. Furthermore the collisions on the fire effect should perhaps be dealt with as most objects place on a basic camp fire often gain a life of their own. Other than these minor detials, the most I can hope for is a slightly more detailed tutorial on lesser functions such as maintaining your health (without disrupting the overall tone of the game of course).
I highly recommend this game even in its early stages, keep up the good work!

I do recommend this game, though certainly not for everybody, and probably not at full price. The graphics are adorable (as can be seen in the screenshots), the gameplay functionality uses a simple point-and-click method, and it is completely free of monsters or anything else scary. This, of course, means that it truly is safe to play with the kids if you have any. In addition to this, it has a nice soundtrack and some interesting puzzles. However, it also has some downsides. For one, the game is full of slow-moving cut-scenes, every time you do something, which cannot be skipped. Also, there is absolutely no background or story provided within the game itself (really no dialog or screen text at all, in fact), and not much of a plot, all of which, depending who you are, might or might not bother you. The major downside to this is that there is also no real explanation given of what you are meant to accomplish in any given puzzle, and several are far from clear just from looking at them. Therefore, there is a lot of either randomly doing things until something happens that works to solve the puzzle, or else seeking an explanation online or in the forums of what your final goal in a puzzle is meant to be. At first glance, it appears to be an awesome action MMORPG emphasizes on fast-paced combat. However, it lacks a strong story line with uninteresting NPC's and contents and soon you'll find yourself skipping every single conversation and just wanting to hit max level ASAP.
Leveling is quite fast in this game. You'll hit level cap at 65 within a few days just by soloing. But when you do, it's also when all the fun stops, as all there is left to do is farming and more farming. And with the lack of contents and crappy drop rate, it gets extremely repetitive and boring. They've made everything about the Combat Rating in this game. It's no longer about player skills but how much you can put up with farming. The more you can farm, the higher your Combat Rating will be. Since all the end game dungeons require ridiculously high Combat Rating, you either have to spend months on farming or buy carries from other high CR players. Be ready to shell out tens of millions of gold. And without spending real cash, you're not going to have enough gold for that.
All in all, this game is just ok for killing time. It's definitely not for long-term serious play. A game where a player's skills don't matter will not last long. Take my advice. If you're going to give this game a try, do not spend any real money. You will regret it. I guarantee it.

This game is difficult to recommend because in it's current state, the game is more of a 👌 than a 👍 or 👎.
Don't get me wrong - the graphic style is great, sound isn't bad, and the polish is there.  The rogue-type aspects (supplies, RNG, etc.) of this game are what kept me wanting to come back for more, but that's just it, there wasn't much more to be had.
When I saw the previews with undead and other fantasy elements mixed into a tactical game, I was sold, thinking it could turn out like a newer version of Ogre Battle.  Except your little mercenary band can't recruit anyone other than humans, and there isn't any magic element outside of Necromancers (who you can't recruit) raising undead.  Women aren't recruitable either, so no Briane of Tarth's or Valkyrie-types.  You're just a bunch of [battle] bros with some weapons.
Which brings me to the next part - the tactics, or the limited amount thereof.  There's essentially two strategies.  70% of the battles are just turtling up from the start, while the enemy wave breaks against your spear wall, inter-parsed with axes for breaking shields.  For the other 30%, when the enemy doesn't rush to it's own death and has ranged units, you either attack at night or slowly march forward with shields up.  That's it.
There are no area attacks that penalizes shield turtling (like grenades or fireballs) and the guys who can do the two-handed melee area attacks get mowed down like grass for not having a shield.  You have a huge amount of weapons to choose from, which is nice, but you basically equip every other guy with a spear or crossbow.
The fatigue system is about as interesting as every battle devolving into a tired slog, unless your characters have that one perk that lets you restore half your fatigue.  Since that perk is available at lvl 2, you pretty much give it to everyone.
Because of the RNG rogue-like aspects, there are a couple other perks that are impossible to survive long without, so the entire perk tree is pretty unbalanced and uninteresting.
The random encounters are few but redeeming.  The quests (contracts) are either fetch/kill the things at some location or escort missions.  Noble contracts are a little more interesting but are still "kill the things in this area".
Overall it's kind of a grind to get to late game, since you pretty much repeat the same two strategies each battle.  The character traits are interesting, and the wound affects & fatigue mechanics add
depth to the game, but the repetitive nature of the quests/battles just is not that fun.  I would have loved to be able to rescue and recruit a wyvern that spews fire, but maybe my expectations are too high.
I don't recommend this game for the price it's at, so wait for it to go on sale.

From the developers that brought you the amazing AdVenture Capitalist and the less-amazing AdVenture Communist comes  Guild Quest, the totally-in-beta, we-know-what-we're-doing-now-guys-we-promise idler based on RPG tropes. The idea sounds great, and it was.
Was.
The grind is always a big part of RPGs and idlers, but HyperHippo's idea of adding more playtime is to simply extend the grind instead of actually adding new content. The last two or three have been particularly egregious; this last one upped the difficulty astronomically and wiped almost all progress. While levels have been a joke for quite some time now (whatever the suggested level was for islands, you could expect to need at least twice as many levels to actually clear it), now being several times higher than the recommended level is necessary just to clear the first mission on level one. Let me repeat that. You must be severely overleveled just to beat the first mission on its easiest possible setting. The power creep has just gotten ridiculous.
That said, I do have some faith remaining. AdVenture Communist looked equally doomed and mismanaged, and yet, it was rebalanced into a pretty solid game, if only one I spend five minutes a day on. However, that faith is fading with each disastrous update, and goodwill is wearing thin. I'm not sure this will ever fully recover.

This review is spoiler free as it gets. And I was playing this game only on PC.
Dog Sled Saga is multiplatform singleplayer simulator involving racing and team management. Suitable for every age. Recommended only for those who can read English as some game mechanics and story are understandable only by reading.
Once you've set up your team the general idea is to win as many races as possible and improve your team along the way either by improving your dogs; using money on several improvements or signing better sponsor as time goes by. Everything leads to more complicated races in higher tier leagues. If we consider day count as a goal of the game, to be the best as soon as possible, then these choices very much matter, but if you just want to have some casual fun, your team will improve over time and the order of things is not an issue.
Controller of choice is my beloved PC Mouse and on few occassions even Keyboard. Everything else I found to be a hindrance to the gameplay.
UI can become a bit confusing at times due to design being done for smart phone devices. I have encountered one bug in main menu few times but nothing game breaking.
Game is very easy to run on pretty much any computer, the choice was once again well crafted pixel graphics and very basic sounds. Even with very little resolution on character models, I found them adorable and very well crafted though they don't make for the best Steam page background.
Sounds can be helpful in this game as they give you clues on what happenings during the race once you learn to recognize them. Some sounds were pretty hilarious especially when something fails, it bounces back with humor.
I preffered playing with loud sounds and music off.
I have to say that first few races proved to be the toughest, the game does explaining it's mechanics very well but over time the game gets much easier than it was in the beginning and increasing in difficulty once again when you start reaching the end of the game.
There has to be only few games of it's kind. This game did an honest job with art style making it stand out among other games using pixel graphics. There's also an option to field a few unusual dog races for dog sledding.
Story is very subtle addition to the game and doesn't affect the way you play the game.
Very enjoyable casual game that you can turn on anytime do a few rounds and then return to it later. Altough the general loop may seem a bit repetitive, I felt this game to be rewarding and cheerful. Ultimately I was not able to put in as high amount of hours as I think I could and I'd blame the repetitivness and rich game library but on other scores the game is very solid with future improvement being teased.
+ Graphics
+ Simple mechanics
+ Cute and cheerful
+ Low HW requirements
+ Price
- Repetitive
- UI
In it's price category I'd say this game can dominate many comers and if you feel like Dog Sledding may be your thing, give this one a try or gift it to a friend. Make your musher dream come true.
I, based on my experience, recommend this game.

Please Don’t Touch anything is a minimalist puzzle game where you are left alone in a room by your buddy and instructed not to touch a button. Naturally, you do, unlocking more and more panels and secrets, with possibly dire consequences for the city on the view screen.
This was a cute idea for a game and they did a surprisingly large amount of stuff with it; there's a lot of puzzles in this game, and some of them are fairly nifty.
Unfortunately, other puzzles are very obscure, and if you miss a few hints, you're likely to be very frustrated, as some of the endings are pretty well hidden and it is not at all obvious what you are supposed to do. In particular, it is easy to miss some of the codes for the ten digit panel and never realize it, because, hey, you've already done that, right? Some of the panels are used time and again, while others only matter for a very small number of things.
In the end, I got it for under a dollar, making it hard to complain too loudly. That being said, I have to admit I got kind of bored after messing around with it for about a half hour or so, beyond which point finding the rest of the endings felt like a tedious process of elimination. In the end, I was forced to go to an endings guide because I just couldn't figure out a few things, and I don’t think I ever would have, either.
All in all, I think that if you like obscure puzzle games - that is to say, a puzzle game which obscures its puzzles heavily - i think this might be the game for you, as this is all about obscure puzzles in a very limited (one screen) environment.
On the other hand, if examining every single freaking detail (and trying to figure out which ones matter and which don't) doesn't appeal to you, you might find this frustrating, and not in a good way. There's nothing really here beyond the puzzles - the gameplay is very simplistic and there's no deeper mesage to any of it. It is just "solve these puzzles and get a little silly animation".

Want to unlock classes by going dungeon-smashing?
Want to only have to manage 3 skills, but stack equipment to make everything explode?
Want a quick dungeon-run that still can pack a challenge depending on how you like to play?
Well that's barely scratching the surface, but this game is a hell of a lot of fun.
Feeling like a cross between Binding of Isaac and Rogue Legacy, hack, slash, cast, summon, shoot and wrench your way through dungeons, fighting some bullet-hell-ish bosses and a heap of different monster types.
The passive improvement system allows you to spend gold between runs to upgrade your character(s) - allowing you to make it further into the dungeon's depths each time.
Dungeon runs last until you die, which so far has been between a few minutes with a squishier class for me, to a couple of hours with some lucky def/damage drops. Shops carry 3 items of which you can buy one, but there are items you can find which reduce price, increase item droprates, or allow you to buy more than one thing at a time. Also, items have a stack count, so you can carry multiples of some items, magnifying their abilities. If you pick up a duplicate of something that's at the max, the item will randomly turn into xp, gold, or crafting materials, which are kept between runs.
After death you restart with no items (duh, rogue-lite) your ability to compile items into a synergy that works for your class is pretty impressive. I'm so far 7 hours in, and although it's feeling slightly grindy trying to beat certain bosses, randomisation of items and choosing other classes and upgrade combinations are keeping me coming back.
Graphics are pixel-perfection, with nice lighting effects, interesting monsters, and mostly orb-based spell effects, or fire.
Controls are pretty tight, unless you combine stupid amounts of speed items, at which point looting becomes a bit hit-and-miss. I've discovered a *little* story so far, but half the fun is finding that out.
10/10 so far, will update if the fun stops.

Alright, simply put.. this game's hugest flaw is the lack of clarity. For example, you, as a new player, are expected to understand that a red target mark on the ground means.. "Beware, huge boulder is about to roll out and one-shot you effortlessly." This is ESPECIALLY annoying when there are literally 30 of them in a SINGLE small map around each and every single corner. Dying to these is just so damn frustrating and is hard to avoid sometimes. Many of the projectiles are really, really, REALLY hard to see, making dying to them also really annoying. Some enemies teleport around and such and tracking them is pretty difficult. You're meant to go around and activate these little areas that spawn a huge hoard of enemies in a circle, yet to DO SO means.. "stand in the center and try not to get insta-bursted by enemies", which happens a lot and is unavoidable. After unlocking the Necromancer, I realized the skeleton summon AI is really crappy. It does.. well, almost nothing useful but soak up damage because the other enemy's AI is smart and attacks them properly. Another hugely irritating thing I found is that levels seem poorly designed. For example, I spawned in an area and I IMMEDIATELY got shot by an arrow-shooting.. machine.. thing.. within 0.5 seconds of spawning (yes, it was NEXT to the spawn point IN THE SHOOTING PATH) with no hope of dodging it. If my HP was low, I would've died. Fair? That brings me to my next point, some enemies and objects that harm you are SO ridiculously hidden that you're wondering what the hell's 2-shotting you in the room. This also happens a lot. One of the more irritating things is that the menu and controls are wonky. Why am I using "WS+space" to navigate a menu? This isn't 1990. Let me just use my cursor or the arrow keys or something. Right now it's just really, really frustrating to navigate the menus. Additionally, some of the audio sounds choppy and crappy. Footsteps sound like crackling noises instead of 8-bit footsteps.
While all of these are big negatives, the game is still fantastic. Irritating and really, really frustrating, but the core concept and design and ESPECIALLY the amazing characters and their lovely design and interactive unique gameplay are enough to make the game worth it. All of those other negatives NEED to be fixed, desperately, but once they are, this will be one of the best Rogue-like games ever produced bar-none. It has so much going for it. Just a long way to go. Apparently the devs are really great at updating this game, which is great to know, so it looks like it has a bright future.

So far I have tried four different tower defense games: Sanctum 2, Orcs Must Die 2, Defense Grid: The Awakening, and Deathtrap.
Deathtrap is most similar to Orcs Must Die in terms of gameplay. Aesthetically it is darker, with a grimmer, far less comedic tone. Being set in the Van Helsing (game, not movie) universe, if you played either of Neocore's excellent Van Helsing Arpg's, the monsters will be familiar to you. There are three character types you can play, representing the classic three Arpg archetypes, Melee, archery, and magic.
The game basically plays as a perfect arpg/tower defense hybrid. Characters have skills and there is loot, crafting, and enhancing runes that give your character different bonuses like damage boosts or reduced traps costs, In addition to defending the gates, there are sometimes sidequests during areas that require you to balance going off-map (in tower defense terms) to hunt for an extra objective while also maintaining and upgrading your defenses.
I have only played for 4.1 hours so far, but I find this to be a lot of fun. Definitely my favorite tower defnese game so far, though my experience with the genre is limited.

Here we are, a sequel to hand of fate and herein lies the rub. I'm not going to review the entire game, but I am going to pickup on what seems to be the commonly stated problem of the game, the combat.
So why all the negative reviews over the combat? Simple, it's a change from the first one and it's not a carbon copy of the batman arkham games. Enemies cannot be stun locked into submission anymore and you can't fly half way across the arena to hit someone. For people coming to this game from the original, it is going to be a jarring experience and I daresay that has led to the acidic response of some people.
But I honestly like it. Combat is now more methodical and rewards knowing your opponents and been able to second guess their attacks. Also there are more responses to attacks now, rather than 'attack' 'dodge' and 'stun/guard break'. The game rewards swapping weapons out and tailoring your loadout to your opponent.
If you liked the first hand of fate and can deal with a change to the combat mechanics, then this is a game you will enjoy.
