I didn't actually care about the Thief series when I got this, nor did i really want to get the game. It was recommended to me, and for whatever reason I got it. The fact that I waited two or three weeks to even touch the game, after buying, reflects how I felt about it.
(P.S, pardon my spelling skills).
Interestingly, when I did finally boot it up, I emediatly got a vibe that I had never really gotten from another game- and I have played alot of games (Ive beaten DaggerFall for ex). The vibe was somewhat alienating, from the main menu's ominous  esteem, the organinc font for "Theif", and the tutorials obscure method of setting the scene- I was not sure what I was getting into. Plus the pause menu was funny.
Unfortunatley, the tutorial of the game made the whole thing feel dumbfounding, with extremely easy motives and wonkey elements. Because of this, I put the game down for about a month, I only came back to it because I was bored and remembered that the game was somewhat intriguing.
Glad I did comeback, as this time I was a little more attune to the controls and had somewhat of a drive to play the game. The tutorial ended and I quickly noted that the main character was fun to use, and I loved his voice. personally that was the first thing I appreciated, the characters charm. But I was met with a new mission, inside a manor which was a family establishment. It was big.
I instantly got lost, the corridors, the gaurds, the lights, all of it was turning me about- But in a good way. I learned that every element, every corner, all of the maps physic, had a purpose- and I would need to comprise them into my own favor. After a hour I had completed the mission, and exhausted all my equipment in doing so. Yes an hour long, I had been spending so much time waiting and tiptoeing, or using the blackjack on all foes. In truth, i was kinda scared, because i felt so vulnerable, and i was invigerated by this feeling. (even dark souls dosn't make me feel this weak).
After that mission, I knew I was hooked, Every inch of the game so far had been thought out intently, inteligently, and fairly. Failure was my own fault, the Ai (though kinda dumb) prooved I had to think a little extra, and the evironment was appropriate to it's own game world.
I loved it, and I was ready for the next mission. Which Garret (main Character) desscribes as his house... house? okay, sure. I start up and sneak around and go through a couple rooms, steal from my land lord, nice. Outside I go, and- To the store... lol wut.
The thing was, i didn't relize it was a world hub. I assumed I was just on a unique level. When more and more I got to move about, -it finally dawned on me that i was indeed in a hub, and my love for the game was intensified. This game has a meenigful way of making zones that respect each other and allucate factional use amazingly. For example, groups will hone an area, maybe spread their presence throughout the game. Gaurds walked about, poor folk, rich folk who you could pit pocket, it was all an emersive realm and i was blown away by how much it all made sense.
To be fair, i didn't know you could pitpocket, I know- its a stealth game, your a thief, but i would just bash people on the head with the blackjack and take it off the ground. Lol.
Anyway, I was greatly pleased with the game and apptly entitled it one of my favourite games. It would however, continue to earn my respect, one of the reasons why was the introduction to supernatural elements (for me it was an introduction as it is my first thief game).
I can remeber being infront of the Church, and I skipped pass a guard to check a dead end. I was caught off gaurd to hear a really raspy voice asking to "Kill" people. In the dark i couldn't really see it, but sure enough, some creature was in a jail cell. I opened it up, to which the creature was revealed to be a fish man, like an atlantic person. I laughed it off as a joke or easter egg, yet i could not shake the feeling of "beyond" intitys.
I also rember a conversation by two street goers, talking about a zombie quaritine. I took it as "Dumb old timey superstition" character types and ignored it, (which is a little unfair, being supersticious myself).
I completely learned that monsters did exist in this game world however, and was happy that it did come true, as secretly i desired it would.
To be fair, I could go on and on and on. But Really i just wanted to share my first experiences and how i almost never got to enjoy what is easly my second most favourite game of all time. I Recommend it, and im off to play the original games.

As a Veteran of most of the Genre defining stealth games (Metal Gear Series, Splinter Cell, etc), I can happily say this game captures the heart and core of what makes a stealth game enjoyable.
The game mostly consists of you (Garrett the Thief-Man) going from house to house and playing Reverse-Santa, taking everything in the house that isnt bolted down, and assaulting lawful residents into submission. Actually way more fun than it may sound.
For a game made well over a decade ago, it still looks decent and will run on just about any computer that can run Windows XP (so basically anything) and the sound isn't bad too. Audio is ok, no audio lag or grainy sounding effects.
The controls take some getting used to, and while a controller is nice to use on occasion, customizing the bindings is fairly simple. The overall control of Garrett is pretty decent, noting one special thing that sets this game apart from most First Person stealth games..... You can see your feet position by looking down!
Anyway, in a nutshell, this game's pretty fun, looks fine, sounds good and will last you a decent amount of time. Its got some mild online modding options, usually goes on sale for about $4 or so, and is a nice and charming stealth/kleptomania simulator game that has a hearty whiff of the PS2/Xbox/Gamecube glory days.

Pros and Cons of Starbound:
Pros: Lots of exploring, perfect for the sandbox/survival genre. Plenty of fun weapons, from cursor-guided missile launchers, to massive swords with elemental power. A ton of quests that will take you all over the galaxy, perhaps the universe. A story and soundtrack perfect for the game, and each species has a different armor set and reactions to certain items. And interesting biomes from an underworld of sorts called "heck" to an ocean planet full of treasure and ocean themed enemies.
Cons: (some of these are pretty small but noticable enough to mention) Sometimes the rendering of planets can be kinda slow. Trying to stream the game fullscreen resulted in the resolution bugging out and caused the framerate to slow considerably. Each species does not have different powers, even if it makes sense that they should. Finding certain meterials can be hard at times. And just trying to get your ship working so you can explore the universe takes a whole process that can be pretty tedious.
Now here's a list of what powers I would give to what species.
Human: Slightly increased currency aquisition, slight dps increase with melee weapons
Hylotl: Ability to breathe underwater, increased mining efficiency underwater
Avian: Increased jumping height, slight gliding effect, lessened fall damage.
Apex: Increased inteligence (allows faster crafting and amount of meterials needed to craft items is decreased)
Glitch: Using electric dps weapons adds a small regeneration effect, recruitment of robotic crew members is easier
Floran: Immunity to poison, chance to poison an enemy hit with a melee attack
Novakid: Small increase to ranged weapons dps, Glows in dark areas due to them being made of energy

'Stacking', while being a game primarily aimed at children, manages to appeal to adults as well, not unlike other Double Fine titles.
Set in a fictional world of european industrialisation, tiny Charlie Blackmore, the youngest member of a family of proud chimney sweepers, finds his family abducted by the evil Baron and sets out to not only rescue them, but put an end to child labour as well.
In doing so, he has to make use of his stacking ability, jumping into bigger persons and animals, since all creatures in this world are Matryoshka dolls. With everyone being bigger than him, one could say that Charlie is the only one not being in some way hollow. Every doll has a special ability that may help Charlie on his way.
Overlooked or ridiculed by the bigger dolls, his only help is Levi, the hobo, who offers him a hideout and chronicles his adventures.
The concept is very well executed, making for lots of fun and at times quite tricky puzzles. There's multiple ways of solving the different situations, with a generous but optional hint system suited to all ages. On top of that there are lots of optional mini quests, involving all kinds of shenanigans, encouraging one to try out all possible combinations of stacking. There's much to explore and delight in in this small world.
Much effort is put into details. Difference in height when using different dolls changes perspective, field of vision, depth of focus and perception of sound. When jumping into a dog the colours fade, and so on.
The humour ranges from fart jokes to more mature themes such as the seductive black widow or that creepy guy who stares at women.
Along with the PC version comes the only DLC, in which Charlie returns the favour done to him by the hobos; finding the lost hobo king of Camelfoot is just as enjoyable as the main game.
This one comes highly recommended, whether you want to play it alone or together with your kids. Since some of it's themes are quite dark, it's probably not suited for toddlers as tiny as Charlie, unless you lend them a hand. Despite the grim tones, there's still a happy end.
If you like titles like Costume Quest, this one's right up your alley, but keep in mind that the alley is in some places quite a dark one, with monsters called men lurking in the shadows.

I'm torn on Stacking.
I love the concept. Anything with matryoshka dolls is excellent. I like the sense of humor it has and there is a lot to look at which is something I always appreciate. The puzzles have obvious and less obvious solutions and if you like finding all possible details in a game this game gives you a lot of options.
HOWEVER, I thought the viewing mechanics were astoundingly stupid. The view you have is the view you keep until you change it; so if you turn around, now you're watching your character walk into the "camera" and you don't see where you're going. It does not shift on its own. I can see some rationale for some elements of the game needing this but it is very tiresome and it made the very last challenge so frustrating I just gave up completely.
The last challenge was also very arbitrary to me, as at no other point in the game are you expected to do anything quickly.
I would recommend the game for the fun of it, but I did get sick of it at the very end. Going between it and another game would probably be a better approach.
Overall, fun game but definite design issues and has the downside of becoming monotonous.

There's also a hidden helix in each level that requires you to think outside the box and experiment in order to locate it. Simply put, this is a fantastic and lengthy game. And that's not even touching upon the incredibly robust level editor and the hundreds of user-created levels available for download without even exiting the game.
Plus the subtitle is "Tactical Espionage ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥." How can you hate that?

This is probably one of the most addictive games I have played recently. I first tried it at my friend's house and immediately had to buy it. I have been playing it like a maniac since then.
So far I have enjoyed the game immensely, though that does not mean that I haven't noticed certain pros and cons to it.
Thankfully the pros outweigh the cons. The game is a pixel game which in my case is awesome because I love pixel games. The dogs and everything is pretty detailed and with pretty darn good animations. The colors and nice and soft and don't hurt the eyes even though the majority of the game consists of various shades of white and gray (the environment).
The game's racing mechanic is simple enough yet it offers a challenge, especially later in the game when you reach higher leagues. For examples, I am currently part of league 6 which involves having up to 5 dogs on your team and I have to admit I am struggling a bit more often to reach the 1st place. It takes a bit of practice and choosing the right dogs for the race becomes a lot more important. Still, it is very fun and enjoyable.
Managing your team is probably my favorite part of the game. Considering all the expanses you have it is really important to keep only those dogs who work for you. However, you usually have to spend some time working with any dog to see if it's really a good match for your team. There are quite a few things to considering when creating a team for a particular race. I also love that you can now specifically train or rest your dogs and manage who will train, and who will be idle for a while. Having staff to help you with that is of great help, especially if you have a lot of dogs to work with.
Unfortunately there are a few things that do bother me, though I am pretty sure they will be improved later.
First of all, yes, I understand that higher leagues are meant to offer a much greater challenge when racing, but sometimes the obstacles you have to face are a bit too much. Sometimes it is a bit too difficult to get to a race that your dogs are ready for and that will give you enough money to pay your bills.
Although the game has quite a few of them, I would love to see more dog breeds, but the ones who are actually suitable for dog sledding. Though I am sure that will come with time.
Also, I wish there were more things to do in the game. At the moment you pretty much just race and spam the rest/train + proceed buttons. I wish we could interact with our dogs more by feeding, playing or petting, maybe make it optional to boost their happiness, or skills or something. Maybe add some real errands where you have to transport things, or help people in need, like a simple quest system that can help you financially or in some other way like free special training or something. Crafting would be a nice addition, maybe make your own food or equipment or something like that. They do plan to add breeding later to the game which will be awesome.
All in all, this is a great little game to play at almost any time and I cannot recommend it enough! :D Regardless of whether you are a dog lover or not, it is a good game to play. The only real issue is that once you start playing it is definitely difficult to stop. On more than one occasion I would start playing and after a couple of minutes realize that in fact almost 2h had passed. It's an awesome game with an awesome concept that has potential to become even greater. It's just needs support! :)

TL;DR -- Dungeon Souls is a unique roguelike that takes the shooting mechanics from Nuclear Throne and marries it with dungeon crawler mechanics a la HackSlashLoot. Though its difficulty feels cheap sometimes, its randomization of items and levels will keep you entranced for hours.
I once had such high movement speed I clipped through the wall and it took 5 minutes' worth of effort to clip back in. (They've sadly fixed this since then :c )
In all seriousness though, I love this game. It's super cool seeing dungeon crawler stats and items being mixed with twinstick shooter mechanics. The randomization is nice and gives you tons of variety in level design, and there's plenty of character unlocks and other tasks to keep you addicted. Seriously, getting every character to their max level took me some cumulative 15 hours, which then got reset after a big update. Thanks for that, devs. >:T
Some minor problems I have: I think that the action is a little slower than most twinsticks, perhaps a result of the dungeon crawler elements. It's also pretty cheap near the endgame, particularly with Judgement and beyond. The devs' updates have become a little less consistent since the initial release, but I have good faith that this won't become another Starbound. There's also bugs, but I haven't encountered many these days. Finally, I think it's brutal to new players. Even if you're an experienced roguelike player, there's things even in early levels that will take cheap shots at you, like boulders and traps. It doesn't take too long to adapt, but it can be frustrating at first.
Overall, this game has fantastic potential. It's got a solid foundation to turn into a truly unique roguelike experience, and I have total faith.

When I first heard about this game and that it is based off Van Helsing quest (been there, done that), I was rather sceptical. I thought it was just another "we wanted to make some money" kind of game, a sad attempt to squeeze more from a known title. Then I've watched the trailers and read the reviews, and it started to look like the game was worth a try.
I started with the Mercenary, and at first glance the game seemed rather slow-paced and easy. And the major difference compared to other TD games like "Defence Grid" and countless Flash versions was very... no, VERY limited number of spots for traps. Furthermore, every spot was restricted to certain types of traps (mechanical tower/floor, magic tower/floor, summoning). So the usual tactic of zones of death was obviously impossible. It seemed that the character was the central figure, and the traps were just a supportive feature.
However, as I've reached higher tiers of maps, it became clear that I was mistaken. More difficult maps had more trap spots, allowing trap combos. And the game itself became harder and more pressing. Sometimes I had to teleport over the map and/or spam skills like crazy to get the perfect score. And sometimes I had to do so to complete the map at all. Maps became way more demanding on trap type and hero skill selection, some of the late Tier 4 maps were absolutely unbeatable without redistribution of skill and trap points.
So, in the end, the game is a solid, worthy and highly enjoyable as a combination of RPG and tower defence genres. Good variety of traps and their upgrades combined with trap-specific and other hero skills leave space for different playstyles, and the maps are different enough to prevent relying on same 2-3 trap types throughout the game. Although some traps do seem somewhat weak compared to other that do similar stuff.
The game is not perfect, though. It has occasional bugs, which might appear after updates and sometimes are rather serious, affecting damage output of hero/traps or simply freezing/crashing the game (haven't frozen or crashed myself, but saw threads in the tech support discussions). And they don't get fixed as soon as one would wish. Nevertheless, I still recommend this game to anyone who is into tower defences, skill/item builds and mobicides.

When this game first released, I wrote a review which had no feedback, but at this point it wouldn't have mattered since the game has grown so, so much since then.
Starbound is like Terraria in space; that's obviously the first thing people see when they see Starbound gameplay footage or screenshots. But unlike Terraria, this game is far, far more interactive. One thing I'm so shocked and amazed by is that Starbound now has a central plot. (Minor spoilers ahead)
In Beta releases, human players' backstories was that they were rather abruptly expelled from Earth by a gigantic tentacle monster that broke the planet apart and shook society out into the cosmos. You never directly see that happen; it's just kind of mentioned every so often. In the full release, however (I've only tested this when you make a Human character), you spawn on Earth, and the story begins right before the monster tears the world a new one. The story is focused on obtaining some sort of mythic stone to keep this horrible destroyer at bay, so "Scooby-Doo! and KISS: Rock and Roll Mystery"'s plot, only lengthier.
But even beyond that, Starbound has quests of all shapes, sizes and colors, which is really cool because each quest has rewards that will benefit your character as you progress. Like Terraria, it has boss fights, which is also really nice; it has different crafting tiers, which is kind of standard for games like this, but that totally works.
What's really cool though, is that Starbound has been many steps ahead of No Man's Sky in terms of the concept of a limitless universe. I honestly am blown away by how many systems and sub-systems of planets and moons there are; each one has its own unique resources and alien life forms, which themselves have unique appearances - you'll never see the exact same alien on more than one planet. And they don't just look different; they have different attacks as well. Early in my full release adventure, I was attacked by an alien that launched rainbows at me, but acidic ones that immediately killed me.
I don't have the usual sort of overwhelmed amazement I usually have in my reviews, since as stated I've been on Starbound for as long as I can remember, but I strongly recommend it due to how interesting it is, even for an old veteran of it. A newcomer with no experience or knowledge of past updates is going to have their mind blown by how much stuff Starbound has to offer.

I cannot give this game a recommended review for 1 simple reason
For a game that is 90% based around the tactical turn based combat you would expect the challenge to be centered around troop placement in lineup, weapon type selection and actualy stategy in the battle...
Well while i did get outplayed by the AI a couple of times tactically (although most of them were vs situations that i wasnt fully familiar with) the challenge of this game is simply getting decent RNG.
No matter how well you execute your plan and how effective it is it's simple down to 1-2 RNG rolls to completely mess up your playthrough (specially if you are playing at Veteran+ and Ironman). I seriously cannot count the times that my ful HP  with 100% armor guy missed his 70% roll only to be critically wounded to 30% health by the guy who was suppoed to die.
Situations like 9 consecutive attackson the same round on a surrounded opponent with chances ranging from 40-60 (nighttime swamps) all fail only to have the guy who was on 1hp attack once and chop of the head of 1 of his 7 attackers.
I wish i could tell you that my campaigns ended because i got ambushed by superior numbers, or got outplayed by enemies who were fielding a better combination of weapons, or because i mismanaged my funds. No that only happened 2-3 times in the first hours of my playtime while i was still learning the game... ever since i have been watching RNG cripple me just because...
This game wanted to be a challenge but i am sorry most of the time it just felt like playing a slot machine that's biased against you and when the game offers extremely little else all you have is turn based combat that ends up feeling frustrating for the wrong reasons.

This game sucks you in with its gorgeous visuals and cute but helpless protagonist, Lilly. The adventure is over far too quickly but you will fall in love and enjoy every minute of it.
Lilly Looking through is a point and click puzzle game. This game is a successful kickstarter and greenlight story and for good reason. There is simply not enough of these types of games. It reminds me of games like Monkey Island, only there is no inventory and every level is its own individual puzzle.
The puzzles are not ment to be hard, simply obstacles. Although, the color puzzles through me for a loop and I find myself asking “what am I supposed to be aiming for?” a few times. Even after beating the game once I still found myself a bit confused and just clicking around until things lined up.
The game’s art and music are very well done. It is easy to tell that the focus of the game is indeed the atmosphere. The music keeps you calm even through some frustrating parts and mixed very well with the art direction.  The art is designed to look like a painting and it succeeds. I found myself captivated by the environment and beauty of this game.
The story is simplistic but enough to set up the adventure. Lilly is trying to save a young boy, Row, as he is swept away by a mysterious red scarf. It is not much to go on, and exists only to move things forward. I actually found myself forgetting about Row and asking more questions about what happened to the world that Lilly is a part of.
I would recommend this game looking for an experience. This game is far, far too short to satisfy anyone looking for a time waster. If you want to kill time, go play COD: Ghost multiplayer.

A game about stacking Russian dolls, saving your family, and . . . stopping child labor industrialists? You got it.
You play as little Charlie Blackmore in this third-person puzzle adventure. Though he is the smallest stacking doll in the game, you can get bigger by stacking into progressively larger dolls, each of which has a unique active ability. Some characters can play an instrument, or give handshakes, or fart out a green cloud of stink, among dozens of others. It sounds like an odd assortment, but you'll need to use most of the powers in this game along with a little imagination to solve the puzzles.
It will take new players up to an hour to grasp what this game is about and how to think in its shoes, but once that locks in, the adventure is great.
There are several solutions to the puzzles in this game, and players are encouraged to repeat the story's challenges to discover them all. You'll use a lot of guess and check, but it's fun to try out different combinations of dolls' abilities in each scenario. In one instance, you are tasked with sabotaging a museum on a cruise ship. You can stack into an illusionist to disguise part of the exhibit, lead rats in to ruin the fun, or just stack into the mummy on display (which happens to be a Russian doll, conveniently) and walk straight out of the museum. Whatever you do, other dolls' reactions will make you laugh.
Other more optional tasks include completing unusual hi-jinks and finding unique Russian dolls scattered throughout the levels. These won't be for everyone, but if you're a completionist with a passion for collecting everything, you'll be right at home here.
The story is appropriately simple. Every so often the cutscenes drag on and become childish, but this is one of the only complaints about the game. The visuals, soundtrack, and sound effects go together really well.
This is an artful game that runs at a nice length and pace. I cared about it enough to 100% it in less than a day. It would be difficult to find another puzzle game like this one.

Dungeon Souls experiments with certain established rules of Rogue-Lites and makes use of multiple elements of other games I've enjoyed. However at this state I cannot fully reccommend the title because after a couple of hours the replay value shrinks to a minimum due to stat grinding mechanics.
However, this might change. After all, the game is still in development.
mechanics I liked (compared to games that I've personally played):
+ Item drops (graphics reminiscent of Risk of Rain)
+ Floor layouts (reminiscent of Nuclear Throne/Crypt of the Necro Dancer)
+ Abilities (reminiscent of Hammerwatch)
+ Portal opening objectives (reminiscent of Hammerwatch/Risk of Rain)
+ Redeemer that kicks you out of the level after last portal (never seen before)
+Animations
mechanics I didn't like:
- Bossfights (hp grind - few interesting AI patterns)
- No gamechanging item drops (as in Binding Of Isaac/Risk Of Rain)
- Levelup progression (grind)
- Powercreep: As soon as you've obtained a certain amount of items you are unstoppable. I literally had a run, where I had 100% damage reduction and couldn't die. I had to force quit, because I couldn't suicide.
- Game might benefit of some sort of lore. As of now it feels rather artificial.
TLDR: If you're really into action Rogue-Lites, this may be interesting in a Sale. Not reccommended as of now.

Dog Sled Saga has finally came out of Early Access and is a full functioning game! Now I can give my final review and thoughts, both the good and the bad. Overall, I find that this game is extremely charming with adorable pixel graphics, but it also shares a few problems like everything else.
I LOVE this game to death, it was really fun to play from start to finish. There's so many dogs to choose from, with lots of sled and leash colors to choose from. The new breeding mechanic also doubles the fun, making me some adorable puppers! Racing is fun, and I enjoy figuring out the ups and downs of my dogs. It's nice to know that each dog is unique in personality and has different skills for your team. Many dog lovers will find this fun and adorable.
Sometimes I do have to put Dog Sled Saga on the shelf, I often get bored when playing for too long as the gameplay can feel pretty repetitive. I also feel the full release has a serious lack of dog breeds to choose from, which is fine since 'most' of them are made for this kind of job, but a lot of them aren't. With so many breeds in the world I understand that they had to stop somewhere, and there is already a nice roster, but there's quite a few popular breeds that weren't included. I do hope eventually there might be some DLC, or just updates continuing to add more.
Dog Sled Saga is a fun and short game to play, it's great for a quick sitdown as it isn't as demanding or as time consuming as other games. Its arcade-like style allows it to stand on its own feet as a fun and addictive game.

This game Is basically Malaysian Airline Simulator 2015, but all jokes aside I'll give my opinion on It.
• First off I want to say, this game Is very well made for early access. Usually their Is tons of bugs and glitches around the game but I have only seen 2 In my play time. These bugs were not major either, but they consisted of 'Menu Glitching for a few seconds' and 'Not being able to drop or pick up Items for a couple seconds'. I can say with confidence that this game Is the most well made early access games on steam at the moment. Next I want to touch up on the 'Crafting System'. This system is very unique, when placing down Items that are craftable on the ground, holding left click on the item/items, dragging your mouse away from the item, and clicking which Item you want to craft It Into. Very unique system that I have yet to see In any game that I have played. Most games that you drop Items In are usually a bit annoying but this one Is very smooth and your items don't roll all over the place when dropped like most games. Gathering Items Is a bit tricky but fun and exciting at the same time. Wether your collecting Items on your Island such as sticks, rocks, rope, etc or your swimming In the ocean under water collecting Items from a abandon ship while sharks attack you. (Which I might add Is a adrenaline rush like no other) It's very entertaining and enjoyable. One other thing I would quickly like to touch on Is the sound. Now don't get me wrong, I love the sound of the ocean In the morning and night just like anyone else. But I would love If they adjusted the sound just a tad bit. Maybe more options for other sounds to turn down. Also, the audio needs to be adjusted a bit as when I put the game to low volume, It still was very loud. But this will be fixed eventually. The last thing I want to touch up on about Is the graphics. These graphics for early access are pretty damn good. I don't they hit they're full potential but they are very enjoyable at 1080p, Ultra settings. They could use some work but they are very, very beautiful and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic. But at the moment they're is some stuff to do that will entertain you for a couple hours, but the game will get boring after that and you will switch. Hopefully they add more things to do In the game In the near future, Instead of just build 24/7.

Storyline:
You start off inside the ditched aircraft and you must escape into the life raft and paddle your way onto one of many islands in the distance, once there you will find trees, rocks, bushes, and fish you must use these resources to craft tools/buildings and survive by keeping your health, hunger, and thirst down.
Survival Aspects:
1. Inability to stay on one island for an extended period of time due to resources.
2. Poisons from eating raw food and coming into contact with venemous plants.
3. Tools have durability.
4. Weather.
5. Hunger, thirst.
Game Mechanic:
The game is procedualy generated meaning the contents/shape of each island are randomly generated as you go along, problem being that all the islands are the same size, restricting that feeling of being in the middle of nowhere.
Pros - Atmosphere, graphics, survival, looting.
Cons - Procedualy generated islands, limited crafting (Still in Alpha though).
Summary:
All in all a very very promising game with a lot more content to come just dont expect more than 5 hours of replayability at the moment.

TL;DR - Wait for a bundle. It's cute but short and tedious with no story and no replay value.
Lilly looking through is a point and click atmospheric puzzle game. I hesitate to even call it an Adventure game because there's no dialog and really no story at all. It's basically a short series screens designed to create an atmosphere of whimsy with puzzles to stretch the time out. The one story element there is, chasing the little boy, is really nothing more than a macguffin to get you to the next screen.
At no time are we ever told who these kids are, where they come from, what world they are in, what the rules of it are, why they are there, where if anywhere they were planning or going and what if anything they were planning on doing before the boy was swept away.
That it appears to be presented in a package of magical whimsical mystery is just covering for the fact that in actuality there is no story at all. It's just an experience game made to set a mood and impression. That the bulk of the short play time is made up of puzzles that once figured out are almost immediately solvable the second time around and beyond just means it's experience game that you'll really only want to play once.
Speaking of the puzzles, every time you have Lilly click to go somewhere or do something you to wait. Having to sit through the slow animations every single time and not being able to skip or cancel them no matter how many times you were redoing the same motions made me want to stab my eyes out. It was just so tedious.
The fact that this game is still very short in spite of all this tediousness and the fact that they reached their Kickstarter stretch goal to make the game longer is really saying something.
If you come to the end and think 'That's it?' a short length of a game is more likely to feel noticeable and problematic than another game of the same length with a satisfying conclusion that feels like a complete, whole experience. To the Moon is a good example of the latter. It is short but that never feels problematic because there's a definite, clear conclusion that makes sense in the context of the game and the journey.
This game in comparison definitely gives a 'Huh? That's it? What does that even mean?' feel at the end which just makes the short length all the more noticeable and unforgivable. If you are going to make a game first and foremost about soaking up the atomsphere framed by gameplay that that gives no replayability to speak of then at least make it long enough so that we feel we get enough time in that world to soak up the atmosphere.
Seeing as it's both short and without a story, all your are left with is a short time with a feeling of whimsy that's mostly padded out by puzzles made tedious due to all the slow unskippable animations between motions.
Lastly, I want to talk about pricing and packages. I bought the 'Deluxe Edition' through their Humble store. The regular version for $10 pre-order at the humble store did not come with a Steam key. The 'Deluxe Edition' for $15 did. It also came with a PDF artbook, which turned out to be very short and mostly just pictures of one particular locale in the game. It's also the same PDF they are giving at GOG for $9, the price of the regular version minus 10% off new release sale. They literally charged $5 extra to for a Steam key if you bought the game from the Humble Store which is not only shady, I've honestly never seen another developer do this.
The music was excellent, relaxing, magical sounding and ambient and the best thing about the game in my opinion. It would have been nice if this had come with the 'Deluxe Edition' for $15. It didn't. The soundtrack will put you out another $10. I'll pass as I've already spent more than I should have for what I ended up getting. It's a real shame because I wanted to love this game.

This is a steam version of a F2P Web Browser game. I strongly recommend you play this on Web Browser first to figure out if you like the game. I still would recommend buying coven before steam client if you wish to play this game more, as coven is the only thing that adds new, non aesthetic, items to the game. This game is not a P2W by any means, sure you could dump 20 bucks into this game, but all it does is get you skins/pets. There are scrolls, which increase the chance of getting a certian role, but thats it, just increase chances. No unfair advantage.
Now onto review of gameplay. This is a strategy game of sorts. Wit and Switfness are key. A match starts with 15 people (99% of the time). I will mainly talk about ranked/practice (chaos is similar, but all random roles) There are 4 maf/coven (bad people), 9 townies, and 2 neutrals (killing and evil). The goal of the town is to lynch all non townies, the goal of the maf/coven is to kill all who oppose them (everyone except neutral evil), the goal of the neutral killing is to kill everone else other than the neutral evil, and the neutral evil is just a wrench in everyones plan. You have no idea who is who day 1, as it does not tell you anyones role. Each role has different jobs, some protect, some kill, and a lot are informational/supportive. All you have to go on is peoples word, so larry, who claims to be an investigator, actually might be a consigliere (mafia investigator), and it is up to you to call his bluff or leave him be. Now there are wills. Each person has one. Wills are only displayed once you die. When you die, your role is shown to everyone, and any information in your will could help town learn who is who. A will is the most effective way to verify your info as a townie, as it also verifies your role. You can use the wills of dead players to call bluffs of evil roles over contradictions with their claims (as their claims are usually random). So this game is a nice break from the usual shooters and mobas everyone plays, and is definitly a fun game to play on lunch break or eating dinner if you live the dorm style life.

From my personal experience thus far, I have concluded that there are two broadly inclusive categories of people who play Starbound: people with very low standards, and sexual deviants. Speaking as a person with relatively high standards, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game in its present state.
To begin with, the basics: Starbound is a side-scrolling crafting sandbox. From the presentation and gamefeel perspective, it's put together decently well. The graphics are charming, the items look nice, characters are cute, some of the tilesets and planet backgrounds are really well made, jumping and running and hitting things and being hit feels all good and proper - on that front, I really have no complaints. The interface is a little♥♥♥♥♥backwards - it took me a while to figure out exactly how to use items from the inventory, and various functions that could have been assigned key bindings are instead done through tedious mouse movement and clicking (to give an example, in order to assign items to quick use slots, you must click on them in your inventory and drag them to the slot in question. I would have preferred to simply hover over them with my mouse and press the quick slot's key in order to instantly reassign. It seems so incredibly obvious that I do it every time before I realize that the developers hadn't thought of this and I must instead waste my time with this piddly cockamamie bull♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm sure you're wondering - they do it that way so that you can still quick swap while your inventory is open and your mouse is on it, right? Well, you'd be wrong. They do it because they're bad at making games. If there is an item held in your cursor (which is the only reason you'd ever open your inventory) the quick swap keys just do not work.)
My second major complaint is with the performance - for what it is, this game runs like grandma's♥♥♥♥♥ Stuttering and FPS drops are common even on screens which don't have a whole lot going on. It feels like the only time I hit 60 is when I'm deep underground, with no other entities within the immediate area and only a single light source. On big colonies with a decent number of characters, sub-20 is common. Bear in mind that this is a 2D side-scroller and I'm running a 390. And this doesn't even have the excuse of Dwarf Fortress, which calculates the anal circumference and life aspirations of every character in the universe every time someone takes a step.
What breaks this game for me, however, is the gameplay. To begin with, it's all good and fun. You dig deep, collect ores, build stuff, upgrade your old stuff. The starting world plays just like you'd expect of a game of this genre. Once you reach a certain point, you're ready to fix your marooned ship and go to other worlds. On the other worlds, you make a beeline for the ore that you couldn't get on the previous planet in order to ascend to the next tier of equipment that immediately eliminates all challenge from your present surroundings. You repeat this three more times and then the challenge is gone from the game as you acquire the highest tier of gear that makes any combat encounter in the game an utter joke. Once you've gotten the highest tier of stuff, likewise, there is no reason to continue exploring, as your reasons for doing it thus far (getting better stuff) will have evaporated.
There are other aspects, as well - you can build colonies, which consist of you building nice homes for people who will give you money in exchange for taking your fps. They will be altogether happy with plain old rectangles made of dirt bricks and a lightbulb each, but any player of such games will naturally surround their plain dirt rectangles with grand architectural monuments of immense scale suitable as to impress their grubby proles. If you're anything like me, by this point in the game your exploration of other worlds will be driven mainly by your desire to acquire new furniture for your home base, as if you were some sort of savage space pirate from a race of honourable and warlike interior decorators. After a while, however, it becomes evident that there's not really a point to the whole colony system - you can contribute more effort, but you don't really get anything in return, your tenants continue to behave entirely like bumble ♥♥♥♥ idiots that just stumble and wander all over your nice place, and it becomes clear that nothing of risk or consequence will ever happen involving your colony.
As I've mentioned, there's exploration, too, but once you've reached the top tier, the only thing that reaching some new tileset or setpiece will give you is the inherent satisfaction of seeing a new tileset or setpiece. You have no way of interacting with inhabitants or environments outside of dismantling, trading and whatnot, and nothing of consequence can happen as a result of your exploration - you don't learn new stories (unless you pick up a book somewhere, in which case the story will be rather short and not very well written), you don't get new things to do, and any sense of intrigue or mystery that might blossom is immediately crushed by the shallowness of the mechanics. There's very little in the sense of player stories, by which I mean when a player goes "oh man I went to X planet and found this dude who told me Y so I went and did Z where Φ happened and it turns out that Λ was the case all along." You know, the narratives that players create naturally as a result of interpreting events in the game. This is because there are only three things that happen in the game - killing a thing with your overpowered weapon, picking up or dropping furniture and terrain with your magic matter gun, and watching cutscenes. Other actors or the unseen game director lack agency entirely and have no power to complicate or interfere with your experience, making the game BORING. In fact, the only stories are those told by the devs through cutscenes, which are boring because every player will see the exact same thing, in which they're not able to participate in the same way as with emergent player stories.
There is a story, by the way. You have to collect the six chaos emeralds in order to seal away the ancient evil that wants to kill everyone. That is figuratively it. This game doesn't need a story. It needs threats and challenges and things that can happen, new mechanics and random events. If not that, then at least something that can breathe some new life into the cycle of dig - fight - collect - upgrade - repeat, like, say, an endgame. Until the issues I've listed are addressed, I strongly recommend that you AVOID this game unless you can pick it up for $5 or $10 or however much you think is fair for an OKish crafting sandbox with an extremely short expiry date.

There are the obvious genre comparisons, that it's a clicker but without automation making it simultaneously a very casual yet very frustrating game; that it's a visual novel with more "game" than is typical.
I think the most apt comparison I actually came up with though is that this game is pretty much in the same vein as an indie game that was lauded on release and which might not be so well remembered now, Tomorrow Corporation's
. It's a story (or a series of stories, in the case of this game) wrapped around a very casual, barely-a-game core, which allows you to experience the story as a series of episodes rather than one long "novel." The other Cavyhouse game I've played,
functions similarly, though is much more elaborate in its core "game," and I would even say that that game takes its genre (elemental mashup and experimentation, ala
) to a new level whereas this game only strips away the conveniences of other clickers, making much of the game very tedious.
But still, the game is interesting. The dark stories and the simple gameplay make for a nice ambience to spend an afternoon where you don't want to think too hard about what you're doing. It's very calming, and has something of a similarity to
style anime like
or

Pros and Cons of Starbound:
Pros: Lots of exploring, perfect for the sandbox/survival genre. Plenty of fun weapons, from cursor-guided missile launchers, to massive swords with elemental power. A ton of quests that will take you all over the galaxy, perhaps the universe. A story and soundtrack perfect for the game, and each species has a different armor set and reactions to certain items. And interesting biomes from an underworld of sorts called "heck" to an ocean planet full of treasure and ocean themed enemies.
Cons: (some of these are pretty small but noticable enough to mention) Sometimes the rendering of planets can be kinda slow. Trying to stream the game fullscreen resulted in the resolution bugging out and caused the framerate to slow considerably. Each species does not have different powers, even if it makes sense that they should. Finding certain meterials can be hard at times. And just trying to get your ship working so you can explore the universe takes a whole process that can be pretty tedious.
Now here's a list of what powers I would give to what species.
Human: Slightly increased currency aquisition, slight dps increase with melee weapons
Hylotl: Ability to breathe underwater, increased mining efficiency underwater
Avian: Increased jumping height, slight gliding effect, lessened fall damage.
Apex: Increased inteligence (allows faster crafting and amount of meterials needed to craft items is decreased)
Glitch: Using electric dps weapons adds a small regeneration effect, recruitment of robotic crew members is easier
Floran: Immunity to poison, chance to poison an enemy hit with a melee attack
Novakid: Small increase to ranged weapons dps, Glows in dark areas due to them being made of energy

When this game first released, I wrote a review which had no feedback, but at this point it wouldn't have mattered since the game has grown so, so much since then.
Starbound is like Terraria in space; that's obviously the first thing people see when they see Starbound gameplay footage or screenshots. But unlike Terraria, this game is far, far more interactive. One thing I'm so shocked and amazed by is that Starbound now has a central plot. (Minor spoilers ahead)
In Beta releases, human players' backstories was that they were rather abruptly expelled from Earth by a gigantic tentacle monster that broke the planet apart and shook society out into the cosmos. You never directly see that happen; it's just kind of mentioned every so often. In the full release, however (I've only tested this when you make a Human character), you spawn on Earth, and the story begins right before the monster tears the world a new one. The story is focused on obtaining some sort of mythic stone to keep this horrible destroyer at bay, so "Scooby-Doo! and KISS: Rock and Roll Mystery"'s plot, only lengthier.
But even beyond that, Starbound has quests of all shapes, sizes and colors, which is really cool because each quest has rewards that will benefit your character as you progress. Like Terraria, it has boss fights, which is also really nice; it has different crafting tiers, which is kind of standard for games like this, but that totally works.
What's really cool though, is that Starbound has been many steps ahead of No Man's Sky in terms of the concept of a limitless universe. I honestly am blown away by how many systems and sub-systems of planets and moons there are; each one has its own unique resources and alien life forms, which themselves have unique appearances - you'll never see the exact same alien on more than one planet. And they don't just look different; they have different attacks as well. Early in my full release adventure, I was attacked by an alien that launched rainbows at me, but acidic ones that immediately killed me.
I don't have the usual sort of overwhelmed amazement I usually have in my reviews, since as stated I've been on Starbound for as long as I can remember, but I strongly recommend it due to how interesting it is, even for an old veteran of it. A newcomer with no experience or knowledge of past updates is going to have their mind blown by how much stuff Starbound has to offer.

I wouldn't say that I recommend this game, yet I wouldn't say that I don't.
The game itself is fun, especially when you have a really good build, but it's got so many faults.
For one, the melee classes are abysmally bad. Getting close to enemies is bad enough, but all of melee classes have a slow attack. With the exception of one, but you still have to get close and personal. Which is bad, because it makes fighting ranged enemies tedious. And fighting some of the bosses is impossible because they either move around a lot or getting close will put you in a bad position, making you die faster a Mayfly. It's just better to use a Ranged class, the best example being Archer and Rogue, because of their quick rate of fire, ability to cancel out projectiles by firing at them, and starting off with the most speed.
Another flaw in this game is the fact that it lags (this one is personal). A Pixelated game that LAGS. This is something that I very rarely see. From what I can tell, it's all the dynamic lighting and particle effects from the torches. It could also be the corpses as well, since the farther I get into a level, the more lag there is. And the worst part is that my game runs at 30 FPS as oppossed to, what I can tell, is supposed to be 60. So my game runs at half the speed it's supposed to. Everything feels sluggish. It's kind of frustrating in its own right.
This game seems to be trying to be a difficult roguelike, somewhat akin to something like Nuclear Throne and Dark Souls (And not just because of the "Souls" in both names). And it achieves that. In all the wrong ways. As Vlambeer, the developer of Nuclear Throne, once said, "it's not fair, it's not right". This game isn't right. Some attacks from bosses and enemies happen so fast, you can barely take in it's coming for you before you take in in the face. Some bosses, especially the final boss, fire so many projectiles that they feel impossible to dodge. And if you focus on dodging, you're likely to get shot in the face with a laser you couldn't even comprehend was there until you lose half your health.
I've unlocked hard mode. It was one of the biggest goals I had for this game. And I don't want to reach any farther. Hard Mode is, from what I can tell, Borderline IMPOSSIBLE. I can only imagine the final boss doing twice the already ♥♥♥♥load of damage. I hate games that do Hard Mode like this. The ones that don't change anything except the damage and health of enemies. Also, I'm pretty sure the final boss wouldn't be that bad, if I wasn't sure it would have twice the health.
Now that I've gotten through some of the flaws in this game, I will talk about the cons... After I take a break because I'm getting tired of typing. But it can all be summed up into 1 thing.
Dungeon Souls is a mediocre game.
There you go.

I've had the game since its release and have seen it go through several stages over the past year and a half. My original review was very positive but after returning to the game and seeing what its new status is I'm afraid I'm gonna have to change my recommendation.
It started off as a very interesting survival game that sold the idea of infinite worlds and realistic survival. Granted there wasn't much to do in the game, but it still had fun gameplay up until you had gathered all the right gear, buildings, etc. I had confidence that in time this game would expand a bit more and become that survival game I'd been looking for. Sadly updates have kinda beaten this game into the ground. They seem to be very far and few, but when they do happen they don't seem to bring very much into the game, adding a few usless items, fixing minor bugs, updating HUD and main menu layouts, and forcing me to restart all over again because my saved game is not compatible with the newest version. Graphical updates have also changed the game greatly. The game is starting to resemble something completely different from what I purchased. New graphical updates have forced me to lower my visual settings in order to run the game without FPS drop. I won't hold this against the game too much since my computer is kind of a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ But I will let it be noted that I ran the game perfectly fine at max settings before these visual updates occured.
At the end of the day, I can't exactly recommend this game anymore. It promised me an in-depth survival experience that entailed hours of fun and interesting gameplay, however it has done very little to deliver such content in a way that lasts me more than an hour at most until I've experienced all the game has to offer. Hopefully the developers use this game as a way to build upon their mistakes in any future titles they may have in their agenda.

Haven't gotten far into the game yet but I can say this: It's Dungeon Fighter Online but in 3D.
If you liked DFO and want an upgrade on visuals, this game is for you. When I say it's DFO but in 3D I literally mean exactly that. Genderlocked characters, class advancement at level 15, the cash shop is sorted identically, etc. It's like they're both developed by the same team but had a better engine to make Kritika. You also fight in dungeon-like instances exactly like in DFO, and of course, you can choose the difficulty (hell mode replaced with insane mode). The exp/rewards gained from clearing is based also similarly based on performance.

It has taken me a long time to feel comfortable writing this review. I have put over twelve hours into Deathtrap and I still am not entirely sure I've seen everything I want to see in the game, despite matches sitting around 30 minutes a piece. I played all the way through tier one and halfway through tier two. It just kept adding new traps, one-offs that were either specific to the level or reused but unable to be upgraded. There was always more. Then the traps started repeating so now I am going to attempt to write this review before I put it off any longer.
I had played The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing before. I was familiar with Neocore Games' work. I found it enjoyable, even. Despite that, I was a bit skeptical of them creating a tower defense game. Would it be something closer to Dungeon Defenders than anything? Would it be grindy? What was this I was hearing about set trap locations, each one of several different types? It wasn't something that seemed to entirely appeal to me.
Then I played the game. It took a few rounds. I found the controller a bit unwieldy at first, especially in the menus, which have a truly awful control scheme, but I eventually got used to it. I got the rhythm of the game down and it started to become something quite special.
It works like this. The view is isometric, like Van Helsing. The setting is taken from Van Helsing, with your character being a hired mercenary that is taking on the creatures of the Ink. The character you control, you control in a hack 'n slash manner, like Van Helsing. Unlike Van Helsing, however, it is a tower defense, as well, rather than an open world hack 'n slash.
It's not a traditional tower defense, though. You have several types of traps, ground and towers, as well as mystical, mechanical, and summons. These sort of mix and match to create a set of nodes in which you can place, for example, a “mystical ground trap” or a “mechanical tower trap.” The summons are the only exception, being an exclusively ground-based ordeal. This can sound limited at first but then you start unlocking traps and it opens up quite a bit. So much so that you eventually stop knowing what to put your points into.
Put simply, there are a lot of traps. At least 30 that can be upgraded using points earned for leveling and at least half a dozen more that can't. You start to realize “hey, I have a summon trap here, maybe I should put an enthropic pillar there so that it can heal the summons.” Maybe you realize that placing a frost pillar next to a lava grill and upgrading it so that it slows and freezes enemies will result in more damage being done to those enemies with less traps. Maybe you simply realize that an upgraded lava grill with the damage-over-time upgrade active is more worth it than that spear trap you haven't put any points into. The fact of the matter is that there are options in the game's limitations and that there are legitimate ways to play a map incorrectly.
Even more so if you are intent on not using your hero. With the exception of a single map, which was designed to be played without heroes doing damage to the hordes, playing each map in order from tier one to tier two, I have never been able to play a map the first time around without using my hero. Even on that map that was designed for it, I wasn't able to go without using my hero's attacks. It's a game that's designed from the ground up to be a careful balance of hero and tower damage and I think they've done a fine job with it.
Towers aren't the only ones that get to have fun with freezing or burning effects, either. Heroes unlock a significant amount of “fun” attacks as they level. I played as a Mercenary and, pretty early on, I was given a dash attack that froze anything I ran through for an amount of time specified by how much I had upgraded it and then set off a small explosion at the end of the dash, damaging nearby enemies. Later, I unlocked an attack where I slam my weapon down on the ground, causing a wave of fire to damage, and attach a damage-over-time effect to, anything within its range. It is insane amounts of fun to find small hordes and either freeze or light them on fire. One of my favorite features of the game was that you could cause a monster to lose interest in moving forward and stop to attack you, sometimes leading them either off the path or even backwards, so long as they did not pick up on the fact that a significant amount of other monsters were nearby and think weren't needed there anymore. It was incredibly fun for me to freeze hordes with the dash attack and watch them swarm together and chase me down.
Attacks aren't all you get, though. Should you want to specialize as support, you can get spells that buff towers, other players, or both. The amount of options for your player character are staggering to the point of confusion. I legitimately had no idea what to do with my points after so long. The max level for each skill is ten but it would take you a long time to figure that out without someone telling you, as you will probably attempt to become a jack of all trades, as I did.
Beyond the basic gameplay, the game also has a relatively simplistic crafting system in which you can either collect or dismantle different items for a small set of resources that can then be used to craft items that you have obtained the blueprints for. The items you craft scale to your level and are generally better than what you find in chests, I found, even if completing side-quests consistently.
Speaking of which, I found side-quests fairly underwhelming. While a nice touch, after the first few levels, they are few and far between, often requiring you to kill some beast that is either a good half the map away from anywhere you might actually use or that is only accessible by Ink portal. Once you do find said beast, you will probably not beat it unless you come back to it after you've leveled a bit. This isn't too big a deal, as you obtain about a level per match, granted you continue to do the levels in order but it is fairly annoying, especially considering the simplicity of them. Some quests are to “not use mystic traps” or “complete without doing damage with your hero” but even those don't help to alleviate the concerns of being underwhelming. It's fortunate, then, that three different difficulty levels with four tiers each help to increase replay value.
There were very few other issues I encountered in Deathtrap. There was an unfortunate bug that seemed to be related to the way the game sorted which trap you were trying to place/upgrade when using controllers where you couldn't place floor traps that were near a Squash Trap and, as mentioned before, I think the menu controls are absolutely awful and unintuitive, but my concerns pretty much ended there. The game is incredibly solid and provides a high amount of graphical fidelity to match.
Deathtrap is one of those games that rarely comes along. One that restores my faith in a genre that is drowning in a sea of games that stick too closely to the tried and true. It may seem limited at first but the game takes those limitations and makes more options out of them than many games with significantly more freedom give. It provides a fast-paced hack 'n slash experience with the necessity to be smart about upgrades, both on maps and on your character sheet and, to be honest, I don't think that happens often enough. The game has easily restored my faith in the tower defense genre single-handed and, with the ability to create custom maps, it will last for a long time to come.

At first glance it reminded me of Banner Saga with Prison Archetect graphics. But I have to say it's far more intriguing than both those titles. You raise up your own mercenary company, hire, equip, and train your guys, design a standard, forge alliances or enemies. Adventure for gold, or to explore a hidden temple of undead.. You'll get attached to your soldiers, whome you can name, customize the look of, and of course train up however you want. Their graphics show the scars of previous battles (missing nose.. ouch!) 10/10. ANY fan of the turn based strategy genre NEEDS to play this !

Most of us who brought this game are probably a fan of clicker and/or visual novel.  Heck, you probably are like me, found this game from the tag.  If you are a VN fan, you will not be disappointed, but if you are a clicker fan, be warned, this game is not your typical clicker, it contain no mindless clicking and idling.
As for the game play, Forget Me Not is a combination of VN, time management, and clicker game.  Your job is easy, cultivate organ fruits for the customers, all can be done with a simple point and click.  At first, you will manage a single tree, all you do is click, wait, collect, and repeat.  So how is this a clicker?  Once the story progress, on top of multiple trees, you will also given the options to turn the organ into mincemeat and pickle.  The game will become overwhelming and the tool given will not handle the abuse, that's where the helper come in.  You can buy helpers to help you, but those helpers like to slack off once in a while, you have to click on them to keep them working, imagine owning 100+ of them, the clicking will not stop.
One of the best thing I love in the game is that each customer come with they own unique story.  Each of them tell a side of human and is very well written.  The visual and the sound track is absolute beautiful and is matching to each of the story.  In the end, all the hard grinding will paid off, the ending for the main and side story is just stunning.
Overall, this game will give you a truly unique experience.  The repetitive clicking may turn you off in the middle but remember, all the hard work will follow with a beautiful ending.  Now, I just wish the developer team will push out a soundtrack DLC.

Very addictive gameplay loop: take on a job, spend all of your money buying gear and supplies and hiring men in preparation, fight, get paid, try to replenish your supplies, hope that you have slightly more money than you did when you began (you probably won’t), and then do it all again. Also, probably watch some of your men get brutally murdered in the process.
Battle Brothers may be brutal, and it may be a grind, but it is also very fun and very addicting. The difficulty and high stakes of permadeath just make any progress you may earn that much more gratifying. The combat itself is great, and any fan of strategic turn-based combat should enjoy it quite a bit; battles require thought and planning, and even then you are always one step away from disaster. Managing your crew of soldiers is a joy for those who like to do a bit of micro-managing and strategizing. Little touches, such as the interesting and humorous character backgrounds and distinctive art of the characters, add a lot of color and personality to the game.  It all comes together extremely well, forming a very distinctive and charming (in a brutally violent kind of way) gameworld. It’s very easy to lose hours upon hours to Battle Brothers without even realizing it.

I don't write reviews that often, but the developers of this game have earned a negative review. I realize this is a free-to-play, so I don't want to be too harsh with them, but it's difficult not to be with how they've developed this, and they are taking steps backwards on minor changes while the core gameplay needs to be completely reworked.
Starting out, I was incredibly confused because the progression you would normally feel from a typical game such as this doesn't hardly exist. The speed progression goes from full-throttle to stale. It seems like a fun game at first, but quickly you'll realize how senseless many of the features are in this game. For example, you have explore nodes vs combat nodes, and the mixture of the two on each map doesn't make sense after a while, and they actually start to play against each other because of limited hero choices and slots, rather than everything working together as a challenging game.
They have loot boxes, which seem okay at first, but very quickly become useless and annoying. Not only that, but they're the only rewards for defeating bosses, which makes defeating bosses useless and annoying as well. At the time I'm writing this review, they have "EPIC" chests, which are supposed to be the best, but it turns out they actually give somewhat less rewards than the tier of chests below them. They offer for you to spend money to buy these things, but they're lackluster and most of the time useless.
At the time I'm writing this, they just did a UI update, and sent the game back into the stone age with it. The new "improved" UI actually makes the whole game cluttered and confusing. This is not the first UI update they've done back-to-back, and each one is making the whole system more confusing, all the while, they've got sections of the game completely unfinished (like the listing for legendary cards that don't exist), and they add in "content" like the Corgi card (you read that right, the dog... a corgi) which is so incredibly useless I'm not even going to waste time explaning.
Overall, don't touch this game. It might lure you in at the start, but you'll see the problems with it very quickly, and I recommend not wasting your time. The developers have no direction where they're going with this, and they seem to just be making things up as they go.

Premise:
Clear each level by killing enemies and activating marks to progress deeper into the dungeon.  Acquire equipment from chests and shops to make yourself more powerful.
Death is permanent, but not to fear, the resources and experience you collect from your previous deaths can be used to make your character even more powerful, thus making your character stronger every time you die and revive.  Death is an integral part of finally achieving victory!
Visuals:
A cute little game with retro sprite graphics.  The dungeons have neat little designs everywhere, and the characters are cute and really fun.  There's not exactly much to say, but it still looks really nice.
I greatly appreciate that the dungeon backgrounds change with every boss battle.  Instead of making every dungeon look the same with more powerful enemies of the same type, Dungeon Souls changes the dungeon and enemy sprites every 4th level.  It is always refreshing to find a new color palette after you defeat a difficult boss.
Menus/Interface:
A lot of things aren't exactly explained from the start.  The menus and in-game interface can be a little overwhelming at the beginning.  Most of it must be learned through trial and error, and a lot of fiddling around.  It all works well once you figure it out though.
Gameplay/Controls:
Overall, gameplay is a lot of fun.  Basic gameplay is just running around and just chop at random stuff.  You collect items from your fallen enemies, and every 3 levels you will be faced with a boss; each one being harder than the last.
The fact that death is an integral part of eventual victory makes dying a lot less painful in the long run; you die knowing that, next time, you will most likely level up and progress even farther.  So in this case, what kills you makes you stronger!  (Bad reference, I know)
Also, enemies do appear on top of you randomly, and I find this a little unfair to the player, as players shouldn't be penalized for something that is not in their control.
Controls are very simple and well laid out.  While playing, you have easy access to all your attacks, and it is not difficult to use at all, after you learn how they work of course, and that may take some time.
Certain things I am still unsure of how they work.  We could use a little more of a tutorial with this game, as the one currently in place is not the most informative.  I am assuming they are planning on adding a more clear and informative tutorial as development progresses.
Glitches:
Being in early access, this game does have its fair share of glitches.  At times, the game slows down to around 30 FPS.  Seeing as how the graphics are very simplistic and un-demanding,  this is a little confusing. Another issue I have experienced is a game crash after picking up an item.  Aside from this, I haven't found any other issues.
As this game is in early access, I cannot hold these minor glitches against the game, as it is still a work in progress.
Summary:
A fun game overall.  I recommend this game.
Pros:
-Leveling up after a death adds an element of fun to dying.
-Combat is generally simplistic, but there are certain more advanced things which can be done to tilt combat in your favor.
-Cute graphics.
Cons:
-Some glitches, but nothing game breaking, although the framerate drop is annoying.
-Needs a more informative tutorial. Current tutorial leaves the user hanging.
-Sometimes unfair combat.
SCORE:  8.5 / 10

NEONomicon is a puzzle platformer where the word "minimalistic" is a fair descriptor.
Before begining ask yourself:
Am I fine with dying over and over, then over some more?
Do I enjoy games with no exposition, so I need to figure it out all myself?
Is the need to remember the layout of a level just to get through it something I can handle?
If the answer is NO to those questions, this game is NOT for you.
There isn't much to say about this game, as it is a simple premise. You start in the dungeon in a random location (the 1st room is always the same) and the goal is to find where the exit is. The dungeon is a 5x5 grid of levels, with each level having 4 entry/exit points. You need to work your way through the dungeon, checking each exit point until you find the correct one. Each time the game is loaded, the layout of the the dungeon changes with the rooms shuffled and it appears that there are more room variations when you see in a single dungeon, so the game offers a large amount of replayability.
There is no save system though, so allow at least an hour to attempt a playthrough. There are 2 types of enemy in the game (I have seen), a small version you can kill by jumping on them and a large version you cant. There are also 2 types of traps, spikes that kill you and leave your body behind and a cog that cuts you up into 4 pieces. On top of that each stage is in the dark and the only constant light is from the player, as well as a slight glow from any dead bodies on a stage. You can drop light orbs, but this ability must be recharged via collectables.
I have enjoyed the challenge, and in 4 hours have got to the exit once. While I feel the player would benefit from a save system, I can understand that it would hamper the playstyle the developer is going for. The gameplay will limit people interested in the game, and the lack of a save might reduce that pool of players further - so I would suggest to the developer to add one in (if its there, I haven't found it).
All that said, I have enjoyed the game and feel its good value for under $2.

This is a pretty amazing game, for the most part. 20 years ago I had a demo for Thief 1 which was the tutorial and the first mission where you rob some rich dude. I played it to death over and over and loved it. Finally got the full game and was devastatingly disappointed when you move on to stalking graveyards, spelunking in caves, fighting/avoiding ghosts, fighting/avoiding zombies, etc... I just wanted to rob rich dudes! Is that too much to ask?! Gave Thief 2 a try when it came out and now we're fighting/avoiding robots in factories or something. Then I dropped the series in disappointment.
Too bad I missed out on Thief 3: Deadly Shadows when it released because this game is everything I wanted from the original Thief 20 years ago! The lore in the series is pretty rich so the ghosts, zombies, caves, etc all make a return but they're very minor parts that weave into the story very well. For the most part you're robbing rich dudes, subverting cults, saving the world, etc all while lining your pockets along the way. This is an old game in a well-known series so I won't write one of my normal detailed reviews. All I want to say is that this game basically repaired a small part of my childhood and for that it's awesome.
It's not completely without flaws. Controversially, this game dropped from a 10/10 to a 9/10 because of the Shalebridge Cradle level. Most people love this level and I know why. When I first started it was extremely atmospheric and tense. This quickly became one of the most tedious and frustrating levels in the game, though. Instant failure states and near invulnerable enemies (unless you want to spend a lot of expensive resources putting them down permanently) mean you'll be save scumming a lot here.
That's just one level, though. Overall, an epic game. A must-play for any Thief fan and a must-play for any would-be Thief fan that was put off by the earlier games in the series, like I was. 9/10

Bought Thief 2014 first. I have to say TDS knocks Thief 2014 into a cocked hat. No annoying context-based jump/climb hassles and no silly eye icon over an NPC's head if you are detected, or when the NPC is suspicious. Paradoxically, 2014 has slicker graphics but the eye icon looks like a clumsy overlay.
After only a few hours into TDS, I'm hooked. The graphics are much better than I anticipated they would be. The player feels like they are moving around in a proper world space in TDS. The world space feels warmer, more realistic and thus more believable. Thief 2014's graphics seem like washed out, pen and ink in comparison; they are unable to create a sense of place that feels real: nicely Gothic on the one hand, yet somehow "flat" on the other. I wonder if the developers of Thief 2014 deliberately tried to create a washed out, dark world. If they did, they partly succeeded but they lost something in the process. I realise this review is about TDS, but comparison with related games is sometimes appropriate. Thief 2014 is ok but TDS...way better.
The stealth mechanics in TDS are very good and make sense (the "swoop" movement in Thief 2014 was off putting/counter intuitive for me). Navigation is difficult because of the absence of a marker icon to follow. Navigating ones way around without an onboard compass is both realistic and assists with immersion/believability. After all, the player is supposed to be finding their way around an unfamiliar environment, rather than being led onwards by the gaming equivalent of satnav. Unlike Thief 2014 there aren't, so far, guards at every damned turn. Even though Thief 2014 had better (for which read "hand holding") navigation, the presence of guards EVERYWHERE made getting around a real pain in the neck.
Having to visit fences to offload loot is also immersive. I didn't like simply finding myself x amount of gold richer after completing a mission in Thief 2014.
After only a handful of hours gameplay, it might seem premature to post a review. However, I've played enough games to recognise quality when I see it. How I overlooked this wee gem I simply do not know. TDS is my winter project and I'm looking forward to it. I've only paused gameplay because I have other things to do.
