Stacking is one of the most original games I’ve played to date, and one of my favorites. I just cannot tell you how much I love this game.
In Stacking you take the role of Charlie, the youngest in a family of Chimney Sweepers. His relatives are all taken away to work for the Baron, an Industry leader. Your task? To find and rescue your family, and while you’re at it, free the children that are being used in child labour by the Baron.
The game is just super charming: the visuals are pretty stunning, the nesting dolls are adorable, and they all have their own powers and personalities. You, being the youngest of your family (and thus smallest) will need to solve puzzles (how to get into and out of places, unlock stuff, etc) by getting into different dolls and using their powers to achieve your goal. You have to respect the sizes, so sometimes to solve a puzzle you have to get inside various different sizes of dolls.
What’s best about it, besides the originality of it, is that:
All the puzzles are very logical, thus making them both challenging but at the same time not impossible.
All puzzles have more than one way to solve it. Meaning you can go back and find all the other ways in which you could have solved the problem. in fact, you will definitely want to do this.
I found the humor utilized through it to be quite adorable and funny too.
The cutscenes are all made like little theater plays, and the music is just beautiful and very in tune with the game’s setting and style.
The only downside I could find to this game, though, is that the cutscenes are almost unskippable (you can actually double tap esc to skip them, but apparently that works only at certain points because most the time I just couldn't skip them).
I would definitely recommend this game to everyone, regardless of age and gender.

Deadly Shadows (the Thief series, really) is still the best atmospheric stealth game ever devised. The Cradle, twelve years later, is still one of the most memorable and stress-inducing levels ever engineered in gaming history.
And the story? Oh, the story! The politics, corruption, faiths and intrigue of the sublimely steampunk-esque City, its denizens, and gritty Garrett that are the fibers weaving the story whole, ranks among the best ever conceived in interactive fiction. And the best part of this? It's not at all heavy-handedly delivered. Through Garrett's interactions with others, his missions, wry and cynical comments, astute observations and indifferent facade, you become incredibly intimate with the goings-on in this universe as though you've always been a part of it.
I played Deadly Shadows in its entirety countless times over the years; every time, I laid not one finger upon another game till I saw Garrett come out unscathed--it's
engaging. I've never encountered anything game-breaking during play, with the original hard copy, GOG or Steam versions. Any reload done was because I'm a purist--it can happen that I miss a few bob, or inadvertently break the neck of some knocked-unconscious person when I toss them on the ground in deeper shadows. As for graphics and game play, Deadly Shadows (released in 2004!) surpasses many lauded and triple A titles of today. With exemplary voice acting and ambient sounds that will

I got this game because I had already played, and liked, Thief 2014. Unfortunately, I've heard so many fanboys giving the game a hard time. "It's nothing like the other Thief games, blah blah blah." So I decided since it was on sale I'd give one of them a try.
Visually this game was closer to what I would prefer to play, with Thief Gold coming in at a close second. So far I haven't completed the game, I'm the type who likes to attempt to look in every nook and cranny. But so far, the game is exactly what I expected. And I have absolutely no regrets in getting it. But due to the games age, there have been some minor problems when running it on my computer. Mind you, my computer is a couple of years old already, and is running Windows 8.1 if I remember correctly.
First things first, maybe it's due to the settings I have for the resolution, but when loading into a level during the loading screens it flashes to an extremely enlarged version of my desktop for a couple of seconds. So far it doesn't seem to have any effect on the the game or gameplay in general, it's just irritating and unnerving. Second, when the animation for the quest to steal the Pagans claw thing ended the game crashed. I reloaded my save and the game crashed again. I reloaded it one more time, because I really liked the game and was hoping for no more problems, and it worked.
Other things I've noticed that show the games age is the sound detection. I dropped a bottle near a door, with the intention of alerting two guys in the other room. Not only were they not alerted, but the moment I started to move away from the door they seemed to "know" someone was there. Then there's their inability to see you in the dark, even if they're inches away from you. Or one I really enjoyed, I unintentionally caught the attention of a guy in the Pagan's tunnel. But he eventually gave up looking for me, because I kept trying to "hide" behind the crate he kept running into. :') Then there's the character models, you don't notice it so much with the guys. But for whatever reason, most of the women in the stone market look like Black Market Bertha. It's a little weird.
Personally, just based off what I've experienced in this game so far, I don't think Thief 2014 is all too different. The story and characters in Deadly Shadows is way better, but the maps have the same amount of vagueness and ability to confuse and frustrate. With the newest Thief being slightly better in that regard. The loot is definitely better in Deadly Shadows, though it has a smaller variation of loot. And if I remember correctly there aren't any guaranteed designated "special loot" in Thief 2014. They both seem to have the same general feel of "free roam" looting. By that I mean you can loot this house or building on the way to your quest location, but that particular place isn't and never will be a quest location. The only difference being, if I'm not mistaken, is that there aren't random shops to loot in Thief 2014. And Deadly Shadows array of random places to loot is small. You also need to be much more careful with your use of weapons in Deadly Shadows. While you can buy more, once you run out in the middle of a quest the chances of finding more are a bit slim.
All in all, I'm really enjoying the game. I highly recommend getting the game, especially if it's on sale. If you're having any doubts about whether it'll play on your computer, because I believe some of the negative reviews have merit, check the community hub. There may be solutions there that will help.
P.S. I may have forgotten some things, or if anything changes, I will update this with that info. Though I doubt I'll be changing my recommendation.

Tower defence games are great aren't they?
If you said no, then Deathtrap, even with its unique take on the genre probably isn't going to change your mind.
Still here? then I'll assume that you agree with me....
They're fun and easy to drop in and out of when time permits, great for a quick level or two at the end of a busy day.
You fire them up, trace the path the enemy will take, find  the  choke points, plan and place your towers, hit the start button and watch wave after wave of "bad guys" get chewed up (hopefully) by your  turrets, fireballs, lighting towers etc.
Upgrade a tower here and there, increasing its range or power, maybe place a few new turrets and then take on the next level.
Rinse and repeat until you win, or if you're skill level matches my own, until you lose and try again!
At its core, that's what you'll find with Deathtrap, a competent, polished and very enjoyable tower defence game, filled with all the varying enemy, tower and trap types you could want to keep you entertain throughout it's increasingly difficult levels.
The levels in Deathtrap are divided up into islands, each island will have several waves of bad guys for you to destroy.
Should you manage to defeat the initial wave of cannon fodder  you will then get chance to spend any points you've earned by placing new towers and traps in preparation for the inevitably tougher next wave.
Stand your ground against each wave and you'll have  to face off against an end of level boss, which will likely be one tough demonic cookie to kill.
Defeat the big bad boss and it's level complete,  the next island will be open for you, but before you take on the next challenge you might want to go shopping first... (more on that later)
RPG's!
Choose your character, collect loot, equip yourself with the best armour and weapons, visit the obligatory adventurers store to sell your junk and buy new stuff, level up your abilities and maybe do a little crafting before heading into battle
That's right, they're great too!
So we've got too great and very distinct genres and as I stated earlier, at its core, Deathtrap is a tower defence game, but it's also more than that...
It's a tower defence game with a generous sprinkling of sweet RPG goodness.
Everything I mentioned above regarding the Tower defence and  RPG genres are available  to you in Deathtrap.
To be an RPG game, you need an avatar, an in game presence beyond your mouse pointer placing towers and traps and that is exactly what you'll find here.
At the start of the game you'll be given a choice of 3 character types, The Sorceress, The Mercenary and the Marksman, each with their own specialities and styles of play.
Whichever character you choose, they're yours to control in the game world as you see fit.
Wander around exploring, go on the offensive and single-handedly  blast wave after wave as they emerge or you might want to hang back and help defend your towers from the onslaught.
Did I say single-handedly blast the bad guys, that's not necessarily true.
You can also play Deathtrap online in a co-op mode or versus modes both of which are huge amounts of fun.
Deathtrap has solid visuals, you can zoom in pretty close to the action and it still looks crisp and moody, although you'll find yourself playing through the majority of the game zoomed out as far as possible to get a bead on the bad guys as they march relentlessly onwards.
If you've ever played the "Orcs Must Die" titles, you'll recall that they are tower defence games with an in game avatar too.
However, "Orcs Must Die" let you experience the world from a first person perspective.
Whilst Deathtrap also places you in direct control of your character, instead of taking the FPS approach, you'll find yourself viewing the action from a top down, isometric view.
This is a little less immediate than the first person view but this decision does make the direct intervention mechanic feel much more tactical.
What you lose in immersion by not having a first person perspective is more than made up for by a clear isometric view of the approaching bad guys which certainly makes it easier to plan your positioning strategically and get in a few long range shots.
As well as the traditional tower  defence  elements you also be taking down specific enemies located on the map (and hoping your towers can take care of the waves of monsters whilst you're wandering off the path to get to them).
These special enemies will drop keys which will open chests full of lovely loot.
You can find all the armour types you would expect in any RPG, including rings, hats, belts etc. each of which will improve your statistics and help you hang in a fight longer.
There is skill system in the game so you can not only upgrade your trap building abilities, you can also upgrade your own prowess with your weapon of choice.
There's a shop where you can buy and sell items, there are health potions, there's even a crafting system!
The  genre mash-up works surprisingly well, there's enough RPG elements to make the game feel refreshingly different without straying too far from its tower defence heart.
Deathtrap is a great game, quick to pick up and  hard to put down,  It's so addictive that I've genuinely found it difficult to stop playing long enough to write this review, and on that note, If I stop writing now I should have time for just one more wave...

An interesting game, a bit different from the norm.
Your objective is to fulfil quests, or orders for organs. You grow organs on trees, and harvest them when they are ripe. You get orders for specific quantities and qualities of organs, for example 10 average kidneys, or 10 excellent kidneys. As you fulfil different quests, you progress through the story of the game. There are animals that you can purchase (eventually) to assist with your organ harvests - frogs to speed up the water refill of the watering can, moles to increase the speed that organs appear, and so on. You can click on them to make them go to plants/where they will be useful.
So the gameplay is of clicking. You click on watering can, click on plant to water it, wait for organs to appear, click on organs to harvest, and repeat. A lot of clicking. However, this game isn't designed or intended to be skipped through quickly. You must wait for pretty much everything, click for water, click to water plants, wait for water to refill.
This means that I strongly recommend that if you are not willing to alt tab while clicking, and have better things to do with your time, don't buy the game. If you can't stand zoning out while clicking and admiring how the fruits grow, it's not a good game. Slow paced, seriously grindy since you fulfil quotas to proceed.
For all of its flaws, it's a pleasant game to play and while away some time. If you purchase this game, buy it to alt tab out of every so often, the gameplay of grindy clicking is horrible. Wait for your watering can to refill, do not watch it refill because there is little-nothing to do while you wait.
Just alt tab to water and harvest the fruits, then alt tab out. If the door to the shop starts glowing (i.e. story progression), click on it, read it, then alt tab and etc. The story is a nice read, and the soundtrack is nice too, so I'm recommending this game.
Gameplay is grindy though, so remember that alt tabbing out and back in to water plants when the watering can is full instead of watching it fill up is better. Because there's not much to distract you.

I just finished the game and I thought it deserves a review. Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is a really beautiful click-based (i'd say story rich) game with a cartoon style. The plot is quite simple: You are Organa, appentrice at Irene's Shop where you tend to the plants. But those aren't normal plants - they grow organs instead of fruits. Now you can buy several animals that help you (frogs restore water quicker, and so on) and the organs come in different qualities (not ripe, ripe, great, excellent). By completing quests you progress further into the story and also meet several very interesting characters.
As for me, the simple concept, the great art and not to forget the great soundtrack made this game so enjoyable. I usually played between 30-90 minutes per session just before going to bed. Being a collector it was very important for me that the game had Steam Achievements as well as Steam Trading Cards. I was able to get all achievements (100%) in about 16 hours of playtime, which also covered 100% of the storyline.
The normal price of 9,99€ is quite high, try to aim for any sales (e.g. Summer Sale right now as of June 2016) where the price is as low as around 3,99€. All in all the game was really enjoyable and I would recommend it to any of you at all times!

I bought the game in 2013 when the game became available, and it looked good and promising. Now, 3 years later, it is labeled "released" but is pretty much all the same we had then, sans the "good and promising" part.
The game had not much to do initially - the usual "explore, dig, fight", but was kinda bad, shallow and repetitive at the latter two. Fast-forward: still nothing to do.
One version after another devs just keep shuffling stuff around; without adding any gameplay value.  Remove hunger, add hunger. Add buffs, nerf buffs to the point you won't bother with them. Add lots of different weapons, dumb down armor mechanic so different weapons don't actually make a difference, just raw DPS. Remove asteroid bases, remove jetpacks, remove half of the techs, nerf the other half, remove crossbows, remove, remove...
Multiplayer sucks at multiplaying: most of the gameplay is legwork, and it is more rewarding to play alone, because leggin is no faster no matter the party size and you'd have to share, and you can do all that alone anyway.  Locations of interest are easy and enemies don't respawn there, so you actually spend more time finding a dungeon then running one. Some versions of combat used to work with team tactics, like front-runner with a shield covered by a gunner - I found that to work poorly in 1.0, now it's "smash and blast and shoot everything wildly".
Monsters in general are scarce and not a challenge, and underground trips are even less a challenge because mobs are stupidly easy to avoid (compare that to Terraria with teleporting, wall-passing, rainbow-spitting monsters). In fact, 1.0 has much, much, much less monsters with ranged abilities then previous version, which is distressing.
They also made a huge chunk of furniture non-printable, also a form of content degradation. Oh, and high-tiered furniture - all gone.
I may missed some more points, but it's already ridiculous enough. BORING. Stay away.

Stacking is a unique puzzle game from the creative collective that is Double Fine, and follows a tiny doll named Charlie, who sets out on a quest through a Steampunk land of stacking doll people, using their unique abilities to solve problems and save his siblings, who have been forced into child labour.
While the game doesn't offer much more than its $10 price-tag would suggest, this neat little casual puzzle-adventure has a lot more going for it than meets the eye. Using Charlie's skill of hopping inside other civilians – in the way which stacking dolls are known for –. the player must solve various puzzles to progress further and rescue his family. Each puzzles has multiple solutions, so there are multiple paths of thinking for each obstacle, and it allows for an extra challenge should a player wish to discover them all. This gameplay mode in itself makes up the majority of the story-driven aspects of the game, and is both fun and difficult in trying to find those last few solutions by thinking outside the box.
The game has other aspects to it, however, all as equally fun. Progress towards 100% completion requires more than just problem solving, as unique dolls and sets of dolls (such as a family of tourists or a magician's troupe) can be jumped into and collected, and 'Hi-jinks' can be completed, by completing unusual tasks such as shattering glass using an opera singer doll. This is fun, and entirely optional, so if one gets too frustrating, it can be skipped with little consequence towards completing the story mode of the game.
The game also has good – if cliched – writing, and an excellent visual style, especially in the quasi-2D designs of the doll characters and the environments.
However, this game is not without its faults, and there are several. If long unskippable cutscenes aren't your thing, you may want to give Stacking a pass; its cutscenes, presented in an old fashioned silent movie fashion, are numerous and can get frustrating. Despite this, the game's runtime is still rather short, and I myself reached the end of the story in only a few hours. The controls are also slightly fidgety – to take control of a doll, you have to stand in a specific spot behind it, and groups of dolls can make it difficult to select the correct one; there is also a "Highlight path" function for if you get lost, but it takes a long time to run, during which you can't move, so hitting it by mistake is equally frustrating. The camera angle is also somewhat annoying when stuck as a smaller doll such as Charlie or another child, where it swings awkwardly and focuses on the floor more often than not.
Despite these shortcomings, I do still highly recommend Stacking as a fun casual puzzler to whittle away a few hours, and is an excellent package for its price; however, if one is put off by the above-mentioned flaws, perhaps waiting for a sale would be advisable.

It's fun, but there are a few unacceptable issues. There is no volume control on the music or sound effects - so you can either have them turned ON (and very loud), or OFF. There is no explanation as to what some of the more obscure options are ("Catch Cursor"? "Sharp scale"?). These should be explained simply so players know whether to turn them off or on.
Also, the other thing that really bothers me about this game are the dog breeds that you can choose from. Husky and Malamute are fine, but Labradors? St. Bernards? Schnauzers? Worst of all, Shih-Poos? Seriously? These breeds are NOT sled dogs by any stretch of the imagination, and they kind of break my immersion in enjoying the game when I see them on the "Hire Dog" list.
The game presents itself as otherwise somewhat "realistic" otherwise - I can't hire unicorns for my team, and I can't put rockets on my sled for speed boosts, plus there are weather and track conditions that affect my run - so having completely unrealistic dog breeds on my sled team really ruins it for me. I wish there was an option to only hire sled-appropriate breeds (and there are plenty actual dog breeds to choose from that are acceptable as sled dogs).
So this game needs a few serious tweaks - some improvements to the Options menu, some more dog breeds to choose from (and the removal of the ridiculous breeds or the option to filter them out in the Hire Dog menu), and possibly some other things to do besides run races. Some simple minigames to play with your dogs inbetween races would be fantastic.
Otherwise, the game is enjoyable, and cute - a good way to spend some time, but it becomes repetitive quickly when all you can do is run races.

TL;DR: Very stylized, very fast-paced Vindictus with waifus. Approx. 12 hours of actual playtime so far, would recommend.
Before I dig into the nitty gritty, a disclaimer: My main character at the time of writing is Level 37. I cannot speak to the depth/longevity of the endgame at this point.
That being said, Kritika is an instance based, action-brawler loot-fest. The first comparison I made was to Nexon's Vindictus, but approximately 14x better. As far as I've progressed, progression is straightforward and not confusing at all. Combat is a fast paced, adrenaline-fueled ballet through the zones mobs, especially on higher difficulties. Crafting is there, and if you do the smart thing and play higher difficulty instances, you'll amass so many crafting resources from junk gear you'll be well off if you begin enhancing/crafting gear. I don't have much experience with the game's PvP offerings, but it feels similar to Blade and Soul's arena gametypes.
The cash shop seems fair at best and reasonable at the worse: Cosmetic costume pieces can be slotted with
stat bonuses on equip, but we're talking +4 points on a stat that offers +16 at half the level cap. These stats may feel "essential" for those willing to min/max a character, but this also brings me to my next point: At the time of writing, betweeen both the current leveling event and the event for leveling the new class, there's opportunities to earn a great deal of cash currency, which can be used to buy the aforementioned costumes. Ultimately, not a big deal.
Something about it keeps me coming back. My two complaints are the visuals are a bit lackluster, and the instances themselves are used in tandem a bit too often (Currently running the same "course" 4x in a row). Otherwise, if you're into brawler-esque games, Kritika is well worth your time. After repeated attempts to get into games of this genre, this is the one that hooked me.

I first played this on the Dreamcast, many years ago.  I'm pleased to say it plays nice and smooth on PC, and although the graphics were never really designed with higher resolutions in mind, they are crisp and clear so visibility isn't an issue.
I'll be honest, Trizeal doesn't make the best first impression.  As with all Triangle Service games, the first level is more of a tutorial on the scoring system and not much interesting happens.  And yeah, even 10 years ago it wasn't exactly the prettiest shooter on the block.
Get to stage 3 though and things heat up quite a bit.  By the time you get to the ending, you'll confront some interesting puzzles to work out.  Pay attention to your weapons and how to use them, and the correct path will appear.  Good luck!
The scoring system is based around medal chaining, however done mostly in short bursts of opportunity than a full-game run of perfection.  Nothing too over the top here.
The Powerup system is pretty great once you figure out how the mix and matching works.  When switching weapons, pay attention to how many items you've grabbed with that primary weapon, and how it becomes universal once you collected enough.  Experiment a bit and it'll become clear.
I'll recommend this game to players who want to spend some time learning and conquering the game.  For players that just want to load up a new game and blast stuff with instant gratification, honestly this is probably not the best game to get.

Trizeal  was initially launched in 2004 for Arcade (Sega Naomi board), in 2005 for the Dreamcast in Japan, in 2006 for the Playstation 2 in Japan and in 2009 for Xbox 360 as part of "Shooting Love 200X" collection, which brought together beyond this game other three: "Shmups Skill Test", "Minus Zero" and "Exzeal", all of them developed by Triangle Service (japanese developer founded by a former employee of Konami) and now in 2016 this game finally comes to Steam at the hands of Degica, publisher that has been noted for bring to the Steam (and thus to the whole world) many shmups (acronym for shoot' em up aka STG) previously restricted only to Japan. Trizeal Remix is ​​a beautiful vertical shmup with a fun and well balanced gameplay, where the player's ship at the touch of a button can be transformed into three different modes: [Wide], where the field of shots is wide, making it easier to hit multiple enemies; [Missile] where guided missiles are fired at enemies, being useful to hit enemies out of the ship's front range [laser] fires a direct and focused beam and is the most powerful shooting and consequently indicated to defeat enemies faster. During the game, you will collect some "orbs" that allow the upgrade of weapons, at the point of being possible to mix into a certain transformation the characteristics of another, for example, missiles with shot wide, laser with shot wide and etc., making the gameplay very interesting. Trizeal's graphics were pretty good for its time and are still pleasant even today. The game's soundtrack is nice and very pleasant to hear. The controls respond well to commands (I used the official wireless Xbox 360 controller through the analog stick). The player can save replays of matches and the game also has an online leaderboard very good where you can watch the replay of other players  inside the leaderboard, something always useful for those who want to know and learn the patterns and techniques used by the best players. It's your job to keep them alive as best you can and nit together whatever supplies and equipment you're able to until eventually you *hopefully* get them into a legitimate fighting force.
It's a gritty game that joins the genres of everything that you think is cool if you find yourself already looking at this game.

First of all the comparisons to other games made in some of the user reviews are just absolutely ridiculous. Don't be mislead by them. Basically the game consists of the open world part and the tactical battles.
The open world part is in my opinion underdeveloped and offers so very little that it is hardly worth mentioning, which is fine for me because I bought it for the battles. But it is important to know that, because if you are looking for RPG elements (i.e. dialogue options/politics/story line in a medieval setting) and discovery you honestly wont find it here - yet at least. It could be improved in future updates of course and there is great potential but it is just not realized yet.
The battlesystem suffers from a couple of flaws that really hurt it badly. For example the fatigue system, which severly limits the actions your soldiers can take. There is a good selection of weapons which provide different abilities and also gadgets like throwing nets, so in theory there are many interesting options in battle. But in reality, your soldiers can only take one or two actions and even less as the battles progresses because they get fatigued. And these actions absolutely count because the game is quite challenging, so you will realize very quickly that from those many interesting options only very few are actually viable. In my opinion this is a balance issue. To illustrate what I mean here is an example: as the game progresses enemies will have increasingly heavy armor. Of all the weapons in the game only some are efficient in dealing with heavy armor. This automatically makes the other weapons less attractive.
Also the hit chances are generally quite low and the RNG in this game is just a ♥♥♥♥♥. Obviously this is where the whole 'git gud' thing starts. I play a lot of turn-based tactical and rogue-like games, so I have a very high tolerance for RNG. But in Battle Brothers it is a problem for me, because unless you want to reload over and over and over again (which I hate and thats why I generally choose Iron Man Mode but I would never play it in this one) you will very quickly figure out and only play one specific tactic that I wont spoil here. So unlike other games, because youre options are so limited as described above, you can do very little to manage the RNG and that is why I am frustrated where as usually I am not.
So over all the combat feels restrictive, frustrating and boring since you have to stick to very few actually viable ways of doing things. It might be better in easy mode but I doubt it. Again, great portential but not quite realized. This might be easier to fix though.
I really like the idea of the game and I appreciate the effort that went into it, but I honestly cannot recommend it especially for that price.

Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is a comfy farming game with a good story to back it up.
TL;DR: It's worth picking up if you're interested, but gameplay is repetitive and it's more of a visual novel with a clicker mini-game. The game takes about 15-20 hours to complete, depending on the player.
Story: 7/10
Gameplay: 5/10
Graphics: 6/10
Without going too far into it, in Forget Me Not, you're an assistant to the owner of a shop that sells fresh-grown organs. You water the trees, and organs grow. The gameplay is simple, if grindy, so it's easy to pick up. In my opinion, it's a good game to wind down with, whether you need a break from more exciting games or if you need to kill some time. It's heavy on clicking, though, so if that isn't your thing the gameplay is going to bother you.
The graphics are pleasing to the eye and relatively simple. Cutscenes are more like slideshows, but it works well for this game and the artstyle. No flashing lights, no bells and whistles, it does what it needs to. It may just be that I haven't played enough games that use graphics like this, but it made the game more comfy and fit the atmosphere well, and I appreciate simple graphics from time to time.
The story is the only thing stopping this game from being filed into the "time-wasting clicker" genre, and is, in my opinion, the major selling point of the game. The story follows Organa, an assistant to the owner of an organ shop. At certain points during gameplay, you can head into the shop to view a cutscene and get more work orders to fill, and sometimes new equipment/trees. Many of the cutscenes were endearing, and had messages to impart to the player. The "main story" arc, however, carries a tone different than what the atmosphere for the game would otherwise suggest. The true ending actually managed to surprise me without making me do mental gymnastics to understand how it happened.

It could make you really boring and tired after several hours of playing, when there're only few story events to "take a rest". Starbound. The sandbox for people who, just about had it with sandboxes.
Everything's a retro game now, huh indie developers. No more contrast, just pixelate my chode to hell and back. You could of at least tried to make it look retro with 256 colors, but that's almost too much to ask for. Nevermind that this is a Terraria sandbox clone, it's the idea of a sandbox without any reason to do things people normally do in sandbox games like exploring or building. Starbound takes most minecraft knockoffs to their logical conclusions. It's the game for people who want a sandbox, but they want a story, quests, blatant hand holding, they don't want anything difficult. Starbound: it's as exciting as consensual sex.
It's the only sandbox available that struggles to introduce any groundbreaking innovations. That would be fine if the 1.5 gigabytes of content was innovative and mechanic improving, but it has less innovations than minecraft in its current state. The 1.5 gigabytes is more of a mixture things most content mods add in. Which is more furniture,  more furniture, more furniture, more furniture, and more furniture. In a sense it follows minecraft when it was first released, innovative, but as time goes on, the creativity dies and we get what would be considered mod content. When often criticized, most people will tell you that "Mods will fix it." while turning a blind eye to the stacks of furniture that would of been made in mods anyways. Besides, buying a game to mod it is like buying a broken car at full price to fix it. Starbound is a broken and unfinished game that had to be released because it missed all of its deadlines since development started in 2012.
Another thing they also pulled off was poor communication between customers on steam who had to wait years for a disappointing furniture update. Chucklefish begged for forgiveness while spouting that the customers were ignorant because they could of went to the developer website if they wanted to see what was going on. The failure to post news on steam like other reputable developers is not unlike the the trajectory of the early access game development. Chucklefish already has money from selling an incomplete game to their customers. Absolutely no reason to actually finish it when you've already got the money, absolutely no reason to treat our customers nicely because the refunding period has expired. The loyal fans would just lick our feet anyways.
Chucklefish should of been talking with the people on steam and listening to criticism so they could improve their game. After all, it has been in early access for some time now. But we find that's to much to ask for when they present us with more furniture after paying and waiting. In the same way Billy in the office masturbates all day rather than doing his work, up until the day he finally gets caught because the project manager wants to know what the hell was going on with Billy because the official launch of the game was, like always, bugged and unfinished. Chucklefish should have gotten the hint that they needed to work on their game, but instead, they thought it would be a cool idea to censor criticisms on the forums and delude themselves into thinking they were doing just fine.
But nope, lets have this. This is solid proof that indie developers are incapable of getting anything done. AAA developers will see this and promptly take over the market with a shiny new sandbox in less than a year once they figure out what people want to play. Speaking of which, when is the next minecraft update going to come out, I want more furniture for my blocky house.
It has a collection of races included in it as a selling point, probably to appeal to the tumblr turd crowd because muh multiculturalism. Unfortunately, ever since they shoehorned them in at the very beginning of development, it made them feel forced in because they didn't really offer any good reason to play as one race or another. I mean, yeah you get race specific furniture, but there is really nothing else to it. For now, I guess they were merely placeholders because they wanted to do something big and innovative with them, but didn't have the discipline to follow through with their ideas. Whatever their idea was back then, it is gone now because they have actually reduced races into a purely aesthetic element, giving absolutely no other reason to pick a different race.
By the time they raised millions of dollars on kickstarter and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it all away before failing to meet deadline and release a steaming hunk of♥♥♥♥♥♥ any hope of Chucklefish doing something cool for once had lost all kinetic energy. If terraria is a symbol of what a sandbox could be if the developers tried through original gameplay ideas, then Starbound, is a letter of resignation for the obnoxious business of doing an honest day of work.

Good mechanics, catchy music, and an art style that's easy on the eyes make this quite the addicting little game! Even though it seems simple at first, there are lots of different things that factor into races that make each one a challenge - especially when adding new dogs to your team or placing up in a higher league. There's more strategy involved than I first realized as well! As fun as this game is, though, I found it fairly easy, and after roughly 5 hours of gameplay I've managed to go as far as I possibly can with my current team. Despite that, this game is definitely worth the price, and I have high hopes that more things will be implimented before it leaves early access.
Pros:
+ You have to interact/race with each individual dog to learn and unlock their quirks; the perfect dog just insn't handed to you (although more traits are visible when buying dogs in higher leagues)
+ The dogs have personalities and can have rapport with teammates!
+ Races truly seem randomized, don't think I've encountered the same course twice
+ Weather and snow conditions affect the race!
+ Refreshing breeds available. Never thought I'd see a Shih-poo or Schnauzer in a dog sled race!
+ Lots of different fault, skills, and other quirks each dog can have
+ Neat color choices for harnesses/names/accents for each dog
Cons:
- Not very many breeds to choose from. Yes, there are 10 "different" dogs altogether, but three of those are just different colors of husky, not individual breeds. Greenland Dogs, American Eskimos, Alaskan Huskies, Pointers, Chows, Mutts even - there are plenty more breeds that are apt for racing that I'd love to see included!
- You can't return/resell dogs once they're acquired. I feel like this would be a very good thing to add to the game, especially once you get to the higher leagues and find you have 12 dogs or so, five of which you don't race anymore because they have undesirable faults that keep you from winning a race. I hate seeing dogs "rot" away in the cabin with no use.
- Only one save file. I know I personally would explore the game much more if I had three or so files to have different teams in!
- No real plot/objectives. Race. Add dogs to your team to qualify for higher leagues. Then what? What happens after league seven? What else is there to do at Firebowl Kennels (not sure if correct name)? Winning race after race and sitting on over 200k with no end goal in mind gets boring after a while.

This game might be good or it might be bad. I honestly couldn't tell you because it was my first stealth game and it astonished me for that reason alone. I haven't had that same experience again, despite playing many stealth games since. (Splinter Cell, Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, Thief I, Thief II, Thief:2014, Dishonored, Betrayer, Styx, some Metal Gear...) Hell, after I played this game I was so infatuated with the genre of stealth that I tried to stealth through Fallout 3. I still find myself trying to stealth through bits of games that are clearly not going to let me (RAGE). It was a good game for me, because I dream of exploring and stealing while staying unseen. And I didn't know it until I played this game. So I love this game.
This game permits both knocking everyone out and going undetected, or leaving everyone alive and going undetected, or leaving everyone alive and not using any items and still going undetected with a lot of quicksaving. The game's stealth is based upon light-levels, sound-levels, and line-of-sight. (mostly light-levels) This is my favorite type of stealth so far. The way you determine alert levels is by observing guard behaviour and listening to guard voice lines. I prefer this to flashing icons. (!) Early game items are useful for the length of the game. Late game items are not necessary to complete the game. (I believe?) The storyline is mostly glue to hold the levels together. The levels are memorable, and your individual encounters with guards will be memorable. It is awkward and broken and gimmicky and clunky and awful, but I still love it.
Here's a water arrow. It's all you need. Keep to the shadows Taffer. Be crafty, be careful, be foolhardy but most of all, be concealed.

The best parts of playing this game were just seeing how clever many of the solutions were, and how much thinking and poking around it really takes. Pure and simple, some of the solutions are so impossibly out there that it ruins the experience in many ways. $5 may be alot to play a puzzle game with some insanely out there solutions (mainly alot of the later endings). If you're one of the people who love sitting at a computer staring at an unchanging screen until you have eureka moments, I would get this game. If you dont mind paying $5 for a really unique and insanely hard 'puzzle' game, this wont be a bad purchase. Beyond that, I would give this game a wide berth. Its out there, and sometimes nonsensical solutions really started to wear me down and ruin what fun I could have had with this game.

Props to the developers for not copping out with Early Access or pre-order bonuses (in fact, you couldn't even pre-order the game at all). It takes a lot of faith and confidence in the quality of your own product to take the route Defiant chose. They deserve the utmost respect for that.
It's rare that we get actual proper sequels these days, upping the ante as far as Hand of Fate 2 does. For a quick comparison, think The Witcher 3 over The Witcher 2 and you get the idea. HoF2 expands and improves on the unique predecessor in absolutely every way you can imagine.
The visuals and sound design is something you can and should expect to get a boost. And the developers don't disappoint. The music que playing every time you successfully complete an adventure is legitimately epic.
But then you have things like the vastly superior combat, with smooth animations and a sense of weight. Additional gameplay mechanics spice up the variables to consider; everything from enemy types, mini bosses, AI companions you can bring along for support and weapons and gear unlocking new abilities. My perhaps biggest gripe with the original was how the combat felt stiff and unresponsive, and rapidly started feeling like a monotonous chore. I am so happy they've worked hard to improve this! The end result is better than I could possibly have hoped before playing the game myself.
During the quests outside of combat, you'll also find a good bunch of improvements. The variety of quests and encounters is upped to 11. You'll never get too settled in before some new mechanic jumps out of the woodwork to whack you outside the comfort zone.
One thing I find to be a big improvement is how there now are more ways to offset the luck factor of the chance cards. You rarely now feel like you died because the game cheated you. You're much more in control of what's going on. Some might find the sequel to be less difficult for it (in the beginning), but I personally find it much more enjoyable now, with less chance of frustrating resets due to some unlucky card draw. You'll still be challenged, you'll still die. But it's more on your own terms now, because you took a risk greater than you could handle, etc.
The new map system gives you a better sense of progression as you push ever further into the campaign. Every quest feel more connected now, not as disjointed as before. It's a great addition I didn't even know I wanted, but I wouldn't have it any other way after I've now experienced it.
Then, there are minor tweaks like the removal of food consumption when backtracking onto cards you've already explored, the ability to visit your camp to consume food to regain health between fights, customizing the look of your character, each newly acquired piece of gear being treated to a quick introductory "cutscene" as you equip it for the first time during combat and so on. Things that on their own seem small, but together add so much more to the overall experience.
There are nitpicks of course - you can't ever make a perfect game. Having both sprint and evade mapped to the same button, for instance, feels unintuitive and unnecessary. And there are a good few typos that could've easily been avoided with a bit more QA. But these are minor things that barely detract from the overall experience, which is just fantastic.
I can imagine that Hand of Fate 2 - much like The Witcher 3 for CD Projekt Red - is the game Defiant Development always wanted to make, but only now had the chance to put the idea to life in a way that does it justice. And for the offensively low asking price, they've succeeded and then some.
If you played the original and found an iota of entertainment in it, I'd say this is a no-brainer. Furthermore, if you haven't played the original but enjoy roguelites that focus a lot on exploration, storytelling and loot, then you can't go wrong here. Easily worth picking up.

It's tempting to write "Deathtrap is Diablo with tower defence mechanics, only less mobile phone than that sounds", stick a score at the end, then walk away. There's not a whole lot more description you need for Deathtrap, but it is deeper than the description might imply
There's very little story to speak of. Demons are seeping in to our world, and you must stop them before they reach our portal. There is lore, but the way it's presented makes it feel like nothing more than flavour. It does work hard to set the tone though, the designs look the part, the levels suitably ancient and dank.
The gameplay is the important part of Deathtrap. You control a warrior in the world, with Diablo style hotkeys and cool downs, and can drop traps on set locations. You can level your character up, buy, find, and craft armour and weapons. There's stat boosts, equipment that can increase your perks etc. It's very action rpg. Enemies spawn from gates, with each new wave usually adding a new gate to occupy your thoughts.
Enemies follow a set route, which can change between rounds, making placement of traps important. At the start of each round you have a set number of ‘essence’ to spend on traps, with set locations where you can place them. As you level up traps will start to cost you less and you’ll be rewarded with more essence, depending on which perks you pick. Over the course of each wave you’ll earn more essence to spend on the next wave, or, if you’re struggling, mid-fight, although this can leave you in trouble for the next onslaught.
As you might be able to tell, Deathtrap is a pretty simple game that’s a bit of a nightmare to explain when you get to the minutiae. It’s tempting to say that there’s not a lot more to it, and certainly I didn’t delve in as much as I could have, but what makes the game fun is the small stuff. Your use of powers in battle is hugely important, it obviously depends which character and which skills you pick, but playing as the fighter one of my skills was to boost the power of a trap for a period of time. My tactic became to wait for a horde of enemies to head towards a ground trap, power that trap up, then position myself in the way, aggroing them, keeping them there so they were taking extra damage from the trap. I then began to couple that with other spells, the one that gave me extra essence for killing enemies, and a continuous AOE attack that increased the damage enemies were taking. This 30 second blast of attacks was designed to help me out with the next wave, letting me buy and improve my traps.
Where Deathtrap falls down a little is in its depth. There’s actually a lot there, with around 15 levels, all with multiple scenarios, and a level cap of, I think, 100 (I was getting up to about 20 when I finished the game). You only get points to spend on upgrading your traps on the first time beating a level/difficulty/scenario, which is understandable but it causes a couple of problems. You can redistribute your skills for the price of some gold, which you'll have an awful lot of, with very little to spend it on (similarly I never got to the point where the crafting was useful), and you can scrap and rebuild traps during levels. However, I still ended up playing levels where I'd built everything I possibly could, with a wave or so left to play. Something to do with that extra essence would be nice.
There's skills in the game where spending a point on them will incrementally improve something, a nice idea, but given how limited upgrade points are even at the point where I’d finished the game, dropping 10 points to get a 3% chance of some bonus just never seemed like a worthwhile spec. If you're going to play through everything in the game then sure, but there were a few occasions in the game where I found myself falling back on the same tactics, the same skills and the same perks.
For £15 there's a ridiculous amount of content in Deathtrap. You may well use the same tactics on each map, not delving in to the minutiae of respecing, never playing the alternative scenarios, and you’ll still comfortably get your money’s worth. Deathtrap is a game that’s done no favours by a written description. Because of the price it’s hard to be too critical that it’s lacking the gloss of a proper story and a more involved campaign, but it still manages to be compulsive enough that I was squeezing games in before work, rushing things to make time between commitments, Deathtrap is a good game, and one hopefully that gets built on

Better than MANY other Early Access games.  The survival is well done.  Plants regrow in a few hours game time, which I thought was broken, but since other resources do not grow back you will still need to travel to new islands to continute building and progressing -- so it balances out.

Horror/Survival games are fun, but I find myself getting lost in trying to kill zombies or finding a house I can bunker down in and make my home.  Stranded Deep Is one of the first games that actually made me want to create my own home on my own island.  This is a game you can quickly become immersed in.  There is no HUD to make it feel like a game, just a handy wrist watch that, until you break your arm, is easy to see :)
Right now, Stranded Deep lacks an "End Game" but that is coming later... however, that only maginfies the sinking feeling that help is NEVER coming (for now), and that you need to survive incase that day ever arrives.
Final review: EASILY a $20 game AS IS.  The fact that it is $14.99 is great, and if you can find this on sale for under $10, GRAB IT!

Have to say I'm really glad this game got localized.
Something this quirky would normally be overlooked in favor of the generic dating sim of the week.  The atmosphere is what really sold me.  The setting is a bit sinister and horrific, but all painted over by bright, peaceful cheer, and that dichotomy of peace with a sense of something being very wrong is very engaging.  The music was really enjoyable (my favorite track was the loading screen bells), though sparse, since you spend most of your time in a garden which ends up rather crowded and noisy!  The story is quiet and minimalistic, and you get the sense that while the story segments all involve individual customers, you're really just being introduced to another world in bits and pieces.  This is appropriate, given you are an apprentice who doesn't really know much of anything!  In that atmospheric 'what is this place' sense, I am most reminded of another visual novel, "Sekien no Inganock -what a beautiful people-", which is also recommended if you can get it.
Then we get to the gameplay.  No lie, it seems the weakest part of the experience at first.  This is a farming game which would be at home on a cell phone.  You water plants, wait for them to ripen, then harvest.  As you go through the cycle, the plants and implements you use for this task level up and progress.  You can buy critters to speed things up a bit, but they also require some poking and prodding to do their job until they level up themselves!  It is a test of patience.  Your fruit won't grow fast enough, and your water can never fills quickly enough, and now you have to click on those darn frogs to get them back to work, and you always want more more more, faster faster faster.  Until you give up and just go at the pace of the game.  Once I stopped trying to micro-manage the critters constantly and maximize my crop speed, what was initially a stressful impatient mid-game magically transformed into a relaxing activity!  Meditative, almost.
This is a clicker game that teaches zen; it's okay to let go, everything will happen in it's own time.  You don't have to make sure every newt and butterfly are on point, or that you optimize your crop to the nth degree.  It will all work out.  By the end game, the process is a little grindy, but if you're in the relaxation zone it doesn't feel like a bad thing, and you can learn little tricks with bonus stuff called sap to move things along.

A resource management, clicker, visual novel game, my, oh my.  And believe it or not in this game these three genres work well together.
Definitely not the usual type of resource management game since one plays as Organa, apprentice to Irene, the owner of a body organ shop who Organa calls Master.  Organa works in the greenhouse behind the shop growing and cultivating (on trees) body organs: kidneys, hearts, stomachs, livers, and colons (intestines).  As the organ trees grow, they level up (top level 100).  As they grow the organs becomes better quality: average, great, excellent.  Of course Organa is tasked with filling orders of certain quantities of each organ from customers of the shop.  Every chapter introduces a new organ and the sixth chapter is an ending.  The credits roll and Organa can return to shop to complete unfinished tasks and gets a whole set of new ones.  This after story gaming is basically for that visual novel "true" ending, and for achievement hunters and completionists since this part is a grind.  A very easy grind, but still a grind.  Also in this after the (first) ending part is the merchant storyline.
Now back to the resource management, clicker, visual novel parts.
As a resource management game, this game is definitely different just in concept alone: body organs on trees.  Plus this is a vertical first person point of view versus a horizontal third person point of view.  Very different.  Fairly easy as far as gameplay goes but some strategy is involved.  Note:  Excellent organs are only able to be created once the tree levels up past a certain point.  Also the player ends up with a meat grinder which also needs to be leveled up.  Leveling occurs though gameplay so the game is not a grind, and though everyone differs, when the game started to feel like a grind for me, some thing occurred such as getting a greenhouse watering system or a meat rake or new tasks to do.  Plus upon completion of certain tasks the player needs to go chat with "Master" Irene, the boss.  This nicely breaks up that grind feel.  Also any time the door in the greenhouse becomes highlighted the player can go to the front and speak with Irene, for information (about animal helpers), task upgrades (watering system and meat rake), or simply to get more things to do (customer orders).
As clickers go I really have no comparison since I generally do not play clickers, but in this game, the player clicks of the organs at the appropriate time to get the desired quality and quanity needed for the task. Plus the player needs to click of the watering can to water the trees.  Now add to that 6 different helpers that need clicked on to encourage them to do their task since they tend to wander about at first while learning their task.  The helpers are toads, moles, woodpeckers, butterflies, lizards and homunculi all tasked with something different to speed along the watering and growing processes.  Later in the game, tree sap comes into play and quickly promotes growth and higher quality body organs.  (This is a strategic tool.)
For the visual novel part, there are 7 storylines plus Irene/Organa's storyline.  Each one has dark undertones and are a bit sinister in nature.  They border on the line of horror, in fact.  The 7 storylines come from the different customers who come to the store wanting and asking for different organs or ground up meat.  There is the boy and his doll, the girl and her cat, the stout (feret) family, the doctor, the boy, the quiet villager, the witch and the lady in black.  Organa makes comments at the beginning of each chapter and occassionally while she is working.  At the end of each chapter Irene has tea with her friend and they chat a bit.   No story segment is very long, and is clicked through manually.  (That is faster then having to reset the 'auto' talk feature each time.)
Warning:  There is NO AUTO-SAVE.  So make sure to save the game before exiting.
Overall, an interesting and for me at least a quite addicting game to play.

An extremely hyped game that boils down to this:
1) Go to a settlement and accept a contract for your mercenary band (you can't have more than one active contract at a time)
2) Do what the contract says (go there and kill that, alternatively go there and take this with you)
3) Go back to the settlement where you've accepted the contract, collect your payment and sell the loot
4) Use the money to hire more mercenaries for your warband and upgrade the equipment of your mercenaries
5) Rinse and repeat
My 18 hour experience of the game consisted solely of these 5 steps.
You will occasionally run into a random event like encountering a wanderer on the roads who tells you some stuff that doesn't effect gameplay or two of your mercenaries may end up in a fist fight and one receives a minor wound for one ingame day. I've never had any random event that influenced my plans in any way, nor do I think that there is any.
The "influence system" is one of the most hyped things - and I don't get what there's to hype about. There are a dozen or so settlements on the map and three major "houses" that own these settlements (about 4 each). If you do jobs for a settlement or a house, you increase your influence with said settlement or house. If you do something to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off, you'll lose influence with them. That said, even when I reached the maximum influence level with a settlement or a house, the effects where underwhelming at best. A settlement may have better prices for you "on average", but random events, that effect settlements and don't have anything to do with your influence, are much stronger when it comes to prices. You will have better prices in a settlement that is under the effect of a positive random event although you have only "neutral" influence on it than you will have in another settlement, with which you are "very friendly", but which is not effected by a positive random event. Random events that influence settlements happen very often, so it may be that you will have slightly better prices on average in settlements with which you have a high influence level, but that difference will be minimal. All in all, the influence system is another thing you don't need to care about.
You move your warband in real time over the strategy map but play in turn-based mode when it comes to battle. The battle system is okay. You have to keep an eye on the ammo of your ranged fighters, your equipment may break, different enemies are prone to different tactics and so on. All in all not bad. That said, I steamrolled the game with a setup consisting of 3 archers, 1 standard bearer and the rest of my men used shields/spears. Spear wall is op. The RNG has way to much impact on the outcome though.
The (few short) stories you get to read while playing are nicely written. The sound is unobtrusive. I've encountered only one bug and it wasn't game-breaking. I had no crashes.
You can't raid settlements, can't conquer lands or any kind of structures, can't own a headquarter. There's no diplomacy system except for that influence thingy I've mentioned above which is neglectable. There are no quests or quest lines, except for the contracts you take (go there, kill that, finished). There's no character or group development in a roleplaying sense, only raising stats and picking perks. Take a look at the five steps that I've listed at the beginning of the review and know that's what you will do for the entire time.
Overall I would hesitantly recommend to buy Battle Brothers IF you can get it at a hefty discount as 28 € is waaaaay to much for a game that has nothing new or special to offer and could easily be a mobile port. 10 € would be fair IF...
...IF...
...they wouldn't have messed up the ending. That is: There is no ending. The devs obviously (and erroneously) thought that their game has enough to offer to be considered an open-end sandbox game like Mount&Blade and the like. Of course it's not. Repeating the five steps that I've mentioned at the beginning over and over and over again (there is literally nothing else to do) doesn't make this game a new Mount&Blade. Not even close. It took me 18 hours of grind to finally give in and look up in Google how the game is supposed to end...and then it comes out that there is no end. What kind of bad joke is this? Of course you see some progress with forming your warband and so on, but that progress gets smaller and smaller and there literally is nothing "big and exciting" that waits for you. There are so called late game crisis, but you don't have that much effect on them and basically they just mean a temporary change in the composition of enemies you have to fight. The crisis will end sooner or later, no matter if you've been digging your nose or fighting for your life.

Not sure if I can add anything extra to 93% of 2048 positive reviews :) There's not much to say other than the game is hands down amazing. I'll try to describe why I loved it though and why I strongly recommended it to all of my real-life friends that enjoy turn-based games.
Disclaimer: I got the key for free.
Battle Brothers has recently left early access, thus marking a full-featured release of long-developed game. Battle Brothers is a mix of a management game / turn-based strategy game where you lead a band of mercenaries in (somewhat) randomly-generated fantasy world. The campaign sets a defined goals that you need to reach, but it’s up to you how you prioritize them. First and foremost: the game is narrative based, expect to read a lot of background stories about your mercenaries, detailed quest discussions. Despite that, it does not really get annoying: if you want to skip the bios of your soldiers and quest texts while just enjoying combat/management – you can do that too.
-	Great tactical combat with lots of depth: there are a lot of factors that can influence how the combat goes: troop morale, wounds / status effects, terrain. The positioning matters: you want your units to be placed on higher ground for better chance to win.
-	Lots of content: a lot of places to explore, cities to visit, treasures to find and fights to fight.
-	Captivating narrative: there are stories all around you, each one of your squad members have a story and random generator is really doing a good job in creating a believable narratives.
-	Most importantly, the game is just fun to play. The story telling aspects, combined with spectacular turn-based combat and lots of mercenary customization option makes a great mix of game mechanics, essentially bringing us an amazing game.
-	The tutorial is not nearly enough. To become somewhat good at the game in combat – you’ll need to watch videos (at least I needed to do it). Not a huge problem, because in this type of games, there’s so much to do that it’s hard to get into how things work at first.
-	No way to compare items: you need to check manually what your mercenary is wearing before equipping the item.
-	As with most of the team-management games, after you get a lot of people – it becomes really hard to manage them. You need to equip your mercenaries, make sure to choose the right stats / perks, which can get tedious after a while (especially if you have close to 20 people in your squad).
Battle Brothers is a perfect example of Early Access game done right: since the time early access started, the game has seen a lot of patches based on user feedback. In the end we get mature, finished product that is very engaging. With the text adventures comparable to Sunless Sea and mercenary management comparable to Mount and Blade – you get a fun mix of both, wrapped in a deeply thought-out turn-based gamplay. If you enjoy playing turn-based / tactical rpg games, this game is not to be missed.

For balance I guess, as some of the old techs were a bit redundant, but I still miss the ability to use them, even if I rarely did.  I've already seen several mods aimed at 'fixing' things like this though, bringing back old stuff.  Similarly there were dungeons and biomes taken out during development as Chucklefish tried to balance the breadth and depth of the game.  Overall I think they did a fine a job, and I only miss some of this stuff because I had seen it before.
Oh, and combat isn't that hard also could be a pro or a con depending on your perspective I guess.  Mostly it comes down to enemy AI not being great, so as long as you level up your equipment as new tiers unlock you'll probably be fine.  I've died more times from accidentally missing a jump or grappling hook swing than enemy attacks.
Finally, Starbound is more like a light sci-fi fantasy than hard science fiction.  The presence of things like "high tech" staffs and wands that essentially cast spells might irk those that prefer hard sci-fi settings.
The story is cliche and forgetable.  In fact the lore of the Starbound universe was much more interesting when there was no real story missions, and you just had to figure things out by finding and reading codex entries, or talking to NPCs, or just by having your character look at something and seeing how they reacted to it.  Having beat the story I've actually destroyed every plot related item I could in an effort to not accidentally remind myself of it.
I recommend Starbound to those who like exploring and building.  I don't recommend it for those that need a great story in their games.

The game is split into two parts; first part is where you pick and add your own cards to a challenge's deck to try and overcome them, and the second part is encounters that features "Freeflow" (Arkham) brawler combat. I'll review the parts separately, because while I like the former, I hate the latter.
The deckbuilding is rather straightforward. You build up your collection of cards as you overcome the challenges; by collecting tokens from the cards, which unlock new cards for you to choose from. There are a few card categories for you to choose from; companions, encounters, equipment, and supplies. Encounters can vary from quest chains to simple one-offs, from combat to gambits and more. Equipment is what you'd expect; by adding an equipment card, you give yourself a chance to obtain the said item. Supplies are cards that you start the game with, and can be resources, equipment, or blessings.
There are a few gambits that you may encounter on your travels; precision, dice, chance card and wheel gambits. Chance card gambit is more of a perception check, you need to pay attention if you want to win. For dice gambits you roll a 3d6 and try to pass a goal. In wheel gambits, you pick a card as the wheel rotates. In precision gambits you try to stop a pendulum at a right moment, and this is by far the worst among the bunch for me as my reaction times are abysmal.
After selecting a challenge, you add your own cards to the deck. Your primary goal is to make best use of what you have to beat a challenge, while trying to also include cards with tokens so you can unlock even more to pick from in the future. Encounters are usually self-contained, but it's the gains you get from them that drives you forward. Each challenge has its own set of dealer cards, and its difficulty comes from these cards. Does a challenge has a card that gives you a curse? How about you bring a card that removes a curse? It is this part of the game that makes it unique; adding your own cards to overcome the hand you're dealt with, defeat the Hand of Fate.
If you fail a challenge, you have to start over. With each restart, you are presented with a different layout. These two alone brings the term, "roguelite" to my mind. But it is more of a flavor; the real meat of the game is rather the unique deckbuilding. You also have a few resources that you need to manage; life, food, gold and fame. Different encounters may provide another use for these resources, but to simply explain them, food keeps you going, gold allows you to trade, fame allows you to equip items, and life is life.
However in my opinion, the quality of challenges go down rapidly as you progress though them. Most challenges focus on something, and end up overusing it. This is one of my main beefs with this game, whereas in the first one you added your own flavor to a deck with your own cards, and played through a challenge with relative ease, in this one you are somewhat forced to use very specific cards in order to have a chance at victory.
For the first game, Hand of Fate, I overlooked the combat and tried to focus on the rest of the game. I overlooked it because for me the real meat of that game was in the cards. I'm sad to say this but it hasn't improved
. I
hate the combat. It's not because I dislike "Freeflow" combat, it's the opposite. The beauty of this system shines when it is smooth. However, when it is executed poorly (twice, I might add), it is only a source of disappointment.
The freeflow combat features simple mechanics that can be expanded upon. For example, at its core, enemies have a normal and a heavy attack, each having its own visual warning with a different color. Against normal attacks, dodging, countering and interrupting (by hitting them first) are your options. Against heavy attacks, your only option is to dodge them. However, Hand of Fate II fails even at implementing these properly, and has a lot of contradictions. For example, you can interrupt the heavy attack of some enemies.
It also expands the combat by giving enemies a counter-attack. I think the idea behind counter-attacks is to keep you alert. If you focus on an enemy and attack it repeatedly, the enemy will do a counter-attack. It can be a normal or heavy counter-attack. However, the normal counter-attacks differ from the normal attacks; you cannot interrupt the normal counter-attacks, even though they are supposed to be interruptible. The way it is executed just creates a(nother) contradiction, as it uses the same visual clue even though it isn't exactly the same. It should('ve) use(d) a different one.
The freeflow combat also has a some sort of "Mob AI" to keep the gameplay as smooth as possible for the player. For example, only a certain number of enemies can attack you at a given time. However, with the added counter-attacks in this game, more enemies than the allowed amount (one) can attack you at the same time. This sometimes results in getting hit unfairly if you can and try to counter it; you can only counter one of them and the other hits you.
Another thing that the freeflow does to keep the combat as smooth as possible is, when you are doing or start doing a special attack (like finishers or abilities), enemies that are already attacking you stand down if they can, if they cannot do so you simply don't get hit. While this game has something like the latter, it feels like a coin flip everytime it happens, as sometimes the damage registers, and sometimes not.
Dodging has its own share of problems. I lost count of how many times I got hit while trying to dodge. Especially against normal counter-attacks, dodging will usually result in you getting hit. Sometimes the attacks don't look like it's going to hit, yet the enemies
towards you and still hit you unfairly while looking stupid. Sometimes enemies lock onto you, and even if you get away or dodge, they still manage to hit you. You usually end up getting hit unfairly, as if game is trying to punish you for taking an action that you were supposed to.
I liked the first game, even with the flaws in its combat. For this game, I was able to do the same for a while. However, instead of focusing on what the first game was good at (the cards, and the deckbuilding), this one feels like the strength of the game comes from somewhere else, as the challenges start to shove combat encounters in your face over and over. And when it is not combat, it is gambits over and over. It feels like there is nothing else in the game; proper
text based encounters feel sparse. Probably they are not, but overusing other types of encounters make me feel that way. It changes the general tone of the game as you further progress in it.
I hope this game's combat will get better in time, I really do because it is simply unique. However looking at where the first game started from, and where it ended up, I'm not too optimistic about combat to be honest; they developed a sequel yet didn't iron out some of the issues that the first game had. But the rest; the art, the music (soundtrack is exceptional), the graphics, the cards are all there and/or interesting, but late game balance and combat gameplay ruins it all for me.
It is the enjoyment I get from a game that sets its value for me. If you had issues with the combat from the first game, or didn't play it but dislike bad implementations of freeflow combat, I don't think you'll enjoy this game that much. If you don't like freeflow combat at all, or cannot stomach the bad implementations of it, you won't enjoy this game. I can only recommend this game to those who had played and throughly enjoyed the first game.

Bad news first: I've taken off 1 point from a perfect score because of slight flaws. Although the combat was generally improved, the targeting and camera controls can sometimes still feel a bit unresponsive. Also, the Dealer seemed to be a stronger character when he was purely your adversary; it's slightly less fun to hate him now that he's technically on your side as your trainer. But don't worry; unlike what Rock Paper Shotgun's review claims, he's still ultimately the same character you know and love (to hate).
Even with these flaws, Hand of Fate 2 remains only 1 point away from a perfect score, simply because it's so fantastic overall. It improves upon its already-excellent predecessor in every way it possibly could. It is more streamlined and elegant, yet simultaneously more diverse and replayable. I won’t elaborate on its mechanics, as there are many other reviews which explore them in detail, but suffice it to say that at only 5 hours in, I feel safe in my prediction that this game will eventually be recognized as one of the best roguelites of all time, and quite possibly the single best digital board game ever created.
Not convinced yet? Why, is “one of best roguelites of all time, and quite possibly the single best digital board game ever created” not good enough for you? Then allow me to persuade you further by contrasting this game with the general state of the AAA gaming industry in late 2017:
“In Call of Duty: WW2, loot boxes drop from the sky onto Normandy beach and open in front of other players”
That is a real headline from Eurogamer. It is referencing a $60 game, which constantly tempts you to spend yet more of your money in exchange for dropping you some loot boxes out of the sky onto Normandy beach, so you can open them in front of other players, and show them what absolutely-worthless piles of digital feces you got for indulging your possibly-very-real gambling addiction in the hopes of getting slightly-less-worthless piles of digital feces. Everyone runs around Normandy beach and watches everyone gambling with crates of digital feces, in a manner that I might honestly say is not all THAT tasteless, were I for some reason to completely ignore the fact that it actually exists, as well as any and all of its discernable attributes.
Hand of Fate is half the price of CoD:WW2, not even including the loot boxes. They will soon be releasing an Endless Mode DLC, which will be well worth their asking price of absolutely nothing. You get an Endless Mode, you get an Endless Mode, all of you get an Endless Mode, because you were smart enough to support the developers that actually think of their customers and community members not as whales, dolphins, and minnows, but as ACTUAL, SENTIENT, HUMAN F***ING BEINGS.
TL;DR: Boycott loot boxes. Buy the best digital board game in the history of video games.

After playing through the first update and a total of a little more than seven hours, I feel I can now write a helpful review.
TL;DR Overall superb, great developers, recommend buying.
This game, while it was nowhere near "hyped," had a very large starting fanbase, so I believe it will go far. Its premise is new and refreshing; I, along with many others, grew tired of the same "survive alone in the woods" game; however, there are some enjoyable games with that premise( The Long Dark or The Forest, for example), but it was becoming somewhat of a cliche.
The mechanics of the game are, by my standards, amazing. The graphics are superb, while only requiring around 1GB of storage. The optimization is great as well, being able to run stable 60 FPS without even heating up my PC very much.
The possibly most important piece, the gameplay, can be given some slack, as it is an early alpha game, but still barely needs to be. There were a few game breaking bugs when it first released: rafts breaking randomly when out at sea, items   disappearing when leaving the "chunks" they were in, getting stuck in boats, loot containers not spawning/spawning in odd places, and a few others; however, most, if not all, of these bugs were fixed in the hotfix, along with the addition of whales and boat motors. Not only did that make the game playable for a long time, It also can be predicted from this immediacy that the developers are invested in their game, thus they plan on making it the best it can be.
If you are on the fence about this game, I recommend buying it.
