Stranded launched with a major bug in the raft. That was Friday. On Tuesday, the devs showed up with the hotfix. Not only did they fix the raft, they improved and patched a whole laundry list of stuff. And added whales! Attentive and competent.
Why is this the first thing I'm telling you about Stranded? Because it's Early Access, which means "Dev Attentiveness" is everything. I couldn't even think of reviewing this game until we'd seen them in action, at least once. Now we have seen them in action, and it was quite impressive. Not unlike the game itself.
Stranded is a beautiful little shipwrecked simulator. It's very basic right now, but what's here is all well done, and they've got some clever ideas.
Crafting, for example, forgoes the usual subscreen, and revolves around you piling up the materials on the ground, in physical proximity. Want a spit to cook by your campfire? You can't just build a spit and place it. You can only do it if the materials are right there, next to the fire. It's tactile. It's vaguely clunky, but it's very organic. You feel like you're really standing there, trying, like Robinson Crusoe, to forge a life out of sticks and palm fronds.
The islands are another interesting design choice. They're very small, and fairly anemic. Sticks and rocks and Yuca twine. The vast majority of the game is actually out there, under the water, with the sharks. Old shipwrecks and reefs and lost containers and such. The sharks are scary. If you're from the ocean/shark phobia branch of unreasonable fears, like myself, you will find the sharks, and their obligatory accompanying obo (edit: piano) music, genuinely terrifying. The sum of all this is that you're in a hyper relaxing tropical island coconut eating game, but if you want to get anything done, you have to get in the water, and play an intensely stressful horror game with roaming bull and tiger sharks. Neat stuff.
It's all gorgeous, as the screenshots suggest. You'd never know the title was indie, or early access, by glancing at it. I thought the whales were good news, not just because whales are cool, but because it shows us that these devs are invested in their wildlife. Anyone who's played The Forest can attest to how much a robust ecosystem adds to a setting like this one.
At this point, I only have one major complaint, and that's the ocean. The ocean is too calm. It's beautiful, and the part where it has depth and you're constantly trying to figure out what's below you is amazing and immersive, but you're way off in the pacific someplace, and sea is calm as can be. Even the Gulf Coast of Florida has itty bitty waves. After the great rolling oceans of Assassin's Creed Black Flag, and the slightly less mountainous but still very rolling seas of this game's own indie cousin, Salt, the planar ocean of Stranded is like a dead rat in the punch bowl. In most games, it wouldn't matter so much, but the ocean is the star of Stranded; it rarely, if ever, leaves center stage. The fact that it is lifeless as a dish towel never stops feeling wrong.
Aside from that, I can't think of anything to complain about. Had they not just introduced the whales, I would worry about the sharks being too large and scary, and wish for a wider variety of sharks, including all the relatively pleasant ones that fill the real oceans. (Back in the 70s, sharks hired Steven Spielberg as a PR guy, and it was kind of a disaster. It would be nice if Stranded helped them dig out of that, a little.) But, whales. There's probably all kinds of critters coming. If there are still no nice sharks a year from now, I'll come edit this paragraph.
TL;DR - Great start on a shipwrecked simulator. Devs seem to care. All is beautiful. Oceans too flat. Sharks need friends. Safe to buy.

My opinion on this game is mixed. It has nice moments, but it lacks quite a few things to be a great game. its attempt on replicating an atmosphere of the early 20th century is rather superficial. Cut scene screen flickering and vignettes are supposed to imitate silent films (for some reason, with theatrical backgrounds). Dialogs expose mediocre writing skills. Although the game characters are all Russian matryoshka dolls, the rest of the game has nothing to do with Russia or Russian culture. The idea of stacking gameplay is fresh, interesting, and somewhat addictive. However, the quests you are given are often depressingly immoral. A player seem to always end up breaking something, ruining something, spoiling something to get things done. The humour in the game mainly manifests itself in characters doing funny things; unfortunately, these things include vomiting, burping and blowing wind, which game creators, obviously, find extremely amusing. I suppose a plastic Chippendale chair imitation with a whoopee cushion would be a suitable analogy to the game's attempt to be artistic.
To summarise, this game is a nice take on an original idea, but it could have been (so) much better if it were made with a bit more sophistication and taste.

Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is a messed up clicker game where you grow organs on trees. It's a waste of time to be frank.
It's literally just a clicker game. It's not like an idle game like AdVenture Capitalist or Clicker Heroes, where you can leave it and it does things for you. Forget Me Not requires you to invest time into it. It kind of has a visual novel type of feeling to it, but the "story" part of the game is kind of useless. You complete "quests" by growing nice, cute-looking organs and fullfill "buy orders" of sorts. There's not much to it. The game is kind of relaxing if you just want to not think about anything.
The art's pretty simple and cute, which is what made me buy this game. I didn't play the game with sound and music on, so I can't really judge that element of it. I liked listening to my own music while playing. There's not much else that can be said.
I wish it was an idle game, but it's not. Constant clicking gets annoying and the game only becomes more of an idle game when you're able to buy more "helpers". Even then, once you exit the game, it pauses. That's the biggest problem I have with this game.
I still would recommend this game if you're looking for a useless clicker game that has more to it than other clickers, like AdVenture Capitalist and Clicker Heroes. The cute art style and unusual premise makes the game fun. Just remember that you're going to be wasting a lot of time until you get to around Chapter 3. Playing this game for achievements is stupid (I'm trying to do this and it's not fun), so I wouldn't recommend it. 5/10

- Some mission and terrain types are frustrating. E.g. when you defend a time from the undead, the town's militia, under AI control, breaks formation and suicides to the undead, both wasting time and making your life more difficult.
- The perk system has the usual problem - a few perks look great, while most look useless.
- The mercs could use a bit more personality.
- The pacing felt off. A full run on beginner took me 25 hrs. Toward the end the game became a grind.

What is "Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden"?
Well, other than just being a strange title, this game is a ton of fun. It is in no way complicated--you'll be clicking *a lot*--but it's still oddly enjoyable. It's one of those little games that you'll find addictive without really knowing why.
Story:
There's not much of a main story. Your master runs an organ shop and you're her apprentice. You grow organs, harvest them, and sell them while she looks cute at the register. There are several side stories, however, in which characters visit and give you quests to do, which activate cut-scenes with unvoiced dialogue. The game is divided into chapters, though I'm not entirely certain why.
Features:
Animals you can purchase, each of which effects your organ trees in different ways.
Levels (for everything) that effect how well your trees/equipment/animal helpers work.
A quirky cast of characters with their own back stories--some cute, some disturbing.
Simple controls; you only need your mouse.
Gameplay:
As mentioned before, you click a lot. That's it. This game is a micromanagement title in which you'll click to water your garden... And to harvest your plants... And to go through text... And to interact with the various animals in your garden. After harvesting your organs (which sounds way more violent than it is), you turn them in for cash via quests. There are quests that advance the story and quests that simply exist to give you a feeling that you're accomplishing something. The game can get hectic depending on how many critters you've got on screen and the level of your plants (which increases the number of organs on your trees and the speed at which they grow).
BGM:
Catchy. It gets old quickly, in my opinion, but it fades into the background or is drowned out by your incessent clicking.
Graphics:
I adore the art style. It's cartoony and colourful. Interactive parts of your garden will go black if they aren't in use/need your attention and easily stand out amidst the bright shades of everything else--which is a very intuitive way to indicate that you need to tend to them.
Price:
I bought this on sale for 4.99USD and I don't regret it. I think 9.99 may be a little steep, however, for what you're getting. I can't see much replayability and, once you see the end, you probably won't pick this up again. I'm not anywhere near finished with the game, mind you, and I'm almost at 4 hours as I write this, so you'll probably get quite a few hours out of this.
Bottom line:
it's a great little time-waster. If you're looking for depth, look elsewhere. This frantic click-fest is a blast, but it is indeed a casual game. You can easily waste hours with this title or just play it in short bursts.
